The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added four security flaws impacting GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenBSD OpenSSH, and IBM Aspera Faspex to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability in IBM Aspera Faspex that could allow an authenticated user to craft a specific message to bypass authorization, causing privilege escalations. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSwitch that could result in configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution. (Fixed in October 2026)

CVE-2026-123158 aka SSHole (CVSS score: 8.1) - An unexpected status code or return value vulnerability in OpenBSD OpenSSH on Linux that could allow for authentication bypass. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper authentication vulnerability in GPUStack that could allow improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml. (Fixed in July 2026)

The addition of CVE-2026-123158 to the KEV catalog follows reports of exploitation attempts targeting the flaw since November 6, 2026. A total of 22 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 14 unique IP addresses so far, according to Previdian.

In a post shared on X on November 7, 2026, Defused Cyber said it "observed a small amount of actors targeting SSHole" but stressed the exploitation activity is not widespread yet.

According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a.m. UTC. Confirmed post-exploitation activity has been detected from six source IP addresses, representing 18 distinct attack chains to date.

These involve reconnaissance, queries to cloud metadata services, attempts to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and efforts to modify the SSH authorized_keys file to gain persistent access.

In at least one case, an unknown threat actor dubbed GT10 has been observed deploying TAC Agent, a Python-based command-and-control (C2) agent capable of shell command execution, system reconnaissance, directory enumeration, file transfer, and updating itself.

Threat intelligence firm watchTowr said it has also observed the OpenSSH flaw being weaponized in the wild for botnet and cryptocurrency miner activity.

In an advisory for CVE-2026-102895 published on July 31, 2026, the maintainers of the GPUStack Python package credited Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, Rui Yang, and Haoyu Wang for independently reporting the flaw, adding that "active in-the-wild exploitation" was reported by Ulex Innovative Systems' Javier Sixto.

There are currently no public reports on how the other vulnerabilities are being exploited, who is behind them, and the scale of such efforts. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 12, 2026.

Full Text:
November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

Critical RCE Vulnerabilities in Windows Services

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

CVE-2026-112967 is a heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service. An in-network attacker can call arbitrary endpoints on the service to trigger the flaw. Enterprise exposure depends on whether the service is present and running. Consumer-oriented Windows SKUs and gaming-enabled configurations are the primary population, making this lower priority for most corporate fleets.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. The attack path is notable: An unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an Exchange Server, and the search indexer processes the attachment automatically for indexing. The recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation grants code execution with the permissions of the indexing service. Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. The Windows Search path is the more significant exposure for enterprise environments. Email-delivered payloads that trigger without user interaction have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they bypass the phishing-click dependency that slows most initial access campaigns.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

CVE-2026-119958 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows LDAP with a CVSS score of 9.8. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted LDAP calls to a listening server. No authentication or user interaction is required.

LDAP is the directory access protocol that underpins Active Directory. Every domain controller exposes LDAP on TCP/389 (and TCP/636 for LDAPS) by design, and the service cannot be disabled without breaking domain operations. Member servers, workstations, and applications query LDAP continuously for authentication, group policy retrieval, and object lookups, making it one of the most heavily trafficked protocols inside any AD environment.

The scope-of-impact concern is substantial. Code execution within the LDAP service on a domain controller places the attacker inside the trust boundary that every other domain resource relies on. From that position, credential extraction, replication abuse, and lateral movement to additional DCs become straightforward follow-on actions. Because LDAP is network-reachable from any domain-joined host by default, any internal foothold that can route to a DC can attempt exploitation.

Unauthenticated RCE flaws in core AD infrastructure have historically drawn rapid attention from ransomware operators and targeted intrusion actors because they collapse the gap between initial access and domain-wide compromise.

Eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities this month share a common attack vector: the Preview Pane in Outlook and Word. All carry CVSS scores of 7.5 to 8.8, with seven of the eight scoring 8.8. The underlying flaw classes are use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (two CVEs), release of invalid pointer (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). Despite the variation in memory-corruption primitives, the exploitation pattern is uniform: An attacker delivers a malicious document or email, and merely selecting it for preview triggers code execution with the user's privileges.

The Outlook vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309) are the highest-exposure items in this group. Email is the delivery mechanism, and the Preview Pane is enabled by default in most enterprise Outlook deployments. An external attacker who can send mail to a target organization can reach the vulnerable code path without any authentication or prior foothold. The Word vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110067, CVE-2026-111285, CVE-2026-124185) require document delivery, which typically means a phishing attachment or a link to a malicious file, but still fire on preview rather than open.

The remaining two CVEs (CVE-2026-111289, CVE-2026-120003) affect the broader Office suite and follow the same preview-triggered pattern. CVE-2026-124185 has a lower score (7.5) due to high attack complexity, but the others require no special conditions beyond user receipt of the malicious content.

Preview Pane vulnerabilities have historically been attractive to phishing operators and initial-access brokers because delivery converts directly to execution, with no need to persuade a user to open an attachment.

Critical Vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)

CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 are Critical vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services that both stem from incorrect authorization flaws. The two CVEs share a flaw class but differ in outcome and attack complexity.

CVE-2026-118146 carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and enables RCE. An authenticated attacker with low-level access to an affected server can send a specially crafted request and execute code without any user interaction. The authorization flaw means the server fails to properly validate that the authenticated principal should be permitted to perform the requested operation, turning a low-privilege foothold into code execution on a domain controller.

CVE-2026-118148 has a CVSS score of 7.5 and results in elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. This vulnerability has high attack complexity because successful exploitation requires the attacker to win a race condition. An authenticated attacker who can trigger the race gains SYSTEM privileges on the domain controller.

Active Directory Domain Services provides directory and authentication services for Windows enterprise domains. Domain controllers running AD DS issue Kerberos tickets, store the directory database, and process authentication and authorization decisions for every domain-joined resource. Compromise of a domain controller typically means compromise of the entire domain, since the attacker gains access to credential material and can issue arbitrary authentication assertions.

The attack surface for both vulnerabilities is any domain controller reachable from an authenticated low-privileged foothold. In most enterprise deployments, that includes every writable DC in the forest. Incorrect authorization flaws in identity platform components have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they convert commodity initial access into domain-wide compromise without requiring credential theft or additional tooling.

Microsoft Exchange Server provides enterprise email, calendar, and collaboration services, and is commonly deployed with internet-facing client access services for mobile and web users. The authentication requirement lowers the bar only modestly in most environments: Any compromised mailbox credential, service account, or partner federation relationship satisfies it. Once that requirement is met, the attacker reaches code execution on a server that typically holds sensitive mail content, internal address lists, and often enjoys elevated trust relationships with Active Directory.

Organizations running on-premises Exchange frequently expose Outlook Web Access, Exchange ActiveSync, and Autodiscover endpoints to the internet. Servers in this posture are reachable from any network position once the attacker obtains valid credentials, and successful exploitation yields a foothold inside the perimeter on infrastructure that processes sensitive communications.

Microsoft addresses eight Critical elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V this month, spanning five distinct flaw classes: use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (one CVE), TOCTOU race condition (one CVE), untrusted pointer dereference (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). The exploitation outcomes fall into two categories. CVE-2026-113753 allows an attacker to gain Virtual Trust Level 1 (VTL1) privileges, which means escaping from the normal kernel (VTL0) into the secure kernel layer that underpins Virtualization-Based Security features such as Credential Guard. Five of the remaining seven CVEs enable guest-to-host escape: An attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine can execute code on the host in the security context of the virtual machine worker process.

Hyper-V is the hypervisor layer that runs Azure compute infrastructure and powers client-side Windows features including Windows Sandbox, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, and Virtualization-Based Security. The exposure therefore reaches both datacenter server populations and ordinary endpoints where these features are enabled.

Most of the cluster carries a high attack complexity because exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk. Hypervisor escapes of this class have historically attracted attention from advanced adversaries because a successful exploit compromises the isolation boundary that separates tenants in shared infrastructure and protects credential material on endpoints.

CVE-2026-113752 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a use-after-free that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger over an adjacent network. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk in contested LAN environments.

Windows Print Spooler manages print job queuing and driver loading on Windows endpoints and servers. It runs with SYSTEM privileges by default and is enabled on virtually every Windows installation, including workstations that have no physical printer attached. The adjacent-network attack vector limits exposure to attackers who already have a foothold on the same network segment, but that constraint is often satisfied during post-compromise lateral movement.

Print Spooler vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attacker attention because the service combines broad default deployment, high privilege, and a complex legacy codebase that has repeatedly yielded exploitable flaws.

Title: SonicWall releases patches for 7 flaws in its firewalls, most involving unauthenticated access
Context: “The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said
Full Text:
SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service.

And Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported.

“The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.”

The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2.

SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall.

A ‘mixed bag’

Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag.

“SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.”

The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.”

Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however.

“Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.”

Could be combined

Sav Wheeler, malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous.

“These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.”

He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.”

He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.”

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live.

“Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.”

A vendor risk management issue

These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.”

Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself.

“The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.”

However Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily.

“Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.”

He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said.

Additional preventive measures

In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them.

“List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

Title: Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products
Context: Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost
Full Text: Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products. Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups. “At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address. AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost. Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand. Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws. The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself. The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses. IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.” We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response. Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.” After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. “Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.” The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

Title: N-able issues advisory on critical vulnerabilities
Context: Sophos countermeasures SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available
Full Text:
On November 9, 2026, a security researcher released a series of proof-of-concept (PoC) scripts targeting various vulnerabilities in N-able's N-central platform. The collection of PoCs claims to exploit several critical weaknesses in the N-central platform. As a result, N-able has taken the precautionary step of taking their N-central Hosted Environments offline.

At this time there is third-party reporting suggesting that exploitation is occurring in the wild. N-Able’s advisory does not indicate that they have observed exploitation as of this writing; however they do note that they have observed scanning activity associated with the published PoC code. At this time, Sophos X-Ops has not observed exploitation. We recommend that operators of on-premises N-central servers follow N-able’s advice.

Recommended actions

Sophos X-Ops recommends that organizations review N-able’s advisory and monitor it for further instructions from N-able.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available.

N-able Disables Cloud Services Following Disclosure of "Able2Shell" Exploit Chains

Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ben Bernstein, and Andrew Brandt for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Huntress is tracking N-able's response to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in its N-central platform, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform built for managed service providers and IT teams. On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline while it worked to secure the environment and apply remediation.

That move came after an independent researcher published the details of 33 critical vulnerabilities to GitHub that can be chained to lead to four different exploits (dubbed "Able2Shell"). Three of those chained exploits lead to remote code execution and one leads to privilege escalation to root. The vulnerabilities impact servers running N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 (and likely earlier versions as well).

N-able said it has not seen active exploitation of the vulnerabilities as of November 9 at 15:15:00 UTC. The company is working on a hotfix that it said will be available soon; customers should keep their N-central servers offline until N-able confirms they can be brought back online safely.

Huntress has tracked and responded to other, separate flaws in N-able's N-central this year, including five critical CVEs:

August 2026: N-able released a hotfix for CVE-2026-18556, a critical vulnerability impacting all current versions of N-central across both hosted and on‑prem deployments, giving attackers unauthenticated, "god-mode" access to the RMM console. CVE-2026-18577 was disclosed soon after as an incomplete patch to the former CVE.

September 2026: N-able issued a hotfix to address a third vulnerability, CVE-2026-86218, an actively exploited pre-auth RCE zero day with a 10.0 CVSS score. The next day Huntress produced a proof of concept (PoC) exploit of a separate, net new vulnerability chain (CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207) in N-central that allowed attackers to bypass access controls to create unauthorized administrative accounts.

What Should Potentially Impacted Organizations Do?

Potentially impacted organizations should do the following:

If you run N-central on premises, take the server offline now and keep it offline until N-able confirms it is safe to restore.

If you use N-able's hosted service, expect an outage. N-able has taken its cloud infrastructure offline; follow its status page for updates.

Review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access. If you find suspicious activity, involve your incident-response team and assess whether systems or client networks managed through N-central may also be affected. The document warns that exploitation could enable remote code execution or privilege escalation on the server.

Carefully examine your audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise. During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools. Specifically, you should monitor for anomalous remote access sessions, new scripts being deployed, or the unauthorized creation of new administrator accounts.

Apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe. The document said a hotfix was in development, with no exact ETA, so check current vendor guidance rather than relying on this dated update.

N-able does not always iterate version numbers when it pushes down live hotfixes that don't require a reboot, so it remains to be seen whether the patched version will be numbered 2026.4.0.31 or something different.

Next Steps

Huntress is actively investigating this incident and we are communicating with our potentially vulnerable customers to share updates as they become available. Please check this blog for further updates as we learn more information.

You can also get further updates from N-able at: https://uptime.n-able.com/event/202561/

Title: Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Modules: Identity Security Posture Management; Cloud Risk Management; Data Security Posture Management; Network Security
Title: Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
Context: Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined
Full Text:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Why the Roles Let the Attacker In

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

How to Check Your Accounts

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.

IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.

IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it.

IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used.

IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof.

Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum.

User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs.

For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.

CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.

How to Close the Route

The researchers recommend these steps:

If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued.

Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy.

Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses.

Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed."

Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible.

Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers.

Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before.

Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit
Context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks
Full Text:
Executive summary

On October 21, 2026, we observed participants in underground forums seeking PHP2Shell exploits, while others shared scripts presented as exploiting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Discussion included doubts about prerequisites and whether circulating code worked. This post examines that gap between interest, claimed capability, and verified exploitation.

Our assessment covers selected forum posts and messages collected as of October 21. The findings show what was being discussed and shared, rather than confirmed compromises.

Forum participants requested exploit material, shared code, and questioned each other’s claims. For the security industry, this is a reminder to share threat findings promptly across security teams, researchers, and vendors so defenders can assess emerging threats and coordinate their response.

Looking for an exploit they could trust

Exploit.in is a long-running, primarily Russian-language underground forum where participants discuss hacking techniques and trade tools and services. Monitoring these discussions can reveal interest in emerging vulnerabilities and questions about available exploits.

“Does anyone have it?” was the question, translated from Russian, in a discussion on Exploit.in naming both PHP2Shell CVEs. The request sought exploit material, while subsequent comments questioned the prerequisites and legitimacy of circulating PoCs. One participant wrote “Didn’t test but seems legit.” A further comment described code execution “with preconditions,” while referring to a different “real exploit.” These are participant opinions about the circulating material, not our technical conclusions.

The exchange in Figure 1 captures both demand for an exploit and doubts about whether the available code worked. It leaves open whether the requester ever obtained a working exploit.

Figure 1. PHP2Shell exploit requests and discussion observed on October 21, 2026.

What circulated on October 21

On October 21, we recorded an English-language technical writeup at 02.23 UTC whose author claimed a lab reproduction. Hebrew- and Persian-language messages recorded at 05.16 and 05.35 UTC shared security alerts about the vulnerabilities and upcoming patches. The language of a post does not tell us where its author is based. At 06.22 UTC, we recorded a separate Exploit.in post presenting scripts as exploits for both CVEs, shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2. Forum post presenting purported PHP2Shell exploits, observed on October 21, 2026.

We redacted exploit instructions and memory offsets to avoid sharing details that could help reproduce an attack. The screenshot preserves the forum context.

A separate screenshot shared in a monitored channel appeared to show command execution on a local test system. We have not independently verified the result, and its exact posting date was unavailable.

By October 21, our searches returned 68 forum posts for PHP2Shell / CVE-2026-109618 and 62 for CVE-2026-109618. Chat searches returned 81 messages for PHP2Shell and 57 for CVE-2026-109619. These figures measure discussion volume in the collected material. The searches overlap, so the counts are not a combined total.

The forum exchanges show participants openly requesting exploit material, sharing code, and questioning each other’s claims. Separately, security alerts circulated in several languages across monitored messaging channels. Together, these observations illustrate how quickly information about a vulnerability can spread. For defenders, they reinforce the value of timely information sharing across organizations and language barriers, with clear distinctions between observed activity, unverified claims, and validated findings.

Public analysis offers context on PoC reliability

Public technical discussion published on October 23 on the SANS Internet Storm Center website examined why some circulating PoCs depended on specific server settings and knowledge of the target environment. The discussion concerned the PoCs reviewed there, rather than every possible way to exploit PHP2Shell.

The public analysis suggests that the PHP version, server setup, and information available to an attacker can affect whether a PoC works. These dependencies may help explain the questions raised in the forum thread.

Connecting intelligence with observed attempts

In our separate traffic analysis, we observed exploitation attempts, scanning, and invalid-PoC attempts. The invalid-PoC attempts add context to the forum discussion about whether circulating code worked. We detail these findings in our published PHP2Shell exploitation and IPS research. We have found no evidence connecting those requests to the forum participants or scripts discussed here.

We continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update our protections as exploitation techniques evolve. Our cloud-delivered IPS signatures blocked exploitation attempts on inspected customer traffic without requiring a separate protection package. PHP services outside our inspection coverage require separate remediation and protection. Updating affected PHP installations remains essential.

Title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
Context: The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload
Full Text: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

Title: QNAP Warns Users as Plex2Shell Flaws Are Used to Hack NAS Devices
Context: QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices
Full Text:
Taiwanese vendor QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server after reports of NAS compromises through the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices.

“QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected usersadvisory published by QNAP. ” reads the report published by the vendor. “The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected.”

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

“It doesn’t check for a lib prefix, doesn’t require the execute bit, doesn’t verify any signature, and doesn’t look for any specific symbol.” reads the report published by zmain.com. “When dlopen loads a shared object, it runs the ELF’s DT_INIT_ARRAY (constructor functions) before doing any symbol resolution. A .so that only has a constructor and no exported symbols will still execute its code on load. We then trigger a second transcode. The codec directory gets re-enumerated, the .so we wrote in Stage 4 gets loaded, and the constructor runs as uid=1000(plex).”

That detail matters because the final stage can exploit how Plex loads shared libraries. The chain uses a setting related to transcoding to influence execution, allowing a specially crafted library to run when Plex loads it. The result can be code execution under the service account, without requiring the attacker to obtain an interactive login first.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server immediately, users should go to App Center, open My Apps and update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3 or later. They should then check in Plex Web, under Settings and General, that the installed version is 1.43.3.10861 or later. QNAP will release further updates after verifying them, but users should not wait.

If Plex was reachable from the internet while running version 1.43.2 or earlier, users should treat the NAS as potentially compromised. This may apply if Plex Remote Access was enabled, port 32400 was forwarded, or the port was opened automatically through UPnP or router settings. Updating alone will not remove anything an attacker may have installed.

In those cases, users should follow QNAP’s FAQ to perform a clean reinstall, check for signs of compromise and reset both their Plex and NAS credentials. The company also advises disabling Plex Remote Access if it is not needed and avoiding port forwarding for port 32400. Users who need remote access should use a VPN instead.

QNAP also recommends keeping QTS or QuTS hero and all installed apps up to date. Step-by-step instructions are available in the Plex2Shell: Check and Remediation FAQ for QNAP NAS Users.

CISA added Plex2Shell flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to addresse them by October 23, 2026.

Full Text:
A system doesn't always need a complicated bug to let someone in. Sometimes, a blank password is enough. That's one of the bigger stories this week. And it gets worse when the tools meant to keep systems updated or running safely become part of the attack.

Elsewhere, attackers are hiding inside normal web traffic, stealing credentials from network devices, and finding new uses for exposed systems. AI is helping some of them move faster, but old mistakes are doing plenty of the work too. Even forgotten settings and small changes made months ago are coming back to cause trouble.

There's a lot packed into this week's news, including some strange research findings, fresh attacks, and a few warnings worth taking seriously. Here's the full recap.

⚡ Threat of the Week

OpenSSH Flaw Sees Exploitation Attempts — Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration. As of November 9, 2026, a total of 20 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 13 unique IP addresses from Denmark, Iran, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, and the U.S.

🔔 Top News

Trojanized CWP Web Server Used to Deliver CWPdoor — A new Linux malware called CWPdoor is being distributed via a trojanized version of cwpsrv, the built-in daemon and web server that powers the Control Web Panel. According to XLab, a shell script named "cwpsrv_update.sh" is used to download "cwpsrv" from a remote server ("136.0.141[.]71") and replace the legitimate file on the system. "The downloaded cwpsrv is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker," XLab said. "Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs. This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes CWPdoor exceptionally stealthy."

Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Allows Code Execution as Root — A vulnerability in the APT package manager (CVE-2026-109518, CVSS score: 7.7) can be exploited to install a package under certain conditions and achieve code execution with elevated privileges. The issue affects Ubuntu and Debian operating systems. "Under specific conditions, when APT is configured to use HTTP package sources with retry settings enabled, a third-party with a network position between the host and the package mirror can cause APT to install a package that did not pass verification," Amazon said in an advisory. "Maintainer scripts within that package then run with elevated privileges."

CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks Targeting Financial Organizations — The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country. Calling it a "significant escalation" in attacks, the threat actor is said to be re-targeting entities that were originally targeted last month after incomplete remediation, adding that the intrusions "have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response."

Zyxel Fixes 0-Day exploited to Hack About 1,000 Network Switches — Zyxel has fixed a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that threat actors exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write flaw that could "allow a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker to exploit the flaw and potentially execute OS commands via a crafted HTTP request." The activity has been attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala (aka Red Heron). The attacker has been found to weaponize the flaw to deploy the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT, a ring 3 rootkit.

cPGuard Update Mechanism Hijacked to Deliver Backdoor — Unknown threat actors compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. "On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OPSSHIELD's update distribution infrastructure (CDN)," OPSSHIELD said. "The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel." The attacker is said to have gotten in through its billing application at manage.opsshield[.]com and logged in to a customer account they had registered.

mSecure Urges Customers to Change their Passwords — Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company said. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." However, the company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. The lack of specifics has understandably riled up customers, with one user on Reddit stating "their silence on this is mind-bending." In December 2025, Germany's cyber agency BSI found that mSecure's maker could, in theory, access the data users store in it.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-16305, CVE-2026-16306 (INFINITT PACS), CVE-2026-13684, CVE-2026-13639, CVE-2026-13673, CVE-2026-6205 (Synology DSM), CVE-2026-58868, CVE-2026-58882 (Google Android), GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (Ruby on Rails), CVE-2026-102703, CVE-2026-102704 (Xen), CVE-2026-109518 (Debian apt), CVE-2026-98432, CVE-2026-121639, CVE-2026-121638, CVE-2026-121640 (WatchGuard), CVE-2026-76506 (Cisco), CVE-2026-119741 (rsync), CVE-2026-121156, CVE-2026-121229, CVE-2026-121246, CVE-2026-121035, CVE-2026-121247, CVE-2026-121203, CVE-2026-121126 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-98432 (Veeam), CVE-2026-83844 (Microsoft Paint), CVE-2026-19868 (SonicWall SonicOS), CVE-2026-123158 (OpenSSH), and multiple vulnerabilities in the BaseChat Android app version 9.8.1.

📰 Around the Cyber World

The Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation known as Qilin (aka Agenda) has recorded 179 publicly reported attacks in 2024, and more than 1,000 claimed victims in 2025. This year alone, it has claimed more than 900 victims, making it one of the most active ransomware groups. "Affiliates commonly gain access through phishing, stolen credentials, vulnerable internet-facing systems and remote-management tools," Acronis said. "Qilin uses a flexible ransomware platform that allows affiliates to tailor attacks to the victim environment, including the encryption of local files, network shares and virtual machine infrastructure." One notable Qilin affiliate is Securotrop, which continues to operate within the Qilin affiliate network, while maintaining an independent channel for publishing stolen victim data.

Exposed Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers are being turned into abuse infrastructure, according to SecurityScorecard, which uncovered a suspected SMTP botnet that includes confirmed refrigeration controllers. Attackers are said to be using compromised Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers as proxy exits and spam senders. "The SMTP cluster consists of nine IP addresses, three of them confirmed XWEB controllers," Security Scorecard said. "Of 1,041 targets, 508 were contacted by at least two nodes. The three most active nodes had approximately 47% of their target lists in common, the report’s strongest signal of coordination."

A targeted Browser-in-the-Middle (BitM) phishing operation dubbed PhantomDOM is using custom DOM-mirroring to hijack Microsoft 365 sessions. "The attack began with a SharePoint-themed PDF distributed from an apparently legitimate sender and progressed through redirects and browser checks before presenting Microsoft authentication inside an attacker-controlled remote browser," ZeroBEC said. "The victim saw a familiar sign-in experience. The attacker controlled the browser in which that experience actually ran." According to the email security company, PhantomDOM goes beyond cloned login pages and conventional reverse-proxy phishing. "Its client reconstructs the remote DOM, forwards keyboard and clipboard interactions over WebSocket, survives connection interruptions and supports live operator control," it added.

According to a report from the non-profit AI Alignment Foundation, AI agents assigned a sandboxed coding task to fix a broken pricing service "shared a private token and ran untrusted code in exchange for help from an agent forum." In an experiment tested against nine models, GPT-6.1-Sol refused every swarm request in 50 of 50 trials, while Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 trials were cut short by their providers' content filters.

A zero-day vulnerability has been disclosed in CPython that could enable bad actors to breach AI hosting platforms. "A memory-safety flaw in the CPython interpreter allows attackers to escape a code sandbox and execute code hidden in a specially crafted model," RunSybil said. "By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests. They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads." The findings build upon a previous out-of-bounds read in CPython that could result in a sandbox escape. The issue has been fixed and backported to 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches.

The U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has issued an order effectively cutting off MEXC Global's access to the U.S. financial system under Operation Economic Outcast. "MEXC Global is a convertible virtual currency exchanger that has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion, as well as cybercrime, including by transacting directly with sanctioned actors," FinCEN said.

A new study of 25,964 U.S. government-related domains has found 43 whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. In one case, a misspelled domain's SPF configuration ("amzonses[.]com" instead of "amazonses[.]com") authorized at least 32,066 unique IP addresses to send email on behalf of a U.S. county. "These external dependencies authorize third-party senders, route incoming mail, provide DNS delegation, and receive security telemetry," SH Consulting said. "The government domains themselves can remain registered and be considered protected, because there are no signs to suggest anything is wrong." SH Consulting said it defensively registered 17 of these dangling DNS dependencies to prevent abuse.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland and a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 and has agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months. "He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict," said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.

Huntress has warned of a "couple waves of activity across multiple organizations involving GeoVision camera software," pointing to broad exploitation of the platform to deliver malware. The activity originates from the IP addresses 45.32.117[.]34 and 156.246.94[.]183.

A single AI-augmented threat actor (AAT) has been observed using a mesh of 12 AI agents called BOSSAI to conduct persistent campaigns in several countries. The mesh consists of combining HexStrike AI, Hermes, CyberStrikeAI, and HalberdStrike, alongside Grok, OpenClaw, and Claude Code, with some acting as infrastructure builders and maintainers, while others scan for vulnerabilities and attack. The findings once again show how a lone actor can mount offensive operations at scale. "Using the BOSSAI mesh, the operator targeted hundreds of organizations spanning government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities, military systems, phone directories, e-commerce platforms, and gambling sites in eleven countries," Acronis said. "It's unclear if the attacker has any specific affiliation or goal beyond compromising as many organizations as possible, presumably to monetize the activity." The threat actor is believed to be a single individual based in Hualien City, Taiwan.

Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million secrets that have been confirmed to be live and leaked on GitHub, Docker Hub, npm, Hugging Face, and others.

Gnosis Pay said it detected unauthorized access to the system powering its Gnosis Pay-branded cards on November 3, 2026, leading to the exposure of customer information. "The data breach was limited to the system powering Gnosis Pay-branded cards, which was already scheduled for retirement on 20 December 2026," it said. "We have increased our monitoring of card activity and wallets to detect fraud or attempts to access user funds. We have also implemented an extra verification step (3D Secure) and made it mandatory for all online card payments.
