Title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
Context: What can we learn from this Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk...
Full Text:
php2shell raised fears of mass exploitation. A week of testing by our research team found that working exploits had to be fitted to each target’s exact PHP setup. Systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are the exception: one tuned exploit can reach every device that runs it.

Key takeaways

The five vulnerable PHP sites we exposed to the internet were not compromised, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) that go beyond version checks do not reliably confirm whether a host is vulnerable. Exploitation has been confirmed elsewhere, on researcher honeypots and on some network appliances.

In realistic environments, turning php2shell into remote code execution usually takes an exploit built for the specific target. That is hard, not impossible, and it puts php2shell in a different category from Log4Shell, even though both received near-maximum severity ratings. Where many systems share one build, such as network appliances, a single calibrated exploit can work against all of them.

Patch now, starting with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP branches. Tenable Nessus and Tenable One Web App Scanning have had version-based detection since October 21.

Background

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced two vulnerabilities, and on October 21 released fixes for flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Each has a CVSSv4 score of 9.2. For a full breakdown of affected versions, fixes and mitigations, see our frequently asked questions blog post.

This post covers what happened after the disclosure, based on what our team observed directly.

From disclosure to headline in under 48 hours

php2shell got big fast. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online before the official release. Within two days, the vulnerability had a name, a logo and coverage in mainstream media.

Several websites went offline as a precaution, as described in our threat actor response blog post. Censys’s php2shell dashboard, which tracks PHP services by reported version, showed about 30.3 million PHP services still on an affected version on October 29, though a matching version does not mean a system can be exploited.

The comparison with Log4Shell came up early, but the two are very different to exploit. With Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), attackers only had to send a short piece of text to a vulnerable application, for example in a login form or a web request. If the application logged that text, the attack worked. The same text worked against almost any vulnerable target without changes, so attackers could launch it at scale within hours, and many of those attacks succeeded.

php2shell is different. Exploitation depends on the state of the heap, the process manager in use, worker reuse and how memory is laid out on a given build. php2shell drew attention quickly, but attackers can't exploit it as easily as Log4Shell.

What changed while we were testing

Several developments that matter for defenders came after our research began:

On October 24, honeypots run by Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three sensors running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, a configuration that favors the exploit.

On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Federal civilian agencies have until October 29 to remediate.

The same day, security firm Dream reported an attack chain that combined php2shell with a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw, Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Dream says the campaign rooted “25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 says it independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results. We have not verified these findings ourselves.

On October 28, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV catalog and noted that it can be chained with php2shell to run commands as root. By October 29, Palo Alto Networks reported active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

These reports are consistent with what we found. The exploit has to be calibrated to a specific build. Network appliances often run the same software across many devices, so one calibrated exploit can reach many of them. That is where we expect targeted exploitation to keep growing.

What we observed during our exploit research

Exposed targets

To measure real-world activity, we kept five vulnerable PHP sites reachable from the internet: four through the evening of October 24, and one still running in a standard, vulnerable configuration at the time of writing.

Over that period, we observed mass exploitation attempts that matched php2shell exploitation patterns. None of our targets had been compromised as of October 29.

Other organizations have reported exploitation attempts and, in the cases described above, successful exploitation. Amazon Threat Intelligence says php2shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.” Our data does not contradict these reports. It shows that attempts, even at scale, were not enough to compromise a default installation in our environment. Attempts and successful compromises are two different numbers, and in the first days after a disclosure people often treat them as the same.

Public proofs-of-concept

We collected and tested almost all public PoCs. An early lead was php2shell poc, published by researcher Daniel Púa (devploit). It let us reproduce the exposure on multiple 8.4 and 8.5 environments with specific configurations. From there, we did deeper research, including white-box testing and code and patch comparison, and achieved remote code execution on PHP 7.4.33.

What we learned from this research is that the exploit inadvertently reveals a clean discriminator: the same multipart POST that begins stage 1 produces a different allocator response on patched vs. unpatched PHP. No heap corruption, no crash, no shell, just a measurable size difference in how the server handles the request. That became signal 1: a large filename in the multipart request produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable versions than on fixed versions, because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Same request, same PHP – different memory behavior depending solely on whether the UAF patch is present.

Tenable Research identified a second signal as well: the compact amplification sequences that exercise the UAF window's existence without triggering corruption. The session upload-progress oracle watches for the crash/recover pattern that vulnerable versions exhibit under controlled amplification.

These two signals became a stateful probe that a Nessus ‘direct check’ plugin could detect. However, the probe would miss some vulnerable systems and flag some patched ones as vulnerable.

The memory corruption is real, and PHP confirms memory disclosure as one of the impacts. Turning it into code execution on a target is difficult and unique to each target. Our working RCE required an exploit tuned to the target's environment, including its PHP build, SAPI, extensions and runtime configuration. A payload that works against one lab setup does not carry over to a different distribution package or a different PHP-FPM pool configuration.

AI-accelerated research: Useful, but it needs checking

AI agents sped up our reverse engineering and testing, and they also produced at least one convincing false positive. During a multi-hour session, an agent built a working shell against our PHP-FPM lab containers and reported it as confirmation of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. It was not. The agent had used a local file inclusion weakness that we had added to the lab, a different attack class that does not exist in default PHP deployments. A researcher caught the error by checking the exploit chain against the vulnerability's mechanics.

The lesson applies to anyone reading exploitation claims this week: a real shell is not proof that a specific CVE was used. We also ran into inconsistent responses from AI tools when doing authorized exploit validation, which slowed parts of the work.

White-box testing

The GDB analysis and heap geometry research below show why: there is no universal offset. Code execution is a real exposure yet it is not as simple as portrayed. The RCE we achieved on PHP 7.4.33 worked only once the exploit matched that one setup. A profile that achieves a shell against one lab container does not carry over to a different distribution package, a different PHP-FPM pool configuration, or a different memory limit.

The chunk-relative offsets pictured in the ‘heap geometry capture method’ visuals below reference _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0, arData at chunk+0x64b80. These values illustrate the measurement method and are specific to PHP 8.3.35 built from the docker-library bookworm image on amd64. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or a PHP 8.3.35 built with different extensions, produces different chunk geometry values. We used GDB against the live worker to measure the actual values for a given target.

Our failure to show that mass exploitation is quick or easy does not make this vulnerability harmless. A well-resourced attacker who wants a specific target can build that exploit, and AI-assisted tooling shortens the time it takes. It does make mass exploitation of the Log4Shell kind much less likely. The exception is any population of systems that share one build, such as network appliances, where the cost of calibration is paid once.

Why exploitation is hard

When possible, Tenable Research releases exposure direct checks to help customers detect exploitable vulnerabilities within their environments. These direct checks depend on finding reliable and safe methods of exercising a vulnerability in a way that simulates an exploit without triggering any destructive actions. This typically involves first researching how to develop an exploit, then figuring out how to test that safely.

Our research found the php2shell exposure difficult to reproduce broadly, even with white-box testing and GDB attached to processes, and even with AI agents analyzing runtime memory and source code for weaknesses and leads in parallel. What we learned from this research helps to inform us on the practical realities of real-world exploitation:

php2shell is a multi-stage memory corruption chain. A direct check triggering an out-of-memory condition alone does not fully guarantee the asset is also exposed to remote code execution.

In-memory offsets are version and system specific. The chunk-relative structure offsets required for heap manipulation change with every PHP patch release and system/software combination. Gaps in an inventory of known offsets and platforms could make a vulnerable system look patched (false-negative).

The OOM trigger depends on application-controlled memory limits. Whether the condition fires depends on the configured memory_limit and on whether the application overrides it via ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives.

The use-after-free requires reuse of the PHP worker across consecutive requests. Under mod_php, keep-alive pins a connection to one worker; under FPM, session affinity (PHPSESSID) is required. Both depend on SAPI and process-manager settings. For example, pm.max_requests recycles workers and breaks the use-after-free chain with no visible sign, so the check returns a false negative.

The exploit crashes PHP workers. Workers appear to respawn reliably, but a direct check that intentionally degrades performance could still affect production systems.

What can we learn from this

Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk reaction is triggered that creates significant fears of mass exploitation and extreme risk. While we do not want to downplay the dangers of this vulnerability, it is valuable to understand the practicalities of exploitation in the real world versus the fear that is built around a CVE during the regular news cycle. In this case, that nuance points remediation first at internet-facing assets, especially appliances such as network infrastructure management interfaces, and anything else that runs a common, basic deployment that reduces overall complexity.

Prioritization matters more as AI finds more vulnerabilities

Calif, OpenAI and Wiz are credited with finding php2shell. Calif says AI assisted the discovery. We expect the number of disclosed vulnerabilities to keep rising as these tools improve, and many of them will come with high base scores. Patching everything rated critical at the speed of the news cycle will not be possible.

Security teams need to understand what a vulnerability takes to exploit, not only how bad the worst case is:

Is there a public exploit that works without changes, or only a crash PoC?

Does exploitation depend on a non-default configuration, a specific build or prior access?

Is the vulnerable component reachable from the internet in your environment?

Has anyone observed successful compromise, as opposed to scanning?

Exploit prediction scores such as EPSS, Tenable's Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR) and confirmed exploitation sources such as CISA's KEV catalog help answer these questions. They work better alongside an analysis of the vulnerability itself than in place of one.

Patch anyway

Our observations do not mean php2shell should be ignored. The conditions for exploitation exist, exploit development will improve and targeted attacks against high-value PHP applications are plausible. Updating to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or applying your distribution's fixed packages, remains the recommendation. For end-of-life branches, plan an upgrade. Until then, apply the configuration mitigations described in our FAQ and limit internet exposure, starting with appliance management interfaces. For network appliances, PHP version numbers do not apply: use your vendor's fixed build or its interim mitigations.

What we are recommending is a different order of work. Patch or isolate internet-facing network appliances, management interfaces, and end-of-life PHP systems now. For the rest of your PHP estate, patch on your critical schedule, and check that less publicized vulnerabilities that are easy to exploit in your environment are not waiting behind php2shell.

Title: Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools
Context: Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the...
Full Text:
Attackers are managing to sneak low-grade phishing emails through brand name email security products, as evidenced by a recent Anthropic impersonation campaign.

The campaign, described in a new blog post by Cofense, won't impress anybody. Since September, an unidentified threat actor has been sending out emails around the world, pretending to grant early access to Anthropic's cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Their goal: stealing Google and Microsoft account credentials.

To avoid being relegated to spam folders, the attacker has been using novice tactics: shortening their malicious URLs, adding CAPTCHAs to their phishing flow, and leveraging legitimate video conferencing tools. The only remarkable thing about the campaign, really, is that it actually seems to be working.

Fake Emails Steal Google, Microsoft Credentials

Even as far as phishing campaigns go, this one's pretty lazy.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Attackers are appealing to targets with VIP invites to a "private preview" of Anthropic's supposed "new social media AI tool." Emails emphasize that this special early look is "private, invitation-only."

Right off the bat, there are ample reasons to be suspicious. The email titles have a grammatical error. The email sender's name includes a typo — "Austin from nthropic" — and their domain belongs to GoTo Webinar, not Anthropic. Visually, the messages are barebones, possessing no visual elements that even attempt to impersonate Anthropic branding.

If for some reason someone actually clicks on the fake registration link — a link that doesn't point to an Anthropic or even a conferencing app domain — they'll end up on a fake Zoom meeting page. If, further, the victim doesn't catch that a GoTo Webinar invite led to a Zoom call, they might choose to sign into Zoom via Google or Microsoft Single-Sign On (SSO). If they choose Google, they won't even be prompted for a password, thus making half of this malicious campaign completely useless, even to the attacker running it.

Inconsistent brand impersonations and missing or broken data theft flows are endemic to AI-generated campaigns; Cofense couldn't confirm if AI was used here. "However, due to the multiple variations of Zoom pages, it's likely generative AI was used," Cofense researcher Jacob Malimban says.

He points to one bit of additional evidence: Beginning Oct. 28, the threat actor began spoofing Anthropic's website instead of Zoom's. The similar but slightly off format of the Anthropic spoofing page, he says, also suggests AI generation.

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

How Weak TTPs Beat Email Security Solutions

The overall package is so maladroit that one can only wonder how such an email bypassed any spam filter in the first place. In fact, Cofense found these emails getting through market-leading email security products like the Proofpoint Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Cofense pointed to a few little details that might help explain why.

First, the emails are sent from a legitimate email address, customercare@gotowebinar[.]com — a shared sender address that any GoTo Webinar user might use to distribute webinar information. The legitimacy and ubiquity of this shared address shields the sender from scrutiny.

Second, the malicious registration link in the emails was run through a URL shortener, Zapier, eliminating a security product's ability to interpret red flags in the domain itself.

Lastly, the phishing flow incorporates two separate CAPTCHAs. The first — a Cloudflare CAPTCHA, presented before the fake Zoom or Anthropic page — is meant to stop an automated scanner in its tracks.

The second CAPTCHA — placed between the fake Zoom or Anthropic page and the fake SSO page — is a malicious twist on the form, designed to block VPN services, Tor browsers, and other tools defenders might use. "Some phish kits used that specific type of CAPTCHA before. It appears to have been actively developed by threat actors to detect the tools of both automated and human activity, as well as see if the IP address was proxied," Malimban explains.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

None of these tactics will knock anyone's socks off but, in the gestalt, they seem to do the trick.

Takeaways for Cybersecurity Awareness Month

To Keeper Security chief information security officer (CISO) Shane Barney, it's no surprise that threat actors are successfully bypassing perimeter email defenses, even with cookie cutter tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

"The reality of modern cybersecurity is that Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) will always have blind spots," he says.

Barney adds that organizations should assume phishing emails will end up in employees' email inboxes, and therefore security teams need to build defenses that focus on identity.

"If an employee is tricked by a fake Anthropic lure and their Microsoft or Google credentials are compromised, strict least-privilege access policies, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and privileged access management are what prevent the attacker from moving laterally, elevating privileges and accessing sensitive data," he advises. Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the lookalike domains used in this attack, neutralizing the threat at the point of interaction."

In the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026, and its emphasis on avoiding and reporting phishing scams, Malimban adds, "We hope that employees are trained using Secure Behavior Management to recognize and report phishing. To defend against suspicious account access, organizations should have robust account monitoring, like with CISA's free tool (Logging Made Easy). All in all, having multiple controls and defense in depth is necessary to defend against modern attacks."

Title: Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes
Context: Related: GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub From Vulnerability Discovery to Chained Exploits Historically, creating such chained exploits would...
Full Text:
An unreleased version of Claude identified critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used browsers and operating systems and chained them into working exploits requiring little or no human interaction, Anthropic said this week.

The exploits included one that enabled data theft from a locked Android smartphone, another zero-click exploit allowed remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on Linux servers, and a third that could have allowed attackers to remotely crash Windows systems. In total, Anthropic said, the model generated five working exploits targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. All affected vendors have addressed the vulnerabilities after Anthropic reported them.

The exploits are the latest evidence that frontier AI models are moving beyond simply identifying individual flaws to combining multiple into sophisticated working exploits. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said in a blog post this week.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

From Vulnerability Discovery to Chained Exploits

Historically, creating such chained exploits would have required special teams with domain expertise, the researchers wrote. "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Anthropic's report described a one-click RCE exploit chain involving Chrome on macOS. The exploit combined four vulnerabilities in Chrome's JavaScript engine, memory protections, browser process isolation, and federated sign-in functionality.

Each of the vulnerabilities that Claude discovered helped overcome a different security control and allowed the chained exploit to escape the browser's sandbox. As a proof of concept, Anthropic's exploit launched macOS Calculator from Chrome when a user loaded a malicious webpage.

Anthropic said it reported 62 vulnerabilities to Google, all of which had been assigned CVE identifiers, rated high or critical, and patched by Chrome 156.

On Safari, Claude's exploit chain allowed JavaScript on any website to bypass the same-origin policy, a security control that prevents one website from accessing another site's data. An attacker could have used the exploit to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and session data, potentially allowing an attacker to read information from authenticated websites.

"For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers," Anthropic said. The exploit chain combined four weaknesses Claude identified in Safari — a use-after-free flaw in Safari's JavaScriptCore engine, a way to bypass WebKit's Gigacage memory protection, a vulnerability in the WebContent sandbox, and a JavaScriptCore flaw.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

Apple has since fixed the issue, Anthropic said.

The Android exploit, meanwhile, targeted a locked Google Pixel 9. Claude chained three vulnerabilities in Android's device-transfer and USB-handling mechanisms, bypassing four layers of protection to extract photos and other personal information from the phone without unlocking it. Anthropic said Google has addressed the issue.

Claude's Windows exploit, which Microsoft has patched, involved a remotely exploitable denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. The flaw was an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's implementation of the transport protocol used by HTTP/3. An attacker could send a small number of specially crafted network packets to a vulnerable server to crash it and repeatedly trigger crashes, disrupting access for users, Anthropic said.

For Linux, Claude developed a zero-click exploit against the kernel's networking stack that would have let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute commands with root-level privileges on affected servers, without requiring any user interaction. "This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches," Anthropic said.

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

Expanding Defender Access to More Powerful Models

With AI getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, defenders need powerful models for patching them before attackers can exploit the flaws, Anthropic said. "Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do," the company said.

To that end, the company is expanding access to its most capable AI models for vetted cybersecurity professionals through its Cyber Verification Program. The program now has three access tiers that give security teams a way to apply for the level of access appropriate for their work.

"It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward," Anthropic said. "Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever."

Andrew Bolster, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, says Anthropic's results are credible where they can be verified. The Chrome, WebKit, Windows, and Linux fixes are all public, he notes, but any claims that Claude discovered them autonomously are Anthropic's own. "The report gives no success rates, cost, or human-hours per chain, which is critical context for security leaders," he says.

Some of the conditions for the exploits to work were also noteworthy, he says. For instance, the Android chain involved a stolen phone and a USB cable, and the Linux exploit required an exposed MPTCP listener. "Exploit benchmarks show model success dropping sharply once ASLR, stack canaries, and sandboxing are enabled, and VulnCheck found only 1.3% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities confirmed exploited in the wild," Bolster says. "Delivery, reliability, and target preconditions remain the attacker’s problem for now, though I'd expect that gap to narrow."

Claude's chained exploits are another indication that AI has lowered the barrier to discovering vulnerabilities and building working attacks, says Jacob Krell, senior director, secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs. But there are still substantial barriers between a proof of concept and a reliable attack in the wild. "A shell on one honeypot tells you little about the next server's worker count, build, or kernel," Krell notes. "AI has made finding the bug cheap. Getting it to work on a server it has never seen is still the expensive part."

At the same time, the gap between a proof of concept and a reliable, broadly deployable attack is increasingly becoming about time and target-specific adaptation rather than specialized expertise, he cautions.

Defenders are making a mistake if they assume this kind of vulnerability discovery always requires the most powerful AI models, adds John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security. "Local systems, including a Mac Studio with 128GB of memory or a DGX Spark, can support AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research. The target, model, tools, and operator's skill matter."

It may take attackers longer, with less capable systems, and attacks may be more practical only against smaller, less-scrutinized code bases. But defenders need to account for that capability, Strand says. "If AI can find vulnerabilities in Windows, Android, Linux, and Chrome, what does that say about code that receives a fraction of that attention? Think about your IP cameras. Think about the firmware on the router running a remote office. All of that is in play."

Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect an industrial control system network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
Full Text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Envoy: 1.36.12, 1.37.8, 1.38.6, 1.39.3, 1.40.0; Istio: 1.29.9, 1.30.6, 1.31.2 (first fixed in each branch)

Two details deserve special attention. Java's brotli4j bundles its own native Brotli build inside its jars, so patching the operating system's libbrotli does not fix it. Bun executables built with bun build \--compile embed the runtime and stay vulnerable until they are rebuilt.

Before the disclosure, Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux ARM64 image. Their exploit needed several attempts and was not released. A public proof of concept appeared on October 22, 2026. On standard builds it produces a crash and a limited memory read. As of October 29, 2026, there have been confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities catalog now lists the CVE.

How to know if you're affected

A service is exposed when it decompresses Brotli data that an attacker controls, which comes through two common paths. A few additional considerations apply to both.

Outbound requests (the quiet path)

Outbound requests are the harder path to see. Node.js's built-in fetch() decodes a Content-Encoding: br response automatically, whether or not the request asked for Brotli. The axios, got, and node-fetch clients advertise and decode Brotli by default. Any feature that fetches URLs supplied by users, such as webhooks, link previews, and feed readers, enables an attacker to force the encoding selection server side since the attacker controls the response headers, and fetch() decodes a body labeled br even when the application explicitly forces Accept-Encoding: identity.

In our testing, no exception surfaced at runtime: one crafted stream completed with an empty body and an HTTP 200, and the only visible signals were CPU usage and, under concurrency, a starved threadpool that still answered health checks.

The same holds outside Node.js: Python HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically whenever Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if application code never imports the package.

Inbound requests (the visible path)

Inbound attacks are easier to observe. A compressed request body is a recognizable attack surface, your reverse proxy or WAF can see the Content-Encoding: br header, and the framework parser is a known place to audit. Express 5 and body-parser 2.x accept Brotli-compressed request bodies by default in their JSON, raw, text, and URL-encoded parsers, and Koa and NestJS inherit the behavior. Express 4 rejects those bodies with an HTTP 415, and a bare Node.js HTTP server does not decompress anything. Parsers mounted before authentication expose the decoder to unauthenticated requests.

Other considerations

Both paths share a versioning trap: process.versions.brotli still reports 1.2.0 on the patched Node.js 24.22.1, because the cherry-picked fix does not bump the embedded version string. process.version is reliable only for official distributions from nodejs.org.

If you cannot patch immediately, set inflate: false on Express 5 and body-parser 2.x parsers, or reject Content-Encoding: br at the reverse proxy. These measures only mitigate the risk, as patching is the only complete solution. These mitigations could also break the functionality as they reject all compressed request bodies, do nothing for the outbound path, and break compressed bodies sent by legitimate clients.

How the vulnerability works

A Brotli stream is divided into blocks, and the decoder moves to a new block only when the current block's length budget runs out. A 23 MB stream of otherwise ordinary commands drains that budget while producing no output, and its closing commands request a block switch that the format forbids. These steps are where the attacker does the proper setup to exploit the bug.

In the next stage, we see the impact of the vulnerability. In Brotli 1.2.0, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns a boolean, and it answers two different questions with the same "false" value: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input". Callers cannot tell the two apart, and on the decoder's fast path the return value is dropped entirely.

The two arms then diverge. The first path is an overflow where the decoder parks the unconsumed bytes in a small internal buffer while it waits for more input. The copy has no bound check, so bytes past the end of the buffer land in adjacent decoder state. The write happens inside a single heap allocation, so the tooling built to catch memory corruption never sees it, and the process keeps running. The other path is that it keeps spinning. The decoder retries the forbidden switch in a loop, which pins a CPU core inside a single call that never returns: a one-request denial of service.

From memory corruption to code execution

In this case, memory corruption has impactful consequences. The corrupted decoder state controls where the decoder reads from and writes to next, so a crafted stream can redirect both operations. This gives an attacker two primitives:

A repeatable read of heap memory that leaves through the decompressed response.

A redirected write. In our lab, we aimed it at an unmapped page and produced a deterministic crash.

Both primitives are real. The read primitive is the most operationally interesting, because heap bytes returning over the wire are the first step of a staged attack.

Three obstacles stand between these primitives and a shell:

The addresses move. The heap layout that the corruption targets is randomized and changes between requests, so what one request leaks, the next request can’t reliably use.

The corruption bytes are also the decoder's input. The decoder consumes the bytes that steer the corruption again as it continues, so the values an attacker needs are constrained by the values the decoder will accept. This is the deepest structural obstacle we found.

A managed runtime stands in the way. Between the corrupted C state and control flow sits the machinery of a language runtime with its own allocator, its own compiled code, and its own defenses, none of which the original C library was designed around.

After measuring all three obstacles, we assess that the flaw is exploitable and that the gap between these primitives and reliable code execution is engineering effort. This matches Imperva's report of successful execution after several attempts on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image.

How the patch addresses the flaw

The patch is small and precise. The block-switch helper now returns a real error code, and both code paths treat a failed check as a hard stop instead of a request for more input. It rejects a crafted stream with a format error (-17) before anything is written to the decoder's state.

The release timeline is the troubling part. The fix was committed to the upstream Brotli repository on February 27, 2026, but the fixed library releases did not ship until October 21, 2026. For eight months, anyone who downloaded Brotli, or a runtime that embeds it, received the vulnerable version even though the corrected code sat in the public repository. The release also ships without a regression test or a changelog entry for this fix.

How to detect exploitation

This CVE involves no attacker-controlled infrastructure, so there are no conventional indicators. Detection rests on behavioral signals, and no single signal is conclusive. Correlate across three layers.

Decoder error signals

The vulnerable and patched builds respond differently to the same malicious bytes. Both responses appear in application logs and APM error spans and the error you see depends on whether the build is patched. On a vulnerable build, Node.js returns Z_BUF_ERROR with the message "unexpected end of file". On a patched build, Node.js returns ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, and Python returns "brotli: decoder is unhealthy". The vulnerable signal also appears for benign truncated input so you have to still look a little closer and differentiate the benign truncated input vs real attacks.

Process signals

A worker that exits with signal 139 (SIGSEGV) right after a Brotli transfer is a crash attempt, and a process pinned at 100% CPU inside a decompression call is the spin arm. Correlate on workload identity (the container, pod, or service) and not the process ID, because the process that crashed is gone and a successful attempt may not crash at all. The strongest signal is behavioral: a shell or new outbound connections from the same workload.

The disclosure channel

Decompressed output that contains bytes the client never sent is the read primitive in action. Investigate any such output immediately. Because the leaked heap memory leaves through the decompressed response, start by listing the endpoints that return or reflect decompressed content back to the caller, such as echo, preview, conversion, or proxy features.

What does not work

Payload byte signatures, because the attacker-controlled parts of the stream change per target and the exploit is the decode process itself, not the decompressed content.

Content matching at the WAF, because the web server forwards compressed bytes and never decodes them.

Body-size limits, because the tested middleware counts decompressed bytes, so the 23 MB compressed trigger still reaches the decoder.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management tracks CVE-2026-111497 and the related vendor advisories as vulnerability findings on hosts and container images, so your patching status lives in one place.

Datadog Code Security reports the vulnerable services that ship dependency inventories. Its library inventory identifies which services to prioritize: those running Express 5, body-parser 2.x, or Koa parsers, and those using HTTP clients that auto-decode Brotli.

Datadog Application Performance Monitoring (APM) helps you hunt for attempts. This query requires capturing Content-Encoding, which is not set by default in Node.js spans, so make sure to check how the language tracer you are using behaves. For example in Node.js it can be enabled by including content-encoding in DD_TRACE_HEADER_TAGS. Pivot on the services that accept Content-Encoding: br request bodies using this query, and review services that fetch user-supplied URLs. Decoder failures surface as APM error spans correlated with the request and the client address. The process telemetry that the Datadog Agent collects shows a crashed attempt as a worker restart with exit code 139.

Datadog Workload Protection includes coverage through the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell Exploit Content Pack. This pack includes a new security policy with three Agent rules that cover post-exploitation that surfaces a CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell exploitation detected signal.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation:

Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or web processes. It uses process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-111497 shows how a single unchecked return value in a widely shared C library can ripple across nearly every major runtime. Because the decoder runs inside the application's own process, the flaw sidesteps the defenses most teams rely on. The eight months between the upstream fix and its release are a reminder that a fix in a public repository protects no one until it ships.

Exploitation has been confirmed, which further proves the primitives are real and the path to code execution is a matter of effort. Patch to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 or your vendor's fixed package, rebuild container images, restart every process, and inventory the other Brotli consumers in your environment.

Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

Title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
Context: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits
Full Text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

Title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
Context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
Full Text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Title: Millions of security cameras at risk: DoS vulnerability in Intelbras devices
Context: During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems
Full Text:
Background

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Firmware

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

How authentication works

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash, where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

Affected endpoint

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo, which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

New firmware version

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

Real risk

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app, which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

Takeaways

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release (R.260804 along with update instructions), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

Title: Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): Detecting the Node.js Brotli RCE
Context: js Brotli RCE Published by: Sysdig Threat Research Team @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research Published: October 28, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security...
Full Text:
This blog was originally published on October 24, 2026.

As of October 28, 2026, Node2Shell is also tracked as HTTP2Shell and there are four important updates:

The Sysdig TRT added an additional runtime rule called Node.js Process Redirected Network Socket to Standard Stream to Runtime Notable Events. The rule detects the post-exploitation step of Node2Shell.

We previously reported there was no confirmed exploitation. On October 26, ELLIO confirmed exploitation.

Initially, we cited only one RCE reproduction. OtterSec has since reported dozens.

Debian was previously unpatched. Debian 12 and 13 now ship a fixed brotli, and Debian's Node.js uses the system library.

A malformed compressed stream, an ignored error, and a write past the end of a buffer. On October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped fixes for an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder it bundles, versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. One day later, on October 22, Imperva reported running code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Docker image for Linux arm64. The vulnerability, now tracked as CVE-2026-111497, received a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2 (Critical) and has been widely referred to as Node2Shell.

As of October 23, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and Node2Shell has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, public proof-of-concept (PoC) code has been tested, and the gap between patch and PoC was about a day. Security teams should work to uncover all instances where their Node.js services decode Brotli data they don’t control, and begin by patching those first.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed public Node2Shell research to help defenders understand who is reachable, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what they can do until their organization can begin to patch.

Timeline

Date

Event

Oct. 14, 2026

Node.js pre-announces the release, naming the affected lines and a top severity of high

Oct. 21, 2026, 10:38 UTC

Node.js publishes v22.23.4, v24.22.1, and v26.12.1

Oct. 21, 2026, 15:47 UTC

The first public GitHub repository for the CVE appears, about five hours after the fixes ship

Oct. 21, 2026, ~19:27 UTC

The Brotli project publishes 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1, each listing CVE-2026-111497

Oct. 22, 2026

Google’s CVE record is published with a 9.2 score on CVSS v4.0

Oct. 22, 2026

Imperva publishes research showing code execution on Node.js 24.22.0

Affected Node.js versions

The bug itself is in Brotli, not within Node.js code. Node.js bundles its own copy, so fixing it means updating the runtime itself.

The Node.js advisory rates the vulnerability as high severity. Google scores it as a critical severity vulnerability, at 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. However, severity may depend on exposure, which is determined by whether your code reaches the decoder.

No fix

Node.js states that end-of-life versions are always affected by security releases. Organizations running Node.js 25, 20, or older should treat those hosts as vulnerable, with no further patches coming.

Distribution packages need their own check. Debian’s tracker, read on October 23, lists nodejs 18.20.4 in bookworm, 20.19.2 in trixie, 24.21.0 in forky, and 24.22.0 in sid as vulnerable, and notes that Debian’s nodejs uses the system Brotli library. In that case, the fix lands in the library, not just the runtime.

Debian’s Brotli package is also vulnerable in every release the tracker lists, and the tracker shows no fixed version for any release. The tracker also shows both brotli and nodejs as unfixed in Debian’s development branch unstable. As of October 23, there is no patched Debian package for either component. Debian rates the nodejs entry as unimportant urgency, which differs from the high rating assigned by Node.js, though the tracker doesn’t state why.

The CVE record places the root bug in Google’s Brotli library 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Any other software that bundles a Brotli build in that range is worth further analysis or vendor inquiry.

But the impact isn’t limited to Debian. Packages for Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine may also use the system Brotli library instead of the bundled copy. Therefore, the fix arrives through the distribution’s Brotli package, and a Node.js version number won’t indicate whether a given instance is patched.

According to Aikido, Bun is also affected. All versions 1.4.3 and earlier are vulnerable, and Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix.

How the Node2Shell bug (CVE-2026-111497) works

Brotli is a compression format. Node.js supports it through the native decoder in its zlib module. The CVE record describes a buffer overflow in c/dec/decode.c and lists two weakness types: out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and unchecked return value (CWE-252).

The second weakness explains the mechanism. The crafted stream declares one type of data block, then asks the decoder to switch block types. A correct decoder stops with an error. The unpatched decoder ignores the error and keeps going, writing past the end of its buffer. Semgrep describes the underlying defect as the decoder confusing incomplete input with invalid input and continuing to process a malformed stream.

The fix is small. Node.js cherry-picked an upstream Brotli commit (0ed4268a) that makes the decoder fail immediately on a block switch when the stream declares only one block type. Node.js also added a new error constant, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH.

What is reachable

Node.js does not decode Brotli on its own. An app is exposed when its code, or a library it uses, decompresses Brotli data an attacker controls. Semgrep confirmed several entry points:

Path

Reaches the decoder?

Details

Express 5 with express.json()

Yes, by default

Express 5.3.0 depends on body-parser ^2.3.0. body-parser 2.x decodes br bodies, and its inflate option defaults to true. A bare Node.js HTTP server doesn’t decode incoming Brotli bodies on its own.

Express 4 with express.json()

Not through body-parser

body-parser 1.20.x handles only deflate and gzip and answers 415 to other encodings.

Server-side fetch()

Yes, for attacker-influenced responses

Node.js fetch decompresses a response with the Brotli decoder whenever the Content-Encoding header contains br. Sending Accept-Encoding: identity does not prevent it. Features that call user-supplied URLs are typically targets, like webhooks.

Direct node:zlib use

Yes

createBrotliDecompress() is exposed when it receives attacker-controlled data.

Koa (via co-body)

Yes

Brotli request bodies pass through co-body to inflation. Semgrep also lists @koa/bodyparser, koa-body, Egg and Strapi.

Fastify with @fastify/compress

Yes

Registering the plugin adds request decompression before Fastify’s content-type parsers run.

The inbound path should be prioritized. When mounted globally, body-parser can reach many public body-bearing routes, subject to the content-encoding and parser conditions. However, the outbound path also matters. If an organization’s service fetches from a server an attacker controls, the response can attack the service.

This doesn’t leave Express 4 with a clean bill of health. That reading covers body-parser only. Other middleware, frameworks, reverse proxies, and an organization’s own code may still decode Brotli.

Node2Shell exploitation: What’s been demonstrated vs. claimed

Imperva has demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux arm64, and noted that execution required several attempts. On freshly started containers without a debugger or modified binaries, the test ended with a marker file, and the patched 24.22.1 rejected the same inputs with a format error. Imperva has not released its exploit code.

As far as what the public PoCs do, on October 22 at 20:28 UTC, a GitHub search returned 11 repositories. One lab reported crashes on Node.js 20.19.5, 22.23.3, 24.22.0, and 26.12.0, and says the fixed 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 reject the same input. Another team reported local command execution in three of three runs, but it needed a build that loads an unfixed system Brotli library plus a predictable memory layout. That team says blind remote execution with address randomization on did not work.

However, some of the evidence is thin. Research has argued that no Brotli stream can reach the bad write and the real impact is denial of service. An independent test of the fix commit’s input on Node.js 24.22.0 produced an error on both the pre-fix and patched builds, so that test alone can’t show the write happens. Konfirmity notes that the fix commit itself describes the bug as low severity and not easy to exploit.

Reliable remote code execution (RCE) has been reproduced in only one setup to date. Crashes, by contrast, have been easy for researchers to reproduce. Organizations should treat a crash as the likely outcome everywhere, and the shell as a credible risk wherever their service decodes instances of Brotli that may be attacker-controlled.

Node2Shell impact

Nothing publicly disclosed at the time of publication shows a worm, a mass-exploitation campaign, or a reliable cross-platform exploit. But researchers have proven the following:

Denial of service: Public PoC authors report the process crashes on unpatched Node.js, per the repositories described above. An attacker can take down any service that decodes Brotli from users.

Code execution under the Node.js process: Imperva showed this on one image and architecture, with repeated attempts. An attacker’s code would run with the permissions of the Node.js process and could steal data.

Memory disclosure: Vercel says researchers showed memory disclosure and command execution in the Node.js process on unpatched 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Even when code execution fails, leaked memory can expose data such as credentials.

How to detect Node2Shell

Sysdig Secure customers who use managed policies now have detections to identify and respond to Node2Shell. A Threat Intelligence entry shows where the exposure is, and runtime rules catch exploitation and the attacker activity that follows.

Threat intelligence

The Sysdig Threat Intelligence feed has published a Node2Shell entry. It lists the hosts and workloads that run a Node.js version below the fixed releases 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4, or an end-of-life line. Select the host or workload count to open a filtered search of the affected assets.

Runtime detectionExploitation is rarely clean. Failed attempts crash the Node.js process, and Imperva’s own demonstration needed several tries. The new managed rule Node.js Process Crash Followed by In-Place Program Execution, in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, correlates a Node.js crash with suspicious program execution that follows it in the same workload. This is the pattern of a Node2Shell exploitation chain.

If the exploit succeeds, the attacker can run commands as the Node.js service user. Common next steps include an interactive shell, a malware download, cryptomining, or theft of secrets and cloud tokens from the container. The managed policies that Sysdig Secure enables by default already alert on this kind of activity. Customers have coverage even if the exploit itself goes unseen.

How to mitigate Node2Shell

Patch

Update Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1. Imperva says only a Node.js update fixes the decoder.

Upgrade Bun to 1.4.4 or newer wherever it runs.

Rebuild container images from a patched base, then verify with node --version in the running container. A floating tag like node:24 stays on the old version if you rebuild from a cached image, so run docker pull first. Move your Dockerfile pin to 24.22.1 or later.

Check package managers before assuming. Homebrew still shipped node 26.12.0, node@24 24.22.0, and node@22 22.23.3 about 10 hours after release.

Replace Node.js 20 and older with 22.x or 24.x. No fix will ship for them.

Reduce reachability while you patch

Disable request decompression where you can. In body-parser, express.json({ inflate: false }) rejects compressed bodies with a 415. Test your clients first. This also rejects gzip.

Reject Content-Encoding: br on request bodies at the proxy or load balancer where your clients don’t send it. Brandefense proposes this as its own suggestion, not vendor guidance. Test it before relying on it. It does not cover responses your services fetch.

Audit fetch calls to servers you don’t control, and any direct use of createBrotliDecompress().

Layer a WAF if you have one. Imperva says it added WAF rules and advises limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths. Treat this just as a layer and not as a fix.

Contain the blast radius

Run Node.js services as an unprivileged user and keep secrets out of the process environment wherever possible. Code execution lands with the permissions of the Node.js process.

Monitor web-facing Node.js processes for shell spawns and unexpected outbound connections.

Across the estate

Inventory every Node.js runtime: containers, CI runners, serverless functions, build servers, and tools that ship their own Node.js.

Conclusion

Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli. Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability.

The timeline, however, is the real warning. In the case of Node2Shell, a public repository tracking the CVE appeared five hours after the fix shipped, and a working PoC was public within a day. Since this flaw sits in a native library that Node.js and other software bundle, each must ship its own fix. Therefore, security teams should also expect more of them to be discovered — in the native libraries under the runtimes — on an increasingly short clock.

For security teams, this week’s work is inventory, then patching in order of reachability, then least privilege for whatever remains unpatched. A runtime sensor will not see the overflow, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next. That’s what makes post-exploitation behavior the backstop worth paying attention to.
