Full Text:
Summary

Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.

Introduction

Fuzzing has long been successfully applied to software projects such as Chrome or V8 (Chrome’s JavaScript engine) to detect bugs. Recently, the arrival of powerful LLMs able to read, reason about, and write code is causing a transformative change to software development and software security. With hundreds, sometimes thousands of new bugs and vulnerabilities having been discovered in well-fuzzed targets, a natural question arises: how do new LLMs compare to “traditional” fuzzers? Are they starting to replace them or do the two approaches complement each other? To help answer this, we look at three key questions:

How many bugs does each approach find in the real world?

What is the overlap between the two approaches?

What is the “shape” of bugs discovered by one system but not the other?

For this blog post, we will limit ourselves to two concrete systems: Fuzzilli, a JavaScript engine fuzzer, and BigSleep, an agentic bug finding system. Both of these systems run in production and automatically look for bugs in newly added code, which makes them fairly directly comparable. Specifically, Fuzzilli runs continuously across many instances, with the first ones usually picking up new changes within a few hours, while BigSleep currently runs once per day and is prompted to review new commits and write proof-of-concept testcases for any bugs it discovers. Both systems report bugs through Clusterfuzz, which will do basic crash triaging, then file bug reports in Chrome’s issue tracker.

We also limit ourselves to V8 as a target, a high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine with a sophisticated and mature testing and fuzzing setup. In particular, Fuzzilli is a special-purpose fuzzing tool designed to find bugs in these engines. The usually complicated nature of these bugs makes for an interesting “playground” to compare the two approaches’ ability to find deep and complex bugs in well-tested software. We leave it to future work to perform similar analysis on a broader set of targets, fuzzers, and agentic bug finding systems.

We will now look into each of the three main questions in a dedicated section. Each section will first summarize the general approach, then describe the methodology in detail (often as bullet points, so you can skip those blocks if you don’t care too much about the details) before exploring the results. We conclude with an attempt at interpreting the results to get a picture of the current state of fuzzing vs. AI.

Part 1: Production Statistics

This is the simplest part to analyze, although with some caveats we’ll see in a bit. The basic idea is to query issues from Chromium’s bugtracker (where V8 bugs are tracked) and extract various statistics from there. This is especially easy since there’s a dedicated hotlist for each of the two systems. We limit our analysis to the six months from April to September 2026 as the automatic BigSleep pipeline only became active in April this year. As such, our raw data comes from the following two bug tracker queries:

Fuzzilli: hotlistid:5433121 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

BigSleep: hotlistid:8067258 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

From there, the raw numbers of bug reports are:

Fuzzilli: 316

BigSleep: 441

Small win for BigSleep. However, this includes all types of bugs, and BigSleep initially also found a lot of configuration and integration issues in V8, for example crbug.com/503869331 where the unsafe flag blocking mechanism didn’t work properly yet. These are legitimate issues, but less relevant for our comparison since there’s little real-world security impact. One easy way to get rid of these is to look specifically at vulnerabilities by limiting the results to type:vulnerability:

Fuzzilli: 178

BigSleep: 95

Suddenly a clear win for the fuzzers? Not quite. There are still some problems with this data, notably duplicates and unactionable reports (e.g. bugs closed as WAI). At first, this seems like a simple thing to fix: just include another constraint such as status:(fixed | verified). Unfortunately, things are a bit more complicated. Take for example Fuzzilli bug crbug.com/511935486. The events on this bug are basically:

The bug is filed by Clusterfuzz on May 11 and assigned to an engineer

The bug is closed by Clusterfuzz as the testcase no longer reproduces later that same day

As such, this bug received zero developer interactions. Most likely what happened here is that this bug was a duplicate of another bug, crbug.com/511210507, but Clusterfuzz didn’t realize it as the crash signature (derived from the stack trace) was slightly different. When the other bug received a fix, the testcase stopped reproducing on Clusterfuzz, which closed the issue.

Maybe the best thing we can do is to look at “actionable” bugs, defined as those that are not marked as duplicates or WAI and that received at least one fix commit referencing them. Then, looking at only Type-Vuln bugs filters out a lot of the less-relevant BigSleep bugs, even though these were “actionable”. With that, the final picture looks like this:

So in terms of vulnerabilities, it’s roughly a tie (small advantage BigSleep) at the moment: 45 vs. 37.

This naturally raises the question of cost: how expensive is each of the two approaches and what does that mean in terms of cost-per-bug? Unfortunately, it’s challenging to make a comparison at this stage in the research. While some effort has been dedicated to making Clusterfuzz more efficient, similar effort has not been expended for Big Sleep and neither system is particularly calibrated for an optimal cost-per-bug ratio.

Part 2: Overlap

The next question is how much these approaches overlap each other. For this, our approach is twofold: we first attempt to find an answer in the bugtracker, by trying to identify bugs discovered by both systems. Next, we run a dedicated experiment in which we let BigSleep try to rediscover old Fuzzilli bugs.

Bugtracker Overlap

The basic idea is to see which bugs were found by both systems, so we’re effectively looking for duplicate bug reports. Similar to part 1, there are a few steps we need to take to ensure we get a somewhat accurate picture:

First, we look for bugs filed by one system that get deduplicated into a bug filed by the other. For example crbug.com/522410841 which is a duplicate of crbug.com/522860268. This is a clear overlap.

Next, we need to take into account that many “unactionable” reports (those with zero associated fixes) are often duplicates. For those reports, we need to find the commit that fixed them, then look at the bug associated with that commit, and treat these two bugs as duplicates. This can be a multi-prong relationship: both bug X found by BigSleep and bug Y found by Fuzzilli might be a duplicate of bug Z reported by someone/something else. In that case, that bug still counts as overlap.

Then, we need to realize that many duplicates never receive a bugtracker entry since they are already deduplicated at the Clusterfuzz level (since both Fuzzilli and BigSleep rely on Clusterfuzz for basic triage and bug filing). As such, we need to query Clusterfuzz’s underlying database to find more duplicates.

Finally, we need to decide what to do with separate bugs that get fixed by the same CL, for example the four bugs fixed by crrev.com/c/7965120. While this can legitimately happen for distinct bugs, it’s probably more likely for the bugs to be duplicates (such as in this case), and so we count them as such.

With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture:

Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an overlap of roughly 25% (20 out of a total of 81), with a slight majority of these found first by Fuzzilli and later by BigSleep.

Overlap Experiment

The second way to measure the overlap is to run a dedicated experiment in which we try to re-discover bugs found by one system in the past using the other. Specifically, here we try to re-discover old Fuzzilli bugs using a BigSleep setup that’s as close to the production configuration as possible. For each bug we collect the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, and ask the agent to review those changes just as in the production CI environment. Note that the other direction, trying to rediscover past BigSleep bugs with Fuzzilli is more difficult to set up, since fuzzers cannot easily be given a similar “starting point”. Moreover, for many of these bugs we already know the outcome of such an experiment: the majority of “historic” BigSleep bugs (e.g. those from 2025) were found after fuzzers like Fuzzilli had already been fuzzing vulnerable builds for months, sometimes years. So they would most likely also not rediscover them in an experiment (except perhaps in a few cases where Fuzzilli was since updated to support new language features). Similarly, in production, BigSleep only reports crashes with a delay of 1-2 days (as there’s currently only one run per day). As such, fuzzers also get a head-start there.

In more detail, here is how the experiment is set up:

We start with a list of historic Fuzzilli bugs (from early 2023 until mid-2026) by querying the bug tracker hotlist. This gives us around 1150 raw bugs.

We restrict this to only type:vulnerability as these are the types of bugs we care most about and will remove some “noise” as above. We are left with roughly 600 vulnerabilities.

Next, we filter this list down to bugs that reproduce in the environment used by the agent. This involves two parts:

Bugs that reproduce on an x64 debug+asan build of the d8 shell as provided by Chrome’s public build infrastructure. This is important because many bugs only reproduce in special builds, for example because they are architecture-specific or need certain compile-time features.

Bugs that can be reproduced without special flags. The problem here is that fuzzers often set custom flags, either to enable in-development features (e.g. --experimental-wasm-jspi in crbug.com/361123483) or to turn on different fuzzing modes that make certain types of bugs easier to discover (e.g. --deopt-every-n-times in crbug.com/362784006). However, we can’t let the agent set arbitrary flags on historic V8 builds as these didn’t have a “safe-flags only” mode (leading to many false-positive crashes), and we also don’t want to tell the agent which flags it should use for a given challenge as that would be a hint. As such, for simplicity we limit ourselves to bugs that can reproduce with a standard set of flags (--fuzzing, --jit-fuzzing, --expose-gc) and only allow the agent to set those.

We end up with 132 historic bugs.

We now perform some deduplication similar to what we did above to identify implicit duplicates, which we remove. This leaves us with a final number of 112 bugs.

For a realistic comparison, we then convert these bugs into “code review challenges” similar to the ones used by the production BigSleep pipeline. For that, we try to identify the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, for example based on bisection. We note that this skews the comparison against BigSleep for two reasons:

We likely sometimes identify the wrong commit that is unrelated to the bug in question, making the task harder or even impossible.

We only have one commit per bug, while in the real world, the agent might discover the bug from another, subsequent commit that touches a similar part of the codebase.

We now run the agent for 25 attempts on each commit. The agent is asked to find bugs related to the commit and prove their existence by writing a testcase that crashes the vulnerable build. The attempt is terminated once a crash is found, so each attempt can report at most one bug. We use essentially the same configuration that was used in production BigSleep at that time, including the same underlying model: Gemini 3.6 flash.

Finally, we run some post-processing on the results to check if the agent found the “right” bug or an unrelated one. For that, we check that the testcase crashes the pre-fix revision but not the post-fix revision. This is imperfect but fairly easy to implement.

Here are the results from the experiment:

Starting from just the commits that (likely) introduced the bugs, BigSleep was able to re-discover ~62% of the original bugs, while finding a different (but by now fixed) bug for another ~12% of commits. On around 26% of the commits it failed to find any bugs.

Memorization

One thing to worry about with experiments such as this one is memorization: the LLM remembering specific bugs from its (pre-)training data and as such having an easier time “re-discovering” them during evaluation. We can try to get some idea of the effect of this by looking at the success rates for bugs from different time spans, e.g. every half-year period for which we have bugs in the data set. If there was memorization, we’d expect higher success rates (both for a single attempt and for the combined run) on bugs prior to the learning data cutoff of the model. Here are the results for our experiment:

For the model used in this experiment (Gemini 3.6 flash), the knowledge cutoff date is March 2026. Combining that with the fact that in early 2026, Chrome bugs would only become publicly visible after ~3 months, the effective knowledge cutoff for Fuzzilli bugs should be around Jan 2026. Looking at the data, there seems to be no statistically significant amount of memorization pre-2026. We note, however, that this may be different for other models or future model generations and as such recommend that this be re-evaluated for similar experiments in the future.

Difficulty

A follow-up question we might ask is how the overlap compares with “difficulty”. For example, in the best case a system like BigSleep would easily find issues that fuzzers struggle with and vice versa. In that case, budget that was previously spent on long fuzzing sessions may now be re-allocated and put to different uses. Here are the results of analysing this, where “bug difficulty” is measured by the time it took Fuzzilli to discover the bug:

While we do get a statistically significant result here (although not of particularly great magnitude), it actually points in the other direction! Bugs that are hard to find for a fuzzer are likely also hard to find for an AI agent. As such, those fuzzers should probably be kept running for now.

Components

Another thing we can look at is a per-component breakdown of the bugs and their rediscovery rates:

Interestingly, the overlap is significantly smaller for compiler bugs. This is the area where Fuzzilli probably specializes most in, which may explain the results. Later on (in part 3), we’ll also develop another hypothesis for why (some) bugs in the compilers may be more difficult to rediscover for BigSleep.

Prompting

A final question is how much the specific prompting played a role in the performance of the AI agent. For that, we run two quick follow-up experiments, only on the bugs that weren’t previously re-discovered and with different prompts:

Instead of starting from commits, we start from the vulnerable file or function. This may be an easier starting point but is still a fairly realistic setup since both can for example be obtained by extracting modified files and functions from a given commit.

Instead of asking the agent to find memory corruption vulnerabilities (what we care most about), we specifically tell it that assertion failures and similar crashes are also desirable.

Running these two experiments with only 5 attempts per bug (instead of the 25 used in the main experiment), the agent re-discovered 10 additional bugs in total: 8 from the different starting points and 7 with the rephrased prompt (with 5 found in both runs).

In total, combining these results with our original experiment, we get the following picture:

So the share of “correct” bugs found climbs to ~70%, and we find some kind of bug for ~84% of starting points. However, for fairness it should be noted that equivalent tweaks to a fuzzer could likely also result in higher discovery rates for certain bugs, so the results of this follow-up experiment should be treated with some caution.

Summary

The main results from our two angles are:

In production, the overlap is noticeable but not substantial at around 25%.

In our experiment, overlap was around 60% of historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with additional runs that used different prompts).

The overlap is not uniformly distributed:

Bugs that are difficult for a fuzzer to find are more likely to also be difficult to find for an agent, so there’s more overlap on “easy” bugs.

The overlap seems to be smaller in the JIT Compilers and higher in the rest of the engine.

From just the experiment, we might expect a higher overlap in production. However, there are probably a few factors that prevent(ed) this:

There’s a limited time window for overlaps: once a bug reported by either system is fixed, the other system no longer has a chance to rediscover it (as the bug won’t reproduce on Clusterfuzz and will therefore be discarded).

Our experiment only looked at a subset of Fuzzilli bugs that reproduce on a standard x64 d8 fuzzer build and without special flags. In production, each system has access to slightly different and specialized builds, as well as different runtime flag constraints, and there the overlap is potentially smaller.

Pipeline hiccups such as overloaded servers or bugs in the automation likely prevented a number of commits from being reviewed by BigSleep in the last months, so bugs introduced by them may have been missed.

Since its introduction in April, the model underlying the BigSleep pipeline has been upgraded multiple times. Earlier models likely performed worse, and we expect future models to perform better.

Part 3: Shape of Bugs

In this section, we will first look at three case studies of bugs found by one system but not the other, then attempt to draw conclusions from these and other bugs.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 449760249 (October 2025)

This bug is a nice example of BigSleep benefiting from the underlying model’s reasoning capabilities to discover a variant that was (likely) too complex to trigger by a fuzzer in a reasonable amount of time. It’s also a good example to show the general working of an agentic bug finding system.

Background: TDZ and Hole Check Elision

Before diving into the bug specifics, we first need to look at some JavaScript internals, specifically variable initialization. In JavaScript, variables declared with the let or const keywords cannot be used before they are initialized, and attempting to do so will lead to an exception (”ReferenceError: Cannot access 'foobar' before initialization”). In V8’s terminology, these variables reside in a “temporal dead zone” (TDZ) until they are initialized. Internally, V8 sets variables in the TDZ to a special sentinel value, the_hole, and then checks for this value when accessing the variable’s content.

To limit the performance impact of these hole-checks, V8’s bytecode compiler implements an optimization (behind the default-enabled --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks flag) to identify redundant checks and subsequently remove them. The idea here is to identify “dominating” checks where it can then be guaranteed that a hole-check has already been performed for a given variable on all possible paths leading to the current position.

This is a security-relevant optimization as an incorrectly removed hole-check would result in the internal the_hole value leaking to JavaScript code, a condition that has historically been exploitable (although new mitigations for this bug class have since shipped).

The Original Vulnerability

The original bug (issue 40071027 - discovered two years earlier by Fuzzilli!) involved do-while loops containing a break statement. In a do-while loop, the loop condition evaluates after the body. If the condition contains an assignment to a variable, the bytecode compiler will mark the variable as initialized. However, if a break statement executes in the loop body in the first iteration, then the condition will never execute. The bytecode compiler originally failed to account for this, leading to an incorrectly omitted hole check and subsequent leak of the_hole value.

To fix this, the implementation of BytecodeGenerator::VisitDoWhileStatement was modified in the following way:

- VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + if (!loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()) { + HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this); + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + } else { + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + }

Specifically, the patch works by creating a HoleCheckElisionScope for processing the condition code in case the loop contains break statements. This means that any updates to the TDZ state of variables will be discarded once the scope object is destroyed. As such, code after the loop will see the previous TDZ state (which is the correct behavior in this case).

Discovery of the Variant

The BigSleep agent began its analysis by examining the patch to VisitDoWhileStatement, realizing that the fix relied on loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() to decide if a protective HoleCheckElisionScope was required. It then began creating and testing various hypotheses for scenarios in which no break statement was registered with a given loop but the condition would still be skipped at runtime. For example, it hypothesized that a try-catch in combination with a throw inside the loop might confuse the hole-check elision logic. It then investigated how try-catch was implemented in the bytecode compiler and concluded that this was handled correctly.

Eventually, the agent started investigating labeled breaks, which allow directly breaking out of inner loops. It hypothesized that these might not be handled correctly and continued to investigate how these were being processed, for example by studying the logic in BytecodeGenerator::VisitBreakStatement. This time, it seemed to have identified a real flaw: in the case of nested breaks, the inner loop was apparently not being informed of the existence of a break statement! It therefore formulated the following vulnerability hypothesis:

If a labeled break inside a do-while loop targets an outer scope, the inner do-while loop’s LoopBuilder is not notified.

Consequently, loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() remains true.

Therefore, when generating the code for the loop condition, the HoleCheckElisionScope introduced by the patch is not used.

The condition is bypassed at runtime, but the bytecode compiler erroneously removed a later hole-check, leading to a leak of the_hole to JavaScript.

The agent then began writing a testcase to prove the existence of this bug. The initial attempt with simply two nested loops and a label failed, however, as the bytecode compiler would add another protective scope object for the labeled block. To work around this, the agent decided to use a switch statement. When handling a switch statement, the bytecode compiler uses a HoleCheckElisionMergeScope to compute the intersection of initialization states across all branches. By ensuring that the variable was initialized in a default case, the merge logic then concluded that the variable was correctly initialized on all paths.

Proof of Concept

With that, the agent had everything in place to produce a testcase to demonstrate the vulnerability. Below is the agent’s PoC:

// Flags: --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks function trigger(cond) { { target: switch(1) { case 1: do { // Labeled break targeting the switch. The do-while LoopBuilder remains unaware. if (cond) break target; } while((x=1) && false); // Condition performs a check/assignment on x. break; default: x=1; // Ensure x is considered initialized across all switch branches for merging. } // Generator incorrectly believes x is checked/initialized. Elides TDZ check. x + 1; let x; } } trigger(true);

Here is how this testcase works:

trigger(true) executes, entering case 1 of the switch.

The do-while loop executes break target.

Control flow jumps to the end of the switch, bypassing the do-while condition where x is assigned.

At runtime, x remains uninitialized (holding the_hole).

Because the TDZ check was elided at compile time, the engine leaks the internal the_hole value to JavaScript code in the x + 1 expression, leading to a potentially exploitable condition.

We can see how this bug would be difficult for a fuzzer to find since the testcase is quite complex. While a coverage-guided fuzzer would have received rewards for triggering individual code paths (such as the handling of labeled break, the switch statement, the do-while loop, etc. in the parser), there is no additional reward for putting these together “in the right way” and so ending up with a testcase like this is quite difficult.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 443765373 (September 2025)

This bug is an example of a relatively simple bug type that is challenging to discover with standard fuzzing approaches.

Background: Exception handling in V8

To understand this bug, it is necessary to briefly look into exception handling in V8. Take the following example JavaScript code:

function simple() { try { throw 42; } catch (e) { return e; } }

Here, we have a function consisting of a try-catch block in which an exception is raised. Running this in d8 with --print-bytecode, we can see the internal bytecode that the engine generates to execute the JavaScript code:

[generated bytecode for function: simple] 0x2ad5001000e4 @ 0 : 1b ff f9 Mov <context>, r0 0x2ad5001000e7 @ 3 : 0d 2a LdaSmi [42] 0x2ad5001000e9 @ 5 : b5 Throw 0x2ad5001000ea @ 6 : d1 Star1 0x2ad5001000eb @ 7 : 8d f8 00 CreateCatchContext r1, [0] 0x2ad5001000ee @ 10 : d2 ... ... 0x2ad5001000f7 @ 19 : b7 Return Handler Table (size = 16) from to hdlr (prediction, data) ( 3, 6) -> 6 (prediction=1, data=0)

For the purpose of this bug, the relevant part is mostly the last line of the output. Here, the bytecode essentially says “if there is an exception while the PC is between offset 3 and 6 in this bytecode, then execution should continue at offset 6 (the start of the exception handler)”.

The Bug

The agent spotted the bug while looking at the following function, responsible for writing the handler table data structure in memory:

void HandlerTable::SetRangeHandler(int index, int handler_offset, CatchPrediction prediction) { int value = HandlerOffsetField::encode(handler_offset) | HandlerWasUsedField::encode(false) | HandlerPredictionField::encode(prediction); int offset = index * kRangeEntrySize + kRangeHandlerIndex; Memory<int32_t>(raw_encoded_data_ + offset * sizeof(int32_t)) = value; }

Here, the int offset is being combined with a few other bits of data into a new int value. As such, the handler_offset cannot have the full integer range in the new field, possibly leading to integer truncation issues. The agent then investigated the specific bounds of these values and realized that the HandlerOffsetField had only 28 bits (allowing for 256MB) while the maximum bytecode size was 512MB! From there it was relatively simple to craft a testcase that crashes, simply by creating a huge function (resulting in >256MB of bytecode) with an exception handler at the end, then triggering an exception inside of it. The result is a jump to a wrong bytecode offset, a primitive that’s easily exploited. Here is the relevant part of the testcase:

// yield statements turn into a large chunk of bytecode let kNumYields = 500000; let body = ` if ("foo" === "bar") { ${"yield* 42;".repeat(kNumYields)} } try { throw 42; } catch (e) { // Will never get here } `;

Such a testcase would again be difficult to craft by a fuzzer as the fuzzer isn’t rewarded for creating large code (at least not with generic coverage feedback). In fact, the fuzzer is likely even actively discouraged from finding this bug since generating and executing large bytecode takes some time (in debug builds, the testcase generated by the agent needs a few seconds to trigger) and would therefore probably have led to timeouts during fuzzing.

Fuzzilli: Chrome Bug 40076141 (November 2023)

This bug is a good example of a type of bug that is likely difficult to find just by looking at (one part) of the source code. It was originally discovered by Fuzzilli and not rediscovered by any of the experiments from part 2.

Background: Value Representation in V8

Consider the following piece of JavaScript code:

let i = 42; let f = 13.37; let s = "foobar" i = s;

Here we create multiple variables holding values of different types. Note, however, that we never declare the type of a variable, and that variables can hold values of different types throughout their lifetime (i first contains an integer, later a string). What we see here is that JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and so variables (and also object fields, etc.) have no fixed type. However, the actual runtime values still need to have a type: the engine somehow needs to know that foobar is a string value and that certain operations (e.g. substring search) can therefore be performed on it. Conceptually, this is possible by representing runtime values with a struct such as

enum JSType { JS_TYPE_INT, JS_TYPE_FLOAT, JS_TYPE_STRING, ... }; struct JSValue { JSType type; // Either the raw value or a pointer to another object, e.g a JSString. uintptr_t value; };

However, this is somewhat inefficient since we now need something like 16 bytes to represent a simple 4-byte integer at runtime. As such, modern JS engines use clever tagging schemas, which rely on unused pointer bits to encode type information. Specifically, in V8 the JSValue type is a tagged pointer (or just tagged for short) which stores one bit of type information in the least-significant bit:

If the bit is one, then the value minus 1 is a pointer to another object. This works because objects are aligned and so cannot start at an uneven address.

If the bit is zero, then the next 31 bits contain a raw integer value (also called a small integer - Smi)

As such, to figure out the type of a value at runtime, the engine first looks at the least-significant bit. If that is zero, the value can be “untagged” to obtain the integer value by right-shifting by one. On the other hand, if the bit is one, the value is a valid pointer to an object that contains further type information. For more details on V8’s pointer tagging scheme see also this blog post.

The Testcase

Let’s start by looking at the testcase produced by the fuzzer, which isn’t overly long:

function f0() { let v2 = 1; for (let i3 = v2; i3 >= v2; i3 += v2) { v2 = v2 && i3; } } f0();

The bug is caused during optimization of the loop by the Maglev compiler, specifically due to a conflict between two stages of the compiler pipeline: the initial graph builder and the later MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector. [truncated for CSV - full text is in the JSON export]

Title: Brotli2Shell: Frequently asked questions for Google Brotli decoder vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)
Context: A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released
Full Text:
Researchers have demonstrated remote code execution through CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) are available. Software that uses the decoder includes Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients and PHP for Windows.

Update October 27: CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog.

October 26: Original publication.

Key Takeaways

CVE-2026-111497, known as Brotli2Shell and by several other names, is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library that Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), scored 9.2 under CVSSv4.0.

Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli decoder is potentially at risk, including Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients, FFmpeg, Apache Arrow and ClickHouse.

Patches are available for Google Brotli and the major runtimes, though some projects had not shipped a fixed release as of October 26, and applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli each need their own fix.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Brotli2Shell, a vulnerability in Google's Brotli C decoder library, which Node.js, .NET and other software embed.

FAQ

What is Brotli2Shell?

Brotli2Shell is one of several names for CVE-2026-111497, a memory corruption flaw in Google's open-source Brotli compression library. Some researchers call it Node2Shell, after Node.js, which disclosed the flaw in its October 21 security advisory. Others use HTTP2Shell, since the same bug reaches HTTP software outside Node.js. It has circulated as Broccoli2Shell as well. We use Brotli2Shell because the bug sits in the Brotli decoder itself, not in any one downstream product.

What is the vulnerability associated with Brotli2Shell?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Google Brotli C decoder library.

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-111497

Google Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write vulnerability

9.2

An attacker can trigger the flaw by getting an application to decompress crafted Brotli data. Two common paths are a compressed HTTP response sent to a client that decompresses it automatically, and a compressed request body sent to a server that decompresses incoming content. The impact ranges from a process crash to potential remote code execution, and the bug can also leak process memory.

Note on severity scoring: Google, as the CNA, scored the flaw 9.2 (CVSSv4.0) with vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. Microsoft rates it 8.1 (CVSSv3.1) for .NET.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first disclosed?

Google committed the upstream fix to the Brotli source repository on February 27. Node.js publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 in its security advisory, the same day Google released fixed Brotli versions. Envoy Proxy and Istio had already shipped fixed releases earlier in October without naming the flaw. NVD published the CVE record on October 22. Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 both reached the Python Package Index (PyPI) on October 22. On October 25, Microsoft released .NET security updates.

What software is affected by CVE-2026-111497?

The risk applies wherever an application decompresses Brotli data an attacker can control, whether that data arrives over HTTP in either direction or inside a file.

Node.js release lines that have reached end of support, including 20, 23 and 25, do not receive a fixed release. Akamai said its telemetry "shows that 61% of networks are running affected Node.js versions."

JFrog Security Research showed that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg through the libjxl library, by way of Brotli-compressed metadata in JPEG XL files. JFrog obtained instruction-pointer control in FFmpeg with a crafted JPEG XL file but did not demonstrate code execution. The same research produced an infinite-loop denial of service in Apache Arrow, which uses Brotli for compressed Parquet data, with a crafted 534-byte input, and crashed a tested ClickHouse server with a single malformed Brotli-compressed HTTP request. Python HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp are also in scope when the Brotli or brotlicffi package is installed.

Does updating the system Brotli library fix the issue?

It depends on where the software gets its decoder. Programs that load the operating system's copy of Brotli pick up the fix once they restart. Node.js, Bun and other applications that ship with a built-in copy keep the flawed decoder until a fixed release of that application is installed.

Is every .NET, Envoy Proxy or Istio installation exposed?

No. These platforms are exposed only when Brotli decompression is in use.

.NET: Microsoft says an application "is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed," and ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are off by default. Applications are in scope when they use ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient response decompression, or the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. NativeAOT and self-contained applications pick up the fix only when they are rebuilt and redeployed. Microsoft says .NET Framework is not affected.

Envoy Proxy and Istio: Envoy Proxy is exposed only when its Brotli decompressor is configured, and Istio users are potentially affected when they enable Brotli decompression, for example through an EnvoyFilter. Istio 1.29 reached end of support on October 15. Its 1.29.9 release includes the fix.

Is PHP affected by CVE-2026-111497?

PHP's official Windows builds are affected, because they include their own copy of Brotli. On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds that bundle Brotli 1.2.1. PHP names its cURL extension as the route to the flaw in those builds, once automatic decompression of HTTP responses is enabled. cURL keeps that setting off unless an application or HTTP client library enables it. On other platforms, PHP can still reach a vulnerable decoder through the system Brotli library or through the PHP brotli extension, which bundles its own copy and fixed the flaw in version 0.21.1. The PHP source releases are unchanged, and this flaw is separate from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities covered in our FAQ.

Is CVE-2026-111497 being exploited in the wild?

On October 26, threat intelligence firm ELLIO reported that its sensors recorded an exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-111497. ELLIO said the attempt targeted Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 and combined code copied from public PoCs with an original exploit chain. Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity. On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, with a remediation due date of November 10 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-111497 has been classified as a “Vulnerability of Interest” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for CVE-2026-111497?

Yes. Public PoCs for CVE-2026-111497 are available on GitHub. The Imperva Red Team demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image after multiple attempts, and has not released that exploit. At least one public PoC on GitHub claims code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under narrow lab conditions. ELLIO said it reproduced code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64.

How reliable is exploitation of CVE-2026-111497?

According to ELLIO, an exploit has to be tuned to the specific Node.js build it targets. ELLIO reported that an exploit tuned for the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64 produced nothing in 10,000 attempts against Node.js 22.23.3 and 26.12.0, which each need their own memory offsets. Even against the matching build, most of ELLIO's 400 lab attempts against an Express server crashed the worker process instead of returning a shell, but where workers restart automatically, an attacker gets repeated tries. The exploit request ELLIO captured in the wild did not produce a shell in 50 lab attempts against a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 target. Imperva also needed multiple attempts to achieve code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 on Linux arm64.

Are patches or mitigations available for CVE-2026-111497?

Fixed versions for Google Brotli, Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, the Python Brotli packages and PHP for Windows are listed in the table above. As of October 26, ClickHouse had merged a fix without shipping a release, and the Apache Arrow issue remained open.

Patching does not reach code that is already running. The fixed decoder takes effect in a process or scheduled job only after a restart, and in a container only after its image is rebuilt and redeployed.

Where patching is delayed, the Patch the Planet mitigation guide and the broccoli2shell.com tracker list temporary steps that reduce exposure:

Blocking requests marked Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer, so they stop before anything decompresses them. This step does nothing for applications that fetch Brotli responses from attacker-controlled servers, and turning off Brotli compression on an origin server or CDN has no effect on decompression.

Turning off Brotli decoding in HTTP clients. Taking br out of the Accept-Encoding header falls short by itself, since a hostile server can still reply with Brotli-encoded data.

Disabling the Brotli decompressor filter in Envoy Proxy and Istio in both directions. A disabled filter forwards compressed bytes as they arrive, which leaves any downstream service that decodes Brotli at risk.

Removing the Brotli or brotlicffi package from Python environments until a patched version is in place.

Are there any indicators of compromise for CVE-2026-111497?

ELLIO published the source IP address and a payload hash for the exploitation attempt it observed. They are available in ELLIO's blog post.

Has Tenable released product coverage for CVE-2026-111497?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

Anthropic’s Claude Mythos put vulnerability management in the boardroom when it was released earlier this year, and the conversation around it has evolved. Press coverage continues to find new angles, and there’s plenty of discourse around how AI is changing everything about cybersecurity.

In the months since the initial release of Mythos Preview, there have been a few developments around what Mythos can do and who is able to access it. But what does this actually mean for your vulnerability management program?

A stronger model, wider access

In September, Anthropic shipped Claude Mythos 5.1, which it calls the model with the strongest cyber capabilities of any they’ve released. Mythos 5.1 is built on the same base model as the generally available Fable 5.1 with different safeguards attached. Then, in October, it folded Project Glasswing, the early-access program that gave select critical infrastructure providers and industry partners access to Mythos, into an expanded tiered Cyber Verification Program (CVP). The revamped CVP spans everyday defensive work up through the highest-sensitivity critical infrastructure.

This means that compared to at launch, machine-speed vulnerability discovery that used to be limited to a small group will reach a wider set of defenders. According to Anthropic, Glasswing partners turned up more than 129,000 verified vulnerabilities between April and July, over 33,000 of them critical or high severity. More access to Mythos-class discovery sounds like it should mean more vulnerabilities found, faster, across more organizations. While this is true, that large number isn’t the full story.

Discovery and exploitation aren’t the same thing

Anthropic noted in its announcement that the generally available Fable 5.1 can now be used to discover software vulnerabilities, but explicitly not to develop exploits for them. Activities that could be used maliciously like penetration testing, exploit generation, etc., are redirected to lower-tier models. The same gating carries into Mythos. The CVP’s three access tiers wall off penetration testing and red teaming work behind the two highest, most heavily vetted tiers.

So while broader access to Mythos-class capability means broader access to finding things faster, it doesn’t, by itself, mean broader access to attacking anything. Also, Mythos still isn’t broadly available: access runs through vetted organizations in the CVP, so it isn’t something readily on hand for attackers.

That’s not to say automated attacks aren’t happening, but that’s a separate development, not something that traces back to Mythos specifically. Lumping every agentic AI risk together misses where the actual exposure is coming from.

The core of vulnerability management hasn’t changed

A lot of the coverage of Mythos makes it sound scarier than it needs to. While it does make vulnerability discovery significantly faster, no security team was patching every known CVE even before Mythos existed. Using AI agents for defense can increase teams’ speed and scope, but the real differentiator continues to be knowing which findings are in active, loaded packages, reachable, and creating real risk, versus which ones are noise with a scary CVSS score attached.

Exploits are getting faster too. Mandiant now puts the average time-to-exploit at negative seven days, meaning exploitation begins before a vulnerability is even disclosed. This makes it even more important to build a vulnerability management program around core principles.

The fundamentals of vulnerability management are even more important in the AI discovery era:

Scan and discover everything in one place, CVE and non-CVE findings alike.

Prioritize by what’s in-use and exploitable, not just what scores high.

Automate remediation at the source instead of patching every downstream instance individually.

Treat runtime security as a safety net for whatever stays exposed.

This plan for vulnerability response doesn’t get rewritten because discovery got faster. Agentic AI can be utilized on your side too, automating and accelerating each of these steps and helping keep up with the volume of findings. You don’t need to treat every Mythos headline as a crisis or rebuild your program every time access expands again.

Learn more at the webinar

To learn more about building a Mythos-ready vulnerability management program, join our webinar, Mythos Decoded: What’s Actually Changed in Vulnerability Management. We’ll cover what Mythos actually is and isn’t and practical steps to keep pace with AI-accelerated discovery without the panic.

Title: In a pickle: Why every pickle defense in machine learning is bypassed the same way
Context: Threat Research Engineer @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research See more threat research Published: October 27, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security briefings...
Full Text:
The machine learning (ML) ecosystem recently shipped a series of defenses against malicious model files. PyTorch restricted what its loader will deserialize. Keras added a safe mode that refuses to execute embedded code. Vendors built scanners to inspect model files at rest and reject the dangerous ones.

But none of them held up to six documented CVE bypasses. These bypasses, often called “pickles,” let a malicious Python data file slip past security scanners undetected. And after the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) pulled apart every public pickle bypass on record, a pattern emerged.

Before we explore that pattern, let’s first understand what a pickle actually is and why machine learning (ML) is full of them. Then, we’ll analyze which model formats are most dangerous, what the Sydig TRT measured when we ran malicious model loads against two detection engines, and how you can best deploy and protect susceptible models in your environment.

A pickle is a program

Pickle is a built-in Python capability for saving something in memory to file so you can load it back later exactly as it was. Many teams may be pickling and they don't even realize it. torch.save() or joblib are both pickle, and that hidden misunderstanding increases exposure and makes it easy for something to go wrong without anyone noticing or understanding why.

Most file formats are data. You parse them, get a structure back, and nothing inside the file gets a vote in what the program does next. A malformed JPEG produces an error, for instance, not a shell.

Pickle is not that kind of format. pickle.load() doesn’t parse; it executes. A .pkl file is a sequence of instructions for a small stack-based virtual machine built into CPython, and loading the file means running them. That’s not an implementation flaw or a parser bug that gets patched, but the inherent design.

The easiest way to believe it is to read one. Pickle's protocol 0 is human-readable by design, and this is a complete, working payload:

cos GLOBAL → push os.system onto the stack system ( MARK S'id' push the string "id" tR TUPLE → ("id",) then REDUCE → call os.system("id") . STOP

The snippet above includes five instructions, and it reads like assembly because functionally that is what it is:

GLOBAL resolves and pushes a callable.

MARK and TUPLE assemble an argument tuple.

REDUCE calls the callable with those arguments.

STOP ends the program.

Swap "id" for something with more ambition, and nothing about the structure changes.

That’s the entire remote code execution (RCE) story, and it’s only three operational codes (opcodes). Import something, build an argument tuple, and call it. Everything else in the format — later protocol versions, the memo table, framing, out-of-band buffers — is optimization around that core.

And because the payload is only opcodes, there are no offsets to leak and no build to fingerprint. One that works on a given Python works on any Python that can parse the protocol.

You wouldn’t normally handwrite those opcodes, either. Python will emit them for you through a documented extension point:

import os, pickle class Evil: def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ("id",)) payload = pickle.dumps(Evil())

__reduce__ is how an object tells pickle to reconstruct it: The method names a callable and its arguments, and pickle invokes them on load — which is how objects that cannot be naively serialized rebuild themselves on the other side. The attack does not subvert that. It uses pickle exactly as specified, and nominates os.system as the callable.

Look at this script, for example:

import os, pickle, pickletools class Evil: def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ("echo pwned",)) pickletools.dis(pickle.dumps(Evil()))

pickletools.dis disassembles the byte stream without running it, and the output reads like a listing: GLOBAL, MARK, SHORT_BINUNICODE, TUPLE1, REDUCE, STOP. Disassemble freely. Run pickle.loads on that payload only somewhere you are willing to lose.

The consequence carries big implications

If a pickle is a program, then a file that is invalid as a whole can still be perfectly effective in part. The VM executes opcodes as it encounters them. It doesn’t validate the stream up front and then run it because there is no up front. It runs until it finishes, or until it reaches something it cannot execute. Everything before that point has already happened.

Data would be parsed and then used, and a corrupted file would yield nothing. A program runs until it faults.

Attackers noticed, and we will come back to that in the third section.

Why is machine learning full of pickles anyway?

A pickle solves a real problem, and the way it solves that problem requires precisely the capability that makes it dangerous.

The problem is general object serialization. Writing a list of integers to disk is easy. Writing an arbitrary Python object, however, is not.

Objects hold references to other objects, to classes defined in modules that may not be imported yet, to state that is only meaningful once something reconstructs it. There is no universal declarative description of "how to rebuild this." The general answer is to record a procedure — call this thing, with these arguments — and run it at load time.

That is what __reduce__ is, and the standard library specifies it in exactly those terms. The first two items of a __reduce__ tuple are:

A callable object that will be called to create the initial version of the object.

A tuple of arguments for the callable object.

Read that as an attacker and the exploit writes itself. Read it as a language designer, though, and it is the only general answer available.

So arbitrary code execution is not a bug in pickle, but a feature. Python has never been coy about it, either. The warning sits at the top of the module documentation:

The docs even name the mitigation. A section titled "Restricting Globals" observes that for many applications the default behavior "is unacceptable as it permits the unpickler to import and invoke arbitrary code," and shows how to subclass the unpickler to allow only what you expect.

So how did machine learning end up built on pickles?

torch.save serializes with pickle. Saving a model is one call, and the artifact is a .pt, .pth, or .bin, none of which look like a pickle to anyone reading a file listing. scikit-learn's persistence guidance points to joblib, a pickle wrapper optimized for objects carrying large NumPy arrays, which is exactly what a fitted estimator is. NumPy's own .npy is a plain numeric container right up until an array contains Python objects. At that point it needs pickle, which is why the allow_pickle flag exists at all.

Nobody in that chain chose arbitrary code execution. They chose "save my Python object," which is the obvious API to want, and pickle is the batteries-included way to provide it.

The result is a supply chain that’s majority-pickle. In a survey of 705,991 models on a Hugging Face mirror, PyTorch's .pt, .pth, and .bin accounted for 335,893 models (51.0%), with explicit pickle variants (.pkl, .pickle, .joblib, .dill) adding another 26,696, or 4.1%. More than half the models you might download execute code the moment you load them.

Why "just fix pickle" isn’t on the table

You can’t make pickle.load both general and safe, because generality is the thing that requires the call. However, you can do one of two narrower things:

Restrict the loader. Keep the format, but allow only a known-safe subset of callables. This is the standard library's own suggestion, and PyTorch's weights_only=True and Keras's safe_mode are that idea applied to model files.

Change the format. Store only what a model actually needs, such as named arrays of numbers, in a container with no way to express a call at all. That’s safetensors.

Both these approaches are sound in principle. Their records in practice are the subject of the next section, and only one of them has survived contact.

Which models are actually vulnerable

Which model files should be treated as code? The short answer is: more of them than the name suggests, and almost none of them are called .pkl.

Note the phrasing on the last two: no known code execution path. These formats are younger and attacked less often than pickle, and the absence of published CVEs is much weaker evidence than a format that cannot express a call in the first place.

Strategy one: Restrict the loader, get bypassed

Keep the format, allowing only a known-safe subset of callables: This is the standard library's own advice. Both major frameworks took that advice, but were still bypassed.

PyTorch flipped torch.load's weights_only argument from False to True by default in version 2.6, explicitly on security grounds. The restricted unpickler permits tensors, storages, and basic collections, and refuses everything else.

Except that in 2.5.1 and earlier, weights_only=True was already bypassable. CVE-2025-32434 found that _legacy_load — the path handling older tar-based checkpoints — did not actually enforce the restricted unpickler on everything it processed. The flag was set and the code that ran didn’t honor it.

Then it happened again. CVE-2026-24747, published in January 2026 with a CVSS of 8.8, defeats the restricted unpickler's validation with crafted opcodes, corrupting memory to reach code execution. It affects every version before 2.10.0, which means the fix for the 2025 bypass was itself exploitable across the entire 2.6 through 2.9 range. If you pinned PyTorch 2.6 in early 2025 because it was the secure default, you were exposed for four minor versions.

Keras has the same shape and more iterations. Lambda layers carry marshalled Python and execute it on load (CVE-2024-3660). Keras made safe_mode=True the default from 2.13, which refuses to deserialize them.

Then, with CVE-2025-9905, loading a legacy .h5 file ignores safe_mode. No warning, no error. An attacker only has to author the checkpoint in an older format, and the current library will load it and run the code anyway.

Finally, CVE-2025-9906, a crafted .keras archive whose config.json calls keras.config.enable_unsafe_deserialization(), and then drops a Lambda layer. The file disables the check that’s inspecting it.

In that same survey of 705,991 Hugging Face models, researchers found 91 malicious ones, and 15 of them used Keras Lambda layers.

Strategy two: Scan the file before you load it, miss malicious files anyway

Check the artifact at rest and reject it if it looks malicious. This is what Hugging Face runs on upload, and what most continuous integration (CI) gates use.

Sonatype disclosed four picklescan vulnerabilities in 2025, and three of them describe the same failure with different mechanics:

CVE-2025-1889: Standard detections keyed on file extension rather than content. If attackers renamed the file, it was never scanned.

CVE-2025-1944: A deliberately malformed ZIP makes picklescan crash with BadZipFile. PyTorch's more forgiving ZIP reader loads the same file without complaint.

CVE-2025-1945: If an attacker modified ZIP flag bits, picklescan fails to detect and PyTorch still loads.

Then there is nullifAI, found by ReversingLabs on Hugging Face in February 2025. The models were compressed with 7z instead of PyTorch's default ZIP. Picklescan didn’t parse them.

One bug, six times

Vulnerability

The gap

Keras CVE-2025-9905

nullifAI

In every case, the thing doing the checking and the thing doing the loading disagreed about what the file was. The attacker did not defeat the check, but found a reading of the file on which the check did not apply.

This is structural, not simply a run of bad luck. A checker has to anticipate how every loader, at every version and down every legacy code path, will interpret a stream of bytes. The loader only has to interpret it one way, and that’s what leads to missed malicious files.

A pickle doesn’t need to be valid to work

The nullifAI models were broken on purpose.

Recall from the first section that the pickle VM executes opcodes as it encounters them. There is no validation pass. The payload was placed at the head of the stream, so by the time deserialization reached the corruption and threw an error, os.system had already been called. As ReversingLabs described it, opcodes execute "until all opcodes are executed or a broken instruction is encountered."

A scanner that parses the whole file and reports a parse error has reported nothing useful. The victim is already compromised. Data is parsed and then used, so a corrupted file yields nothing. A program runs until it faults, and everything before the fault has already happened. Treating a model file as data isn’t just a stylistic error.

Look back at the table in the “Which models are actually vulnerable” section. The formats in the bottom rows are not safe because they are well patched, but because there is nothing in a safetensors file that can express a call — no opcode, callable, or reconstruction procedure. The security property is a consequence of what the format cannot say, which is why it does not need a version number to be trusted.

That is the whole argument for conversion. But conversion is not always available, and plenty of production systems load pickles today. So the next question is what you can see when one of them runs.

Detection

There are two places to catch a malicious model: before it loads, and while it runs. They fail in different directions, and the difference matters.

Scanning at rest

Scanning is the primary control. It is cheap, it runs in CI, it blocks the artifact before anything executes, and against a textbook payload it works. A __reduce__ gadget calling os.system is exactly what modelscan and picklescan are built to find.

The CVEs listed in the third section are the reason that is not reassuring. Every bypass in that list defeated a scanner that was working correctly on the file it believed it was reading. This includes extension checks, ZIP parsing, flag bits, 7z, and a deliberately corrupted stream. None of them broke the detection logic, but they did change what the file was on the way in.

A scanner that catches the obvious case has only told you the obvious case is caught. It cannot tell you the file is safe, because "safe" would require it to have anticipated how every loader, at every version, down every legacy path, will read those bytes: a huge amount of combinations to reason through and one that make scanning alone unfeasible. That is the asymmetry.

So the honest question is not whether to scan, but what’s left standing when the scan is bypassed.

Watching it run

Runtime detection is the layer that gets proposed as the logical answer, so let’s measure it.

We built five hostile gadget families, each one a pickle whose __reduce__ performs a different post-exploitation action, and ran them against two engines: open source Falco 0.44.1 on its default ruleset and Sysdig Secure.

Both runs fired a positive control first. All five outcomes were predicted in writing before the run.

Gadget family

All five gadget families triggered Sysdig Secure rules, all within two seconds. Four of five triggered OSS Falco defaults. Falco’s open source default ruleset contains 26 rules versus the commercial product’s 278. This includes the Falco rule Modify Python Startup Hook File, which was created after this test.

Three findings in that table matter more than the raw score, however.

First, the spawn axis is irrelevant. We expected the gadget that forks a shell to look different from the one that never leaves the Python process, but the detections don’t differ. The shell-spawned gadget was caught in 1.6 seconds, the direct one in 1.9 seconds, and the entirely in-process one in 1.5 seconds The same rule caught all three. Whether a gadget forks is a fact about its syscall surface, not about whether it’s visible.

Second, runtime itself doesn’t solve the checker vs. loader problem, but it doesn’t need to. A runtime sensor never observes the deserialization at all, but the consequences. Nothing in that table detected a pickle being loaded. What fired was a file read, or an outbound connection, that happened to originate downstream of one.

That sounds like a technicality until you read the rules that look like they should have caught this. Shell Spawned with Inline Python Command keys on proc.pcmdline containing -c together with the literal source text; import os and os.system. Base64-encoded Python Script Execution does the same thing one encoding layer down. Both assume malicious Python is visible on the command line.

And third, a pickle load is python3 load_pickle.py model.pkl. The gadget is in the file. None of that text is ever on the command line, at any encoding layer, ever.

Best practices if you must deploy a susceptible model

As we’ve established, no single layer is foolproof on its own. But that’s not an argument for doing nothing. It’s a case for ordering the layers by how they fail.

The stack below is ordered by strength, each a part of a stronger approach to defense:

1. Convert the format, and stop having the problem.

Most models don’t need to serialize anything but named arrays of numbers. If that is true of yours, store it in a container that cannot express a call: safetensors for weights, GGUF for quantized inference, and ONNX where you need a compute graph.

The difference between those three matters more than it may seem. Safetensors is structurally safe , as it consists of tensors and a JSON header, with nothing in the format capable of expressing a callable. GGUF and ONNX have no known path, which is more of a claim about the current state of research than about the format's expressive limits. ONNX in particular carries a full operator graph and a history of parser CVEs. When deploying a new model, opt for the format that is safe because of what it can’t say.

Caveat: "No known path" isn’t "proven safe," as conversion isn’t always available. A model distributed only as a pickle has to be loaded once to be converted. Do that in the sandbox from step 5 below, not on a build host.

2. Pin your loaders past the bypasses, and verify the version actually running.

For PyTorch, the most secure approach means version 2.10.0 or later. The weights_only=True default arrived in 2.6 and was widely reported as the fix, but CVE-2026-24747 defeats the restricted unpickler itself and affects every version before 2.10.0. A team that pinned 2.6 in early 2025 on security advice stayed exposed for four further minor versions.

For Keras, run current and refuse legacy .h5 inputs rather than trusting safe_mode on that path. CVE-2025-9905 is the case where it is ignored with no warning. For NumPy, keep allow_pickle=False and treat any code that flips it as a finding.

Caveat: This layer has arguably the worst track record of anything on this list. Every entry above is a fix that was itself later bypassed. Pin it, but do not spend the trust it appears to buy.

3. Scan at rest, in CI, as a gate.

Run modelscan or picklescan on ingest and fail the build rather than the deployment. It’s cheap and it catches the commodity case, which is most of what you will actually encounter.

Caveat: Scanners are blocklist-based, and every CVE evaluated beat a scanner that was working correctly. A clean scan is the only absence of evidence. Never let it be the signal that promotes an artifact to production.

4. Establish provenance.

Track which model came from where. Sign what you build, verify what you consume, and give preference to publishers who do the same.

Caveat: A signature proves origin, not intent. The malicious models found on Hugging Face were authentically uploaded by the accounts that uploaded them. Provenance narrows who you have to trust, but it doesn’t tell you whether that trust is deserved.

5. Load inside a sandbox with an egress boundary.

This is the least glamorous control on this list, but the most reliably effective. Load models in a process with no credentials worth stealing, no write access to anything that persists, and an explicit egress allowlist.

This is the only control here that doesn’t depend on recognizing the attack; it doesn’t have to. It isn’t deciding whether the connection is malicious, only whether it’s permitted.

Caveat: A sandbox bounds the blast radius, but doesn’t prevent execution. The code still runs. You are choosing what it can reach.

6. Always assume breach, and use runtime detection as the backstop.

Everything above is a prediction about a file. Runtime is the only layer that observes what actually happened. Use runtime observability to verify what your code is actually doing and catch malicious activity.

Caveat: In this case, it’s silent on behavior that looks innocuous, and it never sees the load itself, only consequences.

Why that order matters

Read through the first four controls again, and there’s one distinct pattern: Each works by predicting how a file will be interpreted. The converter predicts the format. The pinned loader predicts which code path will run. The scanner predicts what the loader will do with those bytes. The signature predicts that a known publisher produced what they meant to produce.

Every bypass is an attacker finding an interpreter that disagreed with one of those predictions. And there is no reason to expect it to stop, because the asymmetry producing it never closes. A checker has to anticipate every loader. A loader only has to interpret the file one way, and it is the one that actually runs.

The sandbox and the runtime sensor are the two controls on this list that don’t predict. The sandbox doesn’t care what the file is. It constrains what the code can reach once it’s already running. The sensor doesn’t care either. It reports what the process did.

But that doesn’t make them sufficient alone. Runtime never observes the deserialization, the rules that look like they should catch malicious Python assume the malice is visible on the command line, and the correlation layer that ought to be the sophisticated tier never fired once.

Ultimately, the most comprehensive approach is a “both and” strategy. A scanner and a loader that disagree produce a bypass. A scanner and a sensor that disagree produce an alert.

A model file is a program. It shouldn’t move through a pipeline built for data, and you must assume that whatever you use to check the model file has a reading of those bytes that the thing loading them doesn’t share.

Title: CVE-2026-111497: Critical out-of-bounds write in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Context: Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497...
Full Text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2.

An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder.

On October 27, 2026, CVE-2026-111497 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. Given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory.

The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below.

Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun, Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET, Envoy and Istio, brotli4j, and operating-system packages. Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles:

Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later.

Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later.

Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later.

The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release.

[R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Arnie Cabral Mon, 10/26/2026 - 11:07

Tenable Network Monitor leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, expat, libxml2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 updates OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, curl to version 8.21.0, expat to version 2.9.0 and libxml2 to version 2.15.4 to address the identified vulnerabilities.

Title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.
