Title: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Leaked Ahead of Scheduled Security Patches
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Two vulnerabilities that could affect the servers underlying many websites have been disclosed ahead of the planned security patches, leading major cybersecurity authorities to urge users to prepare for remediation.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ were scheduled to be disclosed on October 21 at 2pm GMT.

However, a user named ‘petecooper’ published a post on the Hacker News forum on October 20 revealing the vulnerabilities’ CVE identifiers, which were supposed to be kept secret until the patches are available.

The post, now deleted, claimed that two maximum-severity (CVSS rating of 10.0) PHP remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22.

It also said that both vulnerabilities affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5 and that exploiting them could allow remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data.

These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

Following the petecooper post, WatchTowr confirmed that CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were scheduled to be disclosed later.

The disclosure was also scheduled to happen alongside the PHP security team releasing patches for both vulnerabilities.

Leaking information on critical vulnerabilities and some of their characteristics, such as the range of affected versions, ahead of an available patch can lead malicious actors to exploit them, for instance using reverse engineering techniques.

CERT-EU Urges PHP Users to Prepare for Patching

In a security bulletin, published on October 21, the PHP security team confirmed it was working on patches, which were scheduled to be released at 2pm GMT on October 21 – not on October 22 as claimed by the Hacker News forum user.

“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” they added.

In addition, the PHP team allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.2 rather than the maximum-severity score suggested by the individual sharing the leak.

Several cybersecurity authorities, including the Computer Emergency Response Team of the EU (CERT-EU) and th UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also released emergency advisories, warning of upcoming patches for the two vulnerabilities.

These authorities advised organizations to prepare for immediate patching of affected assets.

“Where immediate patching is not feasible, organizations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available,” CERT-EU added.

Inferring from PHP’s pre-release builds, Kevin Beaumont, an independent security researcher, said on Mastodon that fixed versions will likely be the following:

8.5.12

8.4.27

8.3.36

8.2.35

Update 4pm BST: The PHP security team has now published a security advisory for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 which can be found here.

Title: php2shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities
Context: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.
Full Text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.

Change log

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Click here to review the change log history

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Update October 26: CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its KEV catalog. Added details on a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 and on PHP's October 23 session upload progress advisory. Added a note on restarting PHP services after updating. Added Adel Karimi's report of successful exploitation against honeypot servers and Trail of Bits' report of working exploits against pre-patch PHP releases. Linked our Brotli2Shell FAQ for a separate fix in PHP's Windows builds.

Update October 23: Updated the Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security patch to SC-202610.2 and added a Tenable knowledge base article.

Update October 23: Added guidance on authenticated scanning and a dedicated view in Tenable Cloud Security. Reorganized the Tenable product coverage section.

Update October 23: Updated the example Tenable Hexa AI prompt.

Update October 22: Added security patch SC-202610.1 for Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security, plus a CyberAgents Exchange skill for reporting php2shell exposure. Added the status of these vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog along with CISA's October 21 alert.

Update October 21: Added Amazon Threat Intelligence's report of exploitation attempts beginning October 17, before public disclosure. Added Tenable Nessus plugins, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions, along with guidance on using Tenable Hexa AI to find vulnerable PHP installations and create remediation tickets.

Update October 21: PHP released patches and published its advisories. This post now includes vulnerability details, fixed versions, source backports for end-of-life branches, interim mitigation guidance, updated exploitation details and Tenable product coverage and Vulnerability Watch classification.

October 21: Original publication based on limited public information ahead of PHP's official advisory.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The PHP security team rates both CVSSv4.0 9.2 and says they can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Amazon Threat Intelligence observed an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." On October 26, CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. End-of-life branches will not receive official releases, but the PHP security team published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that were announced on October 20, 2026.

FAQ

When were these PHP vulnerabilities first disclosed?

On October 20, 2026, the CVE identifiers circulated on Hacker News and social media. Later that day, the PHP security team published an advance notice of a security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM ET) to address two critical vulnerabilities. The notice said the team could release earlier if details became public or if exploitation appeared in the wild. CERT-EU also published an advisory (2026-018) naming both CVEs. According to the PHP Foundation, the release was originally scheduled for October 22 and was moved up by a day after the CVE identifiers leaked. On October 21, the PHP security team published its security advisory and released patches.

A video shared by researcher Kirill Firsov demonstrates the exploit chain, dubbed php2shell. Firsov credited the video and exploit to researcher LCFR of Calif.io, which has since published a technical writeup. The PHP Foundation credited Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, among others, for their research and responsible disclosure. Calif and Wiz have both said they used AI models in their research.

The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2.PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence.

— The PHP Foundation (@ThePHPF) October 20, 2026

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-109618

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (OOM Corruption)

9.2

CVE-2026-109619

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (Stale Global State)

9.2

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 stems from how PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) errors. If memory runs out while PHP's internal request data is only partially initialized, the cleanup that follows can treat that data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw. Leftover state from one request points to freed memory, and a later request handled by the same worker can then use it. According to PHP, both can be exploited by an unauthenticated remote attacker. PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 also lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact.

PHP says every installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit can be triggered by an unauthenticated request before any application code runs.

CVSS scores differ across sources. The PHP security team rates both vulnerabilities as CVSSv4.0 9.2. According to the PHP Foundation, the CVE identifiers that circulated before the release came with an incorrect CVSS score of 10.0.

Which PHP versions are affected?

According to Calif's technical writeup, the earliest affected code path it found dates to PHP 5.4.0. The PHP security team released the following fixed versions:

Affected Versions

Fixed Version

8.2.35

PHP 7.4.x through 8.1.x

No official release; minimal source backports from the PHP security team

PHP 5.4.x through 7.3.x

End-of-life, no fix from the PHP project

According to PHP, Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance. If you use distribution packages, check your vendor's advisories.

On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds, 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, that fix a separate vulnerability in their bundled Brotli library, CVE-2026-111497. The PHP source and runtime versions are unchanged. For details, see our Brotli2Shell FAQ.

How widespread is PHP, and how many hosts are potentially affected?

According to W3Techs, PHP is used by 69.3% of websites whose server-side language is known. Platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Laravel and Magento all run on PHP. Calif says it confirmed pre-authentication remote code execution against specific versions of popular PHP applications, including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento. Security researcher Silas Cutler's rough estimate is that over 1.3 million internet-exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable. A Shodan search by Henk Poley counts over 1.9 million internet-exposed hosts running PHP.

Has exploitation been observed in the wild?

On October 21, Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said the company is "seeing early attacks emerging" and is updating its mitigations as new attack vectors appear. watchTowr says it has reproduced both vulnerabilities and is observing exploitation attempts against both.

Amazon Threat Intelligence said it observed a php2shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It said it is unclear how the attacker obtained exploit information. More attempts followed on October 21, with payloads and infrastructure that Amazon says suggest multiple actors. Amazon says it is unclear whether any of the October 21 attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems. It also says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." It recommends starting investigations from at least October 17, not from the disclosure date.

On October 24, security researcher Adel Karimi reported successful exploitation against three honeypot servers running PHP 8.4.26. The exploit requests started shells that ran attacker commands. The report says the activity is consistent with CVE-2026-109618, and that it does not show use of CVE-2026-109619. It also says the traffic closely matches a family of publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. The honeypots used a single-worker Apache mod_php setup that was intentionally favorable to the exploit, and the report says the results are not a measure of how reliably the exploit works on other setups.

On October 26, Dream Research reported finding artifacts of a campaign that chained a custom php2shell exploit with CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Fragnesia that we covered in a separate FAQ. According to Dream, the attacker gained root access on 24 internet-facing firewalls from an unnamed vendor, then used the same chain on an internal firewall management server reached through one of them. Some of these systems "appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment." Dream said the php2shell exploit was not a public one and needed precise memory offsets for each version of the firewall software. Dream has not named the vendor or the affected versions, and Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity.

PHP sites behind Cloudflare already have an initial set of WAF rules deployed for the known exploit vectors in these vulnerabilities. The rules are available to all customers, including free.We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up.This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as @ThePHPF releases the update at 14:00 UTC today.

— Dane Knecht 🦭 (@dok2001) October 21, 2026

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Code claiming to exploit these vulnerabilities is circulating publicly, but we have not verified that any of it works against CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. Unverified exploit code is sometimes laced with malware, so treat it with caution. The PHP Foundation said the PHP security team inspected PoCs that appeared after the leak but "did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure."

Since then, on October 26, Trail of Bits said it confirmed that php2shell exploits work against pre-patch releases of PHP 8.2 through 8.5, and its demo showed a shell on MediaWiki, Symfony, Laravel and phpBB.

Are patches or mitigations available?

Yes. The PHP security team released fixed versions on October 21 (see the table above). For end-of-life branches, it published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1, for those who build from source. If you run another end-of-life version, upgrade to a supported release or ask your distribution or LTS vendor.

The PHP security team says updating is the only complete fix. For organizations that cannot update immediately, PHP's advisory lists configuration changes that reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe. For CVE-2026-109618, PHP lists setting memory_limit=-1 in a way applications cannot override. For CVE-2026-109619, it lists setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. PHP says to restart every PHP worker after these changes. PHP also suggests a container or cgroup memory limit as an availability boundary, though it says this is not a complete mitigation either.

Installing updated PHP packages does not patch PHP processes that are already running. Google Cloud's guidance, which includes input from Mandiant, notes that PHP-FPM, Apache and other services that run PHP keep the vulnerable code in memory until they are restarted. The same guidance says to capture worker memory from servers that show signs of probing before restarting them, because a restart erases that evidence.

CERT-EU also recommends that organizations that cannot update right away consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is applied and verified.

Cloudflare has deployed WAF rules for the known exploit vectors, available to all customers including the free tier. Cloudflare describes this as a stopgap only. The rules only cover traffic routed through Cloudflare.

Are there known issues with the new PHP releases?

PHP developers confirmed a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 that can crash PHP processes in some applications that use the SimpleXML extension. It is tracked as php-src issue #24488. PHP developers traced it to a separate garbage collector fix included in those releases, not to the patches for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. A fix has been merged into the PHP source but, as of October 26, has not shipped in a release.

On October 23, PHP published an informational advisory about what it calls an unlikely remote code execution vector in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. PHP says it only occurs under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. Until its next regular bugfix release, PHP suggests setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0, the same setting its CVE-2026-109619 advisory listed as a mitigation.

Have PHP vulnerabilities been exploited before?

Yes. Before php2shell, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog included three vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Two of them are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns:

Have these vulnerabilities been added to the CISA KEV catalog?

Yes. On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to the KEV catalog, with a remediation due date of October 29 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified these vulnerabilities as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been classified as “Vulnerability of Concern” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is Tenable affected by these vulnerabilities?

Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security include PHP. Out of caution, Tenable released stand-alone security patch SC-202610.2 for both products on October 23. It updates PHP to 8.2.35. Details are available in TNS-2026-30 for Tenable Security Center and TNS-2026-31 for Tenable Enclave Security. Tenable customers can find patch release notes in this knowledge base article. Advisories for Tenable products are published at tenable.com/security.

Has Tenable released any product coverage for these vulnerabilities?

Yes. The following Tenable Nessus plugin is available for these vulnerabilities:

Title: Rapid Response: php2shell, Leaked Critical PHP Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619)
Context: Sigma / YARA Rules We'll publish detection rules to huntresslabs/threat-intel once technical details are available
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch and Ben Nahorney for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update 10/21/26 @ 4:40pm ET

Since PHP released its security advisory this morning to address the two critical vulnerabilities, several researchers have come forward to release the technical details of the vulnerabilities:

Calif's write-up provides a detailed history of PHP memory-limit vulnerabilities, and then explains how Calif revisited those earlier findings through OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, uncovering multiple interruption point and reliable RCE paths.

Wiz has demonstrated how the unauthenticated RCE works against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla, and showed that a separate memory disclosure path could expose passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates.

As of October 21 at 4:30pm ET, Huntress has not observed in-the-wild exploitation on partner systems. We are continuing to monitor relevant developments linked to these vulnerabilities.

Update: 10/21/26 @ 10am ET

On October 21 around 9:30 am ET, the PHP team released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to address the two vulnerabilities.

According to PHP, all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk (including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed). An exploit exists for mod_php where an unauthenticated request can trigger an attack before any application code runs.

What to do:

Source downloads are on PHP's downloads site; organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 as soon as possible. For organizations that can't update immediately, PHP has also outlined measures to reduce exposure to specific attack paths in its advisory.

Other update guidance from PHP:

Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of publication. Check with your vendor for updated PHP packages.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are no longer supported by the PHP project and won't receive official updates. Some distributions and LTS vendors might backport fixes for these releases, so be sure to contact your vendor for further information or upgrade to a supported version.

Organizations using the volunteer-maintained rpms.remirepo.net repository should move to distribution-provided packages or build PHP from source to apply updates promptly. Updated packages from that repository won't be available today.

The PHP security team has also provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1. These branches are intended for organizations that build PHP from source or don't have access to an LTS vendor.

For those running the older, outdated versions of PHP (prior to the 8.2.x version numbers), it's likely there will be no official patch to resolve the vulnerabilities. For environments running the deprecated, end-of-life versions of PHP, admins should immediately add the line session.upload_progress.enabled = Off to the php.ini configuration on your server. This may require you to restart your web services and/or the server itself in order to take effect, but will mitigate the known abuse cases.

While the software itself in these deprecated versions will receive no official patch from the PHP maintainers, security researchers have produced their own patches that will permit admins to rebuild the PHP modules from source code. Huntress cannot evaluate whether these patches are effective, and recommend that, wherever possible (and with adequate testing to ensure the upgrade doesn't break website functionality), admins should upgrade their version of PHP on the servers they maintain to the most current 8.5.x release.

The vulnerabilities:

PHP released further information about the two vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-109618 is a remote code execution flaw in PHP's out-of-memory error handling. If PHP runs out of memory while setting up request data, it is interrupted and that data is only partially initialized. During request cleanup that partly initialized data is treated as valid, creating a path to code execution.

The impact here is unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) as the web worker account: according to PHP, complete RCE was validated over HTTP against mod_php with default PHP input and memory limits, and normal prefork configurations with multiple workers.

CVE-2026-109619 is a remote code execution flaw caused by PHP retaining request-specific state after its backing memory has been freed. If the same worker processes a later request, PHP may access that stale state before the normal initialization resets it. This vulnerability can lead to unauthenticated heap use-after-free, memory disclosure, and remote code execution with the web worker's privileges.

Huntress has not yet seen in-the-wild exploitation of these vulnerabilities across our partner base as of October 21 at 10am ET; however, others are reporting that they are seeing attacks emerging. As such, updating promptly to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 and following the guidance above is critical.

Huntress is continuing to track developments related to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. We will update this blog accordingly as new information emerges.

Background

On the morning of October 20, a post on Hacker News claimed that two critical PHP vulnerabilities were headed for public disclosure. The post was taken down, but not before screenshots made their way around social media. Within a few hours, our good friends over at watchTowr confirmed the leak, writing that the vulnerabilities were real and that "we were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET."

Shortly thereafter, the PHP security team posted an advance notice of an upcoming security release addressing two critical vulnerabilities, both with a CVSS v4.0 rating of 9.2. The team scheduled that release for Wednesday, October 21 at 14:00 UTC, a day earlier than the original embargo, and noted it reserves the right to release even sooner "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild."

PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood. When a critical bug lands in PHP itself, rather than in one app built on top of it, the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast.

Huntress is monitoring developments related to these vulnerabilities and will update this blog as new information becomes available.

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

The flaws exist in PHP, the popular programming language running behind a huge number of websites. PHP is designed primarily for web development and is widely supported by hosting providers.

Here's what we know about the PHP vulnerabilities so far (and what we don't):

What we know: Both vulnerabilities are rated critical by the PHP security team. Public reporting describes them as remote code execution in PHP's core, which would mean an attacker could get the server to run commands of their choosing.

What it affects: PHP has not published affected versions yet. Reports have pointed to versions 5, 6, 7, and 8 being impacted, and some researchers have said they expect fixes only for currently supported PHP 8 branches. In its official release, however, PHP said that impacted and fixed versions (along with full details of the flaws) will be published with the October 21 security release.

How it works: No technical root cause has been published. We currently don't yet know which part of PHP is involved, whether it's reachable over a plain web request, or whether it depends on a particular configuration. We'll update this post when the advisory and researcher writeups are public.

Why "php2shell"? That's the name circulating among researchers. If you've followed this space for any amount of time, you know a name like that usually means one thing: someone sends a request to your website, and gets a shell on your vulnerable server.

Technical Details

With no public technical details yet, we can't show you the exploit. What we can do is tell you what we're looking for and what our own telemetry says about where the risk lives.

What exploitation will probably look like

Florian Roth, who released a free tool called process-watcher (a Linux-based process monitoring tool aimed at detecting exploitation) put it well: exploitation of these bugs will most likely show up as suspicious child processes spawned by PHP. At Huntress, that lines up with what we see in nearly every PHP intrusion we work.

In practice, that means a PHP worker process like php-fpm, php-cgi, php-cgi.exe, httpd, or apache2 would launch something abnormal:

Shells like sh, bash, cmd.exe, or powershell.exe

Interpreters like python or perl

Download or networking tools like curl, wget, nc, or certutil.exe

It's worth taking a closer look at command lines that include reverse shell patterns:

/dev/tcp/

fsockopen

mkfifo

It's also worth looking at quick reconnaissance commands like whoami, id, uname -a, or ipconfig run straight from the web server.

Attacker PHP abuse: what we've seen recently

Even before this leak, Huntress regularly catches attackers abusing PHP applications.

One pattern from a recent Huntress incident that occurred last week is a good preview of what php2shell exploitation could look like. In this incident, a PHP FastCGI process repeatedly ran a one-liner that wrote a small PHP file with random marker strings into the first writable temp directory it could find, before executing and then deleting it. If none of the directories were writable, it would print !notwrtbl! to flag that.

While this pattern isn't related to php2shell, it's a good example of PHP spawning things it shouldn't.

On the Linux side, most internet-facing PHP lives on web servers and shared hosting, which are not closely monitored. An exposed Linux web server without endpoint detection is the type of system where PHP flaws can be exploited quietly and remain unnoticed.

Proof of Concept

We have not built or reproduced a proof of concept for these vulnerabilities, and we're not aware of public exploit code as of this writing. A short exploitation video was briefly posted online and then removed. Once fixes are shipped, we expect technical details and proof-of-concept code to follow quickly, and we'll update this post.

What should impacted organizations do?

The fixes aren't out yet, so the goal right now is to be ready to patch the minute they land. In the meantime, there are several things you can do to shrink your exposure.

Inventory every PHP install. Start with your web servers, and then go hunting for the less obvious locations: vendor appliances and Windows software that bundle php.exe or php-cgi.exe, control panels like cPanel and Plesk, and anything running WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento.

Plan your patch window for Wednesday, October 21 at 10am ET. Patch internet-facing systems first. Watch the official PHP announcement for the fixed version numbers, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages.

Identify any end-of-life PHP environments. If you're running PHP 5, 7, or 8.0/8.1, you may not get a fix at all. Upgrade, take it off the internet, or put it behind a VPN or web application firewall (WAF) until you can.

Keep an eye on what PHP spawns. Alert on PHP worker processes launching shells, interpreters, or download tools. On Linux servers without endpoint detection, Florian Roth's process-watcher is a free, quick way to get this visibility today. Start it in observe mode.

If you find something, isolate the server, and preserve web server and PHP logs. Look for webshells and new files in your web root, along with new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts.

What is Huntress doing?

Hunting across our fleet. We captured a baseline of normal PHP behavior across our partner endpoints before the release. Once fixes and technical details drop, we'll compare against it to spot new activity quickly.

We already monitor for malicious activity on servers. Huntress already detects web server processes spawning shells and common webshell activity on Windows and Linux. Our SOC is on alert for PHP-related activity.

Watching the patch drop. Our Adversary Tactics team is tracking the release and researcher analysis in real time, and we'll update this post with indicators and detection guidance as they become available.

Auditing our internal PHP use. Huntress has reviewed relevant internal systems and taken appropriate steps to mitigate potential exposure to these vulnerabilities.

Sigma / YARA Rules

We'll publish detection rules to huntresslabs/threat-intel once technical details are available.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

No indicators of compromise have been confirmed yet. This section will be updated as the situation develops.

This alert is intended for technical teams responsible for network security, asset management, and system administration across all sectors.

It is also intended to inform individuals operating PHP workloads, websites and applications.

Background

PHP Foundation have published advanced notice of critical vulnerabilities; organisations are recommended to monitor for the release of relevant patches to address these vulnerabilities.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) is aware of related media reporting which identifies these vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, though no official technical details have been publicly released at this time.

ASD’s ACSC understands that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards may be affected.

ASD’s ACSC is not aware of successful active exploitation within Australia, related to these vulnerabilities.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises individuals and organisations to:

Identify PHP within their environments.

Monitor and review PHP official guidance at PHP Security Release

Prepare to update and apply security patches as they become available.

Monitor PHP applications and associated environments for potentially malicious activity.

Where to get help

Organisations that have been impacted, suspect impact or require advice and assistance can contact us via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371).

Title: PHP2Shell - Critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): detection, analysis, and remediation
Context: What happened On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
Full Text:
Key points and observations

PHP disclosed two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. We independently reproduced them and confirmed that application-level authentication can't block an attack: PHP processes the malicious request before any application code runs.

AWS reported PHP2Shell exploitation attempts in the wild as early as October 17, 2026, four days before public disclosure and the release of patches.

Only patching fixes these vulnerabilities. Mitigations circulating in the community, such as setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in the PHP configuration file, don't fully protect you.

Successful command execution doesn’t necessarily crash the worker. Memory disclosure, including the PHPSESSID technique, can provide addresses needed for exploitation.

To investigate, look for large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors during request initialization, and unexpected shell processes.

Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both have a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2. PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 contain the fixes. Older PHP branches are also affected. Although PHP 8.1 and earlier are outside normal upstream support, the PHP security team provided source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Users of older branches should check their vendor’s security advisory for patched packages or upgrade to a supported version.

Before the public disclosure, our team built exploits for the vulnerabilities so we could analyze them and develop detections. Our reproduction triggers the out-of-memory corruption described in CVE-2026-109618 on PHP 8.5.11 with an unauthenticated HTTP POST request. The request never reaches the target application's code. Instead, PHP runs the attacker's command while it cleans up the failed request. Any PHP script exposes the vulnerable path, even one that only prints a response.

The two flaws affect different stages of the request life cycle:

CVE-2026-109618: After a memory allocation fails, PHP leaves invalid data behind for its cleanup routine to process.

CVE-2026-109619: A PHP worker can reuse stale state from a previous request.

Our detailed walkthrough primarily covers CVE-2026-109618, although we will discuss CVE-2026-109619 as well.

How to know if you're affected

Any PHP runtime that serves HTTP requests is in scope. PHP's release announcement warns that all web deployments are affected, including Apache modules, PHP FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

When you build your inventory, include containers and applications that bundle their own PHP interpreter. Don't rely solely on the command-line PHP installation: it can use a different version or configuration than the runtime that serves your web application.

Fixed versions

The advisories for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 list the same fixed versions for each supported branch:

Remediation steps

For each deployment:

Record the PHP version, the package or image source, the owner, and the update process.

Apply the upstream or distributor update. If you use a vendor package, check the vendor's advisory, because vendors sometimes backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

Rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Restart or replace every worker that still runs the old runtime.

PHP 8.1 and older

PHP 8.1 and older are outside the PHP project's normal support window. To address this vulnerability, PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, but expect slower fixes for these branches as vendors have more work to do in order to validate the fix. If you run those older branches, check whether your vendor covers it or move to a supported PHP branch.

If you can't patch immediately

Restrict public access to exposed applications. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, CERT-EU recommends isolating internet-facing applications. Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

PHP's temporary mitigation guidance also describes measures for each vulnerability:

CVE-2026-109618: Enforce memory_limit=-1 at the administrator level, and pair it with request limits at the frontend and memory limits on the container. Limit the size of decoded request bodies, including requests without a usable Content-Length header. Don't substitute process limits such as RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, because they can trigger the allocation failures this vulnerability depends on. Even with these measures, allocation failures can still happen, and an attacker who exhausts system memory can destabilize the host.

CVE-2026-109619: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply both settings in configuration that loads before PHP parses the request, then restart every worker. Remove any per-request settings that generate early diagnostics. Hiding the errors doesn't prevent access to stale state.

These measures reduce your exposure while you update, but none of them fully fixes the vulnerabilities. Patching is the only complete fix.

How the vulnerabilities work

Both vulnerabilities follow the same pattern: a fatal error interrupts PHP partway through an operation, and PHP later treats the incomplete state as valid.

CVE-2026-109618: Interrupted initialization after memory exhaustion

PHP converts form submissions into the $_POST array. Internally, PHP stores the array's keys and values in a hash table, in entries called buckets. Before application code reads a submitted field, PHP allocates memory for the field name, creates any nested arrays, and inserts the values into those hash tables.

The flaw appears when an insertion stops halfway through. In the version we tested, _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i() increments the hash table's entry counters before it allocates a copy of the new key. Here is the relevant sequence in PHP's source:

idx = ht->nNumUsed++; ht->nNumOfElements++; p = ht->arData + idx; p->key = key = zend_string_init(str, len, GC_FLAGS(ht) & IS_ARRAY_PERSISTENT);

If the key allocation exceeds memory_limit, PHP raises a fatal error and abandons the insertion. At that point, the counters already include the new bucket, but PHP never initialized the bucket's key or value.

PHP still cleans up the failed request. When it destroys the array, it visits every counted bucket and interprets its contents as PHP values. The unfinished bucket holds bytes left over from an earlier allocation. An attacker who controls those leftover bytes controls what the cleanup code does next, up to running a shell command.

This hash table bug is one instance of the broader flaw that PHP's CVE-2026-109618 advisory describes: a memory error abandons an operation while the internal state is incomplete, and cleanup then treats that state as valid. Multiple public PoCs have demonstrated other code paths with the same flaw, so don't build defenses around the specifics of the hash table exploit.

CVE-2026-109619: Stale state crosses request boundaries

A PHP worker handles many requests over its lifetime. Some worker-wide fields point to memory that belongs to a single request. If PHP frees that memory without clearing the fields, a later request can follow a stale pointer into freed memory. This class of bug is called a use-after-free.

According to the PHP advisory, stale state appears in two ways: a fatal error interrupts PHP while it resets state, or a late shutdown diagnostic recreates state after cleanup. The advisory confirms two exploitable cases:

Fatal-error backtraces (PHP 8.5 only): Fatal-error reporting keeps backtrace state after shutdown. A configuration diagnostic in a later request reads that state before PHP initializes it. PHP confirmed that this case leads to command execution on mod_php.

Upload processing: After a fatal error, upload processing can leave session or decoder state behind. A later upload reads that state before normal initialization. PHP confirmed command execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM. On PHP-FPM, the attack also needs the application to perform a suitable operation after startup succeeds.

The upload case matters because of session upload progress, which tracks uploads before the target script runs. PHP enables this feature by default, and it runs even if the application never calls session_start().

To exploit CVE-2026-109619, an attacker's requests must reach the same worker. A larger worker pool lowers the success rate of each attempt, but it doesn't remove the flaw.

Exploitation walkthrough for CVE-2026-109618

Our reproduction runs PHP 8.5.11, built from commit 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8, on Debian 12 (ARM64). It uses Apache's prefork worker model with mod_php, and sets memory_limit=16M, post_max_size=64M, and automatic POST parsing. To make allocations and failures easier to observe, our lab runs a single worker, disables OPcache, and shows errors in responses. The exploit ends by calling glibc's system().

The exploit works in three stages: reach the interrupted insertion, fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data, and turn request cleanup into a system() call.

Stage 1: Reach the interrupted insertion

The request carries three form fields:

=<binary value>&a=1&<very long field name>[x]=1

Each field plays a role:

The empty-name field prepares memory for reuse.

The a=1 field makes PHP allocate hash table storage.

The oversized name field triggers the incomplete insertion.

The array syntax tells PHP to create a nested array. In the version we tested, that path reaches a string-key insertion helper that allocates the key after it updates the hash table's counters. A plain field name takes a different path that uses an already-created key that is not vulnerable.

PHP's filter extension registers the submitted variable in an internal array and then in $_POST. We size the field name so that PHP's first key allocation succeeds and the second exceeds memory_limit. The failed insertion leaves an incomplete bucket in $_POST, which PHP destroys during request shutdown.

The failure happens during request initialization. Nothing in the target script can impact or defend against the exploit (authentication, filtering…).

Stage 2: Fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data

The attacker needs the unfinished bucket to hold useful bytes, not random leftovers. Our reproduction arranges those bytes through heap grooming: a sequence of allocations and frees that steers PHP into reusing a chosen block of memory.

In this build, a small hash table uses a 320-byte allocation. The binary value in the empty-name field is 276 bytes, and once PHP adds a string header and terminator, its allocation lands in the same 320-byte size class.

PHP copies that value while it processes the field, then frees the copies because the field name is empty. The a=1 field that follows makes the hash tables reuse the freed memory, so most of the binary content survives past the first valid bucket. When the oversized field triggers the fatal error, PHP has counted the second bucket but not initialized it, so PHP reads its contents from the stale bytes the attacker planted. The payload shapes those bytes to resemble a PHP value that points to a fake array.

Stage 3: Turn array cleanup into a function call

PHP arrays hold a destructor callback, the function PHP calls to clean up each element when it deletes the array. The attacker sets the expected location of this callback to the address of system() and points the array's element at a command string.

During shutdown, PHP follows the stale value into the fake array and calls the supplied callback with the supplied element. In our lab, the call becomes system(<command>). The attacker controls the callback address and its pointer argument, allowing the cleanup routine to call system() with a command string.

Here is the full sequence:

Request initialization fails → Request shutdown destroys $_POST → PHP interprets the unfinished bucket as an array → PHP destroys the fake array → The destructor callback invokes system(command)

Our system-call trace records a shell running the command, and the process tree shows its children under an Apache worker. The command runs with the worker's privileges, which are www-data in our lab.

Our refined exploit returns HTTP 200 with the memory-exhaustion error in the response body, and finishes in 3.10 seconds. Process snapshots show the same Apache worker still running during and after the command. A successful HTTP status doesn't mean a request was harmless, and the exploit doesn't need to crash a worker. The process trace is stronger evidence of execution than the response delay alone.

Exploit requirements and limitations

An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses. Neither constraint prevents exploitation, and reports of active attacks are already circulating.

Request and memory limits

The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit. When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table.

PHP's default memory limits are vulnerable. Setting memory_limit=-1 blocks the known exploitation path, but don't treat it as a long-term fix: if the underlying allocation still fails, an attacker may still reach remote code execution.

Address discovery is a separate requirement

To turn the cleanup bug into command execution, the attacker needs valid memory addresses for the fake data structures and for the function they want to call, such as system(). Address space layout randomization (ASLR) randomizes those addresses, so guessing them can take repeated requests and crash workers.

A memory leak removes much of that guesswork. Wiz describes using the PHPSESSID cookie to leak process memory back to the attacker. If the leaked bytes include pointers that stay valid in the target worker, the attacker can use them to make the exploit more reliable.

Public reports of exploitation

As of October 21, we have multiple reports of active exploitation in the wild. We’re also aware of broad untargeted scanning going on.

How the patch addresses both flaws

The PHP security patch changes how memory exhaustion interrupts execution. A soft limit now defers the error until PHP reaches a safe point, which lets an in-progress operation finish initializing its data. If memory use crosses a higher hard limit, PHP terminates the worker at once with _exit(137) instead of running normal cleanup over a potentially invalid state.

The patch also resets request-owned global state before anything can reuse it. During shutdown, PHP clears error and exception state, and it initializes serialization and session state before early request processing can reach it.

The hash-table insertion still updates its counters before it allocates the key, even in PHP 8.5.12. The fix changes the surrounding error handling instead, so an allocation failure no longer leaves the halfway-initialized entry for ordinary cleanup to process.

The fix looks complete for the known exploit, but we consider the underlying pattern risky. Updating metadata before allocating the memory it describes leaves the door open to similar bugs. If an attacker finds another way to interrupt initialization so that the surrounding metadata still counts unallocated memory as valid (for example, an array that records a size of 2 when an allocation failure leaves only one item), the same class of flaw can return.

The patch suggests the PHP team knows about the pattern but judged the refactor to remove it too large to finish before the fix shipped. We expect more of these bugs to surface as researchers find exploitable instances of the pattern, and backporting each one may not stay sustainable. It’s also likely that instances of this pattern unique to older versions of PHP will be found and left unpatched.

How to detect exploitation

Look for signals at three layers: the incoming HTTP request, the PHP error log, and the processes that web workers spawn. No single signal is conclusive on its own, so correlate them. A successful exploit doesn't necessarily crash the worker or return an error.

Suspicious form submissions

While there are a number of ways to trigger the vulnerability, each of them relies on delivering attacker-controlled data through PHP's request parser, which runs before the target script. For detection, look for unusual field names, encodings, and transport behavior alongside request size. Start from what your application's legitimate submissions contain and flag departures from that baseline.

Based on an analysis of multiple public PoCs, the majority begin with a similar multipart form upload. An abbreviated request looks like this:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----XYZ ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" aabb00cc ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" pwn ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="a.txt" Content-Type: application/octet-stream ------XYZ ...hundreds more parts, or one multi-megabyte fill field... ------XYZ--

These field names are useful indicators when an application doesn't normally use them. They can also appear in legitimate submissions: PHP documents the upload-progress field in browser forms, and its transparent session handling can add session identifiers to forms. Investigate unexpected use of these fields, especially alongside the structural anomalies below.

The requests create memory pressure in different ways. Some public tools append fill fields of 100 MB or more. Others use deeply nested, machine-generated names, such as files[R00001][a][a][a], repeated across hundreds of parts. Public examples fit roughly 900 parts into less than 1 MB. PHP's allocations while parsing these fields can greatly exceed the size of the body on the wire, so body size alone is a weak signal. Also monitor parts per request, brackets per field name, and nesting depth.

Inspect upload filenames for PHP tags or serialized-object fragments, such as <?php or |O:. These chains can stage payloads in filenames because PHP stores the filename in the session record.

Another path to the vulnerable function can be reached through large application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST requests whose body carries a single field name of many megabytes (3-60 MB, depending on the memory_limit of the target), along with a binary value containing raw null bytes and control characters.

Two other traffic patterns can support these chains. Uploads that declare a large Content-Length and then trickle or never finish can keep a session record alive for the exploit. On deployments with multiple workers, a burst of connections that become slow or silent while other requests proceed normally can indicate an attempt to occupy every worker but one. This helps an attacker send both requests in a state-reuse chain to the same process.

Also inspect response headers. A Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= header containing an unusually long, percent-encoded value or binary content outside the application's expected session-ID format can indicate the memory-disclosure stage returning heap contents. It can follow an otherwise unremarkable request. Compare the value against the application's normal format: valid PHP session IDs aren't limited to hexadecimal characters.

Configure your web application firewall (WAF) or reverse proxy around these behaviors, and verify what its inspection engine actually sees. A rule can't inspect bytes the engine truncates, fields its parser discards, parts it never enumerates, or bodies it handles differently because they arrived chunked.

Memory exhaustion errors

Our exploit attempt generated this fatal error in the PHP error log:

PHP Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 16777216 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 3500032 bytes) in Unknown on line 0

The Unknown on line 0 location means PHP failed during request initialization, before any script started running. Correlate these errors with oversized POST requests, upstream connection resets, and worker crashes. Memory exhaustion alone doesn't prove an attack, because legitimate workloads can also exhaust memory.

When the exploit guesses a memory address incorrectly, the Apache worker crashes with a segmentation fault. In our lab, the Apache error log recorded this message:

AH00052: child pid ... exit signal Segmentation fault (11)

Also treat a short burst of these errors as a possible setup event, prior to the actual exploit payload being sent. Because modern versions of these chains recover addresses without crashing workers and can leave a persistent include active after a single successful fire, a complete attack can produce as few as two to four memory exhaustion errors and then go quiet. A handful of these errors on one PHP worker in a short window (especially paired with any of the request indicators above) deserves investigation even if nothing crashes afterward.

Unexpected shell processes

A web worker that spawns a shell is the most direct evidence of successful exploitation. In our capture, an Apache worker spawned a shell, which then launched the attacker's commands:

apache2 (www-data) └── sh -c <reverse-shell command> └── bash [outbound connection to c2.example:443]

Investigate any shell that a web worker launches, especially when it coincides with the request or error log signals above. If your application runs external commands on purpose, build a baseline of expected activity so you can spot deviations.

Don't make your detection depend on our demonstration's command names, a specific HTTP status, or a worker crash. In our refined exploit, the request returns HTTP 200, and the same Apache worker keeps running after it executes the command.

Signals for CVE-2026-109619

For CVE-2026-109619, review early configuration warnings, shutdown diagnostics, fatal errors, and execution timeouts on routes that attackers can reach. These events can point to the state-retention paths that PHP's advisory describes.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Workload Protection has out-of-the-box coverage for PHP applications executing a shell. This detection will catch exploits of those vulnerabilities. You can check for suspicious activity using this query. Review uncommon or unusual command lines.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes detections that can help identify PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and associated command execution:

Shell spawned by web server or PHP process detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or PHP processes using process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

PHP2Shell session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or upstream crash on nginx uses nginx error logs to correlate PHP memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or upstream worker crashes on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell PHP-FPM session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or FPM worker segfault on the same host and service uses PHP error logs and PHP-FPM master logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or PHP-FPM worker segmentation faults on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell memory exhaustion with worker crash or session decode failure on an Apache host uses Apache and PHP error logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or worker crashes on the same host.

Datadog Cloud Vulnerability Management can help identify PHP vulnerability findings on supported hosts and container images. Its package scanning support covers official operating system packages; self-compiled runtimes such as our lab build need separate inventory checks. PHP application dependencies managed through Composer are also distinct from the interpreter itself.

Conclusion

Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. If you run PHP, update to a fixed release or your vendor’s patched package as soon as possible. Rebuild affected container images and restart or replace workers so they’re running the updated code. Configuration changes can block some attack paths, but patching is the only complete fix.
