Title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: The Trust Gap Attackers Operate Inside
Context: Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums
Full Text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece weighs the trust gap the technique exploits against what the data actually shows.

A long-revoked certificate still loads a driver into the Windows kernel today. Help Net Security traced a 2026 intrusion to a decade-old forensic driver whose signing certificate had expired and been revoked years earlier. The kernel loaded it anyway.

The reason is structural, and it explains why the defensive target most teams chase is the wrong one. Defenders track bad drivers. We pull the LOLDrivers catalog, sync the default driver blocklist, and watch the list grow. The list is not where attackers compete. They compete over signing trust. A signature is the scarce thing. A driver is just the disposable wrapper around it.

Trust Is the Scarce Resource and Drivers are Disposable

Think about a stolen credit card. The number keeps clearing for hours or days in the gap before merchant blocklists sync. The thief does not need a new card. They need the window where the old one still works. Card networks did not win by perfecting the blocklist. They won by scoring the transaction itself in real time, regardless of whether the number was flagged yet.

Signed drivers run on the same broken model. The blocklist is the merchant blocklist. The signature is the card. Attackers live in the propagation gap, and that gap is wide.

The defensive move that follows is to stop chasing the card numbers and instrument the transaction. This is the reframe no competitor owns. Defend the trust anchor, because the list will always trail it. The anchor is the signing trust itself: revocation, signature metadata, and the slow death of cross-signed-driver trust. A list of bad drivers grows forever. The set of trust mechanisms that let those drivers load is small and addressable.

The web learned this lesson the hard way already. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) soft-fail meant a browser that could not reach the revocation responder simply trusted the certificate anyway. The kernel driver model carries the same flaw in a harsher setting. There is no soft-fail to debate, because the kernel does not ask the question at all.

The Proof Is In the Certificates

The economics favor the attacker because trust concentrates. Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums. That one file forged signatures on thousands of malicious drivers.

A small set of compromised keys signs an unbounded supply of drivers. A few stolen keys against thousands of drivers means the list defenders maintain can never catch up. Block a driver and the cost is one recompile. Edit unauthenticated bytes, the file hash changes, and the same key signs a new artifact. The blocklist entry you just earned is already stale, because the signing key did not move and the key is the asset. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report documents loaders that reintroduce effectively the same payload under fresh hashes to outpace simple hash-based blocking.

The trust-pyramid framing from that research describes a real structure. At the base sit individual drivers, cheap and disposable. Above them sit the end-entity certificates that sign batches of drivers, and at the apex sit the cross-signed certificate authorities the kernel anchors to. An attacker who climbs one level multiplies their reach across everything below it, and defenders who fight at the base are fighting where the attacker has infinite supply.

The same research showed how attackers manufacture fresh trust on demand. Tools forge signature timestamps, exploiting the pre-July-29-2015 cross-signed certificate exception by backdating a signature so it appears to predate the cutoff. An expired or revoked certificate becomes a working signing key again. The forgery does not break the trust chain. It satisfies it.

The kernel makes this worse by refusing to check revocation. Windows loads drivers signed with revoked certificates even when a local revocation list is present, and the decade-old forensic driver case showed the same failure in 2026. The operating system's kernel-mode signing policy accepts end-entity certificates issued before July 29, 2015 if they chain to a cross-signed authority. The policy codifies the loophole rather than closing it.

The defensive consequence follows directly. Blocking expired and revoked certificate driver loads, paired with the blocklist, beats the blocklist alone. The blocklist enumerates known-bad files one at a time. Revocation enforcement attacks the reusable key behind all of them, scaling against the attacker instead of with them.

A certificate authority revokes a key when it learns the key is compromised, and in a working system every consumer checks the revocation list and refuses the key. A revoked certificate carries a clear instruction, do not trust anything this key signs, and the kernel loads the driver anyway. The attacker did not defeat the trust system. They used the part of it that was never enforced.

The Driver Persistence Half-Life

Now the data. Against the LOLDrivers catalog, roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable driver samples are not covered by the default blocklist. The June 19, 2026 pull puts it at 36 percent. That is 782 of 2,190 samples, absent from the default list. About 22 percent, 479 samples, load even with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) enabled.

Call this the Driver Persistence Half-Life, the signature data point of this argument.

Be honest about what that number is. The 36 and 22 percent figures are point estimates from a single computed pull against one blocklist version. The method is published and reproducible: parse the enforced HVCI SiPolicy and the official block rules against the LOLDrivers JSON, match by file hash, then by authenticode metadata, and pin both to a commit and a version.

The caveats matter. The denominator is the LOLDrivers catalog, not every driver that exists. "Not covered" means absent from the default block rules, not exploitable on a given host. Hash coverage is brittle, because an edit to unauthenticated bytes changes the hash without changing the abuse.

The corroboration is real, and it is fewer voices than it looks. The catalog's own coverage metrics report that many LOLDrivers entries sit off the default blocklist, and public threat research corroborates the cadence qualitatively, confirming that systems can be attacked with a driver not yet listed. Two open tools reproduce the check itself, Trail of Bits' HVCI-loldrivers-check and a community block-rules checker, but no genuinely independent second count of the exact figures exists yet.

The lag underneath the number is the real exposure. The default blocklist updates only periodically through Windows Update, roughly once or twice a year, and deliberately holds back some blocks to avoid breaking legitimate software. The minimum disclosure-to-block window is a calendar quarter, and the historical window has run to six months or more. Most of these vulnerable signed drivers are reachable without admin rights, so the exposure is wide and the door is low.

The on-device reality runs worse than the stated cadence. Public reporting documented a Windows 10 driver blocklist frozen at a December 2019 version until an October 2022 fix. That is a roughly three-year gap between the published cadence and what shipped on the machine. A defender reading the cadence would assume quarterly freshness. The endpoint disagreed for three years.

Per case, persistence runs to years. SentinelLABS disclosed Dell's dbutil_2_3.sys flaws in 2021, and the signed-but-vulnerable driver was still disabling security tooling in 2024. SentinelLABS noted that the driver's certificate had not been revoked, leaving it abusable long after disclosure.

The half-life metaphor is precise. The catalog grows faster than the blocklist can absorb it, so the gap widens rather than closes, a long, slow decay that the attacker schedules around.

The method is reproducible against your own fleet. Run the same hash and authenticode match against the drivers that actually load, and the result is a number that describes your real exposure, a measurement you can repeat each quarter. The durable claim stays the honest one: roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable drivers are not blocked by default. The precise 36 and 22 percent belong to one computed pull, a snapshot with a published method attached.

Blocking Everything Breaks the Business

The obvious fix is to block every old driver. That fix is impractical, and the platform's own documentation says so plainly: the blocklist "isn't guaranteed to block every driver," and blocks are held back precisely to avoid breaking functionality.

Vulnerable drivers are dual-use. Public threat research catalogued how most abused drivers ship as legitimate software components first. The same signed driver that disables an EDR this week was a working hardware utility last week. The blocklist maintainer weighs one confirmed abuse against tens of thousands of working installs. The hold-back is a rational choice under that math, and the exact gap the attacker schedules into.

The reboot gap makes the DIY approach worse. Independent analysis of the blocklist notes that a driver the policy would block keeps running until the next reboot, so an in-progress kill chain survives the moment you activate the policy. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule that blocks vulnerable signed drivers only stops a driver from being written to disk. It does not block one already present from loading. Defenders who think they have closed the gap have often only narrowed the entry path.

The platform is moving the trust anchor. A Windows security update in April 2026 removes default trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, directly targeting the loophole the timestamp-forgery and pre-2015 exceptions opened. This is the industry bending toward the right target, attacking the reusable signing key itself, which is the correct altitude.

It helps. It does not close the gap. The April change applies to default trust going forward, so the 36 percent that sit off the blocklist today are not retroactively addressed by changing tomorrow's trust rules. The half-life keeps running on the inventory that already exists.

A separate chokepoint also remains in play. Public threat research documented one EDR killer used by multiple ransomware gangs whose coordination point was a shared packer-as-a-service, with no shared driver tying them together. The packer became the chokepoint when the driver did not. That is the pattern to internalize. Each fix narrows one path and exposes the next. Tighten cross-signed trust and the attacker leans harder on forged timestamps. Close the timestamp loophole and they lean on the unsynced backlog. The trust model has many anchors, and the attacker only needs the cheapest one still standing.

This persistence is not an accident of the technique. It is the product of an industry on the other side. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach, with mature automation accelerating intrusions at scale. A trust gap that one researcher could exploit becomes one that a tooled-up criminal market exploits at volume, which is why the half-life persists across so many drivers at once.

This piece builds on prior work. Independent security research argued that admin-to-kernel is not a serviced security boundary and that blocklists are largely performative. That critique is correct and it stands. The contribution here is a measured persistence half-life, the certificate-concentration evidence behind it, and a trust-anchor reframe detection engineers can act on.

Stop Chasing the List. Instrument the Failure.

The card networks made the stolen number unprofitable by scoring the transaction. Defenders should do the same with signed drivers. Watch the trust event, because the catalog entry arrives too late to matter.

That means instrumenting the load itself. Sysmon Event ID 6 logs every driver load with its hash, signer, signature, and signature status, and any non-Valid status warrants investigation. This telemetry is low-volume and high-value, which makes it cheap to monitor and hard to flood. The Splunk detection content keys on exactly this event, with an explicit note that the alert needs triage rather than blind firing.

Signature-status detection and first-seen anomaly detection catch what blocklist matching misses. Alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, including untrusted root, explicit distrust, and bad or invalid signatures, and on any driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before. Both approaches key on the trust attribute, so the known-bad list never enters the decision and the alert fires whether or not anyone has catalogued the driver yet.

The CodeIntegrity Operational log confirms whether your blocklist policy actually applied. Event ID 3099 confirms the policy is loaded, a blocked load logs Event ID 3077, an audited load logs Event ID 3076, and Event ID 3089 carries the signature detail. Pairing the block events with the audit events proves which drivers the policy stopped, which turns coverage from an assumption into a measurement. Given the three-year staleness the frozen-blocklist case showed, that proof is not optional.

The behavioral chain is observable end to end. A service is created via sc.exe, logged as Sysmon Event ID 1, and a System Event 7045 fires for the service install. A driver loads under Event ID 6, then a device control call (IOCTL) drives termination against protected processes. Public threat research watched one such loop run a repeating, fixed-interval termination cycle in kernel mode, stepping past protected-process defenses (PPL), and recent killers also unregister EDR kernel callbacks as a distinct observable before terminating processes. Picus mapped the same sequence across cases. Each step is a tripwire on the trust event, and none of it depends on prior knowledge of the specific driver.

The order of the chain is what makes it durable. The driver name changes every campaign, but the structure does not. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report makes the same point about the kernel: activity at that layer can blind user-space instrumentation and leave a manual disk scan an unreliable assurance of cleanliness. Detection keyed to that shape survives a recompile, and detection keyed to a hash does not.

The mental shift is the point. A driver list is a finite answer to an infinite problem, and the trust anchor is small, addressable, and already moving. SentinelLABS research has lived at that anchor for years. The team co-discovered the POORTRY and STONESTOP WHQL-signed toolkit that drove the security advisory ADV220005, and proposed Authenticode-metadata blocklisting before that was standard practice.

Defenders are not behind because the list is incomplete. They are behind because they were grading the wrong exam. Score the trust event, and the half-life stops being the attacker's advantage.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists To Do

Scoring the trust event instead of chasing the list is the whole argument, and it is the argument SentinelOne was built to win. The platform watches the load itself, the untrusted signature, the first-seen driver, and the masquerading kernel service, from a vantage designed to keep reporting when the kernel turns hostile. Purple AI® carries that telemetry forward. Its Agentic Investigation capability reasons over the trust event the moment it fires, builds the timeline, and renders a verdict in minutes and seconds rather than hours and days. The propagation gap the attacker lives inside narrows when the verdict arrives at machine speed.

A control you have not confirmed is running is a control you are only hoping for, and most teams cannot staff that verification around the clock. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, holds the line when your own team is asleep, fusing human threat hunting with the platform's autonomous investigation and Google threat intelligence. That is the reason the company exists. The trust anchor is small and addressable, and the advantage goes to the defender who instruments it.

Title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: How EDR Killing Became an Industry
Context: In August 2024, public reporting disclosed EDRKillShifter, abusing the RentDrv2 and ThreatFireMonitor drivers and first seen in a RansomHub attack
Full Text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece traces how the technique scaled into an industry.

Ransomware actors successfully disabled security tools in about 48% of intrusions in 2024. That figure comes from security researchers, drawn from incident-response engagements across the year. Attackers attempted to blind the defender in most of those cases. They almost always succeeded. Turning off the sensor was once a flourish. It is now a default move.

That 48% is the broad rate for disabling security tools by any method. BYOVD is the kernel-level technique this series tracks, one fast-growing method inside that number, and public threat research treats it as the part of the tamper problem accelerating fastest. Treat the 48% as the ceiling and the BYOVD slice as the piece that scaled into a market.

The Claim: This Became a Supply Chain

EDR killing industrialized over the last several years. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report, "Defending Against the Industrialization of the Modern Cyber Breach," names that shift directly, with mature automation accelerating intrusions and tradecraft moving from one-off effort to maintained capability. A killer was once a binary an intruder wrote and discarded. Today it is a serviced capability, built, versioned, and bundled into ransomware-as-a-service for affiliates who never touch a debugger. The defender once faced a hobbyist. Now the defender faces a development pipeline.

A pipeline behaves differently from a one-off binary. It ships versions, fixes bugs, and reuses code across releases. The defender reads that cadence like a vendor roadmap, and every release leaves the same observable footprint when it runs. The reuse is visible in the architecture. Public threat reporting describes one current framework spinning eight-plus variants off a single shared design. That also means a detection tuned to one variant often catches its siblings. Code reuse cuts both ways, and the defender holds one of the edges.

The Proof: A Four-Year Timeline

Start at the floor. Public threat research documented an early Process Explorer-driver killer in 2023, used to disable EDR ahead of Medusa Locker and LockBit. The same year, SentinelLABS tracked an actor called "Spyboy" selling the Terminator killer. The price ran from $300 for a single AV bypass to $3,000 for the all-in-one EDR killer, and the tool abused Zemana drivers. These were early-window artifacts. They were standalone, sold, and disposable.

That timeline has a SentinelLABS anchor that reframes the whole story. SentinelLABS attributed the AvNeutralizer killer, also known as AuKill, to the FIN7 cybercrime group. FIN7 sold it on Russian-language forums at prices running from $4,000 to $15,000. The tool abused a Time Travel Debugging driver and the Process Explorer driver to disable defenses. This is the moment a killer stopped being a one-off and became a product with a price list.

The adoption pattern proves the product framing. SentinelLABS tracked AvNeutralizer spreading into Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit operations. One group built it, and six competing crews ran it. A single tool crossing that many rivals is the signature of a supplier, and the new feature was distribution.

Then the model changed inside ransomware-as-a-service. In August 2024, public reporting disclosed EDRKillShifter, abusing the RentDrv2 and ThreatFireMonitor drivers and first seen in a RansomHub attack. Researchers assessed with moderate confidence that the tool served multiple attackers, not RansomHub alone. The SentinelOne RansomHub anthology records the affiliate logic behind that spread, a customized EDR-killer tool made available to higher-level affiliates. One crew's tool became many crews' tool, and the new feature was tiered access.

The driver roster widened fast across 2025. In early 2025, public threat research documented a malicious driver that carried stolen, revoked certificates and imitated a legitimate EDR driver to silence defenses inside Medusa intrusions. By August 2025, GuidePoint tracked Akira affiliates in SonicWall VPN intrusions chaining a ThrottleStop driver, rwdrv.sys, with a malicious helper, hlpdrv.sys, to disable the built-in Windows antivirus. Different crews, different drivers, the same kernel-level objective. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report records the same pattern from the other side of the kill, naming crews that script the built-in Windows antivirus into silence and kernel-mode drivers derived from POORTRY used to terminate EDR processes and delete security files.

The CVE-anchored cases arrived next. In December 2025, security researchers documented DeadLock ransomware abusing the Baidu antivirus driver BdApiUtil, tracked as CVE-2024-51324, to terminate EDR and the built-in Windows antivirus. In February 2026, public reporting documented Reynolds ransomware embedding the vulnerable NSecsoft driver NSecKrnl, tracked as CVE-2025-68947, which terminated more than 30 security processes. Those CVE records do not name the ransomware, and the actor mapping comes from threat intel. The same NSecKrnl driver shows up across unrelated crews, tied to Reynolds and to Warlock. A driver is shared infrastructure, so pivoting on the driver hash groups campaigns by supplier, not by gang.

By 2025 the sharing went structural. Threat-intel reporting found one EDR killer used across several competing ransomware families, distributed as distinct per-attack packed builds, and Singapore's national cyber agency corroborated the same multi-group pattern in an August 2025 advisory, independent of any single vendor. Public threat research also catalogued a forming marketplace of named killers priced from hundreds to thousands of dollars. Rivals were now buying from a common counter.

The 2026 picture is operator-run kits with large affiliate cuts. Public threat reporting documented the Gentlemen RaaS shipping its in-house EDR killer framework, running eight-plus BYOVD variants and targeting over 400 processes across 48 security products through DeviceIoControl calls. The operator reportedly hands affiliates around a 90% revenue share, a 10% operator cut against a 20% industry standard, and bundles third-party killers like HexKiller and ThrottleBlood. By April 2026, researchers saw Qilin and Warlock at the same game, Qilin chaining the rwdrv.sys and hlpdrv.sys pair while Warlock ran NSecKrnl. Public threat research now reads EDR killers as a standard, repeatable phase of the attack playbook. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report measured how far the response window has collapsed, with one chained sequence reaching SYSTEM in roughly 30 milliseconds and a separate intrusion moving from initial download to a persistent service in 49 seconds.

The Turn: Acceleration Over Origination

Here is the correction the timeline forces. Commercial sale of EDR killers predates the 2024 window. SentinelLABS had Terminator on the market in 2023 and dated FIN7's AvNeutralizer sales earlier still. ExtraHop tracked a dark-web market for these tools across 2024 and 2025. Older still, the open-source EDRSandblast project weaponized a vulnerable driver against more than 1,000 security drivers back in 2022. The raw capability was for sale before the surge.

So the real story is acceleration and consolidation. The non-obvious shift is that rival ransomware crews stopped competing on this layer and started sharing it instead. Several groups feeding from one killer is a market choosing a common supplier. The cost of building beats the cost of buying.

The economics pulled the skill floor down. Reynolds ransomware bundled a vulnerable driver as a recruiting selling point aimed at less-skilled operators, and a capability that once required a kernel developer now requires a subscription. The driver is the part most likely to fail in unskilled hands, so researchers documented a practice they call driver decoupling. Affiliates install the vulnerable driver and confirm it loads before running the killer. That is the kind of guardrail a supplier adds to keep low-skill customers successful, packaging doing the work the operator used to do by hand.

What Makes Consolidation Possible

Markets need shared infrastructure, and this one has it. The shared killer that reporting tracked was one tool reissued as distinct packed builds for each attack, with the packer as the common chokepoint several rivals fed through. Singapore's advisory described the same customized-build distribution model, a single supplier serving many buyers.

The driver supply explains why it scales. Public reference lists now track thousands of vulnerable signed drivers, most reachable without admin rights. The live LOLDrivers catalogue alone records hundreds of unique drivers, a large share still missing from the default driver blocklist. That inventory reads as a parts catalog for the kit builder, a dual-use commodity supply where weak driver access controls hand unprivileged users a way in.

The price ladder runs from the low hundreds for Terminator to five figures for FIN7's AvNeutralizer, both tracked by SentinelLABS, while EDRKillShifter spread through tiered affiliate access rather than a flat price. The skill floor drops in step. EDRSandblast showed the open-source baseline back in 2022, already capable against more than 1,000 security drivers, and a buyer in 2026 does not need that depth. The operator maintains the tool and the affiliate just runs it, so each layer of packaging removes a reason an attacker would have failed. A working tool spreads fast once the price of entry drops to a download.

The Payoff: A Top-Tier Threat Getting Cheaper

Put the pieces together and the threat ranking is clear. Disabling defense is attempted in most ransomware intrusions and succeeds in roughly half. The tooling that does it is now maintained, shared across rivals, and sold with affiliate economics that reward volume. Each force lowers cost and widens reach at once. This is a structural threat, and it is getting cheaper to run.

Defenders set the response, and the response is not despair. Public threat research shows BYOVD remains the dominant kill method, and that dominance means the kill chain stays observable. The killer still has to act in a fixed sequence. It installs a driver, registers a kernel service, and issues the calls that terminate the sensor. Those steps leave telemetry behind them.

The defender should still hold the technique apart from its cousins. BYOVD is one entry in a tamper taxonomy. A driverless class is smaller but growing, and it skips the driver-install step entirely. EDR-Freeze suspends the sensor through a Windows error-reporting race, staying fully in user mode. EDRSilencer uses Windows filtering rules to block the sensor's telemetry from leaving the host. Those two break the driver-load observable, so a detection built only around driver loads will miss them.

Prevention narrows the window without closing it, which is exactly why behavioral observables carry weight. The sequence is concrete enough to map to event IDs. Picus Security described the early steps of the BYOVD chain as logged events. A service created with sc.exe surfaces as a Sysmon process-create record (Event ID 1) and a System service-install event (Event ID 7045). The driver load surfaces as a Sysmon driver-load record (Event ID 6). The killer then issues its DeviceIoControl call, followed by callback removal and security-process termination. Each arrow in that chain is a place to correlate and alert.

The behavior inside that chain is even more specific. Public threat research documented a kill loop where a masquerading kernel service enumerates running processes on a repeating, fixed-interval cycle. It passes the process IDs through an IOCTL so the driver calls the kernel termination routine directly, bypassing the protected-process protections that guard the sensor. The repeating rekill cadence is itself a signal, because a normal service does not poll the process list and terminate from kernel mode on a loop.

Callback removal deserves its own hunt, separate from the kill. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write, then loading hlpdrv.sys to remove the EDR's registered kernel callbacks across more than 300 products. Stripping callbacks blinds the sensor without terminating its process. The process still runs and still reports healthy. The defender who only watches for a killed process misses this entirely.

The masquerade is its own tell. Frameworks ship variants that each impersonate a legitimate product to blend into a normal driver inventory, and one documented driver carried stolen, revoked certificates to imitate a real EDR driver. The defender's answer is to treat the signer and the first-seen status as data. Splunk detection content keys on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid. Alert on a driver whose hash, signer, or version has never appeared on the host before.

The witnesses also outlast the endpoint. Once the sensor is silenced, network, identity, and cloud telemetry are what remain, and independent analysis found EDR-killer execution preceding ransomware across multiple gangs, a window enough to intervene before encryption. Singapore's national cyber agency framed EDR-killer activity as huntable through driver-load monitoring, termination patterns, and telemetry cessation. An agent's health drop, a lost heartbeat, or a gap in a constant feed all read as tamper, so alert on the absence of expected signal. A high-fidelity variant is System Event ID 7031, the service-crash log Windows writes when a kill abruptly terminates a security service. It is rare in a healthy environment, which makes it a strong candidate for a tight, low-false-positive alert.

The mental shift for the practitioner is this. Stop modeling the EDR killer as an exotic, once-a-year event and start modeling it as supply. A supplied capability has a pipeline, a release cadence, and paying customers, and every one of those is a place to detect, disrupt, and raise cost. SentinelOne builds for that fight. SentinelLABS co-discovered the POORTRY and STONESTOP signed-driver toolkit and drove the security advisory ADV220005 that followed. SentinelOne then shipped Local Upgrade Authorization on by default for new customers to blunt the tamper bypass. The purpose behind that work is to give the advantage to those who secure our future. The industry built a market for killing your sensor. The defender's job is to make that market expensive.

Why This Is The Work SentinelOne Exists To Do

Read the timeline and the conclusion is plain. You do not out-hustle a development pipeline with manual triage. You answer it with a pipeline of your own. SentinelOne built the Singularity™ Platform on Autonomous Security Intelligence (ASI) for this exact asymmetry, so the response runs at the speed the supply chain ships. Purple AI® is the reasoning interface for that platform, and its Agentic Investigation capability launches the moment a threat crosses the line, detecting, investigating, verifying, and responding without waiting for an analyst to wake up. The capability does not displace the human. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's 24/7 managed detection and response practice, puts seasoned threat hunters on top of that autonomous layer, with managed response and an incident-readiness retainer when the worst happens. The killer industrialized. The defense industrialized with it.

Title: Fifth of CISOs Take Time Off to Avoid Patch Tuesday
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
One-in-five cybersecurity leaders has either called in sick or deliberately booked holiday time off to avoid Patch Tuesday, according to new data from Socura.

The MDR specialist polled 500 UK CSOs, CISOs and heads of IT security to better understand their attitudes to AI and the once-a-month date where Microsoft, Adobe and other vendors release their latest security updates.

While a plurality (41%) revealed that they have worked overtime to manage the patching cycle and over a third (37%) claimed they’ve worked late to deploy patches, a significant 22% said they have tried to swerve the date altogether.

Socura laid the blame on a growing number of patches and rising stress levels. Over a quarter (29%) of respondents said they feel “significant anxiety” the night before Patch Tuesday. The same share admitted they become more irritable with colleagues or family during that week.

Read more on CISO stress: CISOs Urged to Innovate with Talent Retention as Job Satisfaction Declines.

“You expect your accountant to be available for your tax return deadline, and your lawyer for your court date,” argued Socura CEO, Andrew Kays. “It speaks volumes about the unhealthy levels of stress and burnout in our industry that cybersecurity leaders would deliberately avoid the office during their most consequential day of work.”

The workload is rising as AI-powered vulnerability research helps vendors to discover software flaws in greater volumes. Microsoft fixed a record 974 CVEs in its September 2026 Patch Tuesday release, beating the previous record of 570 just two months prior.

By comparison, just 1130 vulnerabilities were published in the whole of 2025.

The data chimes with previous reports on CISO stress levels. In March 2026, a Seemplicity report revealed that 45% of cybersecurity leaders work 11+ extra hours per week – equivalent to an additional day – and 20% work an extra 16+ hours weekly.

A further two-fifths (43%) said they’re unable to take time off without creating a huge amount of stress upon their return.

“It's vital that security teams are properly resourced on Patch Tuesday, and that cybersecurity workers are properly supported emotionally, technically, and financially,” said Kays. “It's a tough job, and most people do it because they love it. That shouldn't be forgotten or exploited.”

AI Can Also Help

The good news for CISOs is that AI could also help to make certain aspects of the job less stressful.

Two-fifths (40%) of respondents told Socura that the technology automates mundane work, which in turn frees up teams to focus on more strategic tasks.

A similar share (37%) claimed that AI is helping them better protect their core corporate infrastructure against active threats.

Title: Notion says Fireworks breach exposed customer AI chat transcripts
Context: Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace...
Full Text:
Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces.

The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers.

Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.

Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data.

Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3.

However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users.

Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text.

Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI.

The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled.

“Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update.

"Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.”

Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data.

According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts.

Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats.

If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset.

Full Text:
Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom.

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

“Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”

According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system.

Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to.

Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site:

WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations.

“”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site. “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.””

Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection.

According to the attackers, the stolen data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 super admin accounts and signed delivery receipts. The group also claims to have stolen inventory records, purchase orders, advance shipping notices and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI numbers. These details come from the attackers and have not been independently verified. Maersk’s statement does not confirm their claims. WhiteArmor also tried to justify its demand, saying the $5 million ransom represents roughly four hours of revenue for the logistics business.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.” concludes the statement. “We will keep customers updated as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings, we will do so.”

The scale of Maersk’s operations explains why this incident matters. A.P. Moller-Maersk is one of the world’s largest integrated shipping and logistics companies, playing a major role in global trade and supply chains. It operates around 700 container ships, representing approximately 13.5% of global container fleet capacity, and manages 60 terminals across 35 countries. The company employs about 100,000 people in 130 countries and provides services covering ocean shipping, port operations, warehousing, customs clearance and end-to-end supply chain management.

Maersk reported approximately $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit in 2025. Its global reach and reliance on interconnected IT systems make cybersecurity a major concern. A breach involving even an older, locally operated platform could expose sensitive business and personal information, including data belonging to drivers, customers and logistics partners, even if the company’s main systems remain unaffected.

In 2017, NotPetya forced the company to reinstall more than 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. It operated without IT for ten days and took damages of up to $300 million.

Title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
Context: When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process
Full Text:
In this article

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Observed attack chains

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.

Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Figure 4: Distribution of affected organizations by sector.

These figures reflect the share of affected organizations and do not indicate that threat actors selected these sectors deliberately. Exposure is the more likely factor: academic institutions often run large, decentralized web estates maintained outside central IT, which are harder to inventory and patch.

Observed attack chains

The RCE-based intrusions in this analysis followed a similar sequence after initial access. Threat actors compromised an internet-facing application, profiled the host, transferred and concealed the relay tooling, and used the resulting channel for command and control. Some intrusions also included persistence and privilege escalation. Figure 5 combines these behaviours into a generalized attack chain. Not every stage occurred in every intrusion.

Figure 5: Generalized GSocket attack chain observed across RCE-based intrusions, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

Initial access and deployment: Threat actors exploited internet-facing web applications and used curl to download and execute a remote script. The script profiled the host, selected a GSocket client matching the system architecture, staged it in writable or memory-backed paths such as /dev/shm, and established encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Figure 6: Encoded RCE command executed through a vulnerable PHP application.

Defense evasion and persistence: Threat actors disguised GSocket with kernel-thread-like process names, persisted through cron, systemd, shell profiles, watchdogs, and redundant copies, then removed staging files and other deployment indicators.

Figure 7: Kernel thread names used to disguise the GSocket process. Figure 8: Persistence entries created during GSocket deployment.

Privilege escalation: After gaining execution as the web-service account, in few observed incidents, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284, one of the recent Linux kernel vulnerabilities also known as Dirty Frag, to elevate privileges to root.

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname. During installation, the deployment script typically generates a random secret and writes it to standard output. The threat actor can choose to read the secret from the console, redirect it to a temporary file and retrieve the file before is deleted, or have it delivered through a supported notification channel, such as Telegram (configured with GS_TG_TOKEN and GS_TG_CHATID), Discord, or a webhook. With this secret, the operator can reconnect later from any compatible GSocket client, without knowing the victim’s IP address, hostname, or network location.

A traditional reverse shell connects to a threat actor-controlled IP address written into the payload. GSocket instead derives its connection identifier and authentication material from the shared secret. The compromised host and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network (GSRN), which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session. Neither endpoint needs a public IP address, an inbound listener, or a permissive inbound firewall rule.

As a result, blocking an IP address or domain is unlikely to cut off access. The connection relies on a shared relay service, outbound traffic that is commonly permitted, and a secret that does not need to be hardcoded in the payload. Anyone with the shared secret can reconnect through the relay without knowing the compromised host’s IP address or hostname.

Mitigation and protection guidance

For an affected Linux server, remediation should address both the initial compromise and the GSocket deployment.

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Remediate the host as well as the vulnerability. Do not treat application patching as complete remediation. Investigate and remove the GSocket client, associated persistence, and staged files, then verify that outbound connections to the relay infrastructure have stopped

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Constrain outbound traffic. Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.

Harden the host runtime. Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible, and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.

Audit persistence surfaces. Review cron entries, systemd units with plausible service names, and shell startup files. Persistence is often layered across several mechanisms, so stopping the running process alone does not remove access.

Prioritize local privilege-escalation patching on internet-facing servers. In the analyzed activity, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284 to escalate from the web-service account to root. Separately, Microsoft FORGE Lab recently documented 59 Linux kernel bug reports, including eight vulnerabilities for which researchers demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled environments.

Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Keep real-time and cloud-delivered protection enabled, with behavior monitoring for anomalous child processes of web services and masqueraded process identities.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following queries to surface GSocket-related activity. The queries use public Advanced Hunting tables populated by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and cover deployment patterns observed in the analyzed intrusions.

Matches should be investigated in context with process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes, and related network activity.

Vanderbilt University is bringing systems back online after a cybersecurity incident claimed by the BYOD ransomware group.

Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. Founded in 1873, it now serves more than 13,800 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students across 12 schools and colleges, with programs ranging from engineering and education to law, medicine, and nursing. Its combination of teaching and research means its systems support not only everyday campus activities but also valuable academic research.

According to Bleeping Computer, BYOD claims it encrypted Vanderbilt’s databases and obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, telephone numbers, student and employee records, and research data. It also claims control of a domain controller (a server that manages network access) and possession of backups.

How the attackers gained access remains undisclosed. Vanderbilt’s November 10 evening incident update states that the following systems and applications are available:

Campus Wi-Fi

Okta: Continue to use multifactor authentication (MFA)

Vanderbilt email (Outlook): Vanderbilt email is available on Vanderbilt and personal devices

CampusPrint

Brightspace

Zoom

YES (Your Enrollment Services): All course registration is proceeding as scheduled

Other Vanderbilt systems and applications remained restricted. The university says fully restoring normal operations could take several weeks.

The university has not confirmed the number of affected people. BYOD claims it obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, but that is not a verified count of affected students or other people. The university says it is still determining what data, if any, was accessed.

How to stay safe

BYOD has threatened to release the data it claims to have stolen.

Students and staff should follow Vanderbilt’s latest IT guidance and be alert to messages asking them to restore access, disclose passwords, or approve unexpected login requests.

Title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
Context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
Full Text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
Context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
Full Text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.

Title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
Context: In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page, the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups

Read application settings and database connection strings

Enumerate debug and error-log directories

Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration

Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

AntiFox Demo

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.

"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.

The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks

The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus.

"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said.

"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."

According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.

In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.

"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."

The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.

In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.

Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.

The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort.

"Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing."

"The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested."

Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories -

Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon

Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT

C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG

Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes

Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares

"Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said.

"Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

Title: Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks
Context: The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration...
Full Text:
Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments.

The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting.

Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities.

Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs.

“In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says.

One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory.

The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note.

Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets.

In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects.

Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials.

The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files.

The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks.

CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.

For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings.

Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions.
