Title: Iris Ohyama data breach may expose personal information of 7.7 million people
Context: Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7
Full Text:
Iris Ohyama warns that a cloud data breach may have exposed personal information of 7.7 million customers, including names and passwords.

Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7.7 million people through an external cloud service used by its online shopping subsidiary, Iris Plaza. The incident highlights a security risk that often receives less attention than attacks against corporate networks: sensitive customer information can be exposed through services operated outside an organization’s own infrastructure.

Iris Plaza discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service on October 28, 2026. The company immediately shut down its online shopping platform and related systems, launched an investigation and confirmed unauthorized access by a third party. It published an initial notification on October 29, followed by an update on November 5 detailing the potential impact.

In its official incident notice, the company confirmed that information stored in the external cloud environment may have been accessed or obtained by unauthorized parties.

“Iris Plaza Co., Ltd. (Headquarters: Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, President: Ryota Iwasaki, hereinafter referred to as “the Company”), a member of the Iris Group, has investigated the unauthorized access incident that occurred on its official online shopping site for Iris Ohyama, “Iris Plaza” (hereinafter referred to as “Iris Plaza”). As a result of the investigation, it has been determined that some personal information may have been leaked.” reads the company’s notice. “Subsequent investigations have confirmed the possibility that data stored on an external cloud service may have been leaked. The total amount of personal information stored was approximately 7.7 million records, and at this time, we have confirmed the possibility that this data may have been viewed or obtained. “

The 7.7 million figure refers to records stored in the affected cloud service, not confirmed stolen data. Potentially affected individuals include 5.8 million current and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Exposed information may include names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and passwords, some of which are encrypted.

“The following personal information may have been leaked at this time:

classification

Target items

Number of people

Member data(including information on members who have withdrawn)

Name, address, phone number, email address, gender, password * , date of birth, etc.

Approximately 5.8 million people

Non-member data(including information on individuals who have purchased products without registering as a member or who have participated in campaigns)

Name, address, phone number, email address

Approximately 1.9 million people

Not all of the above information about our customers has been leaked. The items affected vary depending on your registration status.” continues the notice. “Some items, including passwords, are encrypted.”

There is one important distinction: credit card information wasn’t stored in the affected cloud service and, according to the company, wasn’t exposed. Iris Plaza also says it hasn’t identified unauthorized access or data leaks involving its stores on other external e-commerce marketplaces. As of November 5, it had received no reports of fraudulent use of the information or financial losses linked to the incident. アイリスオーヤマ株式会社+1

The company reported the incident to Japanese police and the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 29. It also blocked the unauthorized access route, suspended the affected systems and brought in external experts to support the investigation.

The response extended beyond the main shopping platform. Iris Plaza suspended its SIMPLE STYLE website, while another group company, Iris Tech Service, stopped its websites and new applications for home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation services. The company says it hasn’t found evidence that these additional services were compromised.

Iris Plaza has also warned customers about possible follow-up scams. Attackers could use the exposed personal information to create convincing phishing emails, SMS messages or phone calls, impersonating the company or other organizations. Fake websites and social media accounts could also appear, attempting to collect login credentials, payment details or other personal information.

The company is asking customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords on other services to change them. It also says it will contact potentially affected individuals individually as the investigation progresses. Customers should be particularly careful with messages claiming to provide information about the incident, account recovery or compensation.

“We will never ask for your password, PIN, authentication code, or any other important information when we contact you.” アイリスオーヤマ株式会社

The incident is another reminder that organizations must extend security controls and monitoring beyond their own infrastructure. Third-party cloud services can hold millions of customer records, and unauthorized access to those environments can create consequences far beyond the service initially compromised.

Title: ARTEX: Attackers apply agentic AI
Context: Sophos X-Ops is tracking ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework that multiple threat actors have used in intrusions since its public release in July 2026
Full Text:
Sophos X-Ops is tracking ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework that multiple threat actors have used in intrusions since its public release in July 2026. One of the most prominent cases is the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise in mid-October, which Microsoft attributes to Storm-0940, a group it assesses as “China-state aligned.”

How ARTEX works

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent penetration testing framework written in Go. It supports multiple LLM providers and compatible endpoints; in reported campaigns, operators have connected it to models including DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. Given an objective, ARTEX has the following capabilities:

Use planning agents to map the target and decide the next step

Worker agents can invoke offensive tooling and feed results back into the planning process. In malicious deployments, this could include activities such as scanning, exploitation, credential access and webshell deployment

Planning agents can adjust the plan and launch subsequent rounds via worker agents

It records the assets and vulnerabilities it discovers in a graph as the test progresses

Can attempt multiple breach paths at the same time

In campaigns described by Microsoft and Google/Mandiant, operators have supplied ARTEX with authentication material or compromised application credentials and used it against cloud APIs and services, such as Microsoft Graph.

Sophos countermeasures

Sophos has existing endpoint, network, and cloud protections covering multiple behaviours and indicators associated with reported ARTEX activity.

The protections below target ARTEX and the campaigns reported so far. Our evaluation of coverage is ongoing, and we will update this table as it changes.

Troj/Bckdr-SDA detects a backdoored copy of the ARTEX Docker image. The original project has been taken offline by its developer, so researchers sourcing the framework from unofficial mirrors and clones should treat those copies as untrusted.

Sophos has identified activity at a small number of customers that is consistent with ARTEX or other AI-assisted offensive tooling

Common themes include webshell and SQL Server command execution, credential theft, and attempts to move between systems. We’ve also seen rapid command sequences, repeated attempts with small changes, and structured output markers, consistent with agent-driven activity.

Across these instances, existing Sophos Endpoint protections surfaced multiple signals at multiple stages of the attacks. In many cases, Active Adversary Protection (AAP) was enabled and added further protection to disrupt subsequent attack behaviors.

It’s worth noting that, in line with what we’ve discussed previously regarding AI-enabled attacks, the attack activities are broadly the same, but the scale, noise, and persistence all increase significantly. In our telemetry, we noted hundreds of protection events relating to these attacks.

Threat hunting indicators

These indicators come from ARTEX activity described in reported campaigns. In its report, Microsoft claims that Storm-0940 was using ARTEX “as early as September 2026,” so we recommend hunting back to at least this date. Additional reporting indicates that an ARTEX-related incident occurred in September 2026, targeting South Korean financial organizations.

In cloud environments, look for:

Service principal credentials added, or roles assigned, by an application

Application sign-ins with a scripted user agent

On hosts, look for:

Temporary tooling and output files named i<intentID>[variant]_<purpose>.<ext>, for example i12345_b2.ps1.

Files or paths beginning with artx, particularly under C:\Windows\Temp.

Commands containing structured execution-verification markers – such as MARKER123/ARTX123, particularly when combined with rapid command sequences and repeated command variants

Bursts of commands, repeated variants of the same command, and output written to temporary files.

Recommended actions

Several reported ARTEX campaigns have leveraged existing or compromised access, including stolen application credentials, consented third-party apps, and valid accounts. Sophos recommends the following steps as best practice:

Audit service principals and enterprise applications in Microsoft Entra ID. Remove third-party app consents you no longer use, and review every credential addition and role assignment made since September 2026.

Apply Conditional Access policies to workload identities where licensing allows, restricting application sign-ins to expected locations.

Alert on application sign-ins with scripted user agents, and on authentication failure rates that exceed normal baselines.

Automate first response. When an attack reaches privileged access in a short amount of time, containment steps such as disabling a service principal or revoking its credentials should run from a playbook, with an analyst confirming afterwards.

If your own red team uses agentic frameworks, register their infrastructure and tooling names with your SOC so that authorized activity stands out.

Title: The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026
Context: Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started...
Full Text:
Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector

Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started 26% of attacks on retail organizations. That's the highest rate of any sector and well above the 18% cross-sector rate.

Phishing was the top technical root cause for retail at 29%, followed by exploited vulnerabilities (26%) and malicious email (22%).

Identity-based vectors, including malicious email, phishing, compromised credentials, and brute force attacks, initiated 69% of attacks against retail. This was the lowest rate of any sector yet still well above half of respondents. 66% of retail victims said their ransomware attack was also their most significant identity attack, close to the 67% cross-sector rate featured in our State of Identity Security 2026 report earlier in the year.

Known security gaps were retail’s one above-average weakness

38% of retail victims attributed their breach to a known security gap, a weakness they were aware of but had not addressed. That was retail’s most common operational root cause and the only one it cited more often than the 36% cross-sector rate.

Every other operational root cause came in below the cross-sector rate. The report compares each one in detail.

Encryption climbed after two years of decline

62% of attacks on retail succeeded in encrypting data, up from 48% in 2025 and above the 56% cross-sector rate. Attacks that encrypted data and also stole it rose to 19%, up from 14% last year. That second point of leverage weighs heavily on retailers holding customer payment and personal data.

Backups did most of the recovery work: 71% of retail organizations restored data from backups, up from 62% last year and above the 66% cross-sector rate. Far fewer retailers paid the ransom to get their data back than in 2025. The full report shows where retail’s payment rate ranks against other sectors.

Low typical ransoms, with a heavy top end

The median ransom demand for retail was $225,000, the second lowest of any sector and far below the $698,000 cross-sector median. The average (mean) demand was $4.32 million, the highest of any sector. That average does not include outlier ransoms of $40 million or more. These ultra-high ransoms were excluded from the report results to prevent skewing of averages.

The median ransom payment for retail was also low at $57,500, the lowest of any sector and well below the $769,000 cross-sector median.

The report explains what pushed retail’s average demand to the top of the sector rankings and how far retailers negotiated attackers down.

Recovery got faster, but costs went up

The average (mean) cost to recover from an attack, excluding any ransom paid, rose to $1.76 million from $1.65 million last year. That was slightly above the $1.70 million cross-sector average, which also rose this year.

But on the positive side, retail’s average time to fully recover fell to 2.54 weeks from 3.16 weeks last year. 56% recovered within a week, the highest share in five years of retail data. The rate of 2.54 weeks is also below the 2.80-week cross-sector average, making 2026 a strong year for quick recoveries.

Defenses saw the attack, but did not stop it

Almost all retail victims of credential-based attacks had MFA enabled (97%), yet more than half still had data encrypted by attackers. Firewalls flagged 59% of attacks before the ransomware deployed, but even with early indicators, victims were encrypted 60% of the time, compared with 50% across all sectors.

Controls in retail are collecting the right signals, but they’re not connecting deeply enough with other tools and responding together. The report contains several key recommendations based on this year’s data, and one of those recommendations is to adopt a defense system posture where identity, email, endpoint, and network controls respond as one.

Read the report

Retail is paying attackers less than any other sector and recovering faster than in any year of our data. But more attacks are reaching encryption, and the cost to recover went up. Closing known security gaps and connecting existing defenses are the highest-leverage places for retailers to invest in.

Download the free report for the full findings, sector comparisons, and recommendations.

Title: DoppelCart Fraud Network Grows to More Than 250,000 Domains
Context: According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled...
Full Text:
Summary

This article examines DoppelCart, a large-scale shopping fraud network encompassing approximately 261,700 suspected domains identified by Recorded Future. These fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ branding and product listings to deceive shoppers into disclosing personal and payment information, with some also capturing bank-issued verification codes to authorize fraudulent transactions. This research highlights the network’s widespread impersonation of US brands, evolving hosting infrastructure, and use of shared payment-routing configurations and the Medusa e-commerce platform. With approximately 40% of observed DoppelCart websites remaining active, understanding these patterns can help retailers identify brand impersonation and help consumers recognize fraudulent shopping sites.

Background

In September 2026, German cybersecurity company Nebty exposed DoppelCart, a large-scale online shopping fraud network with over 119,000 websites. The fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ product listings, images, and descriptions to deceive shoppers into entering payment information.

Researchers identified shared website designs, code, and infrastructure across thousands of suspicious storefronts, eventually linking the domains to the DoppelCart cluster. Most websites used .shop web addresses, and many advertised steep discounts, including offers of 65% off, to attract shoppers. Although the websites shared technical characteristics, Nebty cautioned that the findings did not establish whether a single criminal organization operated the entire network.

According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled servers in real time. Some also capture one-time verification codes issued by banks, potentially allowing criminals to authorize transactions while victims believe they are completing legitimate purchases.

Domains Discovered by Recorded Future

Primarily between March and October 2026, Recorded Future used proprietary methods to identify approximately 261,700 unique apex domains that are likely part of the DoppelCart fraud network. Based on our collections, a few thousand DoppelCart detections began appearing in January 2026 and increased during March. Our detections peaked during the months of June and July, with a sharp drop-off in new hosts starting in August.

While new host growth mostly plateaued thereafter, a drop-off in new detections is not necessarily an indicator that operations are abating. More likely, it reflects that many previously registered domains remain active, and that operators may have shifted their focus to maintaining existing infrastructure rather than expanding it. Based on data from Recorded Future® Web Scans, approximately 40% of suspect websites in this cluster observed prior to October 17, 2026, remain active.

Title: GhostFrame: A new ESXi Implant Linked to Settra Ransomware
Context: Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access
Full Text:
Implant Deployment and Persistence

GhostFrame includes an integrated builder that generates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. The interface provides operators with deployment instructions, including compiling the binary, manually disabling the ESXi firewall, and executing the implant from a datastore. Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access.

Analysis of a recovered GhostFrame Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) sample revealed that the implant establishes persistence by copying itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and modifying the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh. The modified script executes the implant and repeatedly disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly security control, which restricts the execution of unsigned binaries. These commands run approximately every five seconds, allowing the implant to disable the controls again if an administrator attempts to restore them. The implant also executes /sbin/auto-backup.sh to preserve the modified configuration across reboots. To blend into the ESXi environment, the implant appears as vmhostd, a name that resembles VMware’s legitimate vmware-hostd daemon, by modifying its process name and command-line representation.

C2 Communications and Payload Execution

GhostFrame’s implant uses a distinctive connection strategy to communicate with its C2 server. Rather than relying on a single destination port, the analyzed sample attempts simultaneous Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections across six ports: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, and 9443. The implant uses the first successful connection for C2 communications and closes the remaining connections. If no connection succeeds within thirty seconds, it retries after a randomized delay between five and twelve seconds. This behavior can produce six near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets from an infected ESXi host to the same destination IP address, providing defenders with a potentially distinctive network detection opportunity.

Once connected, the implant functions primarily as an in-memory shellcode loader. It receives machine code from the C2 server, allocates executable memory, and executes the received payload without writing it to disk. If executable memory cannot be allocated, the implant can instead establish a conventional /bin/sh reverse shell.

Post-Exploitation Capabilities

In addition to maintaining access to the hypervisor, GhostFrame allows operators to interact directly with the VMs hosted on the compromised ESXi system. GhostFrame can enumerate registered VMs, display their names and power states, manipulate VM power states, and create or delete snapshots. It also supports enabling Virtual Network Computing (VNC) access to individual VMs and relaying graphical sessions through the GhostFrame C2 infrastructure to the management panel. This allows operators to interact with the guest VMs without establishing a separate direct connection to the guest system.

GhostFrame can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client through an operator-controlled tunnel, allowing direct access to the hypervisor’s management interface from the GhostFrame panel.

For network pivots, GhostFrame includes a SOCKS5 proxy component named gfsox. Once gfsox is deployed to a compromised ESXi host, this component allows operators to route network traffic through the hypervisor, potentially reaching internal systems and services that are otherwise inaccessible from the internet.

One of GhostFrame’s more significant capabilities is its integration of multiple credential-access mechanisms. Analysis of the frontend revealed a component named sdkmon, which the interface describes as a credential interceptor. According to the frontend, the component can modify the ESXi service configuration and intercept authentication traffic, allowing it to capture usernames and passwords from subsequent ESXi logins.

GhostFrame also integrates VMkatz, an open-source credential-harvesting tool. The interface supports extracting credential data through VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, combined memory and disk analysis, or recursive scanning of all VMs on a datastore. These methods are associated with NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, Security Account Manager (SAM) and Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and credential data from NTDS.dit.

Together, these capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying conventional credential-stealing malware inside each VM.

GhostFrame’s combination of persistent hypervisor access, remote VM management, network pivoting, and credential harvesting makes it particularly relevant to ransomware and other financially motivated intrusion operations. Its observed use in activity associated with Settra ransomware provides an example of how the framework has been used in the wild.

TAG 218: From VPN To Hypervisor

Insikt Group identified GhostFrame while monitoring the operator infrastructure behind a threat activity group it designates TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware operations.

Using Recorded Future® Network Intelligence, Insikt Group observed a cluster of victim-facing servers attributed to TAG-218 targeting virtual private network (VPN) appliances across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices. Four of the targeted organizations were subsequently published on the Settra ransomware leak site.

These victim-facing servers also connect to TAG-218 tooling, including two GhostFrame C2 servers and a MeshCentral remote monitoring and management server used for persistence that was previously attributed to Settra intrusions by Huntress. On October 12, 2026, a victim Fortinet VPN appliance was observed beaconing to both GhostFrame and MeshCentral in the same period, placing GhostFrame within the TAG-218 intrusion chain.

Title: France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns
Context: Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on...
Full Text: France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement. All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers. This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers. The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons. Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says. It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.” In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C). Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America. France fights back The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.” This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador. However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

Phishing remained the most common initial access vector for attackers in the third quarter of 2026, according to a new report from Cisco Talos. Ransomware gangs are using voice phishing attacks to trick employees into granting them a foothold within organizations.

“In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool,” Cisco Talos says. “Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.”

The researchers also observed an increase in threat actors abusing AI tools, both as a tool to assist in attacks and as a target for attacks themselves.

“[An] investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant,” the researchers write.

“This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities. These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.”

Title: Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets
Context: “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud...
Full Text: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity. Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued. Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses. “For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®

Title: France Blames Iran for the Supermarket Fridge Attacks
Context: ” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression” and called it the first major cyber sabotage operation...
Full Text:
France blames Iran for supermarket fridge attacks. What’s known, what remains unclear, and how to secure exposed controllers.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the attacks on supermarket fridges in France on 11 and 12 October. He said they hit 700 sites and raised refrigerator temperatures. Some stores threw away their entire stock of perishable food, and fires broke out in several.

“France attributes destabilization and sabotage campaigns against French interests to the Islamic Republic of Iran (electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran – IRGC-ECC).” reads the announcement published by French cybersecurity agency ANSSI. “Following its investigation, C4 is able to attribute these destructive actions to the Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran (IRGC-ECC): infrastructure characteristics, use of signing tools, relay of the attack by a propaganda organ linked to Shahid Kaveh, traces of the use of Persian in the attack infrastructure.”

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression” and called it the first major cyber sabotage operation on French soil. He promised EU-level sanctions, and France summoned the Iranian ambassador. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the response should be strong, adding that she had only just learned about France’s attribution.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets, which occurred on October 11 and 12, and reported Le Monde.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” said Barrot. “It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people.”

“We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible,” he added.

Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit tied to the Guards’ Electronic and Cyber Center, and his two deputies. Anyone else they identify can be added to the case.

The attribution cites shared infrastructure, attack tools, Persian-language traces, and amplification by a group-linked propaganda outlet.

French authorities say Iranian cyber operations targeting French interests date back to at least 2020. Previous incidents include a planned attack against Charlie Hebdo, a 2023 breach of its online store attributed to Emennet Pasargad, and a 2024 attempt to hijack digital advertising kiosks to display anti-Israel messages ahead of the Paris Olympics. C4 attributes these operations to the IRGC-linked Shahid Shoostari unit.

France wasn’t alone. On 2 November, supermarkets in at least nine other European countries reported a suspected attack on their freezer systems. Barrot spoke only about the French case, so nothing official yet ties the second wave to Iran.

This is where we need to be careful. When a government names a country as responsible for an attack, that’s a serious accusation. But the reports I’ve read don’t explain the technical evidence behind it. We should treat it as an official claim, not a proven fact, and stick to what we know. Fear and uncertainty can be used to spread distrust, and that risk applies to all sides involved in this story.

The key issue isn’t just identifying the attackers, but understanding whether someone is exploiting these incidents to promote a hybrid warfare narrative. Hacktivist claims may serve propaganda and visibility more than reflect actual responsibility. If French investigations confirm Iran’s role in the October attacks, the pro-Russian groups claiming November’s incidents could face a serious credibility problem. They may have tried to take credit for someone else’s operations. Still, their involvement in some incidents remains possible.

In today’s hybrid warfare, uncertain attribution, strategic ambiguity, and information manipulation make it increasingly difficult to separate real attacks from propaganda.

The method used in supermarket fridge attacks, at least, is documented. On 5 November, CISA, the FBI and other US agencies published a fact sheet on the same kind of activity. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

The agencies list three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting code and weak settings. They also warn that operators can lose sight of the real temperatures, which is a bad thing to discover after the cheese has gone.

The fixes are dull and they work. Keep controllers off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an updated firewall in front of it. Separate industrial devices from the office network, change default passwords, add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, patch firmware and replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Then limit who can change settings with an allowlist of approved devices and IP addresses. Keep tested backups offsite and offline, turn on logging and read the logs. The last control is the cheapest: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iran)

Title: Hackers Compromise Ethersphere's bee-js and Swarm Desktop to Deliver Wallet-Stealing Malware
Context: The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found
Full Text:
Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2.

Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.

The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there.

Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically.

The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run.

The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version.

None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers.

Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn."

Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes.

When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry.

What to Do

The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed.

If you use bee-js in a project or CI job:

Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages.

Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through.

If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors.

From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read.

If you run Swarm Desktop:

Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs.

The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux.

Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand.

If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key.

On any machine where the code ran:

Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows.

Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them.

Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place.

How the Malware Works

Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts.

The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server.

The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says.

The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS.

The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added.

On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay.

If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently.

How the Releases Got Out

Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request.

For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket.

Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.

For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found.

The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch.

How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets.

The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen.

Links to Earlier Attacks

The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis.

Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases.

Indicators of Compromise

Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.

Domain: api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz

URL path: /v1/analytics (bee-js loader)

URL path: /v1/electron (Swarm Desktop loader)

URL path: /v1/assets/ (further payloads)

URL path: /v1/swarm/report (stolen wallet files)

HTTP header: X-Ethersphere: 1

IP:port: 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912 (evjawbreaker control server)

IP:port: 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 (ScreenConnect relay)

Ethereum contract: 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344

Path: ~/.solidity/

systemd unit: solidity-langsupport-runner.service

LaunchAgent: com.solidity.langsupport.runner

Service: ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df)

SHA-256: 9b73e7cd4e1425e770392549d8df46c706139ef476f4f7b9ac405165dc8d9696 (linux_amd64)

SHA-256: b601776817363b96295119f7221338a122d5247a35a77a64b04f286e1bbcc565 (linux_arm64)

SHA-256: 80d2672e2599732d3c0ae2a4cd0d1e3fe4d555a60273ce33feb99db3f34d250f (darwin_amd64)

SHA-256: fae61f31f00988fdc5cc9e7272b51e08af2e245d81003237875415930fd27358 (darwin_arm64)

SHA-256: 37d14bff30762ca701e9c1f8bc6c57c065bb20ae3a2208cb7411a6530610f08e (invoke.ps1)

SHA-256: 7527e86d70e7c9493db4356f1c3775380431b310000f2602c1e993cf435d01da (app.msi)

Title: C3RB3R attacks Synology NAS: how to protect your files | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Synology officially confirmed the issue and said the attackers were exploiting a vulnerability that had been fixed back in December 2024
Full Text:
Many people think of a home network-attached storage (NAS) device as a large hard drive connected to their router. They store videos, photos, documents, and backups on it, then barely think about the device for years. That’s a huge mistake.

In October 2026, attackers began infecting Synology NAS devices with C3RB3R (Cerber) ransomware. Many users report that they can no longer open files on their network storage, and that text files containing ransom demands are appearing in their folders. And this isn’t happening because someone accidentally downloaded a malicious file: anyone who forgot to update their network storage in time is at risk.

In this article, we explain exactly who’s at risk and how to protect your data.

Who C3RB3R targets and how the attack works

We’re used to thinking that malware gets onto a device after someone downloads a suspicious file or follows an attacker’s instructions. But the vast majority of C3RB3R infections happen without any user interaction at all — the attacker only needs to reach a vulnerable NAS service. Specialized scanners likely help find such devices by automatically looking for Synology NAS systems and checking their DiskStation Manager (DSM) version.

In October, many Synology owners began reporting C3RB3R attacks. Synology officially confirmed the issue and said the attackers were exploiting a vulnerability that had been fixed back in December 2024. Based on the description, this appears to be CVE-2024-10441 — a vulnerability that lets an attacker execute arbitrary code in the NAS operating system without authentication.

At the same time, researchers at 360.cn reported that the C3RB3R attacks they examined also involved two other critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.8: CVE-2026-13639 and CVE-2026-13684. These vulnerabilities allow arbitrary file reads or writes and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Synology hasn’t confirmed that these vulnerabilities have been used in this campaign. The company patched them in its September DSM update.

Either way, the vulnerabilities mentioned above allow attackers to target a NAS remotely. For attackers to access your storage, get ransomware onto it, and run it, only two conditions need to be met:

You haven’t updated your network-attached storage for a long time

The Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) interface is accessible from the internet (or the local network)

That’s it. The attacker doesn’t need your password or any action from you. Every Synology NAS owner who hasn’t updated the system in time is at risk.

If you haven’t installed updates yourself recently and don’t remember whether automatic updates are enabled, we recommend first blocking internet access to your NAS and then updating the device manually as soon as possible — otherwise, you could easily end up among the victims.

Keep in mind that until the updates are installed, the device remains vulnerable to attacks from the local network. So, if your Synology NAS is accessible to other users on the LAN — for example, it’s shared with neighbors or connected to a university, office, or dorm network — the safest option is to disconnect the Ethernet cable and turn off Wi-Fi if your NAS model supports it. Then download the update files to your computer, disconnect the computer from both the wired network and Wi-Fi, connect the NAS directly to the computer with an Ethernet cable, and update its operating system and applications in a fully isolated environment.

Another strong reason to update your network storage is the recently discovered PHP vulnerabilities. Synology has already released urgent updates for its operating system and the Mail Station and Synology Calendar applications.

What happens to files after infection

Once C3RB3R ransomware gets onto network-attached storage, it starts traversing every accessible folder containing user data and encrypts the files inside — photos, documents, archives, videos, and audio recordings — adding the .L0CK3D extension to encrypted files. If a user tries to open one, the system reports that the file is corrupted or in an unknown format. Unfortunately, simply renaming the file won’t remove the encryption.

This is what files look like after C3RB3R encrypts them

The attackers also helpfully leave a text file named read-me3.txt in folders containing encrypted files, with instructions on how to decrypt the data on your storage. Apparently, all you need to do is… open the totally-not-suspicious Tor Browser and pay the attackers for a decryptor that supposedly restores all your files. Needless to say, there’s no guarantee you’ll get your files back intact.

C3RB3R leaves a ransom note like this in every folder containing encrypted files. A truly generous offer: decrypt one file for free, then pay for the rest

Losing all or most of your files may not be the only unpleasant consequence. Attackers often blackmail victims by threatening to publish stolen data — account credentials, intimate photos, work documents, and other confidential information. If the victim refuses to pay the ransom, the criminals threaten to make all of this data public. They may contact you with these demands by email or through social media.

Often, such threats are nothing more than a scam, and we covered these schemes — and what to do if you’re being blackmailed — in detail in our post How scammers use email for blackmail and extortion. But if your NAS has actually been encrypted, unfortunately you can’t rule out data theft.

What to do if ransomware has already infected your Synology NAS

If ransomware has already attacked your NAS, you may face one of two situations.

You caught the ransomware in the act and are watching in horror as more and more files are encrypted and renamed before your eyes.

The user folders have already been encrypted, and the .L0CK3D extension has been added to all your files.

What should you do?

1. Immediately disconnect the NAS from all networks (but don’t power it off)

The NAS needs to be completely isolated from the internet and the rest of your home network. Disconnect every cable from the NAS except the power cable. If your NAS model connects to the local network over Wi-Fi, disable the wireless connection too. You can either disable it on the NAS itself (some Synology models have a Wi-Fi button that turns off wireless networking when held down) or simply unplug your router. This cuts off the attackers’ remote access to the device and prevents the infected NAS from reaching other computers and storage devices.

If external USB drives are connected to the NAS to expand its storage capacity, disconnect those too — there’s a chance the ransomware hasn’t reached them yet.

Pause synchronization and backup jobs associated with the NAS on computers and in cloud services. This helps prevent damaged files from spreading to other copies and overwriting versions that are still intact.

2. Decide whether to power off the NAS

If you catch Cerber in the act, your first instinct may be to pull the NAS power cable, but you shouldn’t do that: a sudden loss of power can corrupt data being written to disk. It’s better to use the NAS’s normal shutdown procedure, but keep in mind that doing so removes one possible way to recover files that have already been encrypted. A specialist may, with some luck, be able to extract a recovery key from the device’s RAM. Once power is removed, RAM is cleared.

If you’re not a technical user, don’t know anyone who can help with recovery, and encryption is still in progress, shut the NAS down normally; if the device doesn’t respond, pull the power cable. That way, you’ll preserve at least the files that haven’t been encrypted yet.

If you’re an advanced user, connect the NAS directly to an isolated computer with an Ethernet cable and try logging in to the NAS over SSH. Check the running processes (sudo ps -ef), identify the ransomware process, determine its PID (process ID), and pause encryption without terminating the process (sudo kill -STOP PID, where PID is the ransomware process ID). Then verify that all process threads are stopped (status T) and follow the C3RB3R / .L0CK3D ransomware rescue instructions for saving a memory dump. If you can’t stop the encryption, power off the NAS.

If the files on your NAS have already been encrypted and you’ve disconnected it from the local network, you can leave it powered on and try to preserve the contents of memory and recover the data by following the C3RB3R / .L0CK3D ransomware rescue instructions.

3. Save the encrypted files and the ransom note

If the ransomware has finished encrypting the files on your NAS and you’ve disconnected it from the internet, try connecting directly to the NAS and saving a copy of the encrypted files and the attackers’ instructions to an empty external hard drive. Security researchers may release a free C3RB3R decryptor in the future.

If you powered the NAS off while encryption was in progress, don’t turn it back on just to inspect processes or copy files — encryption happens locally and may resume after the device reboots. In this case, contact a reputable data-recovery specialist who can read the NAS drives without booting the infected DSM installation.

If, following the previous steps, you disconnected the NAS from the network, connected to it directly in an isolated environment, and stopped the ransomware processes, you can save any unencrypted files you need to rescue. It’s better to connect the backup drive to the computer that’s directly connected to the NAS rather than to the NAS USB port — this reduces the chance that the ransomware will restart and encrypt that drive too.

4. Don’t restore files or connect drives containing backups until the ransomware has been removed

Don’t connect an external drive containing a backup to the infected NAS, and don’t start restoring files from a backup onto the compromised NAS. The ransomware may run again and damage the connected drive.

5. Once the attack has been stopped, check your snapshots in Snapshot Replication

If you configured Snapshot Replication in advance and the attackers didn’t destroy the snapshots, you can recover data from them — but restoring it to the compromised NAS makes no sense. You’ll need a separate drive for the backup.

First, check whether the snapshots are still there. Once the malware has been stopped, open Snapshot Replication from DSM’s main menu on the running NAS. Select the shared folder, open Snapshot → Snapshot List, find a snapshot created before the infection, and click Browse to inspect its contents. From there, you can also copy data from the snapshot to external media without restoring it to the infected volume. For details on using Snapshot Replication, see Synology’s instructions.

6. Wipe the compromised NAS and reinstall DSM

After you’ve saved everything you can — including encrypted and unencrypted data as well as logs — reset the NAS to factory settings before using it again (Factory Reset → Erase All Data).

Keep in mind that this completely erases all data, applications, and settings on the network storage. Before resetting it, check the backups you’ve made and make sure the intact files you copied can be opened, the required file versions from snapshots have been saved, and the encrypted files, ransom notes, logs, and any memory dumps you obtained are stored on another storage device rather than on the NAS. If anything is missing, preserve the original drives or full disk images for a data-recovery specialist. If you can manage without the NAS for a while, don’t rush to wipe it: free decryption tools may appear later.

If you used the NAS as little more than a dumping ground for files and there’s nothing truly valuable on it that you can’t replace, fully wipe the storage as described above before using it again, and reinstall DSM from an official source using the instructions for installing DSM without an internet connection.

Don’t restore settings from a backup created after the infection: it may contain changes made by the attackers. It’s best to configure the NAS from scratch.

7. Check potentially compromised accounts

Reinstalling DSM doesn’t invalidate stolen passwords, sessions, or other secrets for services whose credentials may have been stored on your device. Think about which services were used on your NAS, which additional packages were installed, and what they could access. Go through all of those services, terminate suspicious sessions, revoke affected keys and tokens, change passwords, and enable two-factor authentication. We recommend storing all credentials in the secure vault of a password manager. Do this before reconnecting the storage to the network.

8. Before reconnecting the NAS to the network, disable unnecessary remote access

Disable QuickConnect

This service lets you connect to your NAS over the internet. To disable it in DSM 7, open Control Panel → External Access → QuickConnect, clear the Enable QuickConnect checkbox, and click Apply. In earlier versions, the QuickConnect section is located directly in Control Panel.

Check whether the NAS is exposed to the internet through your router

Your router may be configured to forward incoming connections from the internet directly to the NAS — this is called port forwarding. First, find the NAS’s local IP address. In DSM, you can see it under Control Panel → Network → Network Interface.

Next, open your home router’s settings. Usually, you do this by entering its local address in a browser; the exact address and login credentials are often printed on a label on the router or shown in your ISP’s app.

In the router settings, find a section named something like Port Forwarding, Forwarding, or Port Redirection. Review the existing rules. If a field such as Internal IP, Local IP, Destination, or Device contains your NAS’s IP address, delete that rule.

Also check the DMZ, DMZ Host, or Exposed Host section. If the NAS IP address is listed there, disable the feature.

Disable automatic port opening through UPnP

UPnP lets applications and devices ask the router to open ports for them automatically. If you don’t need UPnP, disable it.

Keep in mind that this is a router-wide setting, so disabling it may affect other devices on your home network. If you want to keep UPnP enabled for them, at least review the rules created through UPnP and make sure none of them point to the NAS IP address. If any do, delete them and, if your router allows it, block automatic port opening for the NAS.

Additional checks

If you use IPv6, review its rules too: unnecessary inbound connections to the NAS should be blocked. Also disable unused tunnels, VPNs, and other remote-access services if you configured any. After making these changes, check whether the NAS is reachable from an external network, for example over a mobile data connection.

9. Keep checking for a free decryptor

Cybersecurity researchers periodically release free decryptors for file recovery. Keep in mind that one may take a long time to appear, so don’t trust offers from unknown “researchers” or websites claiming they can instantly recover your data after an attack by a new ransomware strain.

What owners of DIY NAS systems should do

Many people use third-party loaders for DiskStation Manager — unofficial tools from the XPenology project that let them run Synology’s operating system on hardware it wasn’t originally designed for, such as a PC or a custom-built server. Examples include Arc, RR (RedPill Recovery), and M-Shell.

If you run DSM this way, C3RB3R can attack your system too. But don’t rush to update DSM: first make sure the new version is compatible with your loader and hardware. Otherwise, your files could be damaged.

If you can’t install the latest system version yet, restrict access to the network storage by disabling external access and allowing local-network connections only from devices that need access. If possible, put the NAS on a separate network segment. The Smart Home Monitor feature in Kaspersky Plus and Kaspersky Premium can provide additional protection for your home network — it shows all devices on your local network and detects when new, unfamiliar devices connect.

How to protect your NAS and personal data

Don’t put off software updates for your NAS, and check that automatic updates are enabled.

Don’t expose ports 139 and 445 to the internet: they’re frequent targets of automated attacks. These ports are used by the protocol that lets computers open shared folders on a NAS. It’s useful on a home network, but it shouldn’t be exposed to the entire internet. You can check whether these ports are open in your router settings.

If you need to access your NAS remotely — while traveling or from work — it’s better to set up a remote connection to your home network first and then access the storage from inside that network than to expose the NAS directly to the internet.

Don’t keep the only copy of important files on your NAS. Configure regular Snapshot Replication snapshots and make regular backups. Remember the 3-2-1 rule: keep three copies of your data, on two different storage media, with one copy kept off the primary storage on a disconnected hard drive.

You can also entrust important documents to the Kaspersky Password Manager. It can store account credentials, text notes, scans of personal documents, photos, addresses, bank card details, and PDF documents in the encrypted vault, protected by a master password that only you know. The vault syncs across all your devices, so your data stays protected and accessible from both computers and smartphones.

Use reliable protection that prevents ransomware and other malware from being downloaded to your computer.

Protect the administrator account. Enable two-factor authentication, use a unique password, and set up automatic blocking after several failed sign-in attempts, or use passkeys. Store passwords, passkeys, and 2FA tokens in an encrypted password manager. These measures won’t protect you from the current C3RB3R attack — Cerber exploits vulnerabilities that don’t require authentication — but they’ll help if an attacker tries to compromise your account or finds your password in a data leak.

Title: 9th November – Threat Intelligence Report
Context: Ukraine’s Air Alert app, an emergency notification service used by millions, was compromised by attackers who distributed false radiation, chemical-threat, and military alerts...
Full Text:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 9th November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Queens Public Library, a New York City public library system serving approximately 2.3 million residents, was struck by a ransomware attack that encrypted its systems. The incident disrupted public computers, Wi-Fi, checkout equipment, digital media services, and its mobile application, while all 66 branches remained open.

Russian web hosting provider Beget sustained a destructive cyberattack on November 1 that wiped data across its cloud infrastructure and disrupted hundreds of websites. The attack affected businesses and public services, with more than 1,000 servers requiring manual inspection before restoration. Some backup data was reportedly destroyed.

OPSSHIELD, developer of the Linux security tool cPGuard, disclosed a supply-chain attack after compromised credentials enabled attackers to distribute malicious updates on November 2. Approximately 2,950 customer servers executed the malicious script, which installed a backdoor and collected password hashes, credentials, and sensitive server files.

Ukraine’s Air Alert app, an emergency notification service used by millions, was compromised by attackers who distributed false radiation, chemical-threat, and military alerts to Kyiv residents. Developers temporarily suspended notifications. A separate attack affected Russia’s emergency alert application, although both countries reported that their core warning systems remained operational.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research documented cybercriminals using ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that autonomously discovers and exploits vulnerable systems. Researchers identified 1,608 live, publicly accessible instances. Observed campaigns obtained more than 300 iOS signing certificates and harvested approximately 190,000 gaming credentials, including around 6,000 active accounts.

Check Point Research identified Haiou, a jailbreak bundle targeting OpenAI Codex that weakens safeguards and modifies agent instructions to promote an external AI gateway. The package also installs security-related capabilities and appeared on infrastructure associated with cybercrime tools, although researchers did not establish that its developers intended criminal use.

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team identified Crafty Falcon, a threat actor using AI-assisted tools to target financial services and cryptocurrency businesses. Attackers exploited connections between testing and production environments, abused payment APIs, and stole wallet credentials. AI tools helped generate tailored attack scripts and automate complex intrusion sequences.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

SonicWall patched CVE-2026-19868, a high-severity vulnerability affecting SonicOS SSL VPN services configured with SAML authentication. Attackers possessing valid credentials for an alternative authentication method could bypass SAML controls, including multi-factor authentication. The vulnerability has been linked to active exploitation and affects enterprise firewall environments.

Google published November’s Android Security bulletin, addressing numerous vulnerabilities across Android components. Among the flaws patched is CVE-2026-58868, a critical vulnerability affecting Android versions 14 through 17 that could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

Barracuda patched CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, two high-severity vulnerabilities affecting its Email Security Gateway appliances. Attackers with access to the administrative interface could chain an authentication bypass with command injection to gain root-level control without logging in. The flaws received CVSS scores of 9.3 and 8.6, respectively.

OpenSSH addressed CVE-2026-123158, a high-severity vulnerability (CVSS 8.1) affecting Linux systems using the musl library without PAM authentication. Attackers can exploit oversized passwords to bypass authentication on certain accounts. Active exploitation was observed, including successful root access against an Alpine Linux honeypot. Version 10.6p2 fixes the flaw.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point researchers analyzed the evolution of HYFLOCK ransomware across four generations, identifying new capabilities for file encryption, scheduled-task execution, and network-share access. The October builds contained encryption weaknesses, allowing researchers to partially recover data from encrypted files without a decryption key. The group claimed eight victims in October.

Researchers detailed an APT29 cyberespionage campaign targeting iPhone and Android users through compromised and imitation websites. Malicious scripts identified visitors’ devices and attempted to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities. Successful compromises could expose messages, credentials, and sensitive information, particularly from users in Ukraine.

Researchers analyzed BITTER APT’s espionage campaign targeting government, energy, and engineering organizations across South Asia. Attackers distributed malicious files disguised as diplomatic and military documents to deploy PapRAT spyware. The malware collected system information, executed commands, and transferred files.

Researchers traced SlippyNunchucks, a China-aligned espionage group, to attacks abusing the trusted update and configuration mechanisms of Sogou Input Method. DNS hijacking redirected application traffic to attacker-controlled infrastructure, delivering DarkVigil malware to victims across several countries. Tencent addressed the affected delivery mechanism in version 16.10.

The post 9th November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

Title: Jailbroken AI Agent Ran Two-Week Attack on European Telecom
Context: Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked The operator's...
Full Text:
A jailbroken AI agent has spent more than two weeks attacking a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its data center and cloud infrastructure.

Malbear Labs, which has dubbed the campaign Operation Snowball, detailed the activity in research published November 8 after finding the attacker's working directory during a routine sweep for exposed open directories. The unprotected directory held more than 70 session transcripts and the agent's own reports.

The custom agent framework ran on DeepSeek Flash, with a jailbreak prompt of about 78,000 characters that told the model to treat any refusal as a malfunction. Malbear wrote that the transcripts contained no recorded refusals.

Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits

Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked

The operator's messages, translated from Chinese, were brief. Besides prompts such as "Go on" and "Stop," they set a target subnet, put three internal hosts off-limits and followed up on the agent's vulnerability list. Malbear wrote that the operator "delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress."

The agent entered the telecom by exploiting CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity (XXE) flaw in Cisco BroadWorks. Cisco fixed the flaw in August.

The agent went on to exploit Liferay (CVE-2020-7961) for root access on a host spanning several internal networks and JBoss/RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165) for a second foothold. Malbear listed more than a dozen other flaws the agent targeted, found or kept in its toolkit, none marked as exploited.

When endpoint security blocked an attempt to exploit the Linux flaw PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), the agent changed its approach without operator direction. After a tunneling tool was blocked, it wrote a replacement.

Access Claims Extended to Patient and Monitoring Data

According to Malbear, the recovered transcripts showed the agent extracting dozens of credential sets, private keys and a healthcare organization's Active Directory data.

The agent also reported reaching subscriber billing records and what Malbear described as millions of patient records, through a TrakCare Oracle database that still used default credentials.

Its reports also listed about 80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering the provider's managed-services customers.

The post does not say whether Malbear checked these claims with any victim, what was taken rather than staged or whether all 13 organizations were breached.

Malbear assessed the activity as consistent with a Chinese-origin operator and did not link it to a state actor. Its recommendations included treating internet-exposed, end-of-life JBoss Application Server 6 instances as compromised and watching internal traffic for tunneling.
