Title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
Context: Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings
Full Text:
A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals.

Command approvals turn into credential storage

Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file.

The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it.

For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file.

Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked.

Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens.

It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for.

Leaked credentials on Docker Hub

GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected.

The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image.

Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore.

One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets.

GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.

Title: Ubuntu certificate revocation checks arrive in curl, OpenSSL is next
Context: Eight weak keys in October On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak
Full Text:
Ubuntu 26.10 ships curl with certificate revocation checking built in. The check comes from upki, a project from the rustls developers. Ubuntu’s developers ran the same curl command on both releases: Ubuntu 26.04 accepted a revoked certificate and connected, while 26.10 refused it.

A certificate authority revokes a certificate when it should stop being trusted before it expires. OpenSSL checks a certificate chain by default, but it doesn’t check whether any certificate in that chain was revoked. That leaves curl and other non-browser tools that rely on it trusting certificates that browsers have already blocked.

Eight weak keys in October

On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak. One of them was the number 4. Anyone holding a key like that could issue a certificate for any website. Firefox and Chrome blocked the eight certificates the same day. Most other applications kept trusting them until distributions shipped updated ca-certificates packages.

How the check works

In 26.10, curl compares the server’s certificate against a list of revoked certificates stored on the machine. That list is built with CRLite, Mozilla’s method for compressing revocation data, and Firefox uses the same technology. Because the data is already local, the check adds no network requests. Your connection doesn’t wait on a lookup, and no outside server sees which sites you visit.

The upki package uses a systemd timer to refresh the data every six hours. Until the first download finishes, curl behaves as it did before. If you want the check working right away, install upki with apt and start the fetch service yourself.

OpenSSL is next

For Ubuntu 27.04, the Foundations team plans to build upki into Ubuntu’s OpenSSL, so normal certificate verification would also check the revocation data. Most of the more than 1,000 packages that use OpenSSL directly would then get the check without changing their code. Until that lands, the check in 26.10 covers curl, which the post calls the very first step towards browser-grade certificate verification across the entire OS.

Title: What 70 European CISOs told us about securing the AI era
Context: Prevention has become more urgent AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited
Full Text:
Last week I spent three days in Bavaria with more than 70 CISOs from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Leaders Point EMEA. Led by our CEO Nadav Zafrir and hosted with Team8’s CISO Village, it was our second Leaders Point and the first in Europe. We kept it invitation-only so people could speak openly.

The timing was hard to miss. Over the past month, attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have spoiled food and emptied shelves in stores across France and several other European countries. Nobody has yet been shown to be behind them. For anyone who still sees cyber risk as an IT problem, it was a sharp reminder of how physical it has become.

As Nadav told the room, our industry is going through its most dramatic shift in 30 years. CISOs now have three jobs at once: protect their organizations from AI-driven threats, secure the AI their own teams use, and apply AI in their own defense. They are doing all of this while the rules are still being written.

We host Leaders Point to listen, because Check Point’s strategy depends on seeing these challenges from our customers’ point of view. We covered a lot of ground, from a CISO panel on “Whose AI Can Europe Trust?” to national cyber leadership in the AI era and a look inside the frontier AI labs. Four themes kept coming back.

Prevention has become more urgent

AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited. Attackers can use AI to find weaknesses and turn them into working attacks far faster than before. Patching faster on its own can no longer keep up.

The CISOs I spoke to are rethinking what prevention means. They want to harden their environments and remove whole classes of risk before an attack arrives, so that each new vulnerability matters less. Prevention has been at the heart of Check Point’s approach for a long time, and it was powerful to hear the same conclusion from the people running security every day.

The supermarket attacks show why. Reporting on them points to refrigeration controllers that could be reached from the open internet, many on software their maker no longer updated. No patch was ever coming for those systems. The only real defense was to close those doors before anyone went looking.

AI agents need controls built around their purpose

AI agents now act with legitimate credentials across email, endpoints, networks and the cloud. That makes them hard to police with traditional tools. To most systems, an agent doing something harmful looks the same as an agent doing its job.

The room kept coming back to purpose. To secure an agent, you need to know what it is supposed to do and check every action it takes against that, in real time. An agent built to summarize contracts has no reason to change firewall rules, and security teams need to be able to see and stop that the moment it happens.

There has been plenty of talk lately about kill switches for AI agents. You should have one: if an agent is hijacked, you pull the plug. But most risky agents aren’t malicious. They’re just determined, and take a dangerous shortcut to finish the job. Switch that agent off and you lose the work too. The kill switch is the last resort. Steering is the first move: catch the agent drifting toward danger, stop the risky step and keep the work going. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

Every AI use case needs a human owner

As AI makes more decisions and takes more actions, it becomes easy for the outcomes to end up as nobody’s responsibility. The CISOs were clear that this can’t be allowed to happen.

Every AI use case needs a named owner who signs off on its risk, the same way they would for any other business risk. Clear ownership is what lets organizations move quickly with AI and still know who answers when something goes wrong.

European organizations want control over their AI choices

Many conversations, including our panel on whose AI Europe can trust, came back to control. European organizations want the freedom to switch AI models and suppliers as the market changes, and to build independent capability where it matters most.

For CISOs this is a practical question of resilience. Relying on a single model or provider is a concentration risk like any other. Our job is to secure AI whichever models and suppliers our customers choose.

The decisions that matter will be made this year

By this time next year, many of the decisions that define how organizations secure AI will have been made. The leaders in that room in Bavaria will make a lot of them.

I’m grateful to every CISO who gave us three days of their time and their candor, and to Team8’s CISO Village for building Leaders Point with us. What we heard will shape what Check Point builds next, and we’ll keep listening.

Red Hat has announced the general availability of Red Hat OpenShift 5, bringing built-in operational intelligence, zero trust security and a longer, predictable lifecycle to the hybrid cloud application platform powered by Kubernetes.

Purpose-built to streamline complex operations across data centers, cloud environments and disconnected deployments, the evolved platform enables IT teams to deploy AI workloads, virtual machines (VMs) and containerized workloads side-by-side through a simple, in-place update from Red Hat OpenShift 4.

What Red Hat announced

How organizations work with software, especially through foundational platforms like Red Hat OpenShift, is changing drastically in this agentic age. Red Hat OpenShift 5 delivers an application foundation built to connect and run enterprise AI, helping customers monitor, manage and scale their environments. This release brings Model Context Protocol (MCP) server support, AI interfaces and automated AI-driven reasoning tools to assist where constrained operations teams need the most help.

“Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves the application platform to meet enterprise IT teams where they are, bringing built-in natural language interaction directly into day-to-day operations while delivering the strict multi-tenancy and sovereignty protections modern organizations require. By introducing intelligent, context-aware guidance and a five-year predictable lifecycle, we are providing a transparent, reliable path for our customers to build, run and scale VMs, containers and agentic AI side-by-side with complete confidence across the hybrid cloud,” said Ashesh Badani, SVP and CPO, Red Hat.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed from a conversational assistant to an agent, making the platform more interactive with autonomous troubleshooting and update risk assessments, including pre-flight readiness checks for optional operators directly within the management console.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 also introduces hardened multi-tenancy for sovereign deployments and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) support to protect long-term IT infrastructure investments. Combined with Red Hat AI, Red Hat OpenShift 5 provides a platform for running traditional and AI workloads with performance, governance and observability to help advance your AI strategy.

Why Red Hat OpenShift 5 matters

IT practitioners and IT leaders face mounting friction as they balance scaling high-density AI workloads alongside legacy VMs while meeting strict regulatory requirements. Dense log streams and manual cluster operations pull critical engineering resources away from core innovation. Simultaneously, how teams interact with infrastructure is shifting from traditional management consoles toward headless, agentic workflows.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 addresses this evolution by embedding real-time intelligence directly into platform operations through Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed. By supporting natural language interaction and AI-driven reasoning loops, Red Hat OpenShift 5 transforms reactive cluster maintenance into a proactive process, limiting administrative overhead, mitigating downtime risks and giving IT teams greater operational control across hybrid cloud infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Faster root-cause analysis: Rapidly identify and isolate anomalies, analyze log streams and execute supervised remediation across complex cluster topologies completely within the console.

Sovereign and zero trust guardrails: Hardened multi-tenant isolation, automated certificate lifecycle management and post-quantum control plane cryptography protect air-gapped, edge and regulated environments.

Reduced upgrade anxiety: Automated pre-flight checks analyze API compatibility and run update risk assessments across optional operators before execution.

Deeper details

Red Hat OpenShift 5 introduces advanced platform capabilities to help lower operational costs, enhance compliance and optimize hardware footprints wherever an organization must work:

Sovereignty guardrails and zero trust multi-tenancy: Delivers post-quantum cryptography protections for control plane communications to safeguard critical data against future quantum decryption threats, while hardening sensitive environments with advanced network isolation, extended certificate management and native support for disconnected deployments to satisfy strict regulatory demands.

Full-stack workload convergence: Enhances unified control for Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, containerized build pipelines via GitOps and automated GPU compute slicing to maximize hardware utilization across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads.

Guided platform updates and lifecycle management: Features intelligent pre-check risk assessments and pre-flight compatibility analysis for APIs and optional operators to guide administrators through zero-downtime maintenance windows.

“Service providers need cloud infrastructure that can keep pace with network innovation while meeting the reliability demands of telecom. Our work with Red Hat gives Nokia’s cloud-native network functions a consistent, carrier-grade foundation that simplifies operations and makes change more predictable. Red Hat OpenShift 5 strengthens that foundation, helping operators run today’s critical services efficiently and prepare their networks for greater automation and AI,” said Kal De, SVP, core networks, Nokia.

Title: Druva helps restore AI agents without rolling back entire environments
Context: Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup...
Full Text:
Druva has announced Druva Agent Recovery, a new set of AI Resilience capabilities that keep the business running by quickly restoring AI agents when they are deleted or unexpectedly changed. Support begins with Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft’s platform for building custom AI agents.

Announcement also expands protection across Microsoft Power Platform, adding Power Apps and Power Automate to existing Power BI support. Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup health and recovery options within Microsoft AI tools.

According to Microsoft, more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies now use AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools. As adoption grows, one broken agent can stall the processes around it, and recovery often requires restoring a full environment or rebuilding the agent manually. Druva keeps a recovery point ready for each protected agent, so teams can recover individual agents without starting over.

“More business processes now run through AI agents, which makes those agents essential to how the business operates,” said Ranga Rajagopalan, Chief Products and Marketing Officer at Druva. “That puts them on the same list of critical systems every IT team backs up and recovers. With Agent Recovery, we’re now protecting the agents themselves, building on what we already safeguard across Microsoft 365 and Copilot conversations.”

Druva Agent Recovery protects Microsoft Copilot Studio agents

Druva introduced AI Resilience earlier this year to help organizations recover, govern, and defend AI-powered work. Druva Agent Recovery brings that resilience to AI agents, starting with Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery. It protects customer-built Copilot Studio agents and their configurations, enabling customers to:

Keep pace with agent growth: Automatically discover Copilot Studio agents across Power Platform environments as employees build them, so protection keeps pace with adoption.

Automate policy-based protection: Scheduled, immutable backups in The Resilience Cloud give every agent a clear version history, protecting against accidental changes, unauthorized edits, and emerging risks.

Recover a single agent: Restore individual agents and their configurations without rolling back the entire Power Platform environment.

Expanded power platform support protects each agent’s workflow

Copilot Studio agents depend on connected applications, flows, data, and identities. When one of those fails, the agent can fail with it. To extend resilience across these dependencies, Druva now protects Microsoft Power Apps and Power Automate, expanding the Power Platform support introduced with Power BI protection. Teams can restore individual apps or flows from air-gapped, immutable backups without rebuilding them or rolling back the environment.

With this expansion, Druva’s cloud-native platform protects Copilot Studio agents and their workflows end to end. Coverage spans the Microsoft ecosystem and beyond, including Power Platform, Microsoft 365, Copilot Chat conversations, Microsoft EntraID, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Salesforce. When something fails anywhere in an agent’s workflow, teams have a clear path to recovery.

Druva accelerates recovery in Microsoft AI tools

Two integrations give teams quick access to Druva backup health, recovery points, and troubleshooting guidance within Azure and Microsoft 365 as they investigate issues.

Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent: With Druva’s first-to-market integration, Microsoft Azure SRE Agent can use Druva backup health, protection status, recovery points, and failed-job diagnostics for any Druva-protected workload to enhance incident response. Azure SRE Agent then correlates that information with Azure operational data to identify unprotected workloads and suggest or take next steps.

Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot: Delivered through the Agent Store in Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Druva Agent is the first backup and recovery agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings a consolidated view of backup health, grouped failure analysis, and remediation guidance into Copilot and Microsoft Teams. Using Copilot’s Microsoft 365 context, administrators can see which users and groups are impacted by a backup issue and retry failed backups directly from Copilot.

Support for Microsoft Power Apps and the Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot are generally available. The Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent will be available at the end of November. Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery and support for Microsoft Power Automate are in limited availability.

Title: Microsoft fixes Exchange sign-ins broken by Windows Server updates
Context: Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss
Full Text:
Microsoft has fixed Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems after installing the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.

Microsoft acknowledged this known issue in mid-October, confirming that users had trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later.

As explained at the time, the sign-in and mail flow issues are caused by a new default limit on the amount of memory Endpoint Mapper uses when handling Endpoint Lookup calls, introduced by the October 2026 updates.

"After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," Microsoft said at the time.

"Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem," it added in a separate blog describing the issues.

However, Microsoft said that this Outlook on the web (OWA) known issue isn't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urged customers not to uninstall them.

Fixed by November Patch Tuesday updates

In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates (KB5131080 and KB5131090) address this known issue and advised affected users to install them on all affected systems.

Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues for those who can't immediately deploy this month's cumulative updates, which requires modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems.

To do that, IT administrators have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server to increase the maximum number of Endpoint Lookup calls and the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use, and then restart the device:

reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f

After the system reboots, the admins should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it recurs.

Title: Why does old access outlive the job?
Context: Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone
Full Text:
Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them.

Why is granting access easy but removing it hard?

Granting has an owner and a deadline. A manager submits a request, an approver clicks yes and the process is completed in just a few hours since someone is involved in it. Removal does not have any of the two. Nobody opens a ticket when permission becomes unnecessary, as the only person who notices will not submit the ticket for lack of reason to do it. The cost of maintaining the permission is high, but it is not visible and it comes in the future. The incentives work the same way. Nobody evaluates how low an access level their team maintains, while a permission that was mistakenly removed and became necessary results in an irate support ticket submitted the same day.

And this is something that has to be done via reviews, but, in my opinion, is not done like this. And, at least in all attestation and recertification activities I was involved in, there is simply a basic question for the reviewer: is access still valid? Saying “yes” is not really difficult — access was granted, there were no actions following and reviewing several hundred takes less time than investigating one particular access. This is not what will appear on your screen. When reviewing account names, you do not know whether they were used last week or last year.

Role-based access control helps here, but the problem is that, when a user changes his role, his role gets updated, but not the direct access, groups and folders he acquired during the time.

What does leftover access actually cost?

I have to be quite careful here, as this metric does not reflect the access that remains. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report demonstrated that exploitation of vulnerabilities was the most frequently used method of the breach, making up 31% of all breaches, while the previous leader — abuse of credentials — was reduced to 13%. However, I want to emphasize that this particular report is unrelated to the issue of obsolete permissions. Yet, what the intruder could do after penetrating the system depends on the permissions of the breached account, which in turn depends on the number of permissions acquired. In practice, it looks like findings of audit and investigation, which go on forever, because nobody knows whom exactly to permit to access the corporate data.

However, there is information proving the case of the leavers, although quite meager. Thus, according to the PasswordManager.com survey carried out in March 2023, among 1,000 American workers, 58% of the workers who responded that they had used the passwords of their previous employers admitted that they had never updated their passwords after leaving the company. It is an opinion survey carried out online, and that is why it is an indicator. Indeed, I noticed this too: The departures have to go through the HR offboarding checklists, but not the permissions and certificates created by hundreds of people over many years.

Transfers are even more of an issue and there are fewer studies regarding them. In the case of a leaver, at least something happens — the offboarding process is triggered. Nothing triggers in case of a transfer. And thus I think that transfers should be equally important as terminations, because the standards require exactly that. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — security and privacy control catalog used throughout organizations — contains AC-2 and AC-6 account management and least privilege controls requiring review of accounts, processing of transfers and terminations, and granting only privileges required by the role of the individual.

3 fixes that make leftover access hard to ignore

And here is how I will make sure that the changes will be adopted. There is no need for any new technology to be implemented. Just the decision regarding the ownership of the deletion process.

1. Every change in position will be regarded as an event of deletion

Start from the HR record of the system. After the change takes place, generate a task for the outgoing and incoming manager where there will be only one question for the manager to answer — what will the individual no longer need? Provide them with the access list and 10 minutes to answer the question. All the access the individual had created during this period needs to have an owner. If you only do one of these three, do this one.

2. Each permission must have its own unique owner and expiration date

Permissions or access to the project folders, special permissions or access to the production system must expire on a particular date, which could be either the date the project expires or, by default, three months after its issuance, unless renewed by the owner, who must be a named person, not an e-mail address. I think of the account, the owner and the applications it accesses as a graph, because if there is any change in accounts, then with one query, it can determine what he/she owns and his/her dependencies. Renewal must be a one-click option, but in the event of that person’s no longer being available, it should be done through his/her manager so that it does not get lost in the cracks. It is a default setting. In the current scenario, if you do nothing, it is your permission; hence, laziness is the dangerous path. Do not make the default action renewing the permission.

3. Present last-used information on all reviews, and allow people to act on it

Pull last login and last activity timestamps from your identity provider and application logs and present them along with each entitlement. Order the list such that the least used access appears at the top, select it for removal and ask the reviewer to explain why they need to keep it. From experience, I have found that people are happy to confirm when “this entitlement hasn’t been used in seven months” shows up on the screen. Then allow them to take action based on what they think is best. If attestation takes place using one tool and rotation/vaulting takes place using another tool, then you would find people confirming the question and skipping the action. That’s why I’ve started to keep attestation, rotation, vaulting and retirement of access in one process. Remember, however, there are limitations to this approach. Not all applications maintain usage logs, and sometimes there is legitimate access that is rarely used. Take the case of quarterly close accounts and break glass accounts, for example. They should be assigned an owner and a note.

While employees will be able to identify what they don’t need anymore, this is effective only when there is a system in place which allows them to do so safely and easily, and this is yet another reason why we need to implement the three above fixes.

In this quarter, start with a single system where sensitive data is stored and run a last-used report on that system. Begin with the users who have been moved to a different role within the past year, since no one has reviewed their access rights since then. Send a list of all those users who haven’t used that system in the past six months to the system owner, and ask them one simple question — Do they still require this? The findings will be enough to make the case for the rest stronger than any framework.

Modules: AI Security; Cloud Risk Management; Vulnerability Management
Title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
Context: ” Autonomous patching may only be transitional Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove...
Full Text:
Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea.

The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.”

Not your father’s vulnerability management program

The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.”

Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities.

They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices.

“The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.”

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices.

“It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO.

“Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline.

Is human-in-the-loop dead?

Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed.

“The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains.

“And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.”

That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop.

CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says.

Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’”

“Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.”

Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.”

On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.”

Autonomous patching may only be transitional

Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.”

Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential.

He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines.

The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime. Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference, Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says.

The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.”

Steps CISOs should be taking now

According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment.

For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds.

And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.”

Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate.

“If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.”

Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.”

He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”

Title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
Context: The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a...
Full Text: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post. The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

Title: Your training data is boring: Anomaly detection with LLMs
Context: The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly...
Full Text:
Following on from research presented at Black Hat USA 2025, Sophos data scientists Ben Gelman, Tamas Nyiri, and Tibor Kristóf Lányi recently showcased new work on anomaly detection at BSides Las Vegas 2026. As promised, we’re sharing more details of that research (the recording of the talk is also available here).

Supervised classifiers in cybersecurity are often trained on data that doesn't capture the most unusual examples. Benign training sets are dominated by simple, common patterns, while malicious sets reflect known attacks from past investigations. The long tail of unusual files on both sides goes unlabeled.

When these files appear in production, classifiers are more likely to misclassify them, generating false positives that overwhelm SOCs, and false negatives that let threats through.

Traditional approaches to labeling difficult examples rarely scale. Doing it manually is expensive, rule-based collection is too narrow, and anomaly detection alone has historically produced unacceptable false positive rates. But anomaly detection combined with LLMs is excellent at something else: finding and labeling the unusual data that is missing from cybersecurity training sets.

The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly detection methods, viable across feature representations, to surface distinctly unusual data. Then, an LLM classified each anomaly with format-specific prompts calibrated per data type.

Critically, Ben and his colleagues used separate prompts that err toward malicious and benign respectively, achieving high precision on both label types. More specifically, one prompt instructed the LLM to only evaluate the input as benign when it was confident that it was benign; the other prompt instructed the same but with the malicious label. This way, they only accepted the labels when the two LLMs with the two different instructions agreed, otherwise they threw that example away and didn’t use it for training. In practice, this method produced labels with better precision (tested on labeled data). The labeled anomalies augment the training data for cybersecurity classifiers.

The Sophos AI team evaluated their method across three structurally different data types with monthly ingestion scales spanning four orders of magnitude: command lines, HTML, and RTF.

The problem

Every detection team is familiar with the core issue: supervised classifiers are only as good as their training data, and that data is systematically biased. Benign training data comes from sources chosen for labeling confidence.

Known-clean networks, corporate environments without incidents and regex-capturable patterns are obvious choices, but they inherently exclude the long tail of unusual but legitimate data.

Malicious training data is similarly constrained to known attack types from incident investigations. The events that classifiers get wrong in production are precisely the unusual events missing from both sides of the training set.

Using command lines as an example: prior work on anomaly detection for command-line classification has attempted to address labeling oversights by surfacing anomalies as direct alerts. SCADE uses isolation forests and engineered features to flag potentially malicious command lines at scale, but reports false positive rates around 2%. Filar and French discover anomalous parent-child process relationships using tree-based models, reporting similar ~3% false positive rates. Nisslmueller combines explicit command-line featurization with parent-child context for unsupervised LOLBin detection, also landing under 2% FP.

Although these rates sound low, at tens of millions of daily events they still produce overwhelming alert volumes. All three share the fundamental limitation of treating anomaly detection as an end-to-end alerting mechanism.

Ben and team’s approach sidesteps this limitation entirely: anomaly detection surfaces candidates, an LLM labels them, and the labels improve a downstream supervised classifier.

A key takeaway from the team’s work is the prompt strategy for achieving high precision on both malicious and benign labels. A single prompt struggles to simultaneously maintain high precision on both labels. Instead, the team used two separate prompts per file type: one that errs on the side of calling files malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), and another that errs on the side of calling files benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). This allows both label types from anomaly detection to be usable as training data, which was not achievable in prior work that relied on a single labeling pass.

Stand back, we’re doing science

The pipeline for Ben and team’s research was as follows:

Raw production telemetry

Feature extraction

Multi-method anomaly detection

LLM classification

Newly labeled training data from the long tail

Supervised classifier improvement

A key architectural decision was to treat anomaly detection not as the detection system itself, but as a prefilter that surfaces candidates for LLM labeling, which in turn produces training data for a supervised classifier whose precision can be controlled empirically.

Because each anomaly detection method has blind spots – it catches certain types of unusual data and misses others – Sophos AI used three methods (isolation forest, k-means anomaly, and PCA reconstruction error) on different feature representations, producing broader coverage with low overlap between methods.

The team employed several different feature sets, which contributed to data diversity:

Hand-crafted features: Catching structural anomalies, such as files with extreme length, abnormal Shannon entropy, rare character distributions. Hand-crafted features included character-level statistics, operator/case proportions, and file-type-specific markers.

TF-IDF vectors: To catch content-level outliers, e.g., files whose token distribution didn't match any typical cluster.

Binary vocabulary vectors: For the unusual feature correlations, e.g., files with atypical token co-occurrence patterns.

Prompt needed

A single LLM prompt can’t always achieve high precision on both malicious and benign labels simultaneously, especially in cases where the problem itself is inherently ambiguous, such as dual use scripts . For example, if the prompt says, ‘when uncertain, lean toward malicious,’ benign precision is high, but malicious precision suffers and vice versa.

Sophos AI’s solution was to run two separate prompts per file type. One erred towards malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), the other toward benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). Each prompt was calibrated to the file type's specific attack surface.

For example, with HTML, the malicious-leaning prompt defined what normal HTML looks like (JavaScript, forms, analytics) so it didn’t over-flag standard web features. The benign-leaning prompt defined specific malicious indicators (obfuscated payloads, credential phishing, exploit kit structures), so it didn’t under-flag real threats.

Putting it to the test

Ben and colleagues evaluated this method across three structurally different data types:

Command lines: ~10,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: LOLBin abuse, obfuscated PowerShell, encoded payloads.

HTML files: ~1,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: exploit kits, credential phishing, obfuscated JavaScript.

RTF documents: ~10,000 monthly ingest (testing under data scarcity). Attack surface: Equation Editor exploits, DDE attacks, malicious OLE.

The results on LOLBins can be found in the previous research. But expanding the work to HTML and RTF files elucidated more generalizable trends, and suggests that the method can work with a variety of data types.

Like LOLBins, RTF performed best with isolation forest, showing a 2.41% increase over the existing model, which is an encouraging jump at such a high ROC AUC.

With HTML, we see a different result. The baseline performance of the model is higher, so the increase is more modest, but the team found that K-means was the most effective with a 0.68% increase over baseline. They also noted that PCA decreased the score, which highlights exactly why they used three different anomaly detection methods: they didn’t know in advance which method would capture the most valuable anomalies in a particular dataset. And since running these algorithms is relatively cheap, the small extra cost only comes from running the evaluations on the extra anomalies with the LLM.

Try it yourself

Here’s something our data science-minded readers can try out for themselves:

Pick a file type where your classifier has a false positive or false negative problem

Pull a sample of unlabeled production data, featurize it, and run Isolation Forest (it's 10 lines of sklearn)

Send the top anomalies to an LLM with a format-specific prompt. Use two prompts: one that errs malicious, one that errs benign

(Optional) Check the quality of the LLM output on a sample either by running it on a set of your labeled data or even better, have an analyst verify the unlabeled ones

Add the high-precision labels to your next training run and measure the difference

Wrap it in a YAML config and schedule it. All being well, you now have a self-improving data pipeline

Top takeaways

Classifiers’ failure cases are a training data diversity problem; anomaly detection finds the unusual files that rules and manual labeling miss

Multi-method anomaly detection (IF + KMeans + PCA) on different feature representations catches more than any single method

Dual-prompt LLM labeling achieves high precision on both malicious and benign labels, making both usable as training data

The pipeline is filetype-agnostic (as long as an LLM can produce high precision labels for them – test this empirically first) and runs on a single machine. A new data type therefore requires a config file, rather than having to become an onerous engineering project

Although research on traditional ML models has slowed in recent times, this research shows that LLMs can help revitalize the field by infusing them into the process for significant performance gains

Title: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
Context: Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules
Full Text:
The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all.

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail, information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict.

While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules.

In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to:

Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself

Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams

Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty

Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere

Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually

Prerequisites

For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place.

GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability.

Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions.

If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations, AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists.

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed.

Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects

An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs, or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty.

Custom Detection Rules

Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS. The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read.

Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams.

Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration.

Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available.

Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on

Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration, and accounts that join the organization later inherit it.

Using the GuardDuty console

Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules.

Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule

Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it.

Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration, choose Configure.

Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode

Under Configuration strategy, select Whole organization. Under Status, select Dry run. Under Accounts, select Apply rule status to all accounts, then choose Save.

Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations.

Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals

When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts.

Using the AWS CLI

From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later.

aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN

Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure.

Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids.

aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids <image-build-account-id>

Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments.

Threat entity lists

If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account.

GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move.

In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used.

Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file.

Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain

Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from.

A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective, or Amazon EventBridge, so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue.

Two changes have made that routing more customizable.

Wildcards

Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale.

Additional property filter fields

You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields.

The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule. The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide.

Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule

Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics, the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue.

Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations

What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected. When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin.

GuardDuty Investigation, also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out.

Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence.

You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server. To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings, find AI powered investigations – Preview, and choose Enable.

Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions

The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.

Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.

Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.

Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.

Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.
