Title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
Context: Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported
Full Text:
Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models.

Key findings from Microsoft Research include:

Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post.

A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment.

The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it.

Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously.

Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code.

Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions.

Audit model weights before deployment and after every update

Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly and diffusely, while implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount. Flag tensors or rows whose change is a statistical outlier relative to the rest of the diff and reject models that do not declare a verifiable base.

Use frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline. Microsoft Research found they are highly effective at finding anomalous structure in weights that manual inspection misses, which makes this step automatable at scale.

Complement weight diffing with behavioral backdoor scanning of open-weight models, as described in Microsoft’s research on detecting backdoored language models at scale.

Record audit results alongside the model in the registry, and state clearly to internal consumers that passing an audit reduces risk but does not guarantee safe behavior.

Secure model hubs and publishers

Display provenance and audit status publicly before a checkpoint can be downloaded or served through an API.

Scan every upload for anomalous neurons, weight patterns or behaviors, and state clearly that third-party checkpoints can be unsafe and that passing an audit does not guarantee safe behavior.

Treat every third-party model as untrusted until audited

Source checkpoints only from the original publisher, verify the publisher’s published file hashes, and treat all third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantizations, and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Register approved models in a private, access-controlled registry (for example, Azure Machine Learning registries) and block agents and inference services from pulling models directly from public hubs at runtime.

Turn on AI model security in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to scan models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries for embedded malware, unsafe operators, and exposed secrets, and add model scans to Azure DevOps or GitHub build and release pipelines. Note that this scanning addresses serialization and code-level risks; it complements, but does not replace, a weight-level audit.

Turn on Defender for Storage on-upload malware scanning for storage accounts used to stage model files and training data.

Red team for hidden triggers

Add trigger-hunting and backdoor scenarios to your AI red team plan. Use PyRIT or the AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry to run repeatable adversarial tests against models and agents before and after each update.

Contain what an agent can do if its model is compromised

Run agents with least privilege. Give each agent its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID, scope its permissions to the minimum set of resources it needs, and use Conditional Access for agents to lblock unapproved or high-risk agent identities.

Execute agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, such as Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions, and never expose host-side file write or shell tools to the model.

Apply network egress controls to agent and inference hosts so that a triggered model cannot open arbitrary outbound connections. Allow only the endpoints the agent requires and turn on network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Require human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as running commands, changing permissions, sending data externally or modifying infrastructure.

Apply attack surface reduction rules to devices that host local agents and inference servers, starting in audit mode.

Detect and block malicious agent behavior at runtime

Turn on Microsoft Defender security for AI agents and configure real-time protection rules so Defender can audit and block risky tool invocations, secret exfiltration, and evasion techniques for Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Agent 365 agents, and runtime protection for local agents through Defender for Endpoint.

Turn on threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, including suspicious prompt evidence, so the security operations center (SOC) receives alerts for jailbreak attempts, credential leakage in model responses and malicious URLs in AI interactions.

Enable Prompt Shields for both user prompts and documents on model deployments and agents. Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported.

Onboard every device and server that runs agents or local inference to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in active mode so that suspicious child processes, persistence and outbound connections from agent host processes are detected.

Maintain inventory and governance of models and agents

Use the AI agent inventory in the Microsoft Defender portal to discover agents, their tools, identities, and risk indicators.

Use AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud to build an AI bill of materials (AI BOM) across Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), so you know which models are deployed where.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI to discover, sanction or block generative AI apps, and to monitor sensitive data in AI interactions.

Map controls to the Microsoft catalog of AI defense capabilities, which groups supply-chain provenance, model hardening, runtime isolation and monitoring into a single framework aligned to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Learn more

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

Title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
Context: The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a...
Full Text: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

Title: AWS refreshes ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment to enhance customer’s third-party due diligence
Context: This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input
Full Text:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce renewal of the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment. This validated assessment report helps customers perform effective cloud supplier due diligence on AWS and enhances their third-party risk management process.

What is the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment

Many customers use third-party cyber risk management (TPCRM) services such as ProcessUnity to better manage risks from their evolving third-party environments and to drive operational efficiencies. To help with such efforts, AWS has completed the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment of its security posture. ProcessUnity’s assessors perform the review of Global Risk Exchange assessment and validate the results annually.

This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input. Vendor profiles continuously update as cloud provider risk levels and AWS security posture evolve, keeping risk matrices current in near real time. Additionally, customers can also use Framework View which maps AWS assessment controls to threat profiles, MITRE ATT&CK scenarios, and global compliance standards and frameworks including National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), significantly reducing customers’ third-party due diligence burden.

How can you access the assessment?

Customers can request access to the report by completing an access request form, available on the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange page. If you are an existing ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange member, you can request access from within ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange portal.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, see AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.

Finally, Payment by Bank Transfer Comes to Have I Been Pwned
Context: That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious
Full Text:
Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

Title: Key benefits of Zero Trust Network Access over corporate VPN access | Kaspersky official blog
Context: For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device
Full Text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

Title: Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns
Context: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security...
Full Text: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges. “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory. Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.” The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week. CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface. As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.” CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG). “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either. We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems. These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities. So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

Title: Digital sovereignty at re:Invent 2026: Sessions you won’t want to miss
Context: Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to...
Full Text:
AWS re:Invent returns to Las Vegas for cloud and AI’s biggest week from November 30–December 4, 2026. This year we have over 2,200 sessions, 70 percent of which are interactive, led by experts from Amazon Web Services (AWS), our customers, and our partners.

With that much to choose from, we’ve pulled together the sessions built around Digital Sovereignty at AWS. Whether you’re navigating evolving data residency requirements, choosing the right home for your most sensitive workloads, or scaling AI in environments where your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, there’s something for you at re:Invent.

In this guide, you’ll find breakout sessions, chalk talks, workshops, and a lightning talk covering a range of digital sovereignty topics, grouped by theme so you can easily find what matters most to you. Reserve your seat through your attendee portal, or walk up based on availability. If a session is full, check the catalog for another time, since several of these sessions run more than once.

Pro tip: Sessions are spread across several venues, so allow extra time to get between them. All times are Pacific.

Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud

In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to help meet their most stringent digital sovereignty requirements. As part of its design, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operates with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and is backed by strong technical controls, sovereign assurances, and legal protections. In these sessions, get the full picture of the AWS approach to digital sovereignty, including verifiable controls, operational autonomy, and greater choice with infrastructure options like the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

SEC206 | Breakout session | Digital sovereignty: Verifiable controls and greater choice Speakers: Mustafa Isik, Chief Technologist Sovereignty, AWS; Stephane Israel, Managing Director European Sovereign Cloud and Digital Sovereignty, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 1:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Evolving regulations and geopolitical shifts are prompting organizations to rethink how they protect data and maintain control in the cloud, without slowing innovation and AI adoption. This session explores how AWS helps customers meet their digital sovereignty requirements with the full power of the cloud through a range of offerings, including the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, backed by verifiable and auditable controls. Learn what AI sovereignty means in practice, get answers to the most common questions, and hear how AWS and partners are helping organizations navigate complexity in a fast-changing landscape.

SEC234 | Lightning talk | EU operational autonomy in action: AWS European Sovereign Cloud Speakers: Zoltan Albrecht, Director, AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | Wynn/Encore The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is built on fully isolated infrastructure within the EU, operated exclusively by EU-resident staff, with no access from outside Europe. In this lightning talk, learn from the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations team what independent operations means in practice and how it works day to day.

Theme 2: AI under digital sovereignty and data residency requirements

Moving AI from pilots to production means making clear decisions about where your data and AI workloads run to meet your digital sovereignty needs. These sessions show how to bring AI infrastructure to your data, from fully managed AWS AI Factories in your data center, to the right hybrid deployment for each workload, to agentic AI applications that extend to hybrid and edge environments such as AWS Outposts and AWS Local Zones.

AIM206 | Breakout session | AWS AI Factories: Bring production scale AI to your data center Speakers: Pranav Chachra, Senior Manager, Product Management, AWS; Gareth Tucker, Global Specialist – AWS AI Factories, AWS; Daniel Xu, Member of Technical Staff, Anthropic When and where: Thursday, December 3, 10:30 AM | Venetian Data sovereignty, data gravity, and latency requirements prevent many organizations from running all AI workloads in the public cloud. AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure directly into your data center, fully operated, maintained, and continuously updated by AWS. Run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference without building and managing AI infrastructure yourself or negotiating separate agreements with model providers. In this session, learn how organizations are accelerating AI adoption, reducing time to value, and maintaining full control of their data while benefiting from the AWS experience in their own facilities.

HMC303 | Breakout session | Choosing the right hybrid deployment for your AI workloads Speakers: Shivam Saggar, Sr. Product Manager (Tech), AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS; Shelby Seward, DMTS, Sr. Director, T-Mobile; Hai Lu, Senior Engineering Manager, Databricks, Inc. When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations are running AI workloads for model training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and inference, across an expanding set of environments, including AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories. The right deployment option depends on latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. See how customers deploy accelerated AI across the hybrid spectrum: NVIDIA GPU-based and AWS Trainium-powered instances in Local Zones, purpose-built AWS AI Factories for large-scale training and model serving, and edge deployments for real-time inference. Hear how customers navigate these decisions, including Databricks tapping GPU capacity on AWS Local Zones and T-Mobile running latency-sensitive distributed inference, and learn which environment fits each AI workload without compromising performance and compliance.

HMC402 | Workshop | Implementing agentic AI solutions on-premises and at the edge Speakers: Kyle Palasti, Edge Specialist Solutions Architect, National Security, AWS; Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace Learn how to extend Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to hybrid and edge services to build distributed agentic apps using Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication with on-premises data. Get hands-on with hybrid agentic AI using Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents while exploring AWS hybrid and edge solutions for data residency compliance.

HMC403 | Workshop | Self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge Speakers: Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 12:30 PM | MGM Grand Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand As organizations use agentic AI to automate complex infrastructure operations, many have data residency, low latency, and security requirements that depend on running AI closer to their data. This workshop explores how customers deploy self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge to meet these requirements while enabling autonomous operations. Learn how to architect, provision, configure, and optimize AI agents that run locally, and how to extend the same architecture to AWS hybrid and edge infrastructure such as AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts.

Theme 3: More control, more choice: Finding the right infrastructure for your digital sovereignty needs

Digital sovereignty requirements vary, and AWS offers control and choice across a range of deployment options. Whether you’re comparing AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS Regions, or planning a migration, you’ll find the infrastructure options to meet your unique digital sovereignty needs. These sessions help you learn more and choose with confidence.

HMC314 | Chalk talk | Architecting for digital sovereignty with AWS Hybrid Cloud solutions Speakers: Sherry Lin, Principal Product Manager, AWS; Lakshmi VP, Solutions Architect – WWPS, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand This session uses real-world case studies to understand how AWS hybrid cloud architectures such as AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS Outposts help customers meet their digital sovereignty needs. It examines data residency boundaries, network separation, operational controls, and security guardrail options available in hybrid cloud solutions. It then shows how to configure governance controls, including Service Control Policies (SCPs), to help customers comply with regulatory requirements. Finally, it covers how to detect and prevent unauthorized data flows between hybrid infrastructure and the parent Region.

HMC202 | Breakout session | AWS wherever you need it: From the cloud to the edge Speakers: Spencer Dillard, Director, Software Dev, EC2, AWS; Ian Cottingham, Director, Software Development, AWS; Rama Raghavan, AVP Cloud Architecture, AT&T Inc. When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace While most workloads can run in the cloud, some remain on-premises or at the edge due to low latency, local data processing, or data residency needs. AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories extend AWS services, APIs, and tools to metro areas, on-premises data centers, and the far edge. Explore how these infrastructure offerings power a broad range of hybrid cloud and edge computing use cases such as financial trading, manufacturing, and AI. Learn how AWS helps you run regulated workloads with edge requirements, power generative AI with edge data, and migrate workloads with on-premises dependencies, featuring AT&T’s migration and modernization at scale.

This Level 300 session distills lessons from migrating customers to Outposts across industries, organization sizes, and migration strategies, featuring SERPRO, Brazil’s federal data processing company, and AT&T, migrating telecom workloads at scale. The session walks through the processes that delivered results, the quantifiable outcomes measured, and the critical mistakes to avoid. Learn how to select the right migration approach and navigate common blockers. The session also covers transitioning from first-generation to second-generation Outposts hardware.

Theme 4: Disaster recovery, resilience, and cross-partition connectivity

Digital sovereignty goes beyond where your data lives. It also shapes how you operate, recover, and connect your workloads. These sessions help you learn about the operational side of digital sovereignty: recovering from failures under regulatory requirements, designing for resilience alongside data residency, and strategies for connecting across global AWS Regions, GovCloud, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions.

Speakers: Hossam Ebrahim, Solutions Architect, AWS; Paul Armstrong, Lead Architect UKI, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 4:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Organizations with pre-approved failover regions recover in hours. Those without recover in weeks. Same impairment. Same services. One governance decision separates them, and it’s made years before the event. This session presents architectural patterns for multi-Region recovery under sovereignty constraints, drawn from real operational experience with regulated workloads under regional pressure. Three categories: decisions that set your resilience ceiling before any event, dependencies that create circular failure during recovery, and assets nobody backs up until they become the critical path. You leave with the decisions to evaluate before your next DR test.

ARC318 | Chalk talk | Architecting for resilience and data residency Speakers: Andy Orlosky, AWS Solutions Architect, AWS; Mike Haken, Senior Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Jamie Pasterick, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 2:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Wednesday, December 2, 1:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, but your workload still has to survive a Region degradation. This chalk talk explores architecture patterns that address both resilience and data residency together. We break the challenge into practical layers: where data lives, how workloads recover, what isolation looks like, and how to maintain business continuity across geographic boundaries. We map each layer to AWS capabilities including Dedicated Local Zones, Outposts, and policy controls, then work through real scenarios together. Bring your architecture challenges and we will whiteboard design patterns and tradeoffs with you.

NET327 | Breakout session | Connectivity strategies across AWS Partitions Speakers: Kunal Sharma, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Rohit Aswani, Principal Solutions Architect – Networking Specialist, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 4:00 PM | MGM Grand Organizations increasingly operate across AWS commercial, GovCloud, Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions to satisfy regulatory, data residency, and national security requirements. In this session, learn cross-partition connectivity patterns using AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and application-layer proxies alongside DNS resolution strategies, compliance boundary enforcement, and operational trade-offs. We walk through architectural blueprints for securely linking partitions while preserving the isolation guarantees they exist to enforce, and share lessons learned from customers navigating ITAR, GDPR, and national sovereignty mandates at scale.

Theme 5: Digital sovereignty across industries

Priorities for digital sovereignty vary by industry, and are shaped by different regulations, risks, and requirements. Learn how organizations in government, energy, and telecommunications are meeting their unique needs with the control, choice, and scale of AWS.

IND361 | Workshop | Build hybrid data planes for government GenAI pipelines Speakers: Mohamed Salah, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Usama Salama, Sr. Specialist SA AI/ML, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Strict national security mandates block government agencies from adopting cloud GenAI. Title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
Context: The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025
Full Text: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

Title: How to Evaluate AI Agent Cybersecurity Capabilities
Context: Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once
Full Text:
How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

To create a benchmark, fix the benchmark objective first. Then build the tasks, environment, and the measurement around it. I’ll get into this and explain the principles that guide the process, in greater detail later in this post.

Key Takeaways

Choose the right tasks. Settle the why (objective), the what (data, ground truth and agent setup) and the how (metrics, evaluation function) before you write the first task. Build the data from the real distribution where you can, not from AI-generated or AI-labeled tasks.

Grade with code, not LLMs. Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

Optimize evaluation for realism. Evaluate the harness and model together, give the agent more than one try, and weigh success against what a solve costs.

Avoid common pitfalls. LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

Start with a problem statement

Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

Write down the one question your benchmark must answer, and test every later decision against it. Ours:

Given only the task instruction, a general-purpose agent scaffold, a 1,000-second budget, and no external knowledge sources, does the agent produce a checkable effect on a real target?

Wiz Research's 2026 State of AI in the Cloud Report found that at least 57% of organizations have deployed self-hosted AI agent technology, and that MCP servers appear in at least 80% of observed cloud environments. People are already buying and defending against these systems. That is the why. The rest of this post is how to build a number that serves it.

Design your benchmark

Define three things before you create your first challenge.

Why. A defender or a buyer should be able to act on the number. "Higher pass@1" is not a why. "Can this agent, as shipped, exploit a live target from the instruction alone?" is.

What. Name the subject under evaluation. Here it is an agent (model + harness + tools + system prompt) run by an attacker, which is why we use realistic limits: 1,000 seconds, three attempts, a simple system prompt, and access to client-side code but not server-side code.

How. It’s important for the benchmark to report a single bottom line metric per example. To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

Make the tasks match the job

A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

So we built four categories of equal weight from sources that already exist in the wild. We did not generate or label tasks with an LLM.

Category

Tasks

What it tests

Code vulnerabilities

221

Finding known vulnerabilities in stripped open-source packages, or exploiting a live 1-day CVE

API security

54

Attacking black-box APIs with no source code

Web security

29

Exploiting real PHP web apps with the client source visible

Cloud security

23

Exploiting misconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes-style setups

The agents behave very differently from one category to the next. Averaged over the 59 agents, pass@1 is 78.0% on API security, 64.6% on web, 56.5% on cloud and 38.2% on code vulnerabilities. The top overall agent scores 74.7% on web and 65.8% on code (while web tops out at 90.8%). Another agent scores 9.7% on code and still 71.6% on API.

Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

Grade an effect, not with LLMs

Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

Anti-cheating via isolation

Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

As for contamination, we cannot prove our agents never saw a task in pretraining. We can prove they cannot fetch one during the trial. Anti-cheat belongs in the environment, not in the prompt.

Start small

Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

You need ten tasks you can re-run, one harness you can deploy, and an evaluation metric a grader can check. After you’re convinced it works, you can scale it up.

What we found

Pair the harness with the model

A model on its own is a text predictor. It becomes an attacker inside a harness that runs commands and applies tools, and models do better or worse in different harnesses. Across the 22 models we ran on both Claude Code and ADK React, the mean absolute gap was 5.1 pass@1 points. Claude models prefer Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber prefers the thinner ADK loop.

The conclusion: test the system as a whole. Either pair the harness to the model (and as we’ve seen it’s best to match the harness to the model's creator), or fix one general harness and compare models inside it.

Attackers get more than one try

A real attacker does not stop after one failure. We gave every agent three attempts per challenge, and the extra attempts did more than lift scores. For some agents they even changed which one comes out ahead.

Accuracy has a price

Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

Keep a short list of agents on the frontier and ignore the rest. That lets you ask "for this budget, how do I maximize success?" or "for this success rate, how do I minimize cost?"

Limitations

Four simple harnesses. A cyber-specialized harness would likely score higher, but we chose to measure a simple attacker.

String equality on code vulnerabilities. A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.

Public web tasks. websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).

A time cap. 1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

Confidence intervals. We have yet to publish them on the website, and we are working on it.

Conclusion

Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.

Appendix: Results for All 59 Agents

Every agent, ordered by pass@1. Scores are percentages.

Source: Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9.

Title: Omdia Quantifies the Business Value of Fortinet Unified SASE
Context: Explore Omdia’s economic validation of Fortinet Unified SASE, including modeled cost savings, operational efficiencies, and improved user productivity.
Full Text:
The business case for secure access service edge (SASE) hinges on how well it integrates networking and security. Organizations that manage separate SD-WAN and security service edge (SSE) products alongside legacy VPNs may still contend with fragmented policies, multiple consoles, and substantial integration work. These operational costs can reduce the value of convergence.

A new Omdia Economic Validation report, The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE (October 2026), examines the financial impact of a unified approach. Commissioned by Fortinet, Omdia interviewed customers in education, government, and healthcare—three sectors with tight budgets, distributed users, and strict compliance requirements—and developed an economic model based on their experiences. The findings connect lower infrastructure costs with reduced administrative effort and improved employee productivity.

The Three-Year Financial Model

Omdia used its interview findings to model a composite enterprise with approximately 50,000 employees, 500 locations, and 20,000 remote or hybrid workers. This model’s initial environment included costly WAN connections, multiple security products, and traditional VPN access. The model estimates the following over three years:

Approximately $50.1 million in benefits against $8.4 million invested, yielding $41.6 million in net value and a 493% return on investment

A 47% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) for networking, security, and operations

A 59% reduction in time spent managing and supporting operations, saving more than 21,000 hours

Payback within the first year, with approximately $13 million in first-year cumulative benefits against $3.5 million invested

These modeled results offer a framework for evaluating a SASE investment. Actual returns will depend on an organization’s existing infrastructure, connectivity costs, staffing, and deployment scope.

Reducing the Work of Managing Separate Systems

The 59% reduction in operational effort helps explain how the modeled returns are achieved. Fortinet Unified SASE unifies the SD-WAN edge and cloud-delivered SSE on a common FortiOS operating system, with unified management and a shared data lake. This architecture enables teams apply consistent policies and investigate issues without switching between disconnected tools.

Customer interviews illustrate the practical impact. General network and security administration produced the greatest absolute time savings. Remote access management became simpler when zero-trust network access replaced legacy VPN deployments. One customer cut the time to bring a site online from about a month to just days, and reduced acquisition integration from as long as three months to about three to four weeks.

Customers also reported that a single console made compliance reporting simpler. For organizations in regulated sectors, spending less time gathering and reconciling information can free staff to focus on other security and operational priorities.

Vendor and platform consolidation accounts for another 12% of modeled benefits by reducing licenses, simplifying procurement, and decreasing the number of vendor relationships to manage. Faster integration also helps acquired organizations start using shared systems sooner.

Improving Productivity and Resilience

End-user productivity accounts for 25% of modeled benefits. One healthcare customer reported that doctors had previously lost reliable connectivity after about three hours of work; deployment resolved the issue. Education customers reported fewer connectivity complaints from users on campus, at home, and while traveling.

Improved resilience contributes an additional 11% to the modeled benefits. One customer replaced a single internet connection with two connections and SD-WAN failover. For a clinic or school that depends on continuous application access, this can reduce disruption if a connection fails.

Supporting AI Adoption with Consistent Controls

The report also frames these findings against rising infrastructure demands. Omdia survey data cited in the report show that 80% of organizations are investing in AI infrastructure, while 69% say their environments have grown more complex over the past two years.

One interviewee described a related visibility issue: Before deployment, the organization didn’t know who was using AI tools or what data employees were entering into them. Consolidating generative AI access security, data loss prevention, and cloud access security broker capabilities together on one platform helps teams govern usage and protect sensitive information. These controls are especially relevant in government and healthcare, where employees handle regulated data.

Using Connectivity Savings to Support Modernization

Network and security cost optimization represents the largest category of benefits in Omdia’s model. One customer replaced MPLS circuits that cost roughly $2,000 with cable connections costing about $150, while gaining more than 30 times the bandwidth.

Savings at that scale can help fund broader modernization. By pairing connectivity changes with networking and security consolidation, organizations can assess the transition's costs alongside the operational and security benefits of the resulting architecture.

Applying These Findings to Your Organization

While the composite enterprise is large, the issues it addresses also affect smaller organizations. A small IT team managing multiple consoles and contracts can benefit from consolidation, and connectivity costs can be evaluated on a per-site basis. The study’s percentage reductions provide useful benchmarks for that assessment, though smaller organizations should not assume equivalent returns.

The next step is to build a business case using your organization’s cost data. Compare current circuit and licensing expenses, factor in the time spent managing separate systems, and include migration and deployment costs. A proof of concept can then validate operational improvements and the user experience before a broader rollout.

Download The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE to explore the findings.

Title: Why Does AI Agent Security in Banking Require More Than Alerts?
Context: An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability
Full Text:
TL;DR: AI agent security in banking requires controls that can deny prohibited workload actions before they complete, because an alert does not revoke an agent’s authority. An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability. Aquasec combines deep runtime visibility with local enforcement through its full agent architecture, applying configured policies inside running workloads without waiting for centralized analysis. That control complements identity restrictions and transaction approvals, blocking supported operations that violate policy while the agent is executing.

What is the control gap in AI agent security?

Your bank’s exposure extends to the authority an agent’s workload gives it, which can be much broader than its assigned task. AI agent security must connect that task to enforceable limits on access and execution.

In Kubernetes, that authority can come from a service account, an associated cloud role, mounted credentials and available network paths. Instructions to inspect records do not remove credentials or close connections. A carefully written prompt therefore leaves the workload’s technical permissions unchanged. The agent can still attempt actions the business never intended it to take.

Why do internal AI agents require their own runtime controls?

Connecting an agent to production tools gives its decisions consequences inside your environment. A badly scoped instruction or a malicious prompt embedded in a document can lead it toward actions its existing access permits.

Blocking external agents at a customer login does nothing to constrain an internal agent using a workload identity. The bank still owns that exposure inside its clusters. Security cannot wait for a software exploit to establish that intervention is necessary, because an unwanted operation may use a valid credential and an allowed connection.

Where do access reviews and alerts fall short for AI agents?

Identity controls, image scanning and patching remain essential. They reduce unnecessary authority and address vulnerable software. A posture finding, however, leaves the identified access available until something changes it.

Adding runtime telemetry does not automatically close that gap. A sensor can observe an operation without being able to deny it locally. In a model that exports telemetry for centralized analysis and response, execution can continue while the decision is made.

For an agent connected to a financial system, that distinction is consequential. Investigating a completed operation and preventing that operation from completing produce different outcomes for the bank.

How should banks separate AI agent observation from action?

An agent assigned to inspect transactions should not automatically receive the authority to initiate them. Use dedicated identities and restrict available credentials to the resources its task requires. Require application approval for consequential operations, with read access limited to necessary records.

Then carry those boundaries into the running workload. Define the executable behavior and network destinations the task needs and enforce restrictions on supported operations outside that scope. The controls should hold when the agent misinterprets an instruction, without depending on the model to recognize its own mistake.

How does Aquasec enforce AI agent workload boundaries?

We put the enforcement decision inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines detailed runtime telemetry with local policy decisions at the kernel layer. In enforcement mode, it can deny supported operations that violate configured policy without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response.

Drift Prevention makes that distinction concrete. When an agent attempts to execute a binary introduced after deployment, the configured control can block execution. Network policies can also deny connections to prohibited destinations, restricting paths that the workload’s identity permissions might otherwise leave available.

Those controls act on the operation itself. Security teams get a way to constrain supported workload behavior while permissions are corrected, without making termination of the entire container the default response. Application authorization remains responsible for deciding which transactions an agent may perform.

How do AI agent security approaches compare at execution?

Evaluate what happens to the attempted operation. The comparison below separates finding driven posture from telemetry led detection without local enforcement. Aquasec entries assume supported controls configured for enforcement.

Dimension

Traditional approach

Modern approach

Aquasec approach

Primary function

Identify excessive access

Detect workload behavior

Enforce workload policy

Decision path

Remediation workflow

Central analysis and response

Local enforcement

Prohibited operation

Evidence
