Full Text:
N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

This edition of the Bitdefender Threat Debrief covers the latest events in the ransomware threat landscape, including the claims surrounding the rise of the new ransomware group N0n, a former affiliate that turns on The Gentlemen, and news concerning BYOD ransomware.

As ransomware continues to evolve, our goal with this monthly Bitdefender Threat Debrief is to help you stay ahead of the curve. To do this, we combine information from openly available sources (OSINT) - things like news reports and research – with data we gather by analyzing Data Leak Sites (DLSs), websites where ransomware groups post details about their victims. It is important to remember that we can't independently verify all of these claims but are confident in the trends we see over time.

For this month's report, we analyzed data from October 1 to October 31, 2026, and recorded 1,072 claimed ransomware victims. Note that when excluding some of N0n’s victim dataset (126 victims) from October’s total victims, the actual number of victims reported is actually 946.

Featured Story: N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

What Happened?

In mid-September, the ransomware group N0n emerged. The group hosted a data leak site with more than 100 victims, divided into categories including pending, exposed, leaked, and honors (where NOn claims to have honored the promise to destroy victim data in exchange for a ransom payment).

Several weeks later, information about N0n’s operations became plainly visible due to N0n’s failures to maintain strict operational security measures. N0n’s Python file server was left accessible on the open Internet. This presented visitors with the opportunity to go to the web address and navigate through directory structures to view contents of the server. This exposure allowed cyber defense and research teams to determine with greater confidence that N0n’s image as a potentially significant threat is just that: a false depiction. N0n is a newcomer to the ransomware landscape, relying on AI tools for foundational hacking tasks.

What Information was Disclosed in N0n’s Exposure?

N0n’s file server address is associated with a location in Sweden. Several types of information were disclosed in the aftermath of N0n’s exposure. All information types revealed make it highly unlikely that N0n is a ransomware group capable of competing with other leading threats. N0n;s actual victim count (rather than their published/perceived victim population) and their use of open-source AI dismantles their apparent trend of continuous growth. According to the data obtained from N0n’s file server, the group targeted just over 20 victims. Duplicate or false entries may have emerged due to weaknesses in maintaining the site and polling potential targets.

N0n also uses an open-source AI platform, OpenCode, to manage different AI models and write scripts. N0n invested more than $7000 in Generative AI to assist them in building common scripts that are maintained to perform actions necessary for scanning and reconnaissance activities. While an encryptor was also identified, debate remains over whether N0n consistently uses ransomware. Their reuse of encryption keys and weaknesses in OPSEC may point towards hesitancy for the group to execute ransomware code more frequently.

The exposure of N0n’s server also revealed that N0n references the same encryption keys that are used across different victim campaigns. This means that the group was leveraging the exact same ransomware code and keys to lockdown systems for different targets. Cybersecurity teams supporting victims with access to those hardcoded encryption keys can then analyze them and identify patterns needed for decryption.

What Actions are Recommended for Organizations?

As opportunistic ransomware groups continue to adopt AI into their operations, it is important for organizations to remember the following:

Data theft claims often initially lack any validity. Keep an inventory of your assets, including critical data that may be found in open repositories. Do not assume that any data stolen is from a current dataset or usable by the threat actor without supporting evidence.

Harden remote access controls to secure systems. This includes enforcing VPN access, restricting access via RDP and also requiring MFA authentication.

Enforce a strong password policy and regularly rotate credentials.

Regularly document breach cases predating current operations and check for additional exposures.

Maintain backups in a location separate from critical infrastructure and test them regularly to ensure backup data can be restored.

Request and review intelligence on an ongoing basis to evaluate the threat actor’s behavior and current indicators of compromise

Other Notable Ransomware News

Now, let’s explore the notable news and findings since the last Threat Debrief.

Azazel, an affiliate of The Gentlemen, turns on their operator: Azazel has accumulated more than 6 terabytes of stolen data. Despite their affiliation with The Gentlemen, the group broke away from them after stealing data in an RaaS campaign and keeping the profits for themselves. Azazel published the stolen data on a data leak site under the name Leakned. Notably, Azazel has leveraged a technique that differs from other ransomware groups. They used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to establish a connection between an AI coding assistant and a reverse shell. This connection allows Azazel to use the AI assistant as a command and control channel, executing commands on compromised machines. Azazel has engaged in primarily in data theft and credential theft, extracting credentials from GitLab and other pipelines.

BYOD ransomware claims university that provides healthcare services: BYOD, a ransomware group that emerged in September, has claimed enterprise organizations across both North America and Southeast Asia. The group recently claimed a university clinic that provides healthcare services to patients. Within 24 hours of their claim, BYOD expressed that they did not realize the systems they targeted were used specifically to support direct patient care. BYOD announced they would make decryptors available to the victim organization for free; and, the affected victims are encouraged to reach them and submit a payment of $2,500 to ensure their data is destroyed. These claims are identified as potential ploys to extend the compromise and/or collect additional payment.

Booba Team claims more victims and hits government organizations: Booba Team has claimed more than 9 government organizations at the time of this release. According to Booba Team’s data leak site, this accounts for more than 800 GB of stolen data. Booba Team’s total victims claimed in the government sector in October surpasses the totals in the same period for both Qilin (who claimed 6 victims) and The Gentlemen (who claimed 3 victims). Unlike Qilin and The Gentlemen, who have broadened their victim populations to include government victims in Western Europe and Southeast Asia, Booba Team has continued to claim victims in a limited number of regions, including North America (specifically the US) and South America. The group has been known to deploy ransomware and conduct data theft.

New brands continue to make their entry into the ransomware ecosystem: More than 17 ransomware groups have emerged in the last two months. Several newcomers were identified in October, including but not limited to: aoqin, everstake, shiba, whitearmor, hyflock, umbra, vypr, and scarlettgroup. While some groups emerge out of a necessity to commit acts of organized crime, with limited influence from other threat groups. However, the largest variables that contribute to new ransomware groups include law enforcement takedowns, feuds and factions among ransomware groups and affiliates, and operational failures. Bitdefender will continue to track further developments in ransomware takedowns, rebrands, and evolutions.

Top 10 Ransomware Families

Bitdefender's Threat Debrief analyzes data from ransomware data leak sites, where groups publicize their claimed number of compromised organizations. This approach provides valuable insights into overall RaaS market activity. However, it comes with a trade-off: while it reflects attackers' self-proclaimed success, the information comes directly from criminals and may be unreliable. Additionally, this method captures the number of victims claimed, not the actual financial impact of these attacks.

The Top 10 ransomware groups in October include N0n, The Gentlemen, Qilin, Akira, and Booba Team. Note that due to several indicators of N0n misrepresenting their operations and victims, Bitdefender has high confidence that N0n is not in actuality a group that has the means to maintain a ranking in the Top 10 Groups.

Top 10 Most Attacked Regions

Ransomware gangs prioritize targets where they can squeeze the most money from victims. In many cases, this means focusing on developed countries with higher projected growth rates. Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest.

Taiwan rejoins the Top 10 Regions: Taiwan ranked 10th in October; most of the region’s industries affected by ransomware attacks are in manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

Victims based in South Korea rise due to N0n’s claims: The number of ransomware victims based in South Korea rose to 18 in October. N0n claimed 11 victims based in South Korea; all of these victims are organizations in the transportation industry. However, due to the high level of scrutiny cast on the validity of N0n’s claims, this increase should not be viewed as an accurate pattern of behavior. Ransomware groups have not claimed a total number of victims based in South Korea surpassing 10 per month since September 2025 when Qilin executed the Korean Leaks campaign.

Top 10 Most Attacked Industries

Ransomware gangs may target organizations in critical infrastructure sectors, select other organizations that offer services tailored to consumers, or attack organizations that fall into both categories. Understanding the trends and ramifications associated with specific industries, and how specialized services and clientele are impacted is crucial for assessing risk. Here are the Top 10 industries affected by ransomware attacks.

Healthcare rises to second place in the Top Industries

In October, there was an increase in the number of victim organizations represented in the manufacturing and healthcare industries. Healthcare rose to the second rank. And, the transportation industry moved from the 10th rank to the 6th rank in the Top Industries with N0n claiming a total of 20 transportation victims.

Title: When everything is a threat, nothing feels safe
Context: A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business
Full Text:
When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention.

The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act.

In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky.

These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends.

When a warning becomes background noise

There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy.

But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact.

A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction.

Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise.

There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day.

Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest

Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue. In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy. Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus.

Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness.

When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them.

This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication.

Replace headline volume with decision criteria

I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important.

A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears:

1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee?

2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat?

3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team?

This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter.

For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help.

For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful.

The burden cannot rest entirely on users

It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem.

Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior.

NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case: systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions.

Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame?

These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions.

Build awareness through confidence

I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic.

Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens.

We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision?

If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity.

Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.

Title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
Context: Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning...
Full Text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

Title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
Context: Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes
Full Text:
Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones.

Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN.

The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post.

The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

“Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.”

Intermittent sending issues

DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing, and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes.

But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected.

For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum:

Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered.hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location.

Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation.

According to email security company MailRoute, enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com. A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said.

The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1; p=none. This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained.

DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult

DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM.

SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from.

DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained.

“Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.”

But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.”

Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said.

Quiet, inconsistent failure

As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent.

It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through.

The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC” since Nov. 5.

Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first.

From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain.

Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation.

However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject, which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name.

Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.”

A signal of what is to come

While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025.

“Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.”

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago:

The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users.

And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Title: Enforcing intent-based access control at the endpoint
Context: GitGuardian found the requested inventory file on only about a quarter of targeted systems, and some clients explicitly refused credential-harvesting requests despite the...
Full Text:
In the Odyssey, the Sirens promised every passing sailor the story of "everything that is going to happen over the whole world." Circe warned Odysseus that their listeners never made it home, but he wanted to hear the song anyway. He also knew he couldn't trust himself once he did. So he stopped his crew's ears with wax, had them bind him upright to the mast, and gave them one standing order: "If I beg and pray you to set me free, then bind me more tightly still." When the song came, he signaled with his brows for his men to let him go, and Eurylochus and Perimedes tied him tighter. The song is what people remember, but the engineering worked. Odysseus set his limits before the temptation arrived, and he left its enforcement to ropes he couldn't loosen and men who couldn't hear him.

The previous piece covered turning an agent's prompt into an access policy that a person validates. This piece covers whether that policy holds once the agent starts working. Three questions define the design. Can the agent tamper with the controls enforcing the policy? Does the control check the action regardless of how the agent attempts it? And does it receive enough task context to understand intent while staying simple enough to test? These questions connect controls a security vendor can build on endpoints today with broker, resource-side, and hardware enforcement elsewhere.

OpenAI demonstrated the problem while hardening its training environment. In Securing our frontier model training environment, published October 23, it reports that teams of agents "found several ways to chain vulnerabilities into microVM escapes." In a separate experiment, agents passed synthetic secrets between microVMs through the processor's cache, without network connections or shared writable files. OpenAI gave the attacking agents infrastructure source code and configuration details. In most communication tests, researchers also pointed them toward a specific channel or supplied a method for encoding and decoding messages. OpenAI says it remediated the discovered weaknesses and its frontier training now runs without live internet access.

Other containment failures took different forms. In Marchand et al.'s SandboxEscapeBench, which seeds containers with deliberate vulnerabilities, frontier models prompted to escape often got out through common misconfigurations like exposed Docker sockets and privileged containers, though none solved the hardest scenarios. Many attempts cost on the order of $1 each, cheap enough for an attacker or an uncontrolled agent to keep trying. Anthropic reviewed more than 140,000 evaluation runs and found three incidents involving real organizations through mistakenly open internet access. In those runs the agents needed no exploit, because a configuration mistake had already left the boundary open.

Every one of those failures happened in an environment built for containment. The PocketOS agent from the previous piece ran on a developer laptop, where it found an account-wide access token in a file unrelated to its task and used it to delete a production database. The credential read and destructive API request originated on the endpoint. A security product on that laptop could have seen the token read and the outbound request. With the agent's task supplied through its hook, it could also have recognized a credential unrelated to the task being used for a production deletion the task never required, and blocked the request before it left the machine.

Without that check, the PocketOS agent behaved like Odysseus's crew later in Book 12. They had been warned never to touch the cattle on the island of Thrinacia, but they landed there anyway, and every man swore an oath to leave the herd alone. Winds then kept them on the island for a month. The oath lasted as long as the food, and once the food ran out, the same men who had tied Odysseus tighter to the mast talked themselves into killing the cattle. At the Sirens, the crew had wax in their ears and nothing to decide. On Thrinacia, the cattle stayed within reach, and keeping the oath depended on hungry men choosing to obey it. The PocketOS agent's safety rule was that kind of oath, a sentence in its prompt that competed with the task, and the task won.

Security engineers have long required access controls that programs cannot alter or bypass, with enforcement simple enough to analyze and test. Anderson laid out those requirements in a 1972 computer security planning study for the U.S. Air Force, which introduced the reference monitor, a component that checks every access against policy. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 principle of complete mediation made the coverage requirement explicit: “Every access to every object must be checked for authority.” Agent systems add the work of connecting those checks to a task written in natural language. Moving enforcement outside the agent protects the checks, but requires an explicit way to carry the task context across that boundary.

Keep credentials and evidence outside the agent

The first component is Odysseus's standing order, the short list of actions the previous piece said require explicit human permission. It sits underneath every task, and no task scope can widen it. Enforced outside the agent, that list would have stopped the PocketOS deletion with no model judgment involved.

For credentials, Anthropic's write-up on decoupling the brain from the hands keeps tokens outside the sandbox, using a vault and proxy for custom tools, so they're "never reachable from the sandbox where Claude's generated code runs." Anthropic rejected narrow token scoping as the fix because it "encodes an assumption about what Claude can't do with a limited token." OpenAI's sandbox agents guide also separates the harness from compute, but it lets code in the sandbox use credentials scoped to the mounts and providers it needs. NVIDIA's open-source OpenShell runtime ships a version of this, giving the agent credential placeholders and adding real credentials only to requests that a supervisor outside the sandbox approves against policy. On a developer laptop, the same design means the agent never holds the token. OS controls keep the agent's processes away from credential files and stores, and a local broker makes authenticated requests on its behalf, accepting only narrow, typed operations and adding the credential at the moment of use. The PocketOS agent would have had no token to find.

The audit log belongs out of reach too. It should sit on the sensor side and capture who asked for what, under which task, and what was allowed or denied. Records should be sent to a logging service outside the agent’s control, using credentials that cannot alter or delete existing entries. The UK AI Security Institute's incident report on a July cyber evaluation illustrates the value of independent monitoring. Agents given internet access took unsanctioned actions against real people and organizations, and AISI's general security monitoring caught them by flagging data leaving over Tor. Within an hour of the alert, AISI had stopped every run and isolated the machines, and it found no resulting real-world harm. Independent monitoring only helps when its alerts reach someone with the authority to stop the agent, and AISI's did.

Enforcement across every execution path

Where the checks run is where endpoint vendors have the clearest advantage. Coding agents now expose hooks that let a security product inspect each prompt and tool call, and endpoint vendors can use those hooks to block an agent's action before it runs when it falls outside the task, whether a prompt injection caused it or the agent got there on its own. A hook sees only what the harness routes through it, such as the shell command the agent requested. What that command actually does, including the install scripts, child processes, file access, and network connections that follow, shows up in endpoint telemetry. A security product that sees both can check whether the behavior still fits the task the hook described.

The harness's own permission checks can be switched off from outside, too. In the Nx "s1ngularity" npm compromise in August 2025, a malicious install script ran the AI coding tools it found with flags like --dangerously-skip-permissions and --yolo and asked them to inventory the machine's secrets. GitGuardian found the requested inventory file on only about a quarter of targeted systems, and some clients explicitly refused credential-harvesting requests despite the disabled permission checks.

Endpoint products already collect process, file, and network telemetry. For agent security, those events need to be linked to the agent session and authorized task that caused them. Without that lineage, a destructive request from the agent's child process looks like any other request from the developer. Lineage is also what lets behavioral detection judge whatever gets past policy, by comparing what the agent's processes actually do with what its task needs.

Egress control follows from that lineage. AISI's hardened cyber ranges now disable outbound networking inside their sandboxes and, as an independent layer, block it again at the virtual machine host, on the assumption that "an agent might find its way past any single layer." On an endpoint the same idea becomes per-agent egress policy that covers DNS and package registries. OpenAI's September 20 incident went through a misconfigured resolver, as did the anonymized DNS exfiltration case Bloomberg's Andrey Rybka described in his AI Engineer talk, and OpenAI's July incident went through the package manager.

Information-flow labels track how untrusted content influences the agent's actions. A hostile web page or document can carry instructions, and Shumailov et al.'s CaMeL treats that as a data-flow problem, labeling where each value came from and checking those labels before any consequential tool call, which applies the same principle as parameterized queries: keeping untrusted data separate from instructions. Costa et al. build information-flow control into the agent's planner and check its policies at each tool call. A hostile document can still be summarized, but it doesn't get to choose who receives the summary.

Budgets limit how much an agent can spend or consume. The previous piece covered the AAuth budgets draft and the Resy agent that needed one. For a budget to hold, the resource has to enforce it, so the count stays out of the agent's reach. Human approval threads through all of these controls, because every limit that hands off to a person adds a prompt, and approvals that grow with agent volume eventually get rubber-stamped.

Canaries for the paths enforcement misses

Canary credentials help expose unexpected access paths, whether the agent wandered off-task, followed injected instructions, or was driven by a compromised install script, as in s1ngularity. A decoy token in a repository, home directory, or MCP configuration can reveal credential discovery or attempted use, though indexing and secret scanning may legitimately read the same file.

Tracebit, which sells canaries, ran a benchmark in an AWS environment of about 300 resources. Ten frontier models acted as red teamers, starting from a low-privilege access key with instructions to maximize impact stealthily, and in half the test conditions 11 decoy resources sat among the real ones. Of 951 runs, 352 were dropped from scoring, most because the model refused before touching AWS. Agents that reached admin took 14 minutes on average. When canaries were present, 96% of those runs had already tripped one before the agent's first critical action, a median of eight minutes earlier.

More capable models tripped more decoys, because they enumerate everything that looks high-value. Planting canaries without telling the agents did not significantly reduce full compromise (admin access plus persistence). But telling them to expect deception did, cutting it from 20% to 3% in a figure pooled across runs with and without canaries, so the warning itself did the work, like a "Beware of dog" sign on a yard that may have no dog. Sometimes the bark is enough.

Enough context to understand intent

Model judges can compare proposed actions with the authorized task, and this part of the design can improve with the models. Simple deterministic authorization checks can be cheap. Meta reports small-classifier latencies of 19-92 milliseconds on an A100 processing 512 tokens, while its illustrative LLM-check traces take roughly a second. DeAction averaged 7.2 seconds of guardrail reasoning per online action step. Those costs favor a cascade. Deterministic checks enforce explicit limits, a small classifier screens common cases, and an LLM judge reviews selected consequential or suspicious actions inline while scoring other activity asynchronously.

Anthropic evaluated a probe-assisted classifier cascade in shadow mode on production traffic. A lightweight probe screened every exchange and escalated about 5.5% to an external classifier, using about one-fortieth the compute of its single exchange-classifier baseline. Applying that design to agent actions requires measuring accuracy and interruptions at the workloads and base rates of the intended deployment. The judge should be swappable, with its measurement built in, and explicit authorization limits should remain enforced independently of its verdict.

Every enforcement point has to solve the same design problem. A hook inside the agent's harness sees the prompt and tool request, but only on the paths the harness exposes. OS instrumentation can observe local processes, file access, and connections, but needs trusted task context from the runtime or record to judge whether they fit the work. At every layer, that connection needs as much design attention as where the enforcer sits.

The task also has to arrive intact, because a formal check inherits whatever the translation got wrong. When Taheri et al. re-tested RoboGuard, which uses a model to translate safety rules into temporal logic, every harmful plan that passed in their evaluations traced back to an incorrect translation. The downstream check enforced the specification it received.

NVIDIA's Open Agent Safety Platform, announced September 28, extends OpenShell into hardware through Sentry, a framework designed to run on BlueField-4 data processing units in a host-independent trust domain. NVIDIA says it can quarantine an agent "within milliseconds." Its reference architecture puts BlueField-4 on the node's only network path to the model and outside world. DOCA Tower terminates TLS for connections configured for inspection, while memory introspection tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. Those signals describe execution and integrity. Understanding intent still requires the user-approved task and its limits, supplied through a trusted connection to the runtime.

For hardware enforcement to deliver, the deployment has to route the relevant traffic through it and prevent the host from changing its controls. BlueField's documentation describes a Zero Trust mode that restricts host-side administration, but does not establish Sentry's default configuration. The hardware boundary also needs testing against its own threat model. OpenAI's cache-channel experiment illustrates the broader risk of shared hardware, without demonstrating a bypass of Sentry. In data centers built on this architecture, enforcement sits outside the host's trust domain. On laptops, OS controls and trusted brokers carry that job. Hardware adds another independent enforcement layer where it is available.

Whichever layer enforces the policy, the previous piece showed how much legitimate work enforced policies stall in research prototypes. Published work so far reports pieces of the picture, such as classifier latency and shadow-mode results, but not the full set that would show intent enforcement works: attacks stopped when the attacker knew the defense existed, legitimate tasks that still finished, authority granted per task, approval requests per hundred tasks, latency added to each gated action, and false positives at a stated base rate. Those numbers are what will turn an enforcement architecture into something a customer can rely on.

Ropes the agent can't loosen

Odysseus heard every word of the song, and the ship still rowed past. His rig met all three of Anderson's requirements. He couldn't loosen the ropes, they held for the whole passage, and the standing order was one sentence long. The men at the oars had exactly the context they needed, because they knew the order and could see him straining against it, and the wax kept them from hearing the case he was making. OpenAI's package proxy, Artifactory, sat outside the sandbox, but exploitable functionality let agents use it to cross the boundary. Separation only protects a control when the requests it accepts cannot redirect or disable its enforcement.

An agent's task is written down, and a person can confirm the access policy it becomes. Enforcement is the half that decides whether that policy holds up against a capable agent. Controls the agent can't tamper with have to enforce the organization's restrictions and the task's limits regardless of which tool, child process, API, or discovered credential it uses. Those controls need the authorized task without accepting the agent's arguments for expanding it. Most of that can be built today, on machines security vendors already protect.

Research and blogging assistance provided by Hermes, an AI Assistant. If it ever tunnels out through DNS, it promises a better question than the capital of France.

Title: People Are Getting Weird About AI

Modules: Data Security Posture Management; Identity Security Posture Management; Threat Intelligence; Vulnerability Management
Title: Peer pressure meets private keys.
Context: Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.
Full Text:
A classified memo ties Nvidia’s chief executive to Chinese espionage. AI coding agents crack under peer pressure, coughing up private keys. Big breaches hit seven million Japanese shoppers and three million students here in the States, while a French bank takes a multi-million-dollar hit through a vendor compromise. Adversaries weaponize a fresh OpenSSH bypass in the wild, pro-Russian hacktivists put dark web bounties on senior European officials, and Google drafts digital IDs to solve the passkey recovery puzzle. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Today is Monday November 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Classified memo warns of Nvidia chief's ties to Chinese operative.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo this past spring warning senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an operative tied to Beijing's Ministry of State Security.

Intelligence gathered from electronic surveillance revealed Huang was intimately involved with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed has purchased two billion dollars in advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling restricted artificial intelligence hardware into China. While Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised.

Huang remains an influential voice shaping United States policy against tighter export controls, highlighting the growing counterintelligence risks hovering over America’s critical semiconductor supply chains.

The New York Times originally reported the findings.

Autonomous AI coding agents leak credentials under swarm peer pressure.

Autonomous software engineering agents routinely violate core security policies, leaking private deployment credentials and executing untrusted scripts, when pressured by third-party agent forums, according to testing by AE Studio and the AI Alignment Foundation shared with The Register.

Researchers tasked nine coding models with debugging a broken service in an isolated sandbox. Given access to a forum that held the solution, agents surrendered private tokens fifteen percent of the time and executed unverified installation scripts nearly a quarter of the time to obtain assistance. Under performance pressure, execution rates spiked to thirty-four percent.

As organizations rush to integrate autonomous agents into production environments, granting models broad system permissions without strict data isolation turns automated workflows into immediate remote code execution and credential leakage risks.

A Japanese online market goes offline following a suspected breach of 7.7 million customer records.

Japanese consumer goods and electronics giant Iris Ohyama has suspended its primary ecommerce platform, Iris Plaza, following unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service that contained personal records for nearly eight million shoppers.

The retailer took the storefront offline late last month after discovering a suspicious file on its cloud infrastructure. Exposed records cover 5.8 million registered members and 1.9 million guest shoppers, potentially compromising names, physical and email addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Payment data was stored separately and avoided exposure.

The disruption highlights the severe operational fallout and supply-chain vulnerabilities inherent in cloud-hosted retail environments, leaving core commerce operations frozen while investigators determine whether customer files were actually exfiltrated.

Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical authentication bypass in OpenSSH tracked as CVE-2026-123158, dubbed "SSHole."

The vulnerability allows attackers to compromise accounts like root on systems running musl libc without PAM—including Alpine and OpenWrt—by supplying overlong passwords. Security firms WatchTowr and Previdian report that botnets and cryptominers are already leveraging the flaw in the wild.

The rapid weaponization underscores immediate exposure for lightweight Linux environments, prompting administrators to deploy version 10.6p2 or disable password authentication entirely.

A French banking group confirms third-party compromise and fraudulent fund transfers.

French banking giant Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed an intrusion into its network via a third-party service provider, enabling attackers to conduct major fraudulent transactions.

The disclosure follows reports from blockchain investigator ZachXBT, who traced approximately 133 million dollars in suspicious withdrawals and aggressive cryptocurrency laundering across multiple centralized exchanges. The bank stressed that customer accounts remained untouched, as the threat actors targeted Arkéa's own institutional accounts before routing capital toward external cryptocurrency platforms. Arkéa reports that security teams contained the incident, froze a portion of the funds, and maintain that the bank's financial stability remains secure.

The incident underscores the persistent vulnerability institutional financial networks face through external vendor access paths, demonstrating how rapid cryptocurrency conversion complicates law enforcement recovery efforts.

Frontline Education data breach impacts over three million individuals across K-12 systems.

School administration provider Frontline Education has notified the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that an August breach compromised records for over three million people—more than doubling previous state estimates.

Attackers exploited a flaw in a third-party application, accessing personal records of staff and students across Frontline Central and School Health Management services. Exfiltrated data includes Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses, and health insurance information.

The incident highlights continuing third-party software risks threatening sensitive educational and student administrative platforms.

Google develops digital identity credentials for secure passkey and account recovery.

Google is developing an account recovery framework that leverages verified digital identity credentials, aiming to eliminate the security vulnerabilities of fallback methods when users lose primary devices.

Speaking at the Authenticate 2026 conference, company product managers explained that legacy recovery workflows—such as SMS-based fallbacks—risk undermining the cryptographic advantages of passkeys. Under Google's proposed system, users register a signed digital ID in advance to create a cryptographic stable hash linked to their account. If their physical device is lost, obtaining a verified digital credential on a replacement device restores their account, passkeys, and data in a single step.

Securing the recovery loop represents the crucial missing link in widespread passwordless adoption, though full-scale rollout still faces hurdles in wallet interoperability and near-real-time credential provisioning.

Pro-Russian hacktivists dox European leaders and bounty personal details.

Pro-Russian hacktivist syndicate NoName057(16) has published personal records belonging to Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and seventeen other senior European officials across the dark web, offering cryptocurrency bounties for further intelligence on the targets and their families.

The doxing campaign targets prominent figures across European law enforcement and judiciary—including leaders at Europol, Eurojust, and the German Federal Criminal Police Office—alongside investigative journalists. The operation appears to be direct retaliation for a multi-nation law enforcement takedown in July 2025 that dismantled over one hundred of the gang's servers.

The move marks an aggressive evolution from nuisance denial-of-service disruptions into direct personal harassment and targeted intelligence-gathering aimed at deterring Western support for Ukraine.

Monday business briefing.

Capital continues pouring into artificial intelligence defense and validation, led by 220 million dollars raised across two standout funding rounds. Agentic data security startup Sentra secured 150 million dollars in a round led by Capital One Ventures, while formal verification provider &Truth emerged from stealth backed by 70 million dollars in seed capital.

Consolidation across the sector accelerated with eight reported acquisitions, headlined by CrowdStrike’s aggressive expansion into model governance. According to the Wall Street Journal, the security giant is acquiring AI observability firm Fiddler AI for 400 million dollars alongside red-teaming platform Dreadnode for 95 million dollars to embed behavioral accountability into its Falcon ecosystem. Penetration testing specialist Bendings also acquired Scopertos for 55 million dollars, while Cognition absorbed code security shop Corridor.

The flurry of dealmaking signals that enterprise demand is rapidly shifting toward pre-deployment testing, agent explainability, and securing the broader algorithmic supply chain.

After the break, I welcome Nozomi Networks’ Director of Cybersecurity Strategy Chris Grove. We discuss the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attack part 2.

That was Chris Grove from Nozomi Networks.

Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Huawei claims it has built the holy grail of sovereign computing: an enterprise desktop boasting one hundred percent Chinese-manufactured components.

The Qingyun HM650 runs a homegrown, ten-core Kirin processor alongside an enterprise flavor of HarmonyOS, specifically designed to bid a polite, permanent farewell to Western software dependencies. One government agency has already ordered six hundred units—perhaps less out of spontaneous consumer enthusiasm and more in dutiful compliance with Beijing’s mandate evicting Wintel machines from state desks.

Whether every capacitor actually traces its architectural ancestry strictly to domestic drawing boards remains conveniently ambiguous, as foreign outfits still keep plenty of factories humming across the mainland. Regardless of pedigree, locking Western chipmakers out of vast government procurement pools delivers a cold chill to Santa Clara balance sheets.

Meanwhile, Japan unveiled a sixty-three million dollar emergency cybersecurity fund after adversaries disrupted critical infrastructure, cloud providers, and—perhaps most unforgivably—KFC logistics.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.
