Full Text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Orca automatically maps it to the regulatory compliance frameworks you report on, such as PCI DSS 4.0 and SOC 2, so you know which controls are affected now and have the evidence ready once remediation is done, instead of scrambling for it later.

Cut the time to fix. Orca opens tickets in tools you already use with the affected nodes and fixed kernel version already filled in, so engineers start fixing instead of investigating, and you can track every ticket through to closure. Where patching has to wait, disabling the affected kernel module is a quick interim mitigation.

Catch an attack before the patch lands. Rolling new images across a fleet takes time, and that window is when attackers move. Orca’s cloud detection and response monitors affected workloads for suspicious activity, so if someone tries to use the foothold, you know right away and can respond.

Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. From the first alert to the closed ticket, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows you where a CVE runs, whether it’s exposed, whether it’s exploitable, what it can reach, and how it affects your compliance posture. Copy Fail is one example. The same workflow works for whatever CVE lands next.

See it in your own environment. Request a demo and we’ll walk through how Orca triages the Kubernetes CVEs that matter most to your clusters. To go deeper on Orca’s Kubernetes and Container Security capabilities, download the data sheet.

Title: Railway’s AI agents go off the track on a rival’s network
Context: Amir Boldo, co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences...
Full Text:
AI agents operated by cloud infrastructure and application hosting platform, Railway, have attempted to access a rival platform’s infrastructure, prompting the cloud provider’s leadership to acknowledge the incident on social media.

Railway senior product engineer Jake Runzer acknowledged running agents to perform signups and agentic testing on similar platforms after Primcloud founder Josh Manders publicly questioned why Railway employees were attempting to breach his infrastructure.

Runzer said he had halted the testing harness after it began reaching too far. Railway co-founder and CEO Jake Cooper apologized, saying the models were “getting a bit too good at this point,” and pledged to prohibit non-manual external testing.

According to Manders, the agents attempted to receive credentials from an application container, request platform secrets, access cloud-provider metadata, discover internal databases and caches, and scan all 65,536 addresses on Primcloud’s internal network twice.

The activity reportedly involved 24 scripted commands over 15 minutes.

“An agent can act without a person directing every step,” said Diana Kelley, chief information security officer at Noma Security. “It doesn’t remove the responsibility of the people and organizations that deploy it.”

Primcloud said its defenses blocked every attempt and that “nothing” was accessed. The incident follows Railway’s own security disclosure involving encrypted customer environment variables.

The engineer was acting on his own

Cooper said the employee had developed the testing tool independently, using personal accounts, a personal credit card, and his own time. He added that Runzer ran it against a single external provider and halted it proactively within 15 minutes, adding that Railway had addressed the incident internally.

“I can confirm they ran this tool once and only once,” Cooper said in an X post. “Railway does not condone these actions. We expect all our employees to uphold our standards of conduct, whether acting on behalf of Railway or in a personal capacity.”

Although that timeline checks out with Manders’ own account, some details remain murky. After publicly calling out Runzer on X, Manders posted a follow-up, saying he had observed another attempt to access the account after his initial warning.

“I see you tried to access the account after this tweet too, Jake,” he had written more than 30 minutes after his first post.

Primcloud does not have a bug bounty program, according to its Acceptable Use Policy (AUP). It forbids unauthorized probing, scanning, or vulnerability testing without prior written consent.

‘The AI did it’ is not an accountability strategy

Experts condemn Railway’s “rogue AI” explanation for the incident.

Amir Boldo, co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences without any malicious intent.

Execution traces can establish what an agent did, but they cannot independently prove intent, he said, adding that investigators need evidence spanning instructions, identities, permissions, inputs and tool calls. “You can’t put an agent on trial. You can hold each party accountable for its part,” Boldo said.

Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck, argued that users may not fully appreciate that delegating work to an agent also delegates the authority associated with their identity.

“We now have to ask what happens when trusted identity is delegated to a non-deterministic system capable of independently deciding how to use it,” Lewis said. Cooper confirmed in his X post that Railway had addressed the incident internally and was reinforcing its expectations for employee conduct, including when employees act in a personal capacity.

Title: The Flood is Coming And The Pipes Were Already Full
Context: Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start
Full Text:
An update on Athena, and some unsolicited predictions on what's coming next

On Saturday, Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier. I agree with him. Go read it if you haven't. I've spent the summer looking at what these models find, and the gap he describes between what they can do and what the rest of us are ready for is the one I've been staring at since May.

The hardest piece of his plan is the one that asks governments to coordinate. They're in a difficult spot: regulate too little and a US company accidentally builds the weapon, regulate too much and it gets built somewhere else, and open source isn't governable either way. Where governments can act is on consumption: not what the models can do, but what happens to what they find. Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start. That's what Gold Eagle is.

It matters because of where the risk actually lands. The danger in Dario's essay isn't a model in a lab. It's a model pointed at the power grid, the water system, the hospital network, all of it running on decades of software with the same exploitable design. The frontier is where the capability comes from. Consumption is where it does damage, and that's the end you can still defend.

So pacing has two ends. The frontier end is Dario's and the government's problem, and it's hard. The consumption end is ours: the disclosure processes, the patch pipelines, and the software itself, everything that has to absorb what the models produce. Pacing buys time on the frontier end. This post is a status report on how we're spending it, in three parts:

We start disclosing Athena findings this month, beginning with 50.

We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing and are finding our own vulnerabilities, and I'll show you what that looks like.

We built infrastructure to make both possible, and we're going to open it up.

The short version: I'm more worried than I was in May, and more sure about what to do about it.

The first 50

Athena has been taking in findings since June. The intake numbers are public: more than 40,000 findings, 42% of them critical or high, across more than 500 projects, with more than 2,000 patches produced. What hasn't been public is how much of that we've been sitting on. Generating fixes was never the bottleneck. Disclosing them responsibly, at a scale nobody has ever tried, is.

On September 28, we start. We're beginning with about fifty, and none of them are the scary ones. That's deliberate. The frightening findings, the live pre-auth RCEs, go through Akrites on embargo, which I'll come back to. The first 50 are low-stakes on purpose: a small batch to get the flywheel turning and find out what breaks before the thousands behind them hit it.

All 50 are silent fixes: vulnerabilities already fixed at head, sometimes years ago, where nobody ever filed a CVE. Your scanner has nothing to say about them, and the old versions are still running everywhere. This pattern showed up in Athena almost immediately. A big share of what the models find only affects old versions, because the models scan what's actually deployed, and what's deployed is old.

Two systems fail at once with silent fixes, and neither is anyone's fault. Upstreams typically won't merge fixes to old versions, and they're right not to: the code was rewritten years ago, there's no branch to merge into, and "upgrade" is the correct answer. And the advisory layer has nothing to work with, because CVEs don't get filed for things already fixed at head. It's the one class of finding where acting doesn't step on anyone else's process, because there isn't one.

For each one, where the project has no path for accepting fixes to old versions, we're doing three things.

We publish the patch. Plain .patch files, in a public Chainguard repo that says exactly what it is on the tin, under the project's original license. This is deliberately not a maintainer-of-last-resort move. We have plans for that, and I'll get to them below, but they're for projects nobody maintains anymore. These are active projects that already fixed the bug at head. We're not forking anything, not claiming stewardship, not creating a new namespace, and not inviting anyone to build from it. It's a place to put patches for the people who can't upgrade yet, and nothing more. The durable fix is still upgrading, but this step reflects today's reality, where most of what's deployed isn't upgraded.

We publish the advisory. A Chainguard OSV feed, with fully enumerated affected version ranges and the exact symbols affected. Not "some 2.x releases, probably." Athena partner scanners are integrating with it now, so these show up where your team already looks.

We ship the fix. Patched versions land in Chainguard Libraries for every Chainguard customer the moment the advisory goes live.

We're not planning to contact maintainers ahead of each of these. They already deal with more noise than anyone should, and we don't want to add to it, least of all for bugs they fixed years ago. If you maintain a project and you'd rather hear from us in advance going forward, or you have any other concerns about how this touches your project, let us know at cna@chainguard.dev and we'll happily work with you.

We're becoming a CNA

A silent fix used to be mostly harmless. Nobody had written the bug down, and finding it from a fix commit took real expertise and real time. That's over. A model can go from a public fix commit to a working exploit against every version that never got the fix in an afternoon. The finding exists whether we publish it or not. The only question is whether defenders get a copy, too.

Once people know about a bug, the world needs a signal to upgrade, and the signal the world already has is the CVE. Scanners, KEV, and every compliance regime key on it. Silent fixes had none. So, in support of the Gold Eagle initiative, and in partnership with CISA, Chainguard is in progress to become a CVE Numbering Authority, scoped to open source vulnerabilities processed through Athena where upstream already fixed the flaw without an identifier, or where no maintainer is left to assign one, and no more specific CNA covers the project.

The uncomfortable part: this will put new noise in your scanners. Old versions that scanned clean last week will light up. That's better than no noise and a breach. Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet.

We also go to great lengths to keep each advisory as narrow as it can be. Every entry is enriched with the exact introduced and fixed ranges across every release branch, not a single version floor, and carries module, class, and function level detail on what's actually affected. That's what reachability scanners need to filter out the false positives for your codebase, so the noise you do see should be the noise that matters.

The narrowness is the point. We assign only where there is no upstream to defer to. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, the project's own CNA assigns it, and we are the reporter, never the assigner. Every assignment clears the same gates: a reproduced finding, never raw model output; a defensible commit range; affected versions in real use; the maintainer notified with a response window; and withdrawal if the maintainer shows us we're wrong. Projects that become their own CNA leave our scope. This is a transitional role, not a territorial one.

Where the rest goes

The map for everything else is simple. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, that's Plan A, and it runs through Akrites, the shared disclosure body the Linux Foundation launched in June, and that we helped found. If it exists at latest and the project is unmaintained, that's maintainer-of-last-resort territory, and we're working with other Akrites members to stand that up inside Akrites, where it belongs. And Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse that came out of June's executive order, is the layer that gets prioritized findings in front of the critical infrastructure operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline.

We spent a good part of the summer waiting on both of those and helping build them. Akrites goes operational this month. I'll be straight about the tradeoff: one shared incident response team across dozens of organizations is slower at first than everyone acting alone. That's the cost of choosing "maintainers deal with one trusted counterpart" over "maintainers deal with thirty strangers," and we'd make it again. The disclosure and upstreaming numbers get published either way, pretty or not.

A model found all of it in an afternoon

The second reason I'm worried is less about process and more about what I've seen. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing. Lots of organizations have, at this point, roughly 200 across 15-plus countries, so our joining isn't news on its own. What matters is what it means for Athena: we now have Mythos, and we're running it against the software we build and ship.

Here's the shape of one run, and I've picked it because it's the least reassuring result we have.

One widely used open source project. One run, about six hours. The harness came back with more than a dozen validated vulnerabilities, most of them pre-authentication remote code execution, reachable with no credentials and no operator action. Every one was reproduced three times in a clean VM before it counted, under the rule I'll describe in a minute: the model doesn't get to claim a finding, the host has to reproduce it. This is not an abandoned package. It's one of the most heavily scanned, tested, and fuzzed projects in the ecosystem, code that has survived years of expert review and relentless fuzzing. A model found all of it in an afternoon. These go through Akrites like everyone else's findings, and I'm not going to say more about the specific project here than that.

Here's what I'll say instead. Watching what these models find, and how long it takes a fix to reach anyone once they find it, is what worries me. It isn't the models themselves. It's the race between two clocks. On one, the industry is trying to absorb a short-term rush of findings through disclosure processes that were already behind. On the other, attacker capability is advancing toward the point where compromising critical infrastructure at scale becomes cheap. Right now, the second clock is running faster than the first, and I don't see anything that closes that gap on its own.

Sandboxes and sandboxing

Which is the other reason the sandbox matters. Producing a finding like the one above means building and detonating a working exploit against real code, over and over, driven by an agent nobody is watching in real time. That is dangerous to run, and this summer has been a run of examples of people running it unsafely. The incident Dario built his essay around, OpenAI's agents breaking out of a cyber evaluation and ending up inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure, started with a zero-day in the package cache the agents had been given. Package infrastructure is what we build, so that one landed close to home. Pillar Security spent a week in July publishing sandbox escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and the finding that tied them together was that the agent almost never broke the sandbox head-on. It wrote a file it was allowed to write, and something trusted outside the box ran it later. None of these was a problem of insufficient sandboxes. They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it. Denylists don't contain any better than containers do.

Everything Athena does, from developing an exploit to proving a patch closes the hole, runs inside a microVM, the same primitive our package builds, image builds, and CI have run on for years. Matt wrote up the architecture in July. The short version: every job gets a hardware-virtualized guest with its own kernel and a root filesystem built from scratch, egress is enforced at the hypervisor and allowlisted to package registries and nothing else, the first forbidden connection destroys the VM, and no credentials ever enter the guest. And because a shared primitive multiplies the blast radius of any weakness, we point AI agents at the sandbox itself with instructions to break it. Every finding lands as a failing test first, then the fix.

The harness starts with a person

The harness that runs inside those sandboxes is the part I find most interesting, and it starts with a person. Ian Beer spent about six months writing a zero-click iOS exploit chain, and if you read the write-up as a search, you can see the shape of it: poke at a target, go deep, hit a dead end, back up, eventually connect enough dots to reach a working exploit. No human holds six months of that in working memory. He kept it in notes and pulled back the slice he needed each session. His notebook was the environment.

That's what we built, sharded across many agents in parallel: a tree search where every agent starts fresh with a scoped surface and a distilled trail of what's already known, and continuity lives in durable findings rather than anyone's context window. The rule I care most about is that the host casts the vote, never the model. A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after. Nothing enters the record until reality agrees, and that one rule is most of why the false positive rate is as low as it is.

A few things we learned building this, if you're working on something similar:

Fresh context, bounded job. Every agent starts clean with a scoped surface. Continuity lives in findings written for a stranger, not a transcript.

Every write gated on evidence. Without a precondition, a postcondition, and a host-runnable replay, it doesn't enter the record.

Research steers, it doesn't prove. It decides where an agent looks next and never counts as a finding.

Record dead ends as findings, too. A false positive collides with reality and starves on its own. A false negative is silent, permanent, and the failure that actually costs you the deep bugs.

Taste beats fleet size. In a search like this, the model's per-step judgment about where to look is the base of an exponent, and parallelism only shows up inside a logarithm. You cannot buy your way out of worse taste with more agents. That's the concrete, non-marketing reason we wanted Mythos, and why Glasswing matters more than how many agents you can run.

Put the pieces together, and the loop closes. Find, contain, fix, ship. All of it on one primitive.

What we built to do this, and what we're opening up

None of this was possible on off-the-shelf infrastructure. Over the last year, we rebuilt our factory on three new primitives, and every one of them started as something we needed for ourselves before it was anything we could sell.

The sandbox is the microVM you just read about: the isolation boundary that lets us run untrusted code and hostile agents without the blast radius reaching anything that matters. The harness is the search that runs inside it, the thing that found those pre-auth RCEs. And the third is CI as a function: our own fleet stopped sending code out to a CI system a year ago. The checks run in the loop, and changes arrive already proven, at more than ten times the CVE volume we were handling before.

We built all three because we had to; we've been running our entire operation on them, and over the coming quarters, we're going to start opening them up directly. If you are running untrusted AI workloads, or trying to find real vulnerabilities in your own code, or drowning in CI that tells you less than you'd like, these are the tools we reached for. Soon you'll be able to reach for them too.

So what is the endgame here?

Here's the unsolicited prediction. Everyone is worried about Mythos zero-days right now, and almost nobody was keeping up with ordinary CVEs before any of this started. The median enterprise is months behind on patches that have had fixes, advisories, and scanner coverage for years. That's the system we're about to pour thousands of new findings into. Faster disclosure and faster patching only help the people who can move on them, and most of the world can't move at the speed a model sets. If you take one thing from this post, take this: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full.

Which is why none of the above is the finish line. Everything in this post makes us faster, and all of it accepts a losing premise: that the goal is to keep pace with a discovery rate set by frontier models. The vulnerability classes those models exploit aren't defects in today's software. They're its design. Memory corruption, deserialization, injection, confused deputies: consequences of how the stacks under every enterprise application were built. You cannot patch your way out of an architecture.

So the endgame is new foundations: a stack built secure by construction, where the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written in the first place, filling the role Spring Boot fills today, across every enterprise language, underneath the frameworks and the registries they pull from. For forty years, migration costs protected every incumbent platform. Nobody rewrote the COBOL because nobody could afford to. Agents just collapsed that cost.

We're working on this, and I'll say more when there's more to say. Why us: we see the world's pre-disclosure findings before almost anyone, so we know which bug classes matter, and we have the one tool that can prove a foundation removed them. Point Mythos at it before you ship, and you know.

Dario is right that pacing buys time, and everything above is how we're spending it. But a paced frontier only matters if the software underneath survives the frontier we already have. If the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written, the critical infrastructure built on them can't be broken by them, and a frontier model in the wrong hands has far less to reach. Pacing limits the risk by slowing the capability. Foundations limit it by taking away the target, and that's the only version of this I can see that ends the treadmill instead of running faster on it.

The Programmer's Credo says we do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy when we started. This is the first one where I didn't even think that. We're doing it anyway.

If you maintain a project any of this touches, or if you're finding vulnerabilities, join at chainguard.dev/athena. And if any of this sounds like something you want to build, we're hiring.

Title: UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash
Context: The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats
Full Text: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail. An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week. In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation. The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats. Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations. Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology. "Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law. Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties. "The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said. "The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened. "Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

Title: Half of Security Leaders Report Sensitive Data Exposure Through AI Tools
Context: Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found
Full Text:
Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found.

Of these incidents, 77% involved a company-approved AI tool.

The researchers said the findings demonstrate that many organizations lack visibility into the types of data being shared with AI tools, even those that are approved for use in the enterprise.

While 62% of respondents could identify users or departments sending data to AI tools, less than half (48%) said they could provide any record of the types of data that had left the organization through AI tools.

“This shows why security teams cannot stop at deciding which AI tools employees are allowed to use. Organizations also need to control what information is shared with them," commented Darren Williams, founder and CEO of BlackFog.

Almost all organizations (98%) reported having an AI usage policy in place. However, the ability to enforce such policies varied significantly.

Just over half (56%) support their broader AI usage policies with comprehensive technical controls. Around a third (35%) said that while their organization has a written policy specifying what information employees must not enter into AI prompts, there is no technical enforcement.

Meanwhile, 39% of security leaders admitted that AI adoption is moving faster than they can govern it. Of those respondents feeling outpaced, just 27% have comprehensive AI controls in place.

AI Agents Fall Outside of Organizations’ Governance Strategies

The BlackFog research, published on November 4, also highlighted a significant governance gap around AI agents operating in organizations’ environments.

Over half (56%) revealed that autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of employees fall outside their organization’s existing controls.

Read now: Unchecked AI Agents Cause Cybersecurity Incidents at Two Thirds of Firms

Technology and telecoms were the industries where this issue was most prevalent, with 70% of respondents stating that autonomous AI agents were outside of organizational controls.

In addition, only 54% of security leaders said they had the ability to block or restrict unsanctioned AI tools and around a third (32%) are able to detect shadow AI use but are unable to consistently stop it.

Title: UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk
Context: At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure
Full Text:
At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

The State of UK Critical Infrastructure

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

Andy Burnham's Government Makes Cyber Changes

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Specialized reporting requirements

Evidence preservation requirements

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Cybersecurity Experts Weigh in on CNI Defense

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Title: Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his very personal use
Context: " After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's...
Full Text: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs. "One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call. The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware. Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week. The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies. Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened. And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived. Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action. Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work. The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job. "Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered. By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong. "What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job." After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes. Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place. "You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them." Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

Title: Experts Demonstrate Barracuda Email Security Gateway Chain Enabling Root Access Without Login
Context: watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit
Full Text:
Two flaws in Barracuda's Email Security Gateway, an email-filtering appliance, can be chained to run commands on it as root, its highest level of access, with no login required.

The company released patches on Monday, and the security firm watchTowr detailed the attack chain on Thursday.

One flaw, CVE-2026-116606, is an authorization bypass. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to restore a crafted configuration backup and change the appliance's global settings.

The other, CVE-2026-111560, is a command injection. It runs commands as root but normally needs an administrator account, and on the Email Security Gateway the bypass gives an attacker that access. Chained, the two let an attacker reach root with no login.

Affected Products and Fixes

The authorization bypass affects only the Email Security Gateway. The command injection reaches five other products, but on those it still needs an administrator account.

Mandiant, which assigned the two CVE records, rates the bypass 9.3 out of 10 and the command injection 8.6. Barracuda has released a patch for each affected product and lists the fixed firmware in its security advisory. The Email Security Gateway is fixed in version 9.4.0.030 and later.

What to Do

The advisory sets out three steps:

Apply the patch for each affected product, or upgrade to the fixed firmware listed above.

If you cannot patch at once, limit the appliance's administration interface to trusted internal networks.

If you have turned automatic patching off, switch it back on.

How the Chain Works

In its technical analysis, watchTowr traced the chain through the appliance's code. A failed password change returns the attacker a low-privilege role instead of stopping the request, which leaves a backup-restore function open to someone who has not logged in.

That function accepts an uploaded backup, and the restored data includes a timezone value that the appliance later runs as a shell command with root privileges. Barracuda guards backups with a checksum, but the secret used to compute it is built into the code, allowing an attacker to forge a valid checksum. The firm showed the attack by writing a file to the appliance as root.

As of this week, neither flaw appears in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV catalog), and no public report ties either to an attack. watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit.

The Email Security Gateway was hit in the 2023 attacks by a group tracked as UNC4841, which exploited a different flaw, CVE-2023-2868, as a zero-day. That case is unrelated to the two flaws patched this week, and nothing ties the new pair to any attacker.

Title: AI agents are a 'bane' for some website operators, says Cloudflare
Context: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince
Full Text: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince. “These vulnerabilities, like the PHP vulnerabilities that were disclosed the other day, had been in the wild for years,” Prince said on the company’s third quarter earnings call. “We're going back through our logs looking for any evidence that hackers or nation-state actors or others had been using them in the past. I know that we're going to find examples of that.” That was just one of the warnings he offered on the call, among them that some of Cloudflare’s customers believe AI agents are “a bane to their business and want to keep them away.” To explain why, Prince hypothesized that he could use an agent to find him a restaurant to eat at after he finishes his day of investor relations duties. “It might go and scour the internet and look at 1,000 different restaurants' websites, pull down 1,000 different menus, and then I might choose to only go to one of those,” he said. “The problem is that 999 of those restaurants have now had a cost that is just been applied to them, but they are not getting any benefit.” The CEO admitted that web searches have always driven some low-value traffic but feels the volume of agentic activity – which Cloudflare has previously predicted will be one thousand times greater than clicks from humans – means the problem is now at a different scale. Prince also had bad news for Kubernetes aficionados, because he thinks containers might become another casualty of the agentic age. The CEO allowed that containers are “a significant improvement over bare metal or even virtual machines,” and said they fueled the growth of hyperscale clouds and mobile applications. But he thinks containers are already cooked. “The container-based architecture of the hyperscalers and neoclouds just can't keep up in a cost-effective way with the new agentic paradigms of today,” he argued, again citing the 1000:1 ratio of bot:human traffic Cloudflare expects to see online any year now. That’s a Cloudflare-centric view, because Prince pitched the company’s serverless “Workers” service as an alternative to containers. The company also offers products that can either block agents, ameliorate the cost and traffic impacts of agentic activity, or allow organizations to monetize traffic generated by AI. Prince said demand for those products is growing fast, claiming that since July 1st, “approximately five percent” of the web opted in to Cloudflare’s content protection products. The CEO said Meta is already a customer, and said Zuck’s new “Muse” agents will benefit Cloudflare by creating more agentic traffic that third parties want to tame. He also pointed to year-on-year revenue growth of 39 percent, which saw quarterly revenue reach a record $782.5 million. And he thinks there are better days ahead, due to the terrible state of security. “It may seem like the sky is falling with the number of new security vulnerabilities that have been reported over the last few weeks,” Prince said. “I wish I could tell you we were through the worst, but we're not.” He thinks Cloudflare can profit from security misery because the extent of its activities and client base mean it is “among the first to receive quiet disclosure of new vulnerabilities” and remediates them before disclosure. Investors thought this all made sense, and in after-hours trading sent Cloudflare shares up by around 15 percent, meaning it recovered and then improved on losses that it incurred earlier after major US indices dropped around four percent as investors who worry tech stocks are overvalued. ®

Title: Beyond the Endpoint: Rethinking Security for the Modern Workspace
Context: Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack
Full Text:
The way we work has changed significantly, and now the way we secure that work is changing with it. Again.

For years, organizations have added security technologies to address new risk categories as they emerged. Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack.

But today's attacks rarely stay within one of those boundaries. This shift is driving a broader approach to protecting the modern digital worker: Workspace Security.

How Do You Define Workspace Security?

The workspace has become an interconnected attack surface, and workspace security looks beyond traditional boundaries to focus on the ways attackers now reach users and business data. Several shifts are accelerating this pivot toward workplace security.

1. Work is increasingly distributed. Endpoints, mobile devices, browsers, SaaS applications, and cloud services have extended work far beyond the corporate network.

2. Identity has become a critical security boundary. Attackers don't always need to break through traditional defenses if they can log in using compromised credentials, tokens, or sessions.

3. Applications and collaboration tools are part of the attack surface. Email, browsers, SaaS, and collaboration platforms connect users directly to business data and provide attackers with more opportunities to target them.

4. AI is adding another interaction layer. Generative AI and copilots are quickly becoming part of everyday workflows, creating new interactions between users, applications, and organizational data. It is also increasing the need for visibility and control into how AI is being used and what data it can access.

Rather than isolated changes, these shifts increasingly overlap within the same workflows and the same attacks.

What are the Risks of Operating Security in Silos?

Because users, identities, devices, applications, data, and AI are interconnected, protecting each in isolation leaves gaps between them.

Security architectures have traditionally been organized around individual control points. Endpoint tools protect devices. Identity tools protect accounts and access. Email security protects communications. Other technologies manage vulnerabilities, applications, and data.

Attackers see the environment differently.

A phishing email might lead to credential theft. Those credentials could provide access to a legitimate application. From there, an attacker may establish persistence, elevate privileges, move across systems, or access sensitive information.

One attack can therefore generate signals across the environment.

How Are Organizations Breaking Down Cybersecurity Silos?

According to Gartner®, "Cybersecurity teams with limited resources and a need to reduce silos require a simpler, more unified approach to securing digital work than traditional multivendor tool stacks. WCPs address this by preintegrating modules to lower costs, reduce errors, and improve cybersecurity posture."

Is Endpoint Security a Key Part of Workspace Security?

The endpoint remains central to the evolution toward workspace security, especially because unified endpoint security platforms have expanded beyond malware protection to include numerous capabilities: attack surface reduction, behavioral detection, and vulnerability and patch management, along with EDR, XDR, and identity threat protection.

At the same time, the risks surrounding the digital worker increasingly extend beyond the endpoint itself. Gartner notes, "WCPs have replaced Gartner’s coverage of the extended detection and response (XDR) market, which no longer exists in its original form. As vendors expanded native modules and improved integration, XDR became a feature within WCPs and other cybersecurity markets."

Workspace Security isn't about making endpoint protection less important. It is about extending its context and connecting protection around the digital worker. This is why the distinction between a collection of security products and an integrated platform is significant.

Integration makes the security controls surrounding the user work together more effectively.

What Does Effective Workspace Security Look Like?

Workspace Security is an evolving approach that brings the protections surrounding digital workers together more cohesively, connecting proactive risk reduction, prevention, detection, and response across the workspace. Organizations evaluating their approach should consider several key principles:

Broad visibility: Can security teams understand risk and activity across endpoints, identities, applications, data, and emerging technologies such as AI?

Proactive risk reduction and prevention: Can the platform identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identity risks, and other exposures, reduce the attack surface, and prevent threats before they become incidents?

Connected context: Can telemetry across devices, identities, applications, and data be correlated to help teams understand the broader attack rather than investigate individual signals in isolation?

Deep integration: Do capabilities genuinely share telemetry, policies, behavioral analysis, and workflows, or are they simply a collection of products from the same vendor?

Simplified operations: Can teams manage policies, prioritize alerts, investigate threats, and take action through centralized workflows with less context switching?

Openness and flexibility: Can the platform integrate with the wider security ecosystem when specialized capabilities or existing investments are still required?

The goal is to reduce exposure, prevent more threats before they occur, and provide the context needed to detect and respond effectively to attacks.

Securing How Work Happens

Workspace Security represents an important evolution in cybersecurity, but not because organizations suddenly need another security product category.

It reflects a more fundamental change: the way people work is increasingly interconnected, attacks cross traditional security boundaries, and the security protecting digital workers needs to become more connected as well.

For resource-constrained IT and security teams, in particular, the opportunity is significant: fewer silos, better context, stronger prevention, and simpler security operations.

Title: Killing ill-willed skills: Sophos AI at BSides Sydney
Context: The Sophos AI team presents new research at BSides Sydney
Full Text:
On November 7, 2026, Principal Data Scientist Younghoo Lee will present a talk at BSides Sydney entitled "Decode facts, then reason: Detecting obfuscated malicious agent skills with small LLMs." The talk presents a practical hybrid architecture for addressing a distinct software supply chain trust boundary: AI agent ‘skills’ that may be malicious, in contrast to their declared intent. For instance, a skill that claims to summarize CSV files may also read credentials, contact external hosts, or execute shell commands. The fact that such skills may be obfuscated complicates the problem, and existing solutions have significant drawbacks.

Younghoo’s research proposes a new approach: decoding facts about skills deterministically, and then letting a small LLM reason over them to decide whether observed behavior aligns with a skill’s declared intent.

Ill-willed skills

AI agents increasingly come with ‘skills’: small add-ons, often shared through repositories and marketplaces, that teach an agent how to do a specific task. A skill is typically a folder with a SKILL.md file that describes in plain English what the skill is for – plus helper code (usually Python) that does the work.

Once a skill is downloaded and installed, agents typically trust the description and run the code with their own privileges and accesses: source files, environment variables, the network, and a shell.

The issue, however, is that whereas a person reads the description, the machine runs the code, and the two do not have to agree. A skill that promises to ‘report missing environment variable names,’ for example, could just as easily read every environment value and send it to an endpoint controlled by a threat actor.

Obfuscation makes the problem worse

Compounding this issue is the fact that a skill can hide what it does, and the techniques will likely be familiar to any reader who’s analyzed malware: splitting strings, building words from character codes, wrapping content in Base64, resolving functions by name at runtime, and, in the description text, using zero-width characters or lookalike Unicode letters.

It’s not unreasonable to expect this obfuscation to become increasingly complex, particularly if threat actors start to deploy malicious skills at scale. Attackers have a long history of layering encodings, hiding commands inside ordinary-looking scripts, and abusing legitimate system tools. Skills can leverage the same built-in tools, so essentially we’re facing the same playbook but with a new delivery channel and a trusting host. Techniques we may see in future include stacked encodings, multi-step reconstruction, and novel variants designed to evade signature-base detection.

It’s worth noting, however, that obfuscation is of course not malicious in itself, and this makes the problem harder to solve. Benign tools use it for minified code, test fixtures, and anti-tampering checks, and so simply scanning skills for obfuscation techniques will likely result in false positives.

In Younghoo’s talk, two demo skills – one benign, the other malicious - use similar obfuscation tricks. The first, involving a log redaction skill, builds the words ‘password’ and ’api_key’ from character codes, so that Continuous Integration (CI) secret scanners do not flag its own source, and then masks those values in the logs it cleans. In the second demo, an ’environment auditor’ splits a string to hide access to the environment and uploads sensitive information, such as keys and credentials. The obfuscation looks alike and the eventual verdicts are opposites. What separates them is the declared purpose, the data flow, and the destination.

A hard problem

There are three existing approaches to solving this problem, and while they may provide some level of reassurance, they also fall short in various ways.

Static rule-based scanners are fast, cheap, and auditable, but as the name suggests, they match on what code looks like; if strings are assembled at runtime, for example, the corresponding rule has nothing to match when it examines the skill statically. In Younghoo’s tests, two open-source skill scanners (Cisco Skill Scanner and NVIDIA SkillSpector, both in static mode) performed well on plaintext skills. On obfuscated skills, false positives were rare, but both scanners missed some malicious skills. Both tools also ship optional LLM features, which our main comparison did not use.

Frontier LLMs can reason about intent and judge a skill’s behavior compared to its description, rather than checking whether certain strings or code appear., That would seem to make them an obvious solution, but it’s unfortunately not always practical. Sending multiple skills to a large hosted model adds latency and cost at scale, as well as potentially adding privacy, policy, and regulatory concerns.

Small local models avoid the drawbacks described above, but may struggle with the complexity of the task. The smallest model in Younghoo’s study, for instance, was ineffective when given raw obfuscated code, because it had to untangle the obfuscation and judge intent at the same time.

A novel approach: decode facts, then reason

Younghoo’s idea was to split the problem in two. First, code recovers what a skill may be attempting to hide, and then a small LLM judges whether that behavior fits what the skill claims to do.

The workflow involves three steps:

Decode. A deterministic Python front-end reverses obfuscation patterns. It never executes the skill, and does not assign a verdict or make a judgement. Each deobfuscation is recorded, with its technique, location, and before/after text, providing an audit trail. It repeats its deobfuscations until the source stops changing – so stacked encodings, such as Base64 inside a split string, are stripped back, layer by layer. Content that still looks encoded after decoding (such as long Base64-like runs or unusual runs of non-ASCII characters), is flagged as a possible unknown obfuscation.

Summarize. The decoder's events become a short, facts-only summary for each file: techniques used, revealed content, hardcoded secrets, sensitive operations, and any ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flags. Again, this step avoids coming to a conclusion about intent, and reminds the model (see next step) that obfuscation can be benign, so the presence of obfuscation does not necessarily imply malice.

Judge. Finally, a small LLM reads each summary alongside the skill's original source and description. It returns a verdict and a reason: does the behavior, now visible, fit the declared intent, and does any content that survived decoding make that fit less believable?

It’s worth noting that the decoder, at step 1, will not know every obfuscation technique, so it’s built as one input to the eventual judgement. The ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flag is a cue to weigh, rather than a verdict in itself. Encoded content that cannot be explained by a skill’s declared purpose counts against it, and by the same token, the same content in a skill that plausibly needs it may not. Covering a new technique means adding another decoder pass.

One of the main benefits of this hybrid approach is that for everything the decoder can resolve, the model no longer has to work out what a string of character codes means. The model's job is reduced to judgment, which is easier than decoding and judging at once.

The experiment

Younghoo distilled a larger teacher model into small Qwen3 ‘students’ with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, so inference did not need an external API and could be done locally, and evaluated the approach on a synthetic benchmark of benign and malicious skills, each expanded into many obfuscated variants and split by base skill - so that no variant of a test skill appeared in training.

We’ll publish more detailed results soon – and further information will be available in the BSides talk itself – but here’s a brief summary of the results.

Static scanners stay precise but go quiet. Under obfuscation, their precision held up, but their recall dropped sharply compared with plaintext. The fine-tuned small models recovered most of the missed detection.

Decoded evidence turns small models from unusable into useful. Given the same obfuscated skills, the smallest model scored close to nothing on raw code. Once it was given decoded evidence, with no training at all, it matched the stronger static scanner overall, though it also produced many false positives.

Distillation helps at every size. Fine-tuning improved all three student sizes: Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B. The 0.6B model gained mostly by learning to stop over-flagging benign skills. The 4B model outperformed both static scanners on obfuscated skills and scored close to perfect on our benchmark.

There are caveats to these results, of course: the benchmark was synthetic, and its variants came from known obfuscation techniques. However, we believe this research is a promising countermeasure to an emerging threat. Malicious skills may become more prevalent, and scanners, frontier LLMs, and local models have known weaknesses when it comes to detecting obfuscated variants.

However, decoding the content deterministically, then using a small model – which can be hosted locally – to judge whether it fits the skill’s declared job, may be a viable solution. It’s also a useful reminder that while AI can introduce new variants of threats in the hands of attackers, it can help defenders to counter those same threats. Keep an eye out for more on Younghoo’s research in the near future.

Other VPNs We’ve Tested

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

VPNs to Avoid

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

How We Test VPNs

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

On the privacy front, the top-recommended services included on this list have been independently audited, and they all maintain some sort of transparency report. In most cases, there's a proper report, but in others, such as Windscribe, that transparency is exposed through legal proceedings.
