Title: Claude, you've got company.
Context: The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability.
Full Text:
Claude Dispatch opens the door to hijacking. Residential proxies turn up on White House networks. Asian airlines suffer a wave of data breaches. Cisco and WatchGuard roll out critical patches. GhostMap traps Android phones in endless reboot loops. Hackers exploit a Zyxel zero-day to compromise nearly a thousand devices. Ukraine's scam call center crackdown ensnares senior security officials. AI-powered scammers prey on owners of missing pets. A former U.S. government IT worker admits to spying for Ethiopia. Our guest is Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and co-founder of QuSecure, with insights on the NIST PQC roadmap. Voters pull the plug on data centers.

Today is Thursday November 5th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Claude Dispatch proves vulnerable to being hijacked.

A security researcher has uncovered a vulnerability in Anthropic’s Claude that could allow a malicious browser extension to execute commands on a user’s computer, or even another machine connected to the same account. Forever Security’s Gal Weizman discovered that Claude Dispatch, which lets users remotely control Claude Desktop, could be hijacked through an authenticated browser session. His proof-of-concept attack tricked Claude into installing a malicious npm package while automatically approving permission requests. Weizman says the underlying design weakness also affects Claude Cowork and Code Remote Control, potentially allowing attackers to move from personal devices into corporate environments. Anthropic acknowledged the vulnerability in May but reportedly has not fixed it. The researcher warns that Claude’s convenient cross-device connectivity comes at the expense of traditional browser security boundaries.

Not even the White House is immune to residential proxies.

Security researchers say computers connected to the White House network are running residential proxy services that allow outsiders to rent their internet addresses. Layer3 Intel detected proxy activity on 26 of 30 days, recording 236 connections through six White House IP addresses. Researchers identified 28 proxy services using the network, including Infatica, a Russian company whose founder previously operated hosting infrastructure linked to Russian attacks on U.S. election systems in 2016. Residential proxies are often bundled into free applications, sometimes without users realizing their devices are being used. The services can enable cybercrime and potentially expose internal networks to attack. Researchers warn that anyone willing to pay a few dollars could route internet traffic through White House IP addresses. The White House has not commented.

Asian airlines report customer data breaches.

At least six Asian airlines have reported customer data breaches stemming from a cyberattack on Spanish technology provider Amadeus, which operates reservation, ticketing, and check-in systems. Affected carriers include Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana, Singapore Airlines, and Malaysia Airlines. Japan Airlines reported 92,000 affected customers, Cathay Pacific 53,000, and Singapore Airlines 46,000. Exposed information includes passenger names, booking details, travel itineraries, and, in some cases, passport information and frequent flyer numbers. Cathay Pacific says attackers used credentials assigned to an Amadeus system account. Amadeus says it has addressed the vulnerability and found no evidence that financial information was accessed or ransomware was involved. The airlines say their own systems and operations remain unaffected. Singapore Airlines is changing exposed booking numbers and warning customers about phishing attempts.

Cisco and WatchGuard patch serious vulnerabilities.

Cisco and WatchGuard have released patches for several serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and authentication flaws. WatchGuard addressed four critical bugs, although patches remain unavailable for a Linux kernel vulnerability affecting its Dimension platform. Cisco fixed a high-severity flaw in UCS Central Software and confirmed that 19 products are affected by the actively exploited Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell. Meanwhile, SonicWall warned that two vulnerabilities in its discontinued Global Management System platform will remain unpatched. Neither Cisco nor WatchGuard reports exploitation of their newly patched flaws.

GhostMap disables Android phones through a specially crafted app.

Bitdefender researchers have discovered an Android vulnerability called GhostMap that could render phones unusable simply by installing a specially crafted app. The app requires no permissions or executable code. Instead, malformed file information causes a core Android system process to repeatedly crash, trapping the device in a reboot loop. Neither restarting nor safe mode resolves the problem, potentially leaving a factory reset, and the resulting loss of locally stored data, as the only recovery option. Researchers reproduced the flaw on Android 17 and say it affects versions dating back to Android 10. The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. Google acknowledged the report but declined to issue a security update, referring it for possible future consideration.

A recently patched Zyxel vulnerability compromises nearly 1,000 devices.

Researchers at Binarly say a recently patched vulnerability in Zyxel GS1900 switches was exploited as a zero-day to compromise nearly 1,000 devices. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability. Binarly determined the hackers were actually exploiting the previously unknown flaw, rendering earlier patches ineffective. Zyxel released fixes on October 23, covering ten affected switch models.

Senior Ukrainian security officials are fired after a scam call center probe.

Ukraine's security service has dismissed two senior officials amid an expanding corruption investigation into a criminal network allegedly paying law enforcement officers to protect fraudulent call centers. Investigators say the organization included at least 12 people, among them senior security officials, prosecutors, police officers, and organized crime figures. The group's alleged activities extended beyond online scams to drug trafficking, counterfeiting, kidnappings, and violence. During one search, investigators say a senior security official threatened them with a firearm. The investigation, dubbed Operation Carthage, follows earlier allegations that prosecutors accepted bribes to shield scam operations targeting victims in Ukraine and abroad. The scandal has prompted Ukraine's parliament to approve tougher penalties for operating fraudulent call centers, with potential prison sentences of seven to twelve years.

UK scammers target missing pets.

Scammers in Britain are using AI-generated images of missing pets to extort desperate owners, sometimes threatening to kill the animals unless they receive payment. When Stephanie Young's cat Buddy disappeared, a supposed rescuer sent convincing pictures and demanded Apple gift cards. After Young questioned the images, the scammer threatened to murder or sell her cat. Other victims report similar experiences, including one woman whose supposed rescuer demanded £40,000 for her missing cat. Fraudsters create elaborate backstories and convincing images to exploit owners' emotional vulnerability, often demanding payment before agreeing to return the animals. British authorities advise owners to verify claims by requesting live video or arranging an in-person meeting before paying. Experts warn that AI has made these scams remarkably easy to produce, while the urgency and emotional distress surrounding a missing pet make victims particularly susceptible.

A former U.S. government IT worker pleads guilty to spying for Ethiopia.

A former U.S. government contractor with Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to spying for Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a 53-year-old naturalized American citizen from Maryland, worked across several federal agencies, including the State and Justice Departments. Prosecutors say he accessed classified intelligence reports without authorization, copied information from at least 133 reports, and smuggled documents out of secure facilities on discs disguised as containing unclassified material. He transmitted sensitive intelligence to senior Ethiopian military, political, and intelligence officials through encrypted messaging and personal storage devices. According to the FBI, Ethiopian officials used the information in military operations during an ongoing conflict. Investigators also identified more than $66,000 in bank deposits during the period. Lemma has agreed to a prison sentence ranging from 10 years to nearly 22 years.

Voters pull the plug on data centers.

America's data center industry had a rough election night. Across the country, candidates campaigning against massive computing facilities scored victories, as voters expressed frustration over electricity costs, noise, pollution, and the expanding influence of artificial intelligence. Democrats Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire were among the winners, while candidates dubbed “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick” weren't so fortunate. In Texas and Georgia, newly elected governors have advocated pausing data center construction, potentially complicating hundreds of planned projects. Local ballot measures also reflected growing resistance to development. Industry-backed candidates lost several races despite substantial financial support. The backlash crossed party lines, suggesting that enthusiasm for AI infrastructure isn't necessarily shared by the communities expected to host it. And as the returns came in, Elon Musk suggested that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing. Apparently, the zoning regulations are more accommodating up there.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: How to navigate the SIEM correlation rule set | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Go the other way around: first pin down which event sources are actually connected and feeding data into the SIEM, and only then see which rules will work on that data
Full Text:
In describing SIEM features, vendors almost invariably focus on numbers: how many correlation rules come out of the box, how many were added over the past year, and how many MITRE ATT&CK techniques they cover. Admittedly, these numbers matter. They do help gauge how effective a system is, and we share them from time to time too. But correlation rules aren’t a magic amulet, and having more of them doesn’t make a SIEM more effective. In fact, the total number of available rules says more about the variety of use cases the system supports. The question a hands-on SIEM analyst cares about first of all is different: which of these rules will actually work and be useful at my company? The answer is far from always obvious, and the reason isn’t even rule quality.

How correlation rules work

A rule first and foremost describes the logic: what to match against what, in what order, and within what time window. It also specifies particular event types from particular sources. For example, a rule for Active Directory group creation waits for events from the Windows Security log; a rule for suspicious network activity — DNS queries; a rule for process manipulation — triggers on events from endpoint telemetry. In other words, whether a rule works depends on whether the SIEM receives the right data in the first place.

The Active Directory rule above would be completely pointless at a company that avoids Windows on principle. It would load without errors, show up in the interface, and technically “exist” — but it would never fire. The reason is simple: the events it was built for never reach the system.

That dictates the only correct order of steps when setting up an SIEM. Don’t start out from the list of rules and then work your way toward your infrastructure. Go the other way around: first pin down which event sources are actually connected and feeding data into the SIEM, and only then see which rules will work on that data. Doing it the other way around leads to one of two outcomes: unmet expectations (hundreds of rules, almost no detections), or a laborious rule-by-rule manual slog, where the analyst opens every rule’s description, checks its event requirements, and decides whether the rule is worth using.

What the MITRE ATT&CK coverage percentage means

MITRE ATT&CK coverage is much the same story: it’s often used without a second thought as a yardstick for product effectiveness. The catch is that these are numbers in a vacuum, with no real-world conditions behind them. Coverage only makes sense for a specific set of working rules. And as we saw above, that set of rules depends on the set of event sources. That’s why the same SIEM will show different MITRE ATT&CK coverage at two different companies. Where Windows logs, endpoint telemetry, an email gateway, and network equipment are all connected, coverage will be noticeably broader than at a company with fewer sources.

Here’s the right way to read this metric: it’s not a score for the SIEM content, but a map of what your SIEM can see with its current telemetry. A tactic with low coverage is a signal that detecting it requires data you don’t have yet. Framed this way, it becomes a clear argument for a management conversation. Not “we need one more event source”, but “this part of the matrix is currently invisible to us, and here’s what it takes to close the gap”.

What’s worth checking in your SIEM

To get the most out of a SIEM, it’s worth asking yourself a few questions — not just when deploying the system, but regularly:

Is every connected event source being handled by rules? Infrastructure changes constantly: new systems appear and new integrations get connected. Every change like this is a reason to check again whether there are now rules you should enable.

Do I know exactly which events are required for which rules? Sometimes a rule doesn’t fire not because a whole event source is missing, but because a single event type isn’t being collected: the audit policy simply isn’t set up to capture it. Fix that oversight as soon as possible.

Do I understand my coverage in terms of MITRE ATT&CK? The point isn’t to produce good-looking reports. It’s to prioritize which event sources to add next: which ones will give the biggest gain in visibility?

But how can you answer these questions without spending ages digging into every rule description? We have a solution.

How we can help

To help analysts find their way around the detection logic of our solution more easily, we’ve added a knowledge base section with the complete set of Kaspersky SIEM rules. In essence, it’s a tool that holds data from the official documentation for the SOC Package rule set, and makes it easy to work with that data. It has three sections:

Library. A table of all correlation rules that you can sort and filter per any column: category, MITRE tactic and technique, event source, and event type. Search works across all fields, including descriptions. Double-clicking a rule opens a card with detailed information about it.

Builder. A tool for assembling a rule set that suits the event sources you already have. The analyst just checks the boxes for the sources the company has, and gets a list of matching rules, brief statistics, and the event types that need to be set up for collection. The tool also generates a regular expression that you can paste into the search bar of the Kaspersky SIEM web interface to link all the matching rules to the correlator in a single step, with no manual picking.

MITRE. A view of the ATT&CK matrix where tactics expand into techniques and sub-techniques. Each matrix item has a card with the description from the MITRE website, and SOC Package coverage details. Covered and uncovered items are color-coded, and charts show coverage per tactic.

One more point worth stressing: the content in our SIEM is updated constantly, so it makes sense to check your setup against it not only at deployment, but after every notable change in your infrastructure. To follow the development of the Kaspersky Unified Monitoring and Analysis Platform, visit the official product page.

Title: Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
Context: The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions
Full Text: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions. The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled. If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration. That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not. Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration. Dawn of the *sshole The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually. In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account. Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out. The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk. Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going. In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times. On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack. Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set. There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

Title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
Context: Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed,...
Full Text:
On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration, and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now, which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security.

Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now.

Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation.

Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure.

This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default.

Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain.

Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default

Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads.

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. Building on protections available today, it progressively establishes and maintains more of the recommended security posture through the products themselves, adapting the baseline as threats and Microsoft security guidance evolve.

The result is less manual effort and a stronger security posture maintained increasingly through the products themselves. We’re advancing this work across three areas: Patch, Configure, and Protect.

Figure 1: On-Premises Baseline Security Mode builds on capabilities available today across Patch, Configure, and Protect, with greater automation and stronger defaults coming over time.

Patch: close known vulnerabilities faster

The need is clear in our deployment data: many Exchange Server deployments are not running the current security update, including a substantial share on unsupported versions. Closing this protection gap requires both releasing fixes faster and helping customers apply them sooner.

Today. Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed, helping customers address known vulnerabilities sooner.

Next. In Q1 calendar year 2027, we’re targeting automatic application of security updates after a fixed period following release in connected SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server environments.

Release fixes faster, then help those fixes reach servers faster.

Configure: make the safer posture easier to maintain

Security requires more than current software. Configuration and permissions can drift over time, creating gaps between the intended security posture and the environment administrators are operating. Customers need a clearer way to identify those gaps, establish recommended settings, and maintain them as environments evolve.

Today. Tenant Configuration Management can help customers assess supported SharePoint, Exchange, and Skype for Business Server environments and identify where permissions are broader than intended.

Next. In Q1 2027, we plan to introduce hardened default configurations for SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server, moving from identifying configuration risk toward establishing Microsoft-recommended security settings by default. We also plan to identify configuration drift so administrators can see when environments move away from that baseline.

Make the safer configuration easier to establish and harder to unintentionally lose.

Protect: reduce exposure when threats can’t wait for a patch

Some threats emerge before a permanent security update is available and fully deployed. During that window, customers need mitigations that can reduce exposure quickly without replacing the underlying security update.

Today. Emergency Mitigation Service can automatically apply interim mitigations for certain emerging vulnerabilities, helping reduce exposure while a permanent security update is prepared and deployed. Mitigation addresses the immediate risk; the security update addresses the underlying vulnerability.

Next. In December 2026, we plan to introduce Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 for Exchange Server and Skype for Business Server, enabling it by default and expanding the security mitigations it can apply. In January 2027, we are planning to extend Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 to cover SharePoint Server.

When threats move faster, protection needs to move faster too.

Act today, prepare for what comes next

Taken together, these investments represent an important shift: from providing customers with security guidance and tools toward building the recommended security posture into the products themselves.

Microsoft continues to recommend moving workloads to Microsoft 365 wherever possible. Start by identifying which workloads can move and which must remain on-premises. For those that remain, move to supported releases, assess exposure, apply current security updates, and enable available protections.

The Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server teams will publish additional guidance on available protections, upcoming capabilities, and actions customers can take now. We also plan to bring practitioner-focused on-premises guidance to Secure Now to help organizations assess their environment, identify critical actions, and prioritize the steps they can take.

Join us at Microsoft Ignite for Secure your on-prem estate (BRK215) to explore the initiative, upcoming investments, and steps you can take now.

Modernize where you can. Strengthen the security of what must remain.

Title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
Context: The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra
Full Text:
AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action?

“Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits.

Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries. An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it.

This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents").

This post rests on one principle:

The Intermediation Principle: The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation.

A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign.

The intermediary problem

Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd.

The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business.

Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra.

Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra.

None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today.

A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents.

In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost. That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved.

Our vision

Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification.

None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action. It requires that Sites have the means to obtain or require information about the User to hold them accountable, when applicable, with or without an Agent.

What people have tried, and why they fall short

A common proposal is for Agents to pass a Site's CAPTCHA through to the User to solve. That proves some human is present at that moment (“human in the loop”, or HITL), and nothing more. HITL is primarily a mechanism to prevent mistakes from misalignment. Misalignment is an issue between the Operator and the User, and resolving it does not resolve the majority of the problems above. For example, it can't tell Bob from anyone else (Traffic commingling), and it says nothing about who the Agent acts for the rest of the time. Additionally, Agents exist to remove friction, and HITL adds back that friction, so Operators are incentivized to remove or bypass it for the User.

Another common proposal is to use tightly scoped access controls. Agents are built to do anything a User could, so in practice they ask for, and get, permission to do everything. A scope of "everything" tells the Site nothing. And even a narrow scope only says what the Agent was allowed to do. It doesn't say who answers when the Agent gets it wrong, which is the question the Site actually needs answered.

What the web needs

The web needs tools and protocols that allow Sites and Agents to collaborate to determine what behaviors and actions are allowed, as well as express preferences and policies from Sites to Agents, all in a way that can be reasonably supported by all Sites and Agents. Fortunately, work is already underway along all of these fronts, and many, if not all, of these can be addressed by applying existing standards.

Protocols

Agents and Sites can engage in explicit protocols for solving some of the problems above. For instance, MOLE is one upcoming approach that aims for rate limiting without User-specific identifiers, allowing Sites to transition away from implicit identities and towards explicit protocols for accomplishing the same goal. This is similar to the x402 protocol, which aims to enable payments on the web while remaining privacy-preserving. We are actively exploring ways in which we can leverage existing protocols for addressing other problems, as well as exploring designing new protocols when existing solutions fall short.

Identities

When discussing Agent Identity, Web Bot Auth (WBA) is our preferred method. WBA allows an Agent to sign its requests, which provides a secure way for an Agent to identify itself (and, implicitly, the Operator). We must still define a mechanism that supports multiple intermediaries: when Agent A uses Agent B inside Browser C, the Site needs to be able to know this, so that the Site can correctly ensure that access by Agent A is correctly understood and controlled, for example, in order to prevent Policy circumvention.

Other types of identifying information, such as session, account, or even User-specific IDs, might be necessary, depending on the context. We are working with the relevant standards to explore ways to communicate such identifying information.

Let’s take a look into types of Identity in regards to a User. Ultimately, Identity is a spectrum that trades various degrees of information about a user, while ideally practicing principles of data minimization. Identity provides us a mechanism to answer “who are you?” in pursuit of answering the follow-up questions of: “are you who you say you are?” and “can we trust you?”.

In many cases, identifying information isn’t needed, and privacy-preserving methods for moderating access to agents, such as through Privacy Pass and MOLE, can help us answer “can we trust you?” without needing to answer “who are you?”. Private Access Tokens was one early way in which we tried to establish trust without identifying the user, and MOLE is intended to be the successor to this technology However, there are cases where graduated forms of disclosure along this spectrum would be needed, and you can generally characterize them in the following ways:

Nothing - Users may act on the internet while bringing no identifiers to the table.

Session - Sites require some way of linking requests in the same session to a single agent. This allows the Site to establish reputation for a given session and act on it accordingly. For example, Poppy has a notion of a session ID for exactly this purpose.

Account - Sites require a way of attributing requests to the same User across sessions. This might be a stable identifier assigned by an Operator or third party to a User that persists across the account with the Operator, such as a single Agent visiting the same Site every day using the same identifier. An example use case this would enable is: “Bind your Site account to your Agent account”.

Unique - Some Sites might require a unique, per-User identifier provisioned by a third party that persists across Operators, accounts, Agents, and sessions. This may be useful for high risk actions, or for Sites that need to provide limited access to an expensive resource or that have very restrictive obligations or compliance requirements. Government IDs, third party identity verification, and decentralized technologies like Proof of Human are all examples of technologies that can provide this.

Ultimately, Sites determine what information they need for clients to answer “is the entity behind this request allowed to do this action at this time?” In many cases, protocols already exist, or are being developed, to convey this information: WBA for conveying an Agent’s platform identity, MOLE for conveying User reputation, OAuth for conveying account identities, and so on.

Claims

Beyond identities, some actions require a fact about the real person, such as being over 18 or being the cardholder (Identity verification breaks, Friendly fraud). Often the Operator verified this at sign-up or a third party already has this information.

In order to allow Agents access to Sites or actions with these kinds of restrictions, we need mechanisms for Sites to request this information, and for Operators or third parties to provide this information.

Site Agent access policy

Today, an Agent infers a Site’s rules by trying something and interpreting the Site response (usually, whether it gets blocked). That wastes resources on both sides, and in some cases makes honest Agents appear to be malicious. Robots.txt says where a crawler may go, but isn’t fully suited to express what Agents may do.

Sites need a machine-readable way to publish what actions Agents are allowed to do. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is actively working on some preference expression mechanisms for this, primarily in the AI Preferences Working Group. However, the focus of the group is on expressing preferences for use (such as training, inference, and search), and there is still not a group focused on the larger need for preference expression mechanisms discussed here.

On open source and local Agents

Agents that are not run as an “Intermediary” (e.g. on-device Agents, or locally hosted Agents such as OpenClaw) raise different concerns. Primarily, they look like (and are) automation, and they have no single party to build reputation or hold accountability with.

There are many solutions to this, one of which is to ask these Agents to provide a Unique ID. However, addressing this is not the initial focus of Trusted Agent Delegation.

What’s next

Real-world solutions to the problems that Sites face won’t emerge from fragmented, vendor-specific mechanisms. They require open, interoperable standards that are rooted in real world experience. We have been, and continue to actively collaborate across the ecosystem, with major Operators, identity verification companies, payment providers, merchants, publishers, proxy providers, and cloud browsing companies, to align operational requirements directly with active work on these problems in the IETF and elsewhere

Our focus is on bridging the gap between running code and emerging specifications across working groups and activities like Web Bot Auth, AIPREFs, OAuth, WIMSE, and MOLE. We are doing this, in part, by co-authoring and refining open protocols like WBA and MOLE and building and deploying implementations of these protocols at scale.

We are also announcing the Trusted Agent Delegation (TAD) coalition. The goal of TAD is to bring a group of representatives across the ecosystem to have discussions on the overall problem set that was put forth in this document, examine all existing protocols, and then to bring more well-defined problems or problems to the IETF to work through, as needed. We intend to hold side meetings at the IETF and workshops in the future to facilitate discussion.

If you are building agents, agent runtimes, running an edge or cloud platform, or managing commercial or compliance applications or infrastructure, we need you to get involved in these efforts too. Check out this page for more information on how to participate.

What you can do today

An open, interoperable foundation is where we're headed, starting with TAD. But you don't have to wait for new protocols to start regaining visibility and control. As of this week, Cloudflare customers can take three concrete steps:

See which Agents are on your site, and what they're doing. Security Analytics now breaks out Personal Assistants as their own traffic category, and a new widget lists every Agent visiting your site, how many requests each one sends, the paths it hits, and the errors it runs into. Unexplained automated traffic becomes traffic you can reason about. And for the broader picture of AI crawlers and bots affect your business, including how much each Operator crawls versus the traffic it sends back, Enterprise Bot Management customers can use Business Insights.

Set access on your terms, per Agent. Using AI Crawler and Agent access policies, you can welcome the Agents that bring you business and restrict the ones that don't — allow an Agent across your site, block it only on pages with ads, or block it entirely. Your Search and Training policies stay independent.

Tie an Agent back to the user it acts for — and act on it. For sites using Account Abuse Protection (early access), every login and sign-up now shows whether a personal Agent made the request, and which one. When an attacker abuses a shared Agent on one account, you can mitigate that account — with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID — without blocking the Agent for every other legitimate user behind it. This is a first, concrete answer to the Traffic commingling challenge described above: you can finally see past the Agent to the User, and respond accordingly.

These are the first building blocks of the vision, already in production. More will follow as the standards mature.

And if your company has a more restrictive position on Agents, we would love to hear it. Reach out and share your problems with us directly. We are looking to help build an Internet where site owners have visibility and control, but also where Agents have the maximum access that is reasonable within those controls. You can reach out to your Customer Support team, or email us at crawlercontrols@cloudflare.com.

Title: ​​​​What’s new in Microsoft Security: November 2026
Context: Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context...
Full Text:
Endpoint administrators need to keep elevated access accountable at scale. Security teams also need a clearer view of expert-led protection and a simpler way to deploy SQL Server protection in Azure Government. As AI agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to limit their authority and adapt protection as risk changes. This month’s Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender updates introduce capabilities across these areas, alongside new Secure AI capabilities for agent access. A recent Secure Now update in Microsoft Security Exposure Management also connects information on recent threats to focused initiatives for reducing exposure.

Here’s what’s new:

Limit agent authority to the task with Dynamic Permissions

Give agents task-scoped authority and adapt access as risk changes

As agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to manage what each agent is allowed to do. Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires. As the agent works, Dynamic Agent Risk assesses whether the agent’s authority aligns with changing behavior and context. Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond proportionately by narrowing permissions, restricting access to resources, or requiring human approval for higher-impact actions. Together, these capabilities are designed to help organizations tailor agent authority before an agent acts and adjust access as risk changes. See how security can respond when an agent steps outside its task.

Contain local AI agents with Microsoft Execution Containers

Apply least-privilege boundaries to help limit access on Windows

Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, gives organizations an operating system-enforced containment layer for AI agents, designed to limit what an agent can access. Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions, with additional isolation options for higher-risk scenarios. Organizations can tune and validate policies before enforcing them broadly, while upcoming integration with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Agent 365 is intended to extend governance and attribution across the enterprise. Discover more about this policy-driven containment for AI agents.

Scale least privilege with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Expand least-privilege scenarios with new system settings support and simpler tenant onboarding

Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management continues to expand the tasks standard users can complete without broad administrator rights. With new system settings support, standard users can change IPv4, IPv6, and DNS server values on their device’s network adapters through Endpoint Privilege Management, while administrators determine how those changes are elevated. For user-confirmed changes, administrators can require a business justification, Windows authentication, or both before the change is applied. Along with tenant onboarding updates, these improvements support organizations as they get started with and expand their use of Endpoint Privilege Management. Explore how to get started with system settings support in Endpoint Privilege Management.

Get started with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Simplify security operations with Defender Experts

See what Defender Experts are investigating in a consolidated experience

As threats move faster and security environments grow more complex, security teams need to quickly understand what matters and when to act. New Microsoft Defender Experts MDR experiences in the Microsoft Defender portal bring ongoing expert work into focus with a consolidated overview page with updated navigation and visibility into hunts. Teams can review active and completed hunts, see findings from Defender Experts, and identify items that may require follow-up. Learn more about the new Defender Experts MDR experiences.

Get around-the-clock defense with Microsoft Defender Experts MDR

Extend protection and discover local agents with Microsoft Defender

Simplify deployment and expand SQL protection

The enhanced agent for Defender for SQL Servers on machines is now generally available for resource- and subscription-level enablement in Azure Government cloud. The enhanced agent uses existing SQL infrastructure, eliminating the need to deploy the Azure Monitor Agent for this scenario. Security teams can spend less time on deployment and extend protection across their SQL Server environments. Learn more about the enhanced agent and how to get started.

Discover local AI agents and their configured MCPs on Windows and macOS

On endpoints, Microsoft Defender is extending discovery capabilities for supported local AI agents and their configured model context protocols (MCPs) across Windows and macOS. Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to help security teams understand local AI agent activity in their environment. Learn more about local agents.

Explore Microsoft Defender solutions

Improve security posture with Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Prioritize foundational security controls with Secure Now

AI-enabled attacks can take advantage of familiar weaknesses, including excessive permissions, unprotected authentication flows, and exposed systems. Secure Now now pairs information about recent threats with focused initiatives across security domains. Security teams can use that context to identify foundational controls that need attention, review the recommended actions, and prioritize work intended to reduce exposure. The update helps connect information about observed attack patterns with security improvements teams can consider in their own environments.

Learn more about Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Learn how to address agentic AI’s security challenges

From agentic inventory and observability to stopping AI runtime threats

An inventory is only the starting point for managing Al agent risk. Organizations also need to consider ownership, limits on what agents can access, how risk is reassessed as agents operate, and protections against emerging threats. “Don’t Leave AI Exposed” provides security professionals, IT administrators, and developers with actionable guidance on managing risk across the agent lifecycle. Download the guide for considerations spanning agent inventory, ownership, access, monitoring, and runtime protection.

Stay in the Loop

Security teams need a clear account of what is changing across the portfolio and where those changes can strengthen their operations. In the Loop brings together the latest Microsoft Security updates and their implications for your security strategy. Explore earlier editions and check back for the next drop.

See Microsoft Security innovations in action at Microsoft Ignite, November 17-20, 2026, in San Francisco or online.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

Title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber, and promises this one stays within 'rules of engagement'
Context: This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute...
Full Text: OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement." The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do. The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately." In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests. "In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise. OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things. The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing. The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review. OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework. This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks. As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming. Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well. The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products. Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments, and added new bonuses for independent researchers. This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®

Title: Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
Context: He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential
Full Text: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture. Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets. Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it. "I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here." Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client. "My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes." Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company. He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside. The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share." “I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file. Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated. But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all. He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all. "And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe." He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it. "The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

Title: Cyber Resilience Starts with AI Governance
Context: It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response
Full Text:
Today’s cybercriminals are increasingly using AI to scale, accelerate, and evolve their attacks. At the same time, organizations are recognizing that AI can be a powerful force for defense, using it to strengthen cybersecurity, improve security operations, and protect networks at machine speed.

Data in the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report confirms the near-ubiquity of this response, with 91% of the IT leaders in the 2,700+ organizations surveyed stating they are using or exploring the use of AI-empowered cybersecurity solutions. Unfortunately, as we move higher up the corporate ladder, only 50% of respondents believe their boards of directors fully comprehend the cybersecurity vulnerabilities associated with AI. This disconnect highlights a governance gap, which creates risk for the organization.

Why Boards of Directors Need to Fully Understand AI

To defend against AI-powered criminals, organizations need to build cyber resilience, but they can’t do that if leadership doesn't understand AI and its potential risks. That gap becomes even more significant as AI-driven defenses become more embedded within organizations. As AI adoption accelerates, company-wide AI literacy and cybersecurity governance must evolve alongside it.

According to the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report, although nearly three-quarters of respondents say their boards view cybersecurity as a business priority, only 59% say that priority is reflected in spending decisions. This discrepancy suggests many organizations recognize the importance of cybersecurity in principle but struggle to translate that awareness into sustained investment and governance.

The report also highlights what's at stake for leadership. Half of organizations say board members or senior executives faced personal consequences following a cyberattack, including fines, loss of employment, or other penalties. As cyber risk increasingly becomes business risk, executive oversight has never been more important.

AI-Informed Leadership Teams

Board members don’t need to become AI engineers. But they do need enough understanding of AI to ask the right questions, evaluate risk, and provide effective oversight.

AI literacy also shouldn’t stop with the boardroom or the security team. IT staff, software developers, and business leaders also need a foundational understanding of how AI systems work, the risks they pose, and how to mitigate those risks.

For boards and C-suite leaders, education should focus on governance, risk oversight, executive accountability, policies, investment decisions, and regulatory implications. With a shared knowledge base across the organization, leaders can better balance the productivity and security benefits of AI with its potential risks.

The goal is an AI-informed leadership team that can balance AI's potential with its risks and make informed decisions about adoption, investment, and governance.

What Should Organizations Do Today to Build AI Literacy?

Organizations should begin by assessing their current AI readiness and identifying knowledge gaps across leadership, security teams, IT, and the broader workforce.

An organization’s board of directors must understand the benefits that come with AI adoption. First, AI can act as a force multiplier for short-handed IT security teams. It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response. But leadership must also recognize that realizing these benefits requires people with the skills to securely manage, oversee, and govern AI-enabled environments.

Organizations can address these challenges through a combination of governance, workforce education, and structured skills development. Programs that provide AI education and cybersecurity certification can help employees build the knowledge needed to use, secure, and responsibly manage AI.

The Fortinet Training Institute can help your organization acquire AI literacy and workforce education. Training programs are designed to support the acquisition of technical expertise across leadership, security teams, and the broader workforce.

AI is already changing how organizations defend themselves. The next step is ensuring the people responsible for guiding that transformation understand both its opportunities and its risks.

As organizations strengthen AI governance, another workforce challenge comes into focus: finding and developing professionals with the skills to secure, manage, and govern increasingly AI-enabled environments.

Need more guidance on how to educate the board on AI? Explore Fortinet Training Institute programs and certification pathways to learn how Fortinet is helping close the cyber skills gap through accessible training, upskilling, reskilling, and workforce development.

Title: GitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2
Context: A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation
Full Text:
GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases.

The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions.

The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely.

pull_request_target Is Now a Common Attack Vector Vector #

GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors. Unlike the standard pull_request event, which restricts access to secrets and provides a read-only token for contributions from forks, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to its configured secrets and token permissions.

That elevated access makes the trigger useful for legitimate maintenance tasks such as assigning reviewers, labeling pull requests, and posting authenticated comments. The workflow definition runs from the repository's trusted default branch, rather than the contributor's proposed changes.

The security risk emerges when that privileged workflow checks out and executes code from an untrusted fork or passes attacker-controlled pull request data into shell commands. A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation.

Researchers have warned about these vulnerabilities, commonly called "pwn requests," since at least 2021. Variations of this attack pattern contributed to major supply chain incidents involving Nx, PostHog, and TanStack.

GitHub's June changes addressed a common source of these vulnerabilities by making actions/checkout reject unsafe fork checkouts in privileged workflows unless explicitly overridden. The December policy takes a broader approach, preventing the event from triggering a workflow at all unless administrators have authorized it through an applicable policy.

Two Test Windows Before December Enforcement #

GitHub's default restriction currently operates in evaluation mode, allowing affected workflows to continue running before enforcement begins.

The company has scheduled two temporary enforcement periods, known as brownouts, to expose configurations that will stop working under the new policy:

November 9, 16:00–18:00 UTC

November 16, 16:00–18:00 UTC

During those windows, blocked pull_request_target attempts will generate failed workflow runs with an error annotation instead of executing. The default policy will return to evaluation mode after each test.

On December 2, the restriction becomes permanent for affected public repositories without an applicable policy allowing the event. The change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise Cloud, but excludes private and internal repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server.

Maintainers who still require pull_request_target can create an Actions event policy that explicitly permits it. GitHub supports targeting individual workflow files, allowing administrators to preserve specific automation without enabling the trigger across an entire repository. Existing applicable event policies are not replaced by the new default.

Some Open Source Maintainers Face a Complicated Transition #

The broader restriction introduces complications for open source projects that have relied on pull_request_target for legitimate automation, sometimes across dozens of repositories.

A carefully configured workflow that only labels pull requests or manages project metadata may pose little of the risk GitHub is addressing, but it will still be subject to the new restriction. Maintainers must either allow these workflows explicitly or move them to another trigger where appropriate.

There are also differences in the administrative tools available across GitHub's pricing tiers.

GitHub's documentation for workflow execution protections describes policy configuration at the repository, organization, and enterprise levels for public repositories, including those on free plans. However, the ability to create policies in evaluation mode is reserved for Enterprise Cloud, where administrators can examine policy insights before turning on enforcement.

That disparity had already prompted questions following GitHub's September announcement of the new defaults.

In a GitHub Community discussion, open source maintainer George Joseph questioned how smaller organizations were expected to assess the impact without Enterprise policy insights.

"How would us mere mortals who run open-source organizations see what workflows would be affected?" he asked.

A community response suggested manually searching repositories for workflows using pull_request_target, inspecting existing workflow runs, and testing explicit allowlisting policies. These approaches can identify affected configurations, but require additional work from maintainers managing multiple repositories.

The December deadline gives projects several more weeks to prepare, while the scheduled brownouts offer a preview of what enforcement will look like. GitHub's decision also represents a significant shift for a feature originally created to make external contributions easier to manage: privileged pull request automation will now require an explicit exception to continue running under the new default.

Title: Defense Drill Interventions
