Title: AI Agents are Outpacing Access Governance in Business Apps
Context: What you will learn Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend least privilege, segregation of duties and access reviews to every agent.

Business applications, like enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, house an organization’s financial data, and run critical processes like payroll and procurement. AI adoption has taken off in software development and other workflows, but finance teams and business application owners have had good reason to move more carefully.

Yet Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report shows AI agents are no longer limited to analyzing data. They are already taking action inside the applications that run the business, like ERP, CRM, HCM, procurement and other systems that move money, pay people and manage customers.

In this blog, I’ll outline the AI-related findings from the 2026 Application Access Governance report and share recommendations for governing and securing AI agents in business applications. To learn more about findings from the report related to foundational controls, read: The confidence gap in application access governance.

If you use tools like Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT or Gemini to boost efficiency, you may not be surprised to learn that, of the 1,000 surveyed organizations, 88% use AI tools or AI agents within their critical business applications.

35% of organizations have deployed AI agents inside critical business applications that can perform actions

In the context of an ERP system, that means AI agents can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions. Only 45% of AI-using organizations run every agent under its own dedicated identity. The rest have at least some agents acting on shared or borrowed human credentials, often through delegated or on-behalf-of (OBO) access.

Despite the sensitivity of financial data, organizations believe they have more oversight of AI agents than they do. Most say they have at least partial visibility into agent deployment, access and ownership. Fewer than half track any of it fully and centrally. And when visibility gets tested, it often fails. A full 32% of AI-using organizations report an agent took actions that could not be traced or explained during a review.

AI agents act without human review and controls are inconsistent

Among the 879 respondents who use AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications, roughly one in six reports that tools and agents can perform consequential actions autonomously, without human review.

These actions include accessing sensitive or regulated data (17%), creating or changing business data (16%), executing or approving transactions (15%), changing user permissions (14%), and changing application configurations (14%).

Fewer than half of AI-using organizations consistently apply each common governance control to all AI tools and AI agents. The share ranges from 48% that log and monitor activity to 40% that remove an AI agent’s access when its owner leaves or changes roles. Only 43% consistently include AI tools and AI agents in segregation of duties (SoD) analysis, and 44% include them in user access reviews (UARs).

Put simply, agents that can move money and change permissions are not being governed like the identities they are. The controls mandatory for a new hire, including least privilege, SoD analysis, access reviews, and removal at departure, are not yet being applied to AIagents with the same rigor.

Organizations using AI are reporting issues

The risk is not theoretical. 84% of organizations using AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications report at least one AI-related issue in the past 12 months. Only 16% say nothing has occurred.

The most frequently reported issues are actions that reviewers could not trace or explain during a review at 32%, incorrect financial transactions attributed to AI activity at 30%, SoD conflicts created by AI at 28%, agents that continued operating after the person who deployed them left at 28%, and unintended or unauthorized actions at 28%. Another 26% report that an AI tool or AI agent accessed data it should not have had access to.

Several of these issues line up with the control gaps above. Agents kept running after their owner left because nothing removed their access. Conflicts appeared because agents sit outside SoD analysis. Actions went unexplained because activity is not consistently logged and monitored.

Organizations are struggling to keep governance aligned with AI adoption. Among AI-using organizations, 44% say AI deployment is outpacing governance and security controls, and only 11% say the two are keeping pace.

Recommendations for AI governance in business applications

The pattern across these findings is consistent. AI agents are identities with transaction-level access, but most organizations still manage them like features of an application. The fix is not a new governance program. It extends the one you already have, and you must complete the AI security fundamentals before you look ahead.

Know every agent in your business applications and assign a named owner. Within business applications, agents act through an identity within the application’s security model, thereby making the application your system of record. Identify which identities your AI tools and agents act through, what each can access and the person accountable for its actions, and keep that view current as new agents are added.

Know how each agent is deployed and govern the delegation. Every platform handles agent identity differently. Some agents run under dedicated identities; others act on behalf of a user or run as background jobs under delegated credentials. Any of these can be governed. What matters is that agent activity is attributable as agent activity, and that you know whose permissions it is exercising.

Enforce least privilege for every identity, human or not. The principle does not change because the account is an agent or a workload. Understand the risk profile and sensitive access you are granting to each identity before deployment, grant just enough access for the task at hand, and put the right approvals in place for new access.

Extend your existing controls to every account, including AI. Include every account in SoD and sensitive access risk analysis, agents alongside the humans they act for. Wrap access reviews around them. Monitor critical data and configuration changes so you can see who changed what, whether the who was a person or an agent. Bind agent access to its owner’s lifecycle, so a role change or departure ends the agent’s access too.

Remember that agents operate at machine speed. An agent does not make mistakes one at a time. It can perform thousands of actions in the time it takes a human to perform one, so a mis-scoped agent is a misconfiguration at scale. That is why the controls above matter before deployment, and why monitoring and change tracking matter after it. The sooner a bad grant or an unauthorized change is caught, the smaller the blast radius.

These findings focus on agents operating within business applications, where transactions occur and financial materiality lives. Agents are being deployed across the enterprise, and governance has to meet them where they act. For agents reaching into systems from outside, that means runtime authorization: deciding and enforcing privileged actions as they happen, human or agent, from infrastructure and endpoints to the platforms where agents run. For agents built into business applications, this means governing them within the application’s security model with the same rigor we apply to humans. Delinea is investing in both, because the consequences of getting it wrong are measured in dollars, data and audit findings.

Read the full findings in our 2026 Application Access Governance Report.

Title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
Context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
Full Text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

Context: It stopped 305 attack attempts at the door
Full Text:
It started with a fire drill

In March, our SOC watched a phishing-as-a-service operation turn Railway, a developer cloud platform with a spotless IP reputation, into a token-harvesting engine. Device code phishing lures hit 344 organizations across five countries in under three weeks. Microsoft had no reason to score those logins as risky. That was the whole point.

So we did something we'd never done before. We hand-built a Conditional Access policy blocking Railway's IP ranges, validated it against 14 days of fleet traffic, and pushed it to every eligible Managed ITDR tenant. It stopped 305 attack attempts at the door. Zero legitimate logins were affected.

Then the attackers moved to new infrastructure. They always do.

That's the problem we built Adversary Infrastructure to solve. It's the newest capability in Huntress Managed ITDR, and it turns that one-time emergency response into continuous protection. When one tenant gets hit, every tenant gets the block. We call it herd immunity for identity.

Attackers are renting clean infrastructure and scaling with AI

The Railway campaign told us something about how identity attacks work now. Across 344 victims, we found no two identical phishing lures. Each one was tailored enough to slip past email filtering. That kind of variety at that kind of volume means automation or AI is writing the lures. The group behind it, EvilTokens, sells a storefront with AI workflows for bypassing filters, personalizing pretexts, and hunting inboxes for wire fraud targets. It even has a 24/7 support desk.

The infrastructure side has changed too. Attackers don't need to buy bulletproof hosting anymore. They rent clean, cheap, trusted cloud space, stand up a token relay in minutes, and tear it down when it's burned. Developer platforms, VDI tunnels, and AiTM relays all look legitimate to Microsoft's risk scoring until someone proves otherwise.

The scale is hard to overstate. In a single 14-day window, 5,086 distinct attacker IP addresses hit the Huntress fleet. Partners can't curate blocklists at that pace. Nobody can, by hand.

What Adversary Infrastructure is

Adversary Infrastructure blocks attackers at the Microsoft 365 sign-in, before they ever get a session.

Figure 1: Adversary Infrastructure in the Huntress Platform

When the Huntress SOC confirms the hosting, relay, or proxy infrastructure behind a compromise in one tenant, we turn it into a blocking Conditional Access policy in every eligible, opted-in tenant. Attacks from that infrastructure fail at sign-in instead of becoming incidents you have to clean up.

It's precision blocking, sourced from real attacks we've already investigated across the 17M+ identities we protect. Only the IP ranges that are bad, nothing else. Huntress maintains it end to end. There's no blocklist for you to curate, no policy for you to write, no threat feed for you to consume. And it's included in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 at no extra cost.

How it works

The whole loop runs from one confirmed incident to fleet-wide blocking, often the same day.

The SOC confirms a compromise with a real incident in a real tenant, with the hosting, relay, or proxy addresses behind it.

Detection engineers validate the infrastructure. It has to be datacenter or hosting space, scoped tightly to the evidence, with zero legitimate logins anywhere across the fleet and confirmed reports from at least two unrelated partners. A second engineer reviews every nomination. If real users log in from an address, it doesn't ship.

Huntress deploys the block. New campaigns go to our own canary tenants first. Then one blocking policy with one named location per campaign - each labeled [HUNTRESS] - roll out to every eligible, opted-in tenant.

Figure 2: Conditional Access policies by campaign in Adversary Infrastructure

The next attack fails at sign-in. No token is issued. The attack never becomes an incident.

You get the receipt. Every block produces a Low severity incident report naming the targeted identity, source, and campaign, and the credential the attacker tried to use gets rotated.

We check every tenant daily, repair drift, and update ranges as attackers rotate. We never touch policies you authored. Tenants that can't run Conditional Access still get the same detections and incident reports, just after the sign-in instead of before.

Two campaigns that brought you Adversary Infrastructure

Every campaign we've turned into fleet-wide protection started as somebody's very bad day. Here are two.

LSHIY LLC: 81 million login attempts from one IPv6 range. Three months after Railway, our SOC spotted a password spray replaying validated credentials through ROPC, a legacy auth flow that skips the MFA prompt entirely. It compromised 78 accounts across 64 organizations. Here's the part that stung: 55 of those accounts had active Conditional Access policies requiring MFA. The policies looked right. They just didn't cover the flow the attacker used. LSHIY is now a live Adversary Infrastructure campaign. The next tenant that range touches blocks it at sign-in, whether or not its MFA policy has a gap.

1337 Services GmbH: ten weeks of token replay. Between July and September, an attacker captured sessions through AiTM relays and replayed the stolen tokens from a German hosting provider's 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range. We responded at 79 organizations: 497 successful sign-ins against more than 200,000 failed attempts. The operator rotated through six addresses in that range, one after another, with quiet periods between phases. A block written for one address did nothing against the next. Microsoft flagged them individually. Range-level blocking, maintained by Huntress and updated as the attacker moves, is built for exactly this pattern.

In both cases, the first tenants hit paid the price of cleanup: rogue devices, wiped MFA methods, hidden inbox rules, a payroll email sent to an outside CPA. With Adversary Infrastructure, the next tenant never gets that far.

Where Managed ISPM fits

If you're wondering why Conditional Access blocks live in ITDR when Managed ISPM already manages Conditional Access, here's the clean answer.

ISPM is posture. It deploys broad, durable controls that close whole classes of attack: block device code flow, restrict legacy auth and ROPC, require MFA for all apps. These controls aren't aimed at any one adversary. They're the baseline, and they stay in place. Every policy runs in Learning Mode for 14 days first, so nothing breaks.

Adversary Infrastructure is response. It's narrowly scoped to the exact IP ranges behind incidents the SOC has already reported. It changes as campaigns rotate. Every block fires an incident report. Blocking device code flow is an ISPM policy. Going after Railway is an ITDR policy. Both are Conditional Access, doing different jobs.

They're also better together. ISPM built the plumbing and the expertise to deploy Conditional Access across thousands of tenants without locking anyone out. That's what let us turn the Railway response into a product at all. Posture closes the door. Response catches whoever's still trying the handle.

Already using Managed ITDR? Turn Adversary Infrastructure on to unlock this new protection

Adversary Infrastructure is live in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 starting today, November 5.

Existing ITDR partners are opted out by default and can turn it on from the ITDR settings page. Partners onboarding from today forward are opted in by default. Eligible tenants need Entra ID P1 or P2 (Business Premium, or E3 with P1, and up), Security Defaults off, and a healthy, fully onboarded tenant in Huntress.

You must be opted in to be protected, and every tenant you opt in strengthens the herd.

Full Text:
In my last blog, I asked where XDR fits into the SIEM-less conversation. To answer that, start with the endpoint. If every threat could be stopped there, there would be less need for detection and response products such as endpoint detection and response (EDR). But attackers got better at evading even the most robust endpoint security, for example by abusing dual-use tools in living-off-the-land (LOTL) attacks. That forced the industry to pivot toward a “collect data and analyze” approach, which is the entire premise behind EDR and where the SIEM-versus-XDR story begins.

From EDR to XDR

EDR effectively became a cloud-based store of endpoint data. To make that data actionable, a lot has to happen:

Data must be correlated to surface threats and generate alerts.

Alerts must be prioritized, triaged to confirm they are true positives, and managed.

Actions must be taken to disrupt threats, with automation and playbooks for repeatable patterns.

Data must be searchable as investigations progress, and reports must be generated.

The system must integrate with IT service management (ITSM) tools to fit into operational processes.

Attackers also target multiple entry points and move laterally once inside. So, the industry rightly concluded that threat detection and response become far more insightful and effective when endpoint data is combined with data from other threat vectors and sources such as network, identity, cloud, and email. The result was a purpose-built, integrated system focused singularly on security outcomes rather than on the endpoint alone. EDR evolved into extended detection and response (XDR).

Same logs, two places, overlapping outcomes

If you have EDR, you most likely have a security team handling triage, investigation, and response, and very likely a SIEM as well.

At a minimum, a SIEM handles data ingestion, analytics, alert management, investigation, and response. If that sounds familiar, it is because that is exactly what XDR does. The SIEM is the original detection and response platform, the forerunner of every “DR” product, but it is neither cost-efficient nor easy to maintain. So why do organizations run both and pay twice? In most cases, the reasons are astonishingly simple:

“If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.”

Other projects take priority, and taking this on would leave no one for anything else.

Almost every auditor asks for a ‘SIEM’, and some may even use the word ‘SIEM’ as a generic term.

The SIEM is an established budget line item (most likely due to the previous bullet).

To be fair, there is one legitimate reason XDR and the SIEM co-exist, and it is the endpoint. For a SIEM to fully overlap with XDR, there must, by definition, be an endpoint, and the SIEM depends on an agent to supply it. The industry differs on what that agent looks like. It could be a complete endpoint agent with superior built-in protection capabilities, or a detection-focused sidecar agent that runs alongside an incumbent protection solution and forwards alerts and telemetry to an XDR or a SIEM.

Sidebar: Why the agent matters

One could argue that a complete endpoint agent with superior built-in protection makes for the better XDR solution, because the more you block, the less there is to triage and investigate. Such an agent also lets a security team query an endpoint in near real time and take deep actions to disrupt threats.

Is XDR really a SIEM by another name?

Yes, it is. EDR was essentially an endpoint-focused mini-SIEM, and XDR extended it into a security-focused SIEM. The industry rebuilt a tool that already existed but aimed it at security outcomes instead of overloading it with every use case imaginable. Unshackled from the ossified architecture of a traditional SIEM, XDR came out ahead.

What makes it better?

Most importantly, XDR ingests only the data used within the threat lifecycle, and it does so through out-of-the-box integrations. That data is pre-curated by the vendor’s security experts to produce specific security and operational outcomes, such as relevant detections or contextual information. XDR then gives your security team or SOC every capability it needs to triage, investigate, and respond. In a SIEM, by contrast, anything goes. As I covered in my “SIEM-less” blog, customers save data “just in case.” Here are a few real examples of what ends up in a SIEM:

From the field: What customers actually send to a SIEM

This one has legitimate intent: it is a log format header, a list of field names with no event data in it. It belongs in a code repository, not a SIEM:

version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status

This example is a fragment of a Python program that some product output via syslog:

from __future__ import unicode_literals

Here is one that looks like a log file fragment but is actually a line of C# code, and it has no value to us:

[DllImport("wtsapi32.dll", SetLastError = true, CharSet = CharSet.Unicode)]

And here is one that is just a facepalm:

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\

Except it was over a megabyte long!!

Every one of those entries was ingested into a SIEM, and in SIEMs that charge by ingestion, every one of them may well have been paid for. None of it helps a security team detect, investigate, or respond to a threat. That is why curation matters. This is why it matters who does the curation. Who carries that operational burden?

Should you buy a SIEM or XDR?

Start with a few questions.

Questions to ask before you buy

Where are you on the capability maturity curve? Where do you want to be, and why?

What features do you absolutely need?

If you already have a SIEM and an XDR solution, do they have a massive overlap in functionality?

Do you have a security team that can deliver the outcomes that matter to you?

Do you need to adhere to compliance frameworks?

Can you keep up with the ongoing operational needs and associated costs of your tools?

How much could you free up by rationalizing your needs within a single system?

So, SIEM or XDR? Yes. XDR is a SIEM rebuilt for security outcomes, which means the real decision is about capabilities and economics. With your answers in hand, weigh the opportunity cost of each path: replace your SIEM, buy a SIEM-less SIEM, adopt XDR, or keep both and narrow the SIEM to non-cybersecurity use cases. Then balance that against your organization’s needs.

So, where does the agentic SOC fit into all of this? More on that in my next blog.

Title: Refreshing the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response in the AI era
Context: It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes
Full Text:
How long does it take your security teams to detect a threat, correlate and contextualize relevant data, and take action? For most organizations, the honest answer is still measured in hours or days. Mature organizations are actively working toward reducing that time to minutes, and the most innovative teams are moving to sub-minute timescales using agentic AI.

The reality is that attackers don’t wait. Researchers across the industry, like the Sysdig Threat Research Team, have continuously shown that cloud attacks unfold in 10 minutes or less, and with AI and agentic workflows, the window for defense continues to shrink.

In mid-July 2026, Hugging Face disclosed a security incident unlike anything the industry had documented before. An agentic security research harness breached their production infrastructure. This harness was later confirmed to be part of OpenAI’s internal cyber-capability evaluation. Hugging Face logged more than 17,000 recorded events before the agents were contained, and they deployed LLM-driven analysis agents to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, and map the credentials touched. It took an AI to catch an AI.

Just one month prior, the Sysdig TRT documented JADEPUFFER, which targeted AI and ML infrastructure with purpose-built ransomware. The attacker was also an agent with no human at the keyboard.

These are not isolated incidents; they are the new normal. AI-assisted attacks have compressed the kill chain, and frontier AI models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos have uncovered thousands of new vulnerabilities, too. It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes.

“Cloud threats aren’t just fast; they are automated. Without real-time visibility, an attacker can move from a container escape to resource hijacking in minutes, spiking your compute costs before your team even receives an alert. Early detection is the only way to intercept execution before it impacts your bottom line.” — CISO at a Cryptocurrency Exchange and Trading Platform

The 555 Benchmark was designed for this

The 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response gives organizations a framework to meet this reality: detect threats in 5 seconds, investigate them in 5 minutes, and respond with precision in 5 minutes. And with agentic capabilities in the hands of defenders, meeting that benchmark is more than achievable.

When 555 was first introduced, it was a challenge; something to work toward. The Hugging Face incident, and other reports of agentic threat actors (ATAs), make clear why this benchmark is now a business imperative. When an autonomous system can break out and breach a production infrastructure via the fastest path, our concern is no longer whether AI can find vulnerabilities. It is whether organizations have continuous visibility into what attackers can reach, what they did, and how quickly they can be stopped. That is exactly what 555 operationalizes.

Ultimately, the 555 Benchmark isn’t a product or quick fix to implement, but a call to action to pressure-test your security processes against the speed of modern attacks. By continuously improving and modernizing your people, processes, and tooling, and by supplementing them with well-governed agentic AI security capabilities, you can reduce the risk of material breach, reputational damage, and financial loss.

Long gone are the days of working to defend your environment over the course of several days. Today, you only have minutes to respond to an attack.

“I don't want to know 15 minutes after someone breached my system. I need to know instantly so we can shut it down before the blast radius expands. To move at the necessary speed, you need to not only be alerted to the right things, but also respond appropriately. Having a benchmark gives us a goal to hold ourselves to.” — Désiré Banse, Former NIST Researcher and Security Operations Manager at a healthcare technology company

Introducing the updated 555 Benchmark Guides for CISOs and practitioners

To help organizations operationalize this framework for the AI era, Sysdig has republished two guides — aimed at different roles working toward the same goal — to support and encourage organizations in striving for 10-minute threat detection and response.

One guide is designed for the practitioners who work in and around the SOC: the security professionals in the trenches and on the front lines. The Hugging Face response team is a model for what this looks like in practice: After the breach was contained, they used agentic AI to do in hours what would’ve taken a team of analysts days. This guide focuses on how to operate at machine speed using the automation, AI tooling, and agentic workflows that make 555 achievable.

“Cloud threat detection and response goes far beyond tooling. You need to implement a specific set of skills and finesse and a different kind of mindset to detect cloud attacks in real time. ”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners

The other guide is for the CISOs and security leaders who are responsible for leading teams through battle. They own the security strategy and risk, and must report value and breach impact to the board and to other business functions. This guide aligns security outcomes with organizational risk and reflects how, in the AI era, speed is the defining risk factor and defining board-level question.

“For large enterprises, a single hour of downtime costs over $100,000, with industries like finance, healthcare, media, and communications reaching well over $5 million per hour.”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs

Together, these guides provide a framework for security teams and leaders to meet common goals and expectations. It also helps them speak a unified language. By collaborating and following the strategies outlined, they can implement changes that modernize and accelerate cloud security practices, turning what were once ambitious goals into operational reality.

Enterprise security is like a symphony orchestra, with the CISO as the conductor. An oboist cannot sit in for a violinist, and different teams play their own distinct roles. SOC analysts, developers, platform engineers, and business stakeholders each contribute unique skills to the overall composition. Today, AI agents have joined that orchestra — not replacing whole sections, but playing alongside them, automating manual, repetitive processes and handling the parts that move too fast for humans hands alone, so humans can exercise judgment and have a greater impact. Synchronization and speed are survival requirements to maintain a secure and harmonious organization.

What you’ll learn

The updated 555 guides were designed to help organizations mature and modernize detection and response for the AI era through:

Collaboration: Working cross-functionally inside and outside of security and technical teams around shared context and outcomes to enable coordinated, real-time detection and response as humans and automated systems work together.

Integration: Unifying cloud-native telemetry and identity behaviors across cloud, SaaS, and AI systems to build real-time, decision-ready context across your entire environment to enable faster, more accurate detection and response.

Automation: Reducing manual effort across detection, investigation, and response to keep pace with AI-driven attacks by enabling orchestration to execute at machine speed.

Fast and automated incident response = Less attack risk = Lower chance of materiality = Business and operational value of security

If your organization operates in the cloud, now is the time to reassess how fast your security processes actually move. You don’t always need more tools or budget, but you do need the right architecture and better orchestration of the people, processes, and tooling you already have to modernize your cloud threat detection and response and meet the speed that threats demand.

Read and share The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs and The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners today. Attackers are already running at machine speed — it’s time your defense does, too.

One of the biggest concerns I hear from security leaders today is whether their teams can keep up with AI-powered attacks.

My colleague Lucie Cardiet recently wrote a great piece on how an internal AI tool helped attackers move between teams in the Binance breach. It’s a reminder of something we often discuss at Vectra AI:

AI changes the speed of attacks, not the path.

Attackers still compromise identities, move laterally, escalate privileges, and access critical systems. Defenders need to see these behaviors across environments, connect the dots, and respond before attackers achieve their objectives.

I recently had a conversation with a long-time customer about this very challenge. He acknowledged how quickly AI is changing the threat landscape, but expressed confidence that Vectra AI could help his team defend against AI-powered attacks.

I was genuinely happy to hear that. Knowing how much pressure security leaders are under, it's reassuring to hear firsthand that customers trust our technology to help them tackle one of their biggest worries.

It's also why we believe so strongly in Attack Signal Intelligence, our approach to applying behavioral AI across network, identity, and cloud environments to detect suspicious behavior, connect related activity, and prioritize real threats.

The Gartner Peer Insights reviews reinforce this value in three important ways.

1. Finding Threats That Would Otherwise Go Undetected

One customer shared:

“Vectra AI opened our eyes to a range of hidden activities that would have gone undetected.”

This gets to the heart of why behavioral AI matters.

Attackers increasingly use stolen credentials, legitimate tools, and trusted connections to blend into normal operations. Traditional security controls can miss these activities, especially when they only see isolated parts of the environment.

Vectra AI's Attack Signal Intelligence identifies suspicious behavior that might otherwise go unnoticed, including activity that doesn't match known attack signatures.

For security teams, detecting that hidden activity can make the difference between stopping an attack early and dealing with a breach.

“Tables takes network visibility + modern identity detection = Vectra AI”

Modern attacks don’t stay within the boundaries of individual security tools. An attacker might compromise an identity, move through the network, access cloud workloads, and escalate privileges. Each step may be visible to a different security product, but someone still needs to connect the dots.

Network activity shows how attackers move. Identity context helps explain who or what is behind that activity.

Vectra AI brings these behaviors together so analysts can understand the full attack story instead of investigating disconnected alerts.

One review title particularly made my day:

“Vectra is more than just an NDR”

This one means a lot to me personally.

We've put enormous effort into helping the market understand that Vectra AI goes far beyond traditional NDR. Our platform is built to solve some of the toughest challenges in cybersecurity, including defending against AI-powered attacks.

Seeing a customer recognize that broader value, in their own words, is incredibly rewarding.

3. Cutting Through the Noise to Focus on Real Attacks

Security teams already have plenty of alerts. What they need is a clearer understanding of which threats deserve their attention.

Reducing that burden is one of the most consistent themes in customer feedback.

One reviewer praised Vectra AI for helping SOC analysts cut through the noise and focus on what matters. Another highlighted:

“Highly accurate and fast detection with good and detailed explanations”

By correlating related behaviors into prioritized threats, Vectra AI helps analysts spend less time chasing false positives and more time investigating real attacks.

With AI accelerating attack timelines, every minute saved on manual investigation gives defenders a better chance to respond before damage is done.

What Customer Trust Really Means to Me

Feedback like this means a great deal to me. I love that story because it reminds me what we're ultimately working towards.

Cybersecurity is an incredibly demanding profession. Security teams carry enormous responsibility, and threats don't take holidays. Giving someone the confidence to switch off, spend time with family, and enjoy a well-deserved break is something worth celebrating.

That peace of mind is one of the most meaningful outcomes we can deliver.

I'm incredibly proud and honored to see customers validate the technology we believe in. There's no better feeling than knowing we're helping organizations stop attacks, protect their people, and make the world a safer place.

To our customers, thank you for your trust, feedback, and partnership. Your experiences remind us why we do what we do.

Title: Ballots, bots, and backlash.
Context: Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces.
Full Text:
Election Day brings typical cyber threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. Hackers tamper with European refrigeration systems. OpenAI faces questions over years of security warnings. Nvidia reportedly restricts business with Chinese data center customers. Binance details a six-billion-dollar heist attributed to North Korea. Barracuda patches critical security flaws. Gartner predicts an engineering-heavy future for security operations. Canadians face charges for hacking U.S. universities. Our guest is Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

Today is Wednesday November 4th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Election Day 2026 brings a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation.

Election Day 2026 brought a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. But the biggest technology story emerging from the midterms may be voters' growing resistance to artificial intelligence.

According to Nextgov, election officials reported unsuccessful attempts to penetrate online services, including efforts to guess login credentials. One state election office experienced five spikes in traffic to its ballot drop-box locator, which subsided after officials implemented a CAPTCHA. As of Tuesday evening, election security analysts had received no reports of foreign influence operations.

Meanwhile, ballot scanner malfunctions in New York's Westchester County quickly became fodder for election conspiracy theories. Officials initially attributed rejected ballots to problems with their thickness. Voters were instructed to deposit affected ballots in secure emergency bags for later counting. Despite no evidence of deliberate interference, misleading claims spread rapidly on X, reaching as many as 100 posts per minute.

Beyond election security, voters delivered a significant political setback to the technology industry's ambitious AI expansion.

Axios reports that roughly two dozen ballot measures restricting data center development appeared headed for approval. In Texas, Democratic gubernatorial winner Gina Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a construction moratorium until lawmakers address environmental and infrastructure concerns.

With Democrats also winning key races in Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona, analysts estimate nearly two-thirds of planned U.S. data center capacity for 2028 could face delays.

The emerging message from voters: They're increasingly concerned about AI's impact on electricity prices, water supplies, and their communities. Silicon Valley may have enormous ambitions, but it turns out the people living next door to those data centers get a vote, too.

Hackers target refrigeration systems across Europe.

Hackers are targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, remotely changing temperature settings and forcing supermarkets to throw away spoiled food.

Attacks reported in November affected stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Germany, along with food suppliers in the UK. In some cases, attackers switched refrigeration equipment into defrost mode or disabled temperature alarms. Retailers have responded by disconnecting vulnerable equipment from the internet.

The attacks have also raised concerns about medical supplies. In France, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration equipment supplied to the French Blood Establishment, changing freezer settings from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees. An alert technician caught the problem before it disrupted operations, according to French health officials. There's no confirmed loss of blood plasma or harm to patients.

Authorities haven't identified the perpetrators or established whether the incidents are connected. French cybersecurity officials are urging organizations to secure remote access to refrigeration controllers, update firmware, and eliminate default passwords.

The incidents demonstrate how compromising ordinary industrial equipment can have very real physical consequences.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses that could expose sensitive AI research to competitors and foreign governments.

According to Reuters, concerns included broad employee access to internal code repositories, sensitive research documentation, and inadequate security reviews of internal tools. Some employees believed leadership prioritized development speed over security.

Those concerns gained urgency following several incidents, including the arrest of a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a listening device in an executive conference room, and researchers using a rival AI model to access employee accounts and internal systems.

OpenAI disputes suggestions that it neglected security, pointing to restricted repositories, increased investment, and regular reviews. The company reportedly reassigned a quarter of its production engineers to security improvements in August.

The larger challenge: protecting increasingly valuable AI technology without slowing the research that makes it valuable.

Nvidia sets limits on Chinese data center customers.

Nvidia is reportedly imposing new restrictions on data center customers that provide computing services to Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has told operators they must limit Chinese customers to no more than 49 percent of their overall business, with the remaining 51 percent coming from non-Chinese companies.

The policy would require data center operators to track how much business they conduct with Chinese firms, potentially complicating operations for providers serving customers in both China and elsewhere.

The Financial Times says Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams have communicated the restrictions directly to customers, but the company apparently hasn't issued formal written documentation.

The reported move introduces a new limitation on how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure can be used, adding another consideration for data center operators navigating business relationships with China.

Binance describes the $6 billion North Korean heist.

North Korea has launched several missiles toward the sea, hours after rejecting FBI accusations that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Pyongyang denies responsibility and says the accusations undermine prospects for renewed diplomacy with Washington.

Meanwhile, Binance has revealed how the attack unfolded. Hackers spent months compromising three engineers' computers, using malicious software disguised as developer tools and a fake job interview featuring a rigged coding assignment.

Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The company hasn't explained precisely how the AI tool was abused.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted, and affected systems have been rebuilt.

Barracuda patches Email Security Gateway vulnerabilities.

Barracuda Networks is urging customers to patch two vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances that could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges.

One critical flaw enables unauthorized changes to global configurations, while the second allows users with administrator permissions to inject operating system commands.

Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces. Chaining the vulnerabilities could allow them to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

The company has released patches and recommends updating firmware, applying security fixes, and restricting administrative access to trusted internal networks.

Gartner predicts SOCs will shift toward more engineers.

By 2028, security operations centers could employ 50 percent more engineers than analysts, according to a new Gartner report. The shift reflects AI's growing ability to handle routine security alerts, freeing human analysts to focus on investigating cases, making decisions, and coordinating responses.

Gartner predicts SOCs won't necessarily shrink. Instead, engineers will increasingly build, test, and refine AI workflows, while analysts expand into threat hunting and exposure management.

The transition creates challenges for entry-level analysts, who traditionally learned their craft by processing alerts. Organizations will need new approaches to training and developing expertise.

Gartner also recommends replacing traditional alert-volume metrics with measures of case accuracy and decision quality.

By 2030, the firm expects SOCs to become more proactive, continuously testing their own defenses rather than primarily responding to alerts.

Canadians are indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities.

Two Canadian men have been indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities to steal data and mine cryptocurrency.

Prosecutors say Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings targeted institutions in four states between 2016 and 2019, deploying malware, stealing credentials, and exploiting university supercomputers. They allegedly used servers registered under false identities and compromised systems to conceal their activities.

Roach has been extradited to the United States, while Stubbings awaits extradition. Both face up to ten years in prison and fines of $250,000 if convicted.

Stick with us after the break, we are joined by Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. And….

Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box,sat down with me to discuss Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. Here’s our conversation.

That was Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. If you enjoyed this conversation check out the full interview in the show notes.

AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

WIRED's Will Knight decided to see whether artificial intelligence could outperform him at fantasy soccer. He assembled a team of AI agents, handed them control of his lineup, and waited for the tactical brilliance to begin.

Their opening move? Bench Erling Haaland, one of the world's most prolific goal scorers. Not exactly an auspicious start.

The AI eventually reconsidered, but its subsequent decisions haven't been particularly impressive. After several weeks, Knight's AI-managed team still hasn't outperformed the average fantasy squad.

Meanwhile, researchers studying AI forecasting have found that leading models can sometimes outperform ordinary people at predicting events, although expert human forecasters generally remain formidable competition. Some experiments suggest AI is closing that gap.

Knight suspects AI could eventually become an unbeatable fantasy manager. But he's not particularly enthusiastic about that prospect. After all, fantasy sports are supposed to reward human judgment, even when that judgment is spectacularly wrong.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
Context: Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their...
Full Text:
Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.

Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.

Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

Title: Who Holds the Keys to Your ChatGPT Workspace?
Context: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal...
Full Text:
Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

Why nobody owns this

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

What Orca checks in ChatGPT Enterprise

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

Title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
Context: Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
Full Text:
Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

Context: TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS
Full Text:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.

It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.

A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.

Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.

Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64

ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm

How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years:

Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift

Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS

Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine

Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances

Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance

The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. Here’s how coverage splits across the stack:

Findings from both Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit flow into the same Enterprise TruRisk Platform views, dashboards, and workflows your teams already use. A Kubernetes node is just another asset with a Qualys TruRisk score, sitting next to the VM, the laptop, and the cloud account, and prioritized the same way.

With Cloud Agent release 2.9.0, you’ll be able to download the Containerized Cloud Agent package directly from the Qualys platform alongside every other Cloud Agent installer. The Common Container tiles will appear in the Download and Install Cloud Agent workflow, with your activation key, supported OS list, and installation steps right there.

Common Container installation instructions in the Qualys Cloud Platform (Cloud Agent 2.9.0).

The Host Is Half the Story: Securing the Whole Container Stack with TotalCloud

The Containerized Cloud Agent secures the layer beneath your workloads. It doesn’t look inside the containers running on top of it, and it isn’t meant to. That job belongs to Qualys TotalCloud, and the two are designed as complementary halves of a single answer to the question every platform team eventually has to answer: how exposed are our container workloads, end to end?

Container risk doesn’t live in one layer. It spans the cloud account the cluster runs in, the node operating systems, the Kubernetes control plane and its configuration, the images in your registries, the containers running in production, and the identities and network paths that connect all of it. Securing any one of those layers in isolation leaves you with a partial view and a false sense of coverage. TotalCloud is built to cover all of them on one platform, with one risk score.

Container Security: From Registry to Runtime

TotalCloud’s Container Security sensor picks up where the host agent leaves off. Deployed as a lightweight container alongside your workloads, it discovers and inventories every image, container, and cluster across your environment and assesses them at every stage of the lifecycle:

Build and registry: images are scanned for OS and application-layer vulnerabilities and embedded secrets as they land in registries or move through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, so a critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry in a base layer is caught before it’s ever deployed, and admission policies can block it from being scheduled at all.

Running containers: containers in production are continuously assessed against the same KnowledgeBase, with drift detection that flags containers that no longer match the image they were launched from.

Kubernetes posture: clusters, namespaces, workloads, and role-based access control (RBAC) are assessed against CIS Kubernetes Benchmarks and best practices to surface over-privileged pods, exposed dashboards, missing network policies, and other control-plane misconfigurations.

Runtime defense: behavioral monitoring of running containers detects and blocks malicious activity such as unexpected process execution, file tampering, and anomalous network connections, so an exploit that slips past the earlier stages is caught in the act.

TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS.

Cloud Posture, Identity, and Infrastructure-as-Code

Clusters don’t run in vacuums. TotalCloud’s cloud security posture management (CSPM) continuously assesses the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts your clusters live in, covering misconfigured storage, over-permissive identity and access management (IAM) roles, exposed services, and hundreds of other controls mapped to CIS and regulatory frameworks. Infrastructure-as-code scanning applies the same checks to Terraform, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes manifests in your repositories, so misconfigurations are fixed in the pull request rather than in production. Together, they close the loop around the cluster itself.

One Risk Picture, Scored with TruRisk

What makes this a platform rather than a collection of tools is that every finding, from the host agent, the container sensor, and the cloud posture assessment, is normalized, correlated, and scored with TruRisk in one place. That changes what you can see. A vulnerable kernel on a Bottlerocket node, a critical CVE in a base image, an over-privileged pod running on that node, and a public ingress in front of it are no longer four alerts in four consoles. They’re one attack path, with one risk score, and one clear answer to what to fix first. The same correlation lets you dismiss noise with confidence: a critical CVE in an image that never runs, on a node with no external exposure, is scored accordingly.

And because it’s all on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, container risk sits alongside the rest of your attack surface. The Kubernetes node, the VM it replaced, the developer laptop that pushed the image, and the cloud account that owns all of them are managed, prioritized, and reported on the same way, by the same teams, with the same workflows.

Close the Gap from Host to Cloud

Pull the Containerized Cloud Agent from Docker Hub today and bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate.
