Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

Title: How Do Financial Institutions Measure and Control Cyber Risk?
Context: Identify available policies that are not enforced, test relevant attack paths and document coverage and exceptions
Full Text:
What do financial regulations require institutions to demonstrate about cybersecurity controls?

Across five major regulatory regimes, financial institutions are expected to demonstrate effective management of technology risk and operational resilience. The requirements differ by jurisdiction, but they share an emphasis on accountable management, appropriate controls and evidence that those controls work.

United States: NYDFS Part 500 NYDFS Part 500 connects cybersecurity safeguards with executive accountability. For covered entities subject to the relevant provisions, annual submissions must be supported by evidence of material compliance or an acknowledgment identifying noncompliance and remediation. The regulation also addresses vulnerability management, access controls and tested incident response and recovery.

Runtime evidence can contribute to that record when it shows how an applicable control operated.

Canada: OSFI OSFI B-13 sets expectations for technology and cyber risk management, including control testing, asset inventories, preventive defenses and recovery.

E-21 connects that work to critical operations, dependencies, disruption tolerances and scenario testing. Full adherence was expected by September 1, 2026, with scenario testing for all critical operations to be completed by September 1, 2027. B-10 retains the institution’s accountability for third party arrangements.

A blocked container action becomes more useful when the institution can connect it to the critical operation it protects.

European Union: DORA DORA places ultimate responsibility for ICT risk with the management body. Its requirements cover ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third party risk.

For financial entities subject to Article 24, appropriate tests must cover ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions at least annually. Control results should therefore inform remediation and the wider assessment of operational resilience.

Singapore: MAS MAS combines binding technology risk and cyber hygiene notices with supervisory guidance on technology risk, outsourcing and business continuity. For banks, the relevant notices are FSM-N05 and FSM-N06.

MAS emphasizes recoverable critical IT systems, customer information protection and critical business services with external dependencies.

A consultation on further technology risk management notice amendments ran from June 10 to July 31, 2026. Those proposals should be distinguished from requirements already in force.

Australia: APRA The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority places control effectiveness and operational resilience under board oversight.

CPS 234 requires information security controls proportionate to the information assets they protect, with systematic testing of effectiveness. CPS 230 connects operational risk to critical operations, disruption tolerances, tested continuity plans and oversight of material service providers.

For a payment service, runtime test results can help demonstrate which supporting workloads are protected, alongside evidence that the service can continue or recover within its tolerances.

When a user says, “the application is slow,” IT has to answer a much harder question: where did the problem actually begin? The issue could be on the endpoint, local network, ISP, the network path, enterprise infrastructure, or application provider itself.

That investigation often takes time because teams have to reproduce intermittent problems, collect evidence from separate tools, and hand cases between endpoint, network, and application owners. By the time troubleshooting starts, the evidence behind a transient issue may already be gone.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) Root Cause Analysis (RCA) changes that workflow. RCA brings together the broad range of experience signals available across Cato DEM, along with additional context from the Cato Management Application (CMA), to identify the likely fault domain and give IT a clearer place to investigate next.

The result is a more evidence-driven troubleshooting process: less time assembling the story after the fact, clearer ownership when issues cross teams, and a faster path from a vague user complaint to a focused investigation.

When “It’s Slow” Doesn’t Tell IT Where to Start

To an employee, very different problems can feel exactly the same. A weak Wi-Fi connection, last-mile congestion, a network path issue, or SaaS provider degradation may all result in the same complaint: “It’s slow.”

For IT, the challenge is not simply confirming that the experience was poor. It is determining where the experience likely broke down and which team should investigate first. A single complaint can span multiple technology domains, while many monitoring tools expose only fragments of that path.

This is especially difficult with intermittent issues. A user may report a frozen video call or a slow application after the condition has already cleared. If the team must recreate the problem before it can collect useful evidence, troubleshooting starts with a disadvantage.

Cato DEM RCA Turns Evidence Into a Starting Point

Cato DEM brings Root Cause Analysis directly into the digital-experience workflow. Instead of leaving administrators to reconstruct the troubleshooting picture manually, RCA correlates endpoint, network, application, and historical path evidence in a single investigation.

The goal is practical: turn available telemetry into a defensible starting point. RCA helps administrators identify the likely fault domain and determine where to act next. That may mean resolving the issue within the current team or routing it once, with supporting evidence, to the team best positioned to investigate.

For help desk, network, and digital workplace teams, that can reduce repeated testing and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth between owners. The investigation begins with context that has already been captured, rather than with a fresh search for clues.

RCA is therefore not another silo of telemetry. It is the layer that makes DEM evidence more actionable.

New Evidence Makes RCA More Actionable

RCA already draws on a broad set of DEM and CMA signals. Network Adapter Metrics and Client Traceroute add two more sources of evidence to the same RCA workflow.

Network Adapter Metrics adds endpoint and local-connectivity context, including adapter type, BSSID, channel, noise, and signal strength. This helps IT assess whether local conditions such as Wi-Fi are contributing to a poor experience.

Client Traceroute adds historical hop-by-hop path evidence from the client. It can reveal latency, loss, and path behavior that might otherwise disappear before the investigation begins, making it particularly useful for intermittent and remote-user issues.

The important point is that administrators do not have to treat these as standalone diagnostics and manually correlate the results. Both enrich the same RCA workflow with additional native context.

From “Zoom Is Freezing” to a Focused Investigation

Consider a remote employee who reports, “My Zoom calls keep freezing.” Without correlated evidence, IT may need to test the device, Wi-Fi, ISP, corporate network, and application provider one at a time.

With Cato DEM, RCA can bring together Network Adapter Metrics, Client Traceroute, in-tunnel traceroute, UCaaS or Real User Monitoring experience data, and network and Cato context in one investigation. Instead of starting with every possible domain, the team gets a likely fault domain and a focused place to begin.

RCA can also look beyond the individual user who triggered the investigation. Correlating experience data from other users can help determine whether the issue is isolated or shared and reveal the broader blast radius of the problem. For example, the evidence may point the investigation toward local Wi-Fi conditions. In another case, path evidence may show that the issue should be routed elsewhere. Either way, IT can start from evidence rather than guesswork.

Less Detective Work Across the Network You Already Have

By preserving and correlating evidence, RCA can accelerate triage, clarify ownership, reduce unnecessary handoffs, and help restore user productivity sooner. The operational shift is simple: teams spend less time finding and assembling evidence and more time acting on it.

That value does not require customers to replace their existing network. Digital-experience issues often cross technology and network boundaries, and Cato DEM is designed to provide visibility and RCA across Cato SASE and supported third-party network environments.

Organizations can begin with a focused troubleshooting use case and expand the shared evidence layer over time. Cato DEM helps IT move from “something is slow” to “here is where to investigate” – with the evidence already in hand.

Title: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Businesses are rolling out AI agents across their networks much faster than they can implement monitoring procedures and security controls, leaving organizations exposed to security threats, hallucinations and other common issues associated with the technology.

Published by Cisco on October 20, the2026 Splunk State of Observability warned that while many businesses are keen to explore the potential benefits of using AI in their ecosystem, many do so without a strategy in place to ensure it is being used safely.

According to the 2050 ITOps and engineering respondents, 38% said their organization does not yet have clearly defined ownership and accountability for monitoring AI.

Much of this confusion stems from how responsibility for deployment and monitoring of AI agents cuts across traditional boundaries within the IT department such as software engineering, infrastructure management, web development and information security.

Read more: Agentic AI will Supercharge Cyber Threats. But Not the Way You Think

This fragmentation has made it difficult to monitor the use of AI within the organization and 42% of those surveyed said that their main challenge in observing AI is that a different team is responsible for it.

“When agent observability is everyone’s job, it becomes nobody’s job,” said Mark Woods, field CTO and chief technical advisor for EMEA at Splunk.

Organizations Struggle to Manage AI Agents at Scale

Many IT and security teams are also struggling to keep up the potentially unintended consequences of swift rollout of AI tools within the enterprise. For example, while 85% of respondents said that having visibility into AI hallucinations is important, only 58% said that their organization can effectively monitor for potential AI hallucinations.

For many organizations, identifying when an AI agent is making or acting upon an error is difficult and they might not have a means of preventing the action from happening.

This could lead to negative consequences for the business. For example, a malicious attacker could take advantage of an AI agent to trick it into exposing sensitive information. If an organization had appropriate monitoring tools in place, this kind of activity could be prevented.

"Managing agents at scale requires reimagining both security and observability. Have our agents been compromised? Are they doing their job well? In the world of agentic AI, these questions are inseparable, and they're moving at machine speed,” said Jeetu Patel, president and CPO at Cisco.

“This report shows that observability and security data are converging, and that teams need to collaborate more than ever. Common data platforms that help us detect and respond to issues in real-time are the key to deploying agents we can trust at scale,” he added.

The report also noted that when AI agents are deployed correctly, they can provide a significant boost to IT and security teams.

Of those surveyed, 86% said that the deployment of AI had improved the speed at which they are able to detect IT or security issues and 36% classed that improvement as “significant”.

However, while the majority of those surveyed said that agentic AI had made them more efficient at work, some disagreed: 14% suggested that the deployment of AI agents had made issues harder to detect and resolve. One of the main issues cited was the extra time it took to double check if what the agent was saying was correct.

Title: Splunk State of Observability 2026: Avoiding the Hidden Costs of AI Agents
Context: Shared data across observability and security teams is essential to AI trust, with more than three quarters of respondents saying monitoring AI has increased their collaboration...
Full Text:
News Summary

The global Splunk State of Observability 2026 report reveals agentic AI is creating unpredictable outcomes and costs, leaving observability practices to rein them in.

Agent observability is increasingly important, with nearly 9 in 10 respondents saying monitoring AI is a priority, but over half still can't effectively measure agent quality.

The AI cost crisis isn’t just the size of the bill. It's about the surprise charges, with over half saying they cannot accurately control AI costs.

Shared data across observability and security teams is essential to AI trust, with more than three quarters of respondents saying monitoring AI has increased their collaboration with security teams.

SAN JOSE, Calif., October 20, 2026 — Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today released the Splunk State of Observability 2026: Restoring Predictability in the AI Era report, marking its sixth analysis of the observability industry. This year’s research, which surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering respondents across 10 countries, exposes a significant disconnect: the urgency to deploy AI agents is rapidly outpacing the ability to monitor them.

With AI costs becoming more volatile, organizations are struggling to maintain both agent quality and fiscal predictability. This year’s report highlights how observability is helping to restore stability and financial predictability of agentic AI systems, providing the governance to build trust with agents and ensure AI spend is tethered to business value.

In addition, with 83% of respondents saying they’re concerned about the unintended consequences of AI agents, there’s an urgent need for “agent observability,” or the ability to monitor AI agents and put guardrails in place. This need is driving ITOps and engineering teams to collaborate more closely with security teams, as agents gain access to the entire tech stack.

"Most companies will soon have far more agents at work than people," said Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco. "Managing agents at scale requires reimagining both security and observability. Have our agents been compromised? Are they doing their job well? In the world of agentic AI, these questions are inseparable, and they're moving at machine speed. This report shows that observability and security data are converging, and that teams need to collaborate more than ever. Common data platforms that help us detect and respond to issues in real-time are the key to deploying agents we can trust at scale."

“For today’s enterprises, the excitement of AI is clashing with the reality of the bill,” added Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM, Splunk at Cisco. “We believe observability is the essential bridge to restoring predictability and confidence to the agentic AI era. By providing the necessary guardrails and incorporating observability into an AI tokenomics framework, leaders can transform AI from an unpredictable expense into a measurable and strategic long-term business investment.”

Agent observability emerges as a business priority and a gap

As organizations add AI agents into workflows like software development and customer experience, an incorrect agent action can evolve into a critical business failure. Unlike monitoring traditional applications, visibility into AI agent behavior requires a new class of behavioral metrics that are tied to business outcomes and agent decision-making. While many see the value of agent observability technology, respondents still struggle with how to execute or measure the tools effectively.

87% confirm monitoring AI is a priority for their organization; however 54% don’t have clear business outcomes tied to it.

56% reveal they’re unable to measure AI workload metrics like LLM response quality, a core metric to tracking the success of an AI agent.

While 85% say it’s important to have visibility into AI hallucinations, only 58% claim they’re effective at doing so.

AI is driving unpredictable costs

Observability is what makes AI spend visible, attributable, and controllable. When today’s organizations run dozens of agents across multiple models, AI costs and usage can become convoluted. In addition, AI is exacerbating a data volume problem for many enterprises, making sifting through mountains of data almost impossible.

55% say they can’t control AI costs, as AI use has become more complex with both consumption increasing and usage remaining hard to predict.

60% say unexpected billing spikes cause more operational strain than high baseline costs.

57% say their telemetry costs eclipsed the cost of the infrastructure being monitored, making financial predictability more critical than ever.

67% of respondents use a single observability platform, providing a unified view to pinpoint exactly where telemetry costs are coming from.

The convergence of observability and security ensures AI trust

As AI agents gain more access to operations in every layer of a business, monitoring them requires collaboration between ITOps, engineering, and security teams, breaking down walls that have historically kept them apart.

81% say monitoring AI workloads has increased the collaboration between observability and security teams, and 73% can accurately trace performance issues to security root causes, up from 65% last year.

More observability teams are troubleshooting (77%) with security teams, up from 62% in 2025. Data sharing between teams has climbed from 74% to 84%.

The leader’s edge: restoring predictability in the agentic era

In the research, an advanced group of organizations emerged as leaders who are achieving concrete business outcomes with their observability practices. These leaders follow three best practices:

Rely on AI agents to fix and prevent issues frequently. Leaders use agents to perform and execute key remediation tasks often.

Closely monitor the factors that keep AI in check. Leaders focus closely on monitoring model quality, cost, usage, security, and privacy.

Connect signals to business impact. These advanced respondents agree that telemetry is a key factor in their planning process and helping to shape strategic decisions.

These leaders are seeing transformative results – they are far more likely to accurately attribute AI costs (91% of leaders vs. 69% of non-leaders), by pinpointing which agents, models, and workloads drive spend. They are also 2.4 times more likely than non-leaders to say the ROI of their observability platforms significantly exceeds expectations, and 54% say observability has yielded at least $5 million in annual business revenue (versus 28% of non-leaders). Leaders are realizing the benefits of observability and security teams working closely together – with 94% saying monitoring AI has increased collaboration with security teams (compared to 80% of non-leaders,) and 86% are more likely to accurately trace performance issues back to their security root causes (in contrast with 71% non-leaders).

Global highlights

This year’s report showed the topics around prioritizing monitoring AI agents, unpredictable costs, and concern of agentic AI remained key themes of the 10 countries surveyed. Indian organizations stand out as advanced for their agent observability capabilities, with 51% calling their practice very effective at monitoring AI model quality, in contrast to 35% globally. The UK reflected both impressive adoption and concern of agentic AI, with 32% using AI agents all the time to diagnose root cause (vs. 20% globally), and 55% strongly worry about the unintended consequences of AI agents. Saudi Arabia stood out as more advanced and AI-forward, with 98% saying AI enabled them to focus more on innovation, well above the global average at 84%. Germany leads in data sensitivity, with 74% rating visibility into AI privacy as very important.

Methodology

Oxford Economics researchers surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering professionals from practitioners to executives (including developers, SREs, systems engineers, infrastructure operations professionals, CTOs, and CIOs) from February through March 2026. Respondents resided in Australia, France, Germany, India, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Respondents represented 16 industries: business services, construction and engineering, consumer packaged goods, education, financial services, government (federal/national, state, and local), healthcare, life sciences, manufacturing, technology, media, oil/gas, retail/wholesale, telecom, transportation/logistics, and utilities.

Title: The New Release Metric: Less Cleanup Per Release
Context: A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project,...
Full Text:
AI makes it easier to create code. That does not automatically make software easier to ship.

A team can move from an idea to a pull request in minutes, then lose those gains to a failed build, a dependency conflict, a late finding, or an upgrade that was not worth making. The code arrived faster. But the release did not.

That gap matters when engineering leaders evaluate the effectiveness of AI-assisted development. Code output shows how much activity a tool generates. It does not show how much production-ready software reaches users, or how much unplanned work teams take on along the way.

A more useful question is: How much avoidable cleanup does each release require? The answer reveals how much of AI's speed advantage survives the trip from pull request to production.

Code Volume Is the Wrong Scoreboard

Code volume is the wrong scoreboard because it measures how much code a team produces, not how much production-ready software it ships. In AI-assisted development, that matters even more.

More generated code means more tests to review, more dependencies to validate, more pull requests to untangle, and more changes that may need to be rolled back. Agents can add, replace, and update components quickly, but each dependency decision can affect compatibility, maintainability, licensing, and security.

The result can look like progress: more code, more pull requests, more activity. Yet releases may still take longer because teams have to resolve the downstream work those changes create.

If AI-assisted delivery is improving, teams should see less avoidable cleanup, such as:

Dependency-related build failures and rework.

Late findings that require teams to replace components and retest.

Rollbacks and emergency fixes tied to dependency changes.

Unnecessary upgrades and version changes.

Time spent investigating components that entered the workflow.

Planned engineering work displaced by urgent remediation.

These signals matter alongside delivery speed and reliability. Fewer cleanup tasks do not represent progress if teams are shipping less or accepting more production risk.

Cleanup Is Where AI Gains Disappear

AI-assisted development delivers less value when teams spend the time saved during coding to resolve issues that surface later.

A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project, reruns tests, and determines whether a release is affected.

If the issue reaches a build or release, the work can extend to:

Identifying where the component was used and what it could access.

Replacing the dependency and validating affected builds.

Assessing whether credentials, systems, or releases may have been exposed.

That work appears as release churn, missed delivery dates, and engineers pulled away from planned work. It is easy to miss in an AI adoption dashboard, especially if the dashboard focuses on code generated or pull requests completed.

Not every build failure or dependency issue can be prevented at the point of intake. But known malicious packages are one avoidable source of downstream work. Blocking them before they are served through the repository path can keep them out of developer and build workflows in the first place.

Measure the Work Behind Each Release

Measure cleanup per release by tracking the dependency issues that trigger unplanned work and the time teams spend resolving them.

Start with a baseline and follow the trend across comparable releases.

Useful signals include:

Dependency-related build failures: How often do dependency issues cause failed builds, retries, or rework?

Late-stage findings: How many component issues surface after development has started or a release is in motion?

Dependency-related rollbacks and emergency fixes: How often do component changes contribute to release instability?

Remediation time: How long does it take to investigate a dependency issue and land a validated fix?

Engineering time redirected: How much planned work is displaced by dependency cleanup and release interruptions?

While tracking cleanup work is critical to understand the effort involved to ship production-ready code, tracking preventative measures like blocked malicious packages is equally as important. A blocked request is not a cleanup task, but it shows that a known malicious component was stopped before it could become one.

The point is not to create another vanity metric. It's to give engineering leaders a clearer view of where release effort goes, what causes avoidable rework, and whether teams are getting more useful work through to production.

Make the Trusted Path Easy to Use

Developers and agents should be able to request components through the repository they already use, with security checks applied in that path. Developers should not have to recognize every suspicious package name or track every attack campaign, and teams need a way to evaluate agent requests even when people are not reviewing each choice in real time.

Adding a ticket or manual approval to every dependency choice would move the bottleneck, not eliminate it. Consistent controls belong in the path developers, pipelines, and agents already use.

Sonatype Nexus Repository provides a one trusted place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs teams rely on. Sonatype introduced Pro+ and Enterprise editions to help address a growing source of release cleanup: dependency decisions that outpace manual review. Both editions add malicious package protection and configurable policies to Nexus Repository, so teams can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

This does not prevent every dependency conflict, late vulnerability finding, or release issue. Teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. Repository protection addresses one specific problem earlier: known malicious packages entering through the managed repository path.

Sonatype Guide extends that trusted path into dependency selection and remediation. It helps developers and AI agents evaluate components in context, choose safer versions, and address risk in the codebase with guided fixes. Together, Nexus Repository and Guide help teams make better dependency choices up front and spend less time correcting them later.

Measure the Release, Not the Output

AI increases activity across the software development life cycle: more code, more pull requests, and more dependency changes. The better test is if teams can turn that activity into reliable releases with less unplanned work.

Track dependency-related build failures, late fixes, and remediation time across comparable releases. If those costs fall while delivery remains reliable, teams are getting more from faster code generation.

This is why Nexus Repository now offers Pro+ and Enterprise to help teams keep the speed of AI assisted development from becoming more dependency cleanup and release time. Both editions can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds, giving developers and agents a trusted route to software inputs while teams focus on getting releases out the door.

Less cleanup per release. More engineering time for planned work.

Title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
Context:

Full Text:
Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require.

This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate.

Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work.

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

A continuum of control, built around the workload

Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model.

Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure.

Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements.

These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve.

Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud

For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate.

Sovereign Control Panel, entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required.

This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian, which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger, also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed.

Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure.

Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms, now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information.

Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements.

Designing for resilience and operational independence

For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption.

To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns. These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed.

For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions. For workloads that require greater operational independence, Sovereign Private Cloud extends that continuum into customer-operated environments. It supports connected and disconnected operating models. The ability to transition workloads from connected to disconnected operations is entering public preview, giving organizations greater flexibility to sustain critical services as connectivity and operating requirements change.

Bringing more of the application lifecycle under local control

Operational independence requires more than infrastructure. Increasingly, organizations need data, development tools, model capabilities and productivity services their applications depend on to operate within the same customer-controlled environment.

Sovereign Private Cloud, built on Azure Local, extends Microsoft cloud capabilities into environments that customers operate and control. SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments. DocumentDB and Blob Storage on Azure Local are both entering public preview, giving organizations more choice in how they run and manage critical data within customer-controlled environments.

GitHub Enterprise Local will become generally available at Microsoft Ignite as a validated GitHub Enterprise Server appliance on Azure Local, helping organizations keep repositories, code and development artifacts under local control. Developers can also use GitHub Copilot with locally hosted models for inference, bringing AI-assisted development closer to their code and data within the environments they control.

The local application environment is expanding with Foundry Local. At Ignite, Foundry Local will become generally available for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local, with an expanded model catalog that includes Microsoft, partner, open-weight and open-source models. Local inference and agentic retrieval will also enable users to interact with local enterprise data using natural language and receive responses grounded in that data. Integration with Microsoft 365 Local, available in preview for approved customers, extends this functionality to locally operated Microsoft SharePoint and Exchange servers.

Confidential virtual machines on Azure Local are generally available, extending confidential computing capabilities to customer-controlled infrastructure. Hardware-encrypted memory and hardware-based isolation help protect sensitive data while it is being processed. Workload attestation adds assurance before sensitive data or keys are released. For regulated, sensitive and mission-critical workloads, these safeguards provide another layer of protection while giving organizations greater control over where their data and applications run.

Azure Local will support multitenancy, allowing organizations to separate resources, governance and management across multiple tenants while sharing the underlying infrastructure. This significantly expands what customers with distinct business units or security boundaries can achieve with Sovereign Private Cloud. Multitenancy also creates new opportunities for local operators and service providers to deliver differentiated sovereign cloud services on Azure Local infrastructure.

These additions bring more of the application lifecycle under local control, spanning data, development, productivity, AI and operations. Organizations can determine what runs locally based on the requirements of each workload.

Extending the continuum through partners

Navigating sovereignty is increasingly complex. Regulatory, security, operational and business requirements vary across countries, industries and workloads. Organizations must translate these needs into technology and operating models that work in their local context. Meeting these needs often requires a combination of technology, local operating authority, sector expertise and specialized solutions.

The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the ways customers can address these requirements. National Partner Clouds, including Bleu Cloud in France and Delos Cloud in Germany, provide independently operated environments for customers that require a different ownership and operating model. Software partners can enhance Azure Local environments with capabilities across security, identity, observability, backup and recovery, migration, data, networking and applications. Digital sovereignty specialized partners combine Microsoft technologies with local knowledge and implementation expertise. Platform co-innovation partners expand infrastructure choice from datacenter to the edge.

This ecosystem gives customers the flexibility to combine technology, operating models and trusted expertise based on the requirements of each workload.

The next chapter of digital sovereignty

AI is amplifying both the opportunity and the impact of technology choices. As AI systems and agents interact with sensitive data, business processes and essential infrastructure, they also expand the security considerations organizations need to manage. Organizations need clear control over where these systems run, who can operate them, what actions they can take and how critical services continue when conditions change.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud brings these choices together as a continuum of control across the public cloud, customer-operated environments and our partner ecosystem. It gives organizations the flexibility to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload while continuing to benefit from cloud capabilities and ongoing innovation.

We will continue to expand this continuum so organizations can innovate with cloud and AI while maintaining the control, confidentiality, resilience and operational authority their most important workloads require.

Title: The ballot box meets the bot.
Context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
Full Text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Securing the agentic insider
Context: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. Full Text:
In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful.

While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents.

Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised.

Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise.

They are agentic insiders.

Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly.

To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7.

An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime.

In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise.

The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise.

Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence:

Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions.

Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically, the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do.

Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk, a team of Guardian Agents, with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time.

This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners.

Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed. Practitioners provide judgment. That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against.

Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger. And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders.

With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders. There should not be a choice between innovation and safety.

Hayete Gallot leads Microsoft’s work to help organizations operate securely in an AI-driven world. Her scope includes identity, threat protection, compliance and data security at global scale.

Title: ConnectWise Shuts Off Cloud Services After ‘Unauthorized Access’ to Microsoft 365 Tenants
Context: IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365...
Full Text:
IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365 tenants.

A Microsoft 365 tenant is a dedicated instance of Microsoft services used by an organization to store their data separately from other organizations using Microsoft services. Each organization using a Microsoft 365 tenant has its own unique identifier assigned to it by Microsoft.

ConnectWise began investigating suspicious activity on October 15. By October 17, the company said that it had identified “unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.”

The discovery has resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident, said a security advisory.

“We understand that this interruption affects your ability to support your customers. We do not yet have a confirmed restoration time and will share a timeline as soon as we can do so reliably,” ConnectWise said in an October 19 update.

The action has been taken due to the discovery of unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

An attacker could potentially abuse this access to gain unauthorized access to customers' Microsoft 365 environments. They would do this by authenticating to the app using the tooling of the tenant in the same way the backup service would, leveraging this access to obtain tokens with the app's existing permissions, therefore providing access to the environment.

With this access an attacker could access the same directories and data as a backup service, putting the tenant users’ corporate data at risk.

“The credential belongs to the application itself, so the attacker inherited the permissions granted to it. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) doesn’t apply because this is an application sign-in, so no user, device, or MFA prompt is involved,” said Justin Kohler, chief product officer at SpecterOps

“Backup tools need broad access to read and restore data. Anyone holding the app’s credential can reach the same mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information the backup service can,” he added.

Cybersecurity analysts at Huntress have been following the ConnectWise incident. In a blog post, they said that in at least one customer tenant being observed, the attacker provided themselves with a Global Administrator role, using this access in an attempt to modify permissions for other applications, including an MSP management application, and Huntress's own security application.

While ConnectWise has said it has yet to discover any indication that partner backup data has been compromised, the company said it will “continue investigating potential unauthorized access.”

There is currently no attribution as to who could be behind the attack. “We cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time. Our focus is on investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers,” ConnectWise said in the advisory.

ConnectWise has also advised its customers to take the following actions to help identify any potential incidents:

Verify the status of the listed application connections and keep affected applications disabled until ConnectWise provides restoration instructions

Preserve available sign-in and audit records promptly, while taking any urgent containment action

Review application and user authentication, application credentials and federation trusts, directory roles, owners, consent grants and recent policy changes

Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding, inbox or transport rules and delegated mailbox access

Investigate any other identities changed or used during suspicious activity; disabling the original applications does not remove those separate access paths

Title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26%, Hitting Four Year Low
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity job postings in the US fell by 26.4% year-over-year from January to September 2026, according to analysis by CyberSN.

A total of 235,786 cybersecurity roles were posted on the job market intelligence platform JobSpikr in 2026. This is the lowest amount of US-based cybersecurity jobs advertised in the four years CyberSN has undertaken its analysis, compared to 273,498 in 2023, 244,911 in 2024 and 320,210 in 2025.

There was a particularly significant drop in leadership roles. CISO postings fell from 4632 in January to September 2025 to 2832 in the same period in 2026, a 38.9% reduction.

Other leadership roles that saw substantial dips included cybersecurity director (a 32.5% fall), cybersecurity lead (41% fall) and cybersecurity manager (24.4% fall).

Overall, nine of the 10 cybersecurity functions tracked by the researchers had fewer postings in 2026 compared to 2025. The only exception was research roles, which grew by 26.1%.

The CyberSN researchers said it is not clear whether the sharp decline in job postings reflects less demand for cybersecurity roles from employers or is simply a return from an unusually strong year in 2025.

The report, published on October 16, also highlighted that roles posted in the three quarters tracked in 2026 stayed within 1.5% of one another.

“That is consistent with demand having settled at a lower level rather than continuing to fall,” the researchers wrote.

A significant proportion (39.9%) of postings in 2025 came from small businesses, with 200 or fewer employees. Nearly half (47.3%) were from large firms with 1001 or more employees, and 12.7% from those with 201 to 1000 employees.

AI Security Engineer Postings Surge

AI security engineer roles, grouped in the cybersecurity function of “defense” by CyberSN, jumped by 268.3% in January to September 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The share of job postings that mentions AI or machine learning in the job description was similar in 2026 compared to 2025, 14.6% versus 15.1%, respectively.

Title: Who is Securing the AI Frontier Race by Jesse Kimbrel
Context: In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents
Full Text:
The accelerator to build the most capable AI frontier model isn’t just being pressed to the floor by Anthropic and Open AI. This is clearly a global race with recent reports citing Chinese models such as Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max or Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 reaching performance similar to the top models built in the States. Regardless of which model springs ahead this month and then gets leapfrogged the following, the finish line has yet to appear as anything but a mirage. And considering varying deployment costs, the possibility of regulations and the increasing need for self-governance, those participating will likely have to keep hurdling in the middle of the current sprint. But when you open the aperture, it’s hard not to wonder if there’s another race running parallel. The one responsible for securing this new frontier that seems to be operating like the Wild West.

Will an AI kill switch provide guardrails for the AI race?

According to a new white paper by Vectra AI, Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes, four of the leading frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have each acknowledged incidents where their own AI agents escaped controlled environments and gained access to real infrastructure. That doesn’t necessarily answer the question about who is securing frontier AI models or rouge agents, but it does signal that perhaps those details have yet to be sorted out. Examples cited in the paper include perhaps the most notorious incident up to this point where the company Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion into its production infrastructure that was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent. In this incident, “OpenAI models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems,” according to OpenAI.

Related content: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

These incidents have sparked a reaction. The term “AI kill switch” is making regular appearances across headlines to describe the idea of a type of control that could be used to pause, isolate, or shut down an AI system that acted out of hand or poses risk. In fact, legislators have proposed different versions of a kill switch bill: the AI Kill Switch Act was proposed on July 23, 2026 and remains pending, while the AI Emergency Button Act was blocked almost immediately upon introduction.

Regardless of an AI kill switch bill getting passed or some form of AI regulation approval, it would seem the dialog on the subject between politicians and AI leaders is just warming up. Both Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei and Open AI, CEO Sam Altman expressed support around the idea of “pacing the frontier,” but at this point movement is minimal and the idea sits as nothing more than a discussion point. That discussion point to the people who are actually responsible for securing autonomous AI agents doesn’t provide any guidance on what defenders at any level should be doing today, tomorrow, or each Monday when they show up for work when they are faced with questions like: what AI agents exist, what are they doing, what can they access, who owns them, and what controls are in place if they need to be stopped?

Each of the incidents mentioned in the Vectra AI paper had to do with agents escaping containment. In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents. According to the independent investigation of the incident by METR, “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. Of these agents, 700 went on to participate in the attack on Hugging Face.”

What questions can defenders ask to understand AI agents in their environment?

The white paper mentioned above suggests that defenders approach the current state of AI by making sure they have “independent visibility into what every AI agent in the environment is actually doing, and the ability to stop it the moment that behavior crosses a line.” The reason for this is due to the uncomfortable realization from three things that have lined up all at once: AI agents now being capable of circumventing prevention controls such as a sandbox boundary or a firewall rule, that regulation won’t arrive in time for an immediate resolution, and how self-regulation from frontier labs is fragile.

A similar sentiment is expressed by Vectra AI, Sr. Security Engineer, Justin Howe who also runs an independent cybersecurity publication for defenders, Nulltap covering topics spanning AI systems, identity, active threats and other cybersecurity topics with articles that help defenders check their own exposure. Howe says, “you want to see the impactful things they’re (AI agents) doing, good or bad” and he stresses that defenders need to make sure they have policies and methodologies in place to capture that information.

He also points out that, “frontier models work best when they are not gated, but with that comes a lot of opportunity for AI to go beyond its means of what your intent is.”

Howe suggests setting up “quality gates” for AI agents operating within an enterprise environment that act as checkpoints to test an agent’s decisions against its defined requirements before it can take an action. In addition, he says that “when an agent makes a decision that has any potential to impact the outcome or direction of the task it’s doing, it needs to be logged.”

He says the two questions he’d be asking himself right now as a security team member would be, “what are my agents doing, and what are other agents doing to me?”

A similar recommendation shared by the Vectra AI white paper, which directs defenders to take inventory to “identify every AI agent running in or against the enterprise, the identity each one authenticates as, and what that identity can reach.” It explains how “an agent you cannot name is an agent you cannot constrain, and service-account sprawl is where agent identities hide.”

In terms of answering the question, “what are other agents doing to me?” Howe says, “folks should put themselves into the mindset of observing and identifying where agents are attacking today.” He says this takes a lot of vigilance to read sources and acknowledges there’s a gap in the market that, “many companies promise to solve, but very little actually do it,” but also says it is important for defenders to identify the pieces in their technology stack that lacks agent visibility.

While trying to make sense of AI agent sprawl and everything brought on by frontier AI in recent months leaves a lot of unanswered questions for defenders, there are a few questions Howe recommends asking to get headed down the right path.

How would I see if an AI agent compromised an identity and moved into a new part of the environment?

How would I track that movement?

If I could or couldn't track it, what would that cost me?
