Spot multi-stage attacks that span multiple systems

Relying on complex dashboards without clear guidance

Reduce blind spots between separate security tools

Assuming a single point of visibility equals full coverage

Simplify licensing and vendor relationships

Neglecting core risks like compromised endpoints and phished credentials

The majority of successful attacks still start with a handful of familiar paths:

Compromised endpoints

Phished credentials

Malicious email

The Huntress Managed Security Platform focuses on securing these primary threat vectors. In return, you get deeper visibility where attackers are most likely to strike, without drowning in a bloated toolset you don’t have time to manage.

5. Focus on identity-first security and zero-trust architecture

Trend: Perimeters have dissolved, and identities are the new battleground. Securing logins and access credentials is now central to protecting every endpoint.

With so many apps in the cloud, identity has become the real perimeter. The best phishing protection guards identities to keep them out of the wrong hands.

Threat actors often find it easier to steal or phish credentials than to exploit a local vulnerability. Then, they use those stolen accounts to blend in with normal activity. That’s why identity-first security and zero trust architecture (ZTA) are now central to modern security strategies.

ZTA doesn’t grant long-lived trust. It assumes every session could be risky and leans on continuous verification, like repeatedly checking on:

Device health

User behavior

Usage context

Managed identity threat detection and response (ITDR) builds on that by watching for post-compromise behavior, like unusual logins and multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue.

When ITDR works alongside EDR, your team can spot both the compromised laptop and the compromised account it’s impersonating. It strengthens detection across every layer of your environment and closes the gaps attackers rely on.

6. Treat your supply chain as a major initial access risk

Trend: Attackers are exploiting trusted vendors, turning supply chains into backdoors for compromise.

The software and service providers your business relies on can become stepping stones for attackers.

High-profile incidents like the Kaseya supply chain attack show how compromising one vendor can give broad access to hundreds or thousands of downstream environments. That risk has only amplified with automation and remote tooling, making these relationships even more attractive to bad actors.

Protecting your endpoints now means monitoring how connected systems behave, which includes:

Locking down remote management tools

Enforcing least privilege for third-party access

Pairing vulnerability management with continuous monitoring

This is all to ensure unusual behavior from a trusted vendor doesn’t slip by. Even if you can’t control every partner’s security posture, you can watch how tools behave on your endpoints and be ready to contain abuse quickly.

Quick Checks for Vendor-Related Endpoint Risk

Ask vendors how they secure remote access tools and admin accounts.

Limit vendor access to only the systems they truly need.

Require MFA and strong logging for all third-party connections.

Review vendor activity regularly for unusual sign-ins or changes.

7. Ride the wave of posture management

Trend: Misconfigurations are still the easiest way for attackers to get in. Fixing small mistakes prevents big breaches.

Endpoint security posture management helps find and fix these configuration issues at scale. These tools also keep an eye out for drift as settings change over time.

For many businesses, tying this to dedicated Microsoft 365 security monitoring is key. They need to watch for risky settings and data access patterns that might indicate someone is abusing those misconfigurations

Misconfigurations in Microsoft 365 and other cloud services and productivity platforms are a quiet but consistent source of breaches. Attackers are more than happy to walk through open doors left by occurrences like:

Over-permissive sharing

Weak access rules

Ineffective legacy protocols

8. Prevent alert fatigue and close skill gaps

Trend: Even the best tools fail if security teams drown in alerts or lack the time to respond effectively.

Security tools can generate an overwhelming amount of data. It’s common for small or mid-sized teams to see thousands of alerts per day across EDR, email security, identity platforms, and cloud services. With a lean staff, this can lead to alert fatigue. People either tune out the noise or burn out trying to keep up.

A human-led 24/7 managed SOC like Huntress can make that data workable.

Instead of expecting your team to triage every event, you can count on security experts to investigate alerts, confirm or dismiss threats, contain and remediate threats, and provide guidance to bolster defenses when something is actually wrong.

That support closes skill gaps, reduces time-to-response, and lets your in-house team focus on projects that move the business forward instead of living in alert queues.

9. Look for stealthy living off the land (LotL) attacks

Trend: Attackers are hiding in plain sight, using your own tools to evade detection.

More attackers are skipping traditional endpoint security threats like malware and turning to LotL techniques like living off the land binaries, or LOLBins. They’re using built-in tools like PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), and command-line utilities to do their dirty work.

Because these tools are part of normal Windows environments, their activity can blend in easily if you’re only watching for known malicious files or signatures.

Detecting LotL activity takes endpoint visibility plus context from a human who knows what normal looks like for your environment. That might mean actions like:

Flagging an unusual PowerShell script launched by a user who rarely uses the command line

Spotting a lateral movement tool running from a workstation that has no business doing remote admin work

These are subtle clues, but they often surface well before data is encrypted or exfiltrated. Download our LOLBins Attack Playbook to learn how to spot these attacks and shut them down.

10. Tighten security on all your IoT and OT devices

Trend: IoT and OT devices are expanding the attack surface faster than security can keep pace.

Think about smart cameras, printers, sensors, badge readers, and industrial controllers. They're all part of the endpoint landscape these days, even if they aren't running standard security agents. And your business needs endpoint protection across all of your endpoints, not just the obvious ones.

A lot of these IoT and OT devices don't have strong security built in, or they ship with insecure default settings that people rarely bother to change.

Instead of trying to run endpoint agents everywhere, isolate these devices with network segmentation so these systems have limited access to critical assets and can’t freely talk to everything else. Then, monitor the systems they communicate with using managed EDR.

That way, in IoT cybersecurity instances, you still see the lateral movement and can respond before real damage is done.

Title: What Cybersecurity Leaders Must Prioritize in 2027
Context: Identity attacks and business email compromise (BEC) This is the threat that breaks the traditional security model most completely, because there's often no malware, no exploit,...
Full Text:
The challenges of 2025, tight budgets, rising AI anxiety, and increasingly organized cybercrime, didn't go away. They matured. The threat landscape of 2026 is sharper, faster, and more brazen than what we faced previously, and the leaders navigating it deserve an honest, updated picture.

So let's talk about where things actually stand and what you can do about it.

The threat landscape has shifted under our feet

Back in 2025, we were watching the early signs of trends that are now defining realities. Ransomware was rampant. AI was the new buzzword. Phishing was getting sneakier. Today, those trends have compounded into something more sophisticated, more coordinated, and more personal.

The good news: defenders have leveled up too. The question is whether your defenses have kept pace with what attackers are actually doing in 2026.

Here are the five concerns that should be at the top of every security leader's list, and what proactive defense looks like for each one.

1. Abuse of trusted IT tools (RMM and Remote Access)

Here's a threat that should keep you up at night: attackers aren't breaking down your door anymore. They're using a key you handed them.

Remote monitoring and management (RMM) platforms like ScreenConnect were built to make IT teams more efficient. Attackers figured out that hijacking those same platforms lets them blend seamlessly into normal admin activity, completely evading traditional defenses that assume "if it's an approved tool, it's safe."

Huntress data shows RMM abuse jumped roughly 277% year over year, making it one of the defining attack patterns of 2026.

What proactive defense looks like:

This is a problem that requires distrusting your trusted tools. Huntress Managed EDR is built to watch for behavior, including persistence mechanisms, unusual process chains, and lateral movement, even when that activity originates from a sanctioned RMM tool. Ransomware canaries and tradecraft-driven detections are designed to catch abuse while attackers are still staging, not when encryption has already started. And with a 24/7 AI-Centric SOC delivering around an 8-minute mean time to respond on endpoint incidents, the window for RMM abuse to escalate into something catastrophic gets very small, very fast.

Instead of asking, "Is the RMM set up right?" we need to shift our thinking to, "What are we going to do when it inevitably gets misused?"

2. Malicious use of AI and AI-powered cybercrime

Generative AI has given threat actors capabilities that would have required significant resources and expertise just a few years ago: deepfakes that impersonate executives, adaptive malware that morphs to evade detection, automated vulnerability discovery at scale, and hyper-personalized phishing emails crafted to match a target's communication style, role, and relationships. AI-powered cybercrime is no longer a future threat. It's the current operating model for sophisticated threat actors.

What proactive defense looks like:

The answer isn't to build an "AI-only SOC" and call it a day. Huntress uses AI to triage and correlate massive telemetry across endpoints, identities, and logs, then passes validated findings to human threat hunters who make the actual call. AI for scale, humans for judgment.

On the human side, Managed Security Awareness Training includes content specifically focused on generative AI scams, deepfakes, and AI-crafted phishing, so your employees know what these attacks actually look like, not just what last year's phishing emails looked like. Pairing that user behavior change with technical detection of AI-enabled attack patterns gives security leaders something they can actually measure and manage.

We need to shift from seeing AI as a vague, uncontrollable risk to implementing clear controls: combining policy, user behavior, and technical detection.

3. Social engineering and phishing (ClickFix, fake CAPTCHAs, smishing, vishing)

Social engineering has always been the path of least resistance. But the techniques have gotten nastier.

ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA flows trick users into executing malicious commands themselves, bypassing endpoint defenses entirely because the user is doing the work. Smishing and vishing attacks are increasingly AI-assisted and targeted. More than half of observed loader activity in Huntress telemetry is tied to these kinds of scams. The human is no longer just the last line of defense. In 2026, they're often the primary attack surface.

What proactive defense looks like:

Effective security awareness training has to reflect real threats, not generic phishing simulations. Huntress Managed SAT is built on actual threat intelligence pulled from millions of monitored endpoints and identities, so the training maps to the phishing, smishing, and vishing techniques attackers are actively using, not what they were using two years ago.

But training alone can't carry the weight. When a user does click, Managed EDR catches footholds, loaders, and post-click persistence at the endpoint. Managed ITDR spots the downstream identity abuse, including suspicious inbox rules, rogue OAuth apps, and impossible travel, that often follows a successful phish. And Managed SIEM correlates signals across VPN, firewall, and endpoint logs to surface phishing-driven lateral movement before it becomes a business-impacting event.

Instead of just checking who clicked on a phishing link, let's start looking at the bigger picture: how much damage a single click could actually cause before we shut it down.

4. Ransomware and multi-extortion attacks

Ransomware groups have gotten patient. That's the part that's changed most dramatically.

The days of "spray and encrypt" are giving way to a slower, stealthier approach: exfiltrate first, negotiate later. Double and triple extortion, where attackers threaten to publish stolen data or notify customers and regulators on top of encrypting systems, means paying the ransom doesn't even guarantee the problem goes away. And with time-to-ransom stretching from roughly 17 to 20 hours as gangs trade speed for leverage, there's a longer window of adversary presence inside the network before encryption begins.

That's actually an opportunity, if you have the right detections watching for it.

What proactive defense looks like:

Huntress focuses detection on the steps before encryption: lateral movement, credential abuse, data staging, and pre-ransom tradecraft across EDR, ITDR, and SIEM. Ransomware canaries combined with a 24/7 SOC mean that when something is caught, it gets validated and acted on, not just alerted on. Rapid containment, not just rapid notification.

Equally important is resilience planning. Offline backups, network segmentation, and a tested incident response plan are what separate a recoverable disruption from an existential event. Security leaders who've done that work sleep better when an incident happens, because they know what comes next.

The mindset shift: ransomware isn't a question of "if." It's a question of how fast you find it, how well you contain it, and how cleanly you recover.

5. Identity attacks and business email compromise (BEC)

This is the threat that breaks the traditional security model most completely, because there's often no malware, no exploit, and nothing for an endpoint agent to catch. Attackers just log in.

With stolen or purchased credentials readily available, adversaries increasingly skip the hard part and authenticate as legitimate users. From there, they move quietly: abusing inbox rules to intercept and reroute financial communications, compromising OAuth apps for persistent access, and stealing session tokens to bypass MFA entirely. About 37% of identity threats in Huntress telemetry involve suspicious login footprints, and credential theft remains one of the most common breach vectors across the board.

BEC alone costs organizations billions annually, and most of it isn't stopped by endpoint tools because the attack never touches an endpoint in a meaningful way.

What proactive defense looks like:

Huntress Managed ITDR treats identities and email as first-class attack surfaces, not afterthoughts. That means detecting session hijacking, rogue OAuth apps, suspicious access rules, and BEC flows in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, with an MTTR of around 3 minutes to lock a compromised account. Managed SIEM pulls in VPN, firewall, and identity-adjacent signals so that identity abuse doesn't disappear into log noise.

But technology alone won't stop BEC. Huntress guidance leans hard into the human and process side: verification workflows for financial transactions, strong MFA enforcement, least-privilege access, and building a security culture that extends to accounting, HR, and executive teams, the people BEC attackers are actually targeting.

Instead of asking, "Did we block that phishing email?" let's start talking about "How quickly can we catch identity misuse, and how little damage can it do before we shut it down?"

From reactive to resilient: The new bar for security leaders

The 2023 version of this post talked about innovation, adaptation, and collaboration as the path forward. That's still true. But in 2026, the bar is more specific.

Proactive, resilience-first security means covering the real attack surface, endpoints, identities, logs, and people, where modern attackers actually operate. It means using AI for scale and triage while keeping humans in the loop for judgment and accountability. And it means being able to tell a clear story to your board, your insurers, and your auditors: here's our exposure, here's how we detect it, here's how fast we respond, and here's how we recover.

Common 2026 attack patterns aren't going away. The question is whether your environment is designed to expect them, contain them, and recover from them, or just to hope they don't happen.

That's the difference between security as a cost center and security as a business enabler, and it's the conversation worth having with every stakeholder in your organization this year.

Title: Texas HB 3834 Cybersecurity & AI Training Requirements
Context: In August 2019, the computer systems of 23 Texas municipalities were hit with a ransomware cyber attack that locked access to all computer files in one instance
Full Text:
Did you know that Texas passed a new regulation for state employees to participate in a mandatory cyber security awareness training program?

In June of 2019, Texas State Legislature passed HB 3834, a bill requiring local and state government employees, and even state contractors, to complete a Department of Information Resources (DIR) approved cyber security awareness training program like Huntress! Hint: We’ve made security awareness training more flavorful than your favorite steak house!

Depending on your organization’s role as a state agency, local government entity, or contractor, you may be immediately impacted by this annual compliance training requirement, known as HB 3834. If your organization falls into scope, HB 3834 requires that a security awareness training program has been rolled out and completed by all required employees every year, with your organization certifying completion to DIR by August 31st. That’s a pretty big burden if you haven’t established a formal security awareness training program yet.

And there’s a new factor. As of September 1, 2025, HB 3512 added a second annual requirement for the same people: a DIR-certified artificial intelligence (AI) awareness training. In-scope employees now need to complete both cybersecurity and AI awareness training each year.

But don’t worry, we are going to show you what is required, why this regulation came to be, and how you can comply with HB 3834 without stressing out.

Why is the HB 3834 Regulation Necessary?

It’s no secret that governments are now prime targets for hackers more than ever. In August 2019, the computer systems of 23 Texas municipalities were hit with a ransomware cyber attack that locked access to all computer files in one instance. The ransomware even revoked the ability to process utility payments in another municipality. The Mayor of one unnamed Texas city came forward with claims the hacker demanded $2.5 million in ransom. It goes without saying that the Lone Star State is no exception and hackers are officially messing with Texas.

Now is the time to make a change. With the human element involved in 62% of breaches, according to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, it’s no secret that a strong security awareness program is the key to staying out of the news headlines.

It’s time to fight back, Texas. It’s time to train your employees on how to defend themselves and beat the hackers.

How do I Comply With the HB 3834 Cyber Security Awareness Training Requirements?

HB 3834 is in full force and all state agencies, local governments, and contractors need to complete their compliance training each year. Let’s look at the steps you need to take to get you and your team compliant with the HB 3834 cyber security training requirements. And if you are looking for advice on building your security awareness training program for HB 3834, our expert security awareness team is happy to help.

Texas HB 3834 Scope

Step 1: Are you in Scope?

First step is to determine if your organization is in scope of HB 3834. If you are reading this, you probably already have a hunch that you may be. To confirm, the personnel in scope of HB 3834 cyber security awareness training compliance applies to state agency, local government, and even contractor employees throughout the state of Texas.

State Agencies – Employees who use a computer to complete at least 25 percent of the employee’s required duties, and elected or appointed officers of the agency.

Local Government Entities – Employees and elected or appointed officials who have access to a local government computer system or database and use a computer to perform at least 25 percent of their duties. For school districts, only the district’s cybersecurity coordinator is required to complete the annual training. Other school district employees complete it as determined by the district, with the coordinator.

Contractors of State Agencies – Those contractors who have access to a state computer system or database must complete training during the term of the contract and during any renewal period. There are no exceptions for state agency contractors.

Employees and officials on certain types of extended leave (military or FMLA leave, for example) are exempt as long as they no longer have access to the organization’s systems and databases.

Step 2: Choose a State Certified Vendor

Now that you have confirmed your scope, you must choose a security awareness training vendor that is certified by the State of Texas, such as Huntress. Certified vendors must complete a rigorous training content assessment, certify with the State of Texas that their training program meets all cyber education requirements, and ensure that those requirements are upheld on a continuous basis year over year. Certifications expire every August 31 and have to be renewed annually, so make sure your vendor is certified for the current fiscal year. Simply put, selecting a vendor that’s already done the heavy lifting is required to get started.

With Huntress Managed SAT, you can satisfy the cybersecurity requirement using our Intro to Cybersecurity, Infosecurity, and Texas-specific episodes in our library. Most people can finish them in less than 30 minutes.

The AI requirement works a little differently. Thanks to the free, certified AI awareness training video on YouTube provided by DIR, you can also satisfy the AI requirements via Huntress Managed SAT as well. All you need to do is create a custom episode in Huntress Managed SAT, add the video, and include one question: “Did you complete it?” That way, completion gets tracked right alongside the rest of your training.

Step 3: Launch your Program

Okay so you picked your vendor, but now you need to launch the cyber security training program to your employees. It’s critical to communicate how important completing this required training is. If your employees don’t understand why they are required to participate in this training, they won’t have the motivation you need to have it completed. Motivation is a key component of getting your cyber security training program off the ground and supported by employees.

Step 4: Ensure Completion

Now that you have launched your training program, that doesn’t mean you are done. As part of HB 3834, you need to ensure your employees complete the required cyber security training. Remember it’s important to discuss how this cyber security training program will help your employees become more cyber-savvy both at work and at home. Make it fun by promoting the training across your organization similar to a marketing campaign. This will help drive completion records, and you may even offer incentives for early completion.

Once everyone is done, state agencies and local governments must certify their compliance to DIR by August 31 using DIR’s online certification form. You don’t send DIR individual training records or certificates, but you do need to keep your own, so hang on to those completion reports.

Step 5: Keep it Going

Congrats, you’ve finished your first round of security awareness training! This is a big accomplishment, but the party doesn’t stop here. Remember that you need to keep this momentum going. The best way to do that is to reinforce your security culture to help make security top of mind. Once a year security awareness training is not going to stop the hackers. You need to continue this effort throughout the year, using different methods to communicate and reinforce security concepts in every employee’s mind.

What NOT to do with HB 3834

Although it’s easy to recognize HB 3834 as another compliance regulation to just check the box, it shouldn’t be.

The consequences of falling victim to a cyber attack are well known and your focus should be to ensure all employees understand the risks they face.

You don’t want to be tomorrow’s news headline and your employees are your first step as the most powerful defense for your organization. A strong cyber security training program is the key to protect beyond the regulations of HB 3834. Remember we are all working towards a common goal to beat the hackers, not the regulations.

Ready to check the HB 3834 box without the snooze fest? See how Huntress Managed SAT helps you meet Texas HB 3834 requirements in less than 30 minutes.

Full Text:
Today’s mission environments are operating under a rapidly increasing operational tempo. Security teams face a shrinking mean-time-to-exploit (MTTE) as threat actors leverage artificial intelligence to automate and scale their campaigns. Concurrently, agencies are deploying AI to accelerate and drive mission outcomes. This dual imperative forces security teams to simultaneously adapt to an AI-augmented threat landscape and verify that internal AI workloads are securely architected.

To outpace modern adversaries and secure mission AI adoption, organizations cannot depend on human speed alone. They need an approach that enables risk remediation at machine speed, while maintaining the strict security requirements for protecting public sector environments.

From CNAPP to AI-APP

For many, the Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) has become the foundational standard for achieving continuous visibility and risk assessment across multi-cloud and connected hybrid environments. CNAPPs analyze infrastructure, identity, and applications with connected context. However, AI continues to transform how risk emerges and the speed at which teams must identify and remediate those risks.

This is why Wiz transformed CNAPP through AI-accelerated insights driven by the Wiz AI Agents. These agents enhance insights from signals across development, infrastructure, and live runtime behavior to elevate CNAPP into an AI-Application Protection Platform (AI-APP).

Today, we are excited to announce that the Wiz AI Agents are available within Wiz’s FedRAMP High authorized environment, Wiz for U.S. Government (Wiz for Gov). This makes Wiz for Gov the first AI-APP available for U.S. public sector organizations to protect systems managing highly sensitive, national security and mission-critical data.

This latest announcement signals our ongoing commitment to serving public sector entities, and it is especially meaningful that it comes on the heels of our Scan for Good initiative. Scan for Good is a program that is specifically geared towards supporting under-resourced organizations that play a vital role in the communities they serve, from non-profits to critical infrastructure.

At the core of Wiz for Gov remains the Wiz Security Graph and our agentless CNAPP architecture, which provides deep, ground-truth data and context for cloud and connected on-premises environments. This foundational context ensures that Wiz AI Agents act as a force multiplier for human operators, providing AI-enhanced insights and guided remediation, without relying on predictive risk modeling which can lead to false positives and/or negatives.

Introducing Wiz AI Agents in Wiz for Gov

To execute this unified risk model, Wiz AI Agents translate ground-truth Security Graph context into actionable, machine-speed operations across the application lifecycle.

Wiz AI Agents provide configurable operational boundaries, allowing security teams, for specific workflows, to authorize agents to execute routine remediations autonomously or require human-in-the-loop approval before applying changes on sensitive systems. This flexibility ensures operators maintain complete command and control over mission workloads.

Wiz Green Agent: The Wiz Green Agent delivers actionable remediation plans directly into developer workflows. It provides a transparent Investigation Summary detailing the root cause and generates ready-to-merge Pull Requests to resolve issues at the source.

Wiz Blue Agent: The Wiz Blue Agent provides automated investigation and response for security operations teams. For threats that fire in Wiz Defend, the Blue Agent immediately starts triaging, providing a comprehensive investigation summary and verdict on threat severity.

Wiz Red Agent: The Wiz Red Agent focuses on continuous runtime risk assessment. It will continuously analyze live production environments to map multi-step attack paths, prioritizing exploitable risks so defenders can remediate toxic combinations before threat actors exploit them.

Connecting Dev, Prod, and SOC: A Unified Risk Model

Title: Passkey Authentications Double but Adoption Remains Slow
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Passkeys are an increasingly common feature on log-in screens but widespread adoption remains relatively low, according to new data from Dashlane.

The credential security specialist analyzed millions of aggregated, anonymized passkey authentications that it managed between July 2025 and June 2026 to compile its third annual Passkey Power 20 report.

It revealed that passkey authentications by Dashlane users have nearly doubled year on year, reaching 2.5 million per month in 2026.

Additionally, over half (57%) of its users now store at least one passkey, compared with 40% last year.

However, the phishing-resistant authentication technology still accounts for a minority of logins on major sites like Google (28%), PayPal (18%), Amazon (17%) and eBay (8%).

Read more on passkeys: Half of Cybersecurity Pros Still Rely on Passwords Despite Security Concerns.

Passkeys are much harder for scammers to crack as there’s no password to guess or steal: the user logs in via a device PIN or biometric such as a face scan.

They are cryptographically tied to legitimate websites, and even if the latter were breached, the hacker wouldn’t have access to the user’s private key, which stays on their device.

That’s why institutions like Report Fraud recommend passkeys as one of the most effective ways to mitigate account takeover attacks.

Closing the Gap to Passkey Adoption

For businesses, passkeys can keep sensitive corporate data and systems safe and reduce the password-reset workload for IT support.

In this space, Dashlane noted an expansion in the number of applications supporting the login mechanism.

HubSpot and Cisco Duo led the way in terms of volume of authentications, but there were also new entrants to the top 20 in the form of HR and payroll platforms like isolved HCM and BambooHR, as well as AWS and Dropbox.

The key will be closing the gap between passkey support and adoption, Dashlane argued.

It pointed to four approaches:

Making passkeys highly visible and easy to use within existing workflows

Promoting passkeys as a faster alternative to passwords, with higher completion rates

Starting to remove alternatives like one-time passcodes and passwords

Setting a deadline for mandatory passkey use

Application developers forcing users to adopt passkeys are few and far between, although Japanese internet company LY Corporation has announced a spring 2027 deadline for Yahoo Japan users, the report noted.

More should at least make the system their default method for user logins, argued Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“Despite sustained growth, we’re not on the other side yet,” he said. “There’s still more work to be done to make passkeys easier to use, and more companies need to go from soft adoption to enforcing the change, so that passkeys become the main authentication method rather than a secondary one, as they still are today.”

Title: Beyond Deployment: Evaluating the Operational Impact of an SD-WAN Refresh
Context: Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently
Full Text:
Many SD-WAN refreshes start with an expiring contract or edge equipment reaching end of life. But replacing the edge should not be the measure of success.

For network and infrastructure leaders, the real test is what improves after the refresh. Will the refresh put IT on another appliance cycle, or move the WAN to a cloud service? Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently? Can the WAN respond when network conditions change? Can the team support new locations and changing requirements without creating more operational work?

The answers depend on how the new WAN is built and run.

Decide first whether the WAN runs on hardware or in the cloud

An appliance-based refresh replaces old boxes with new ones. IT still patches that hardware at every site, and the replacement cycle starts again when the new boxes reach end of life.

A cloud-delivered SD-WAN moves routing and policy into a cloud service. The device at each site connects the site to that service.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, the Cato Socket at each site connects automatically to the nearest Cato Point of Presence (PoP). The Cato SASE Cloud Platform handles routing and policy enforcement, and Cato maintains the software that runs it. New capabilities can reach every site through the cloud service without a hardware upgrade.

Where the WAN runs shapes the rest of the refresh. The next three sections cover application priority, path control, and day-two work, and each one depends on where the WAN runs.

When you compare SD-WAN options, start by asking whether the refresh puts IT on another appliance cycle or moves the WAN to a cloud service.

Application priority should follow traffic past the branch

SD-WAN can prioritize important applications and steer traffic across available links. But in many architectures, that prioritization stops at the branch.

Once traffic leaves the branch, the application still has to cross the middle mile (the long-haul path between sites and clouds) to reach another site, a datacenter, or the cloud. If bandwidth gets tight along that path, the priority IT set at the branch should still count.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT defines application-aware quality of service (QoS) centrally. Cato applies that priority at the Cato Socket and within the Cato SASE Cloud Platform, so the priority follows traffic into the middle mile. Business-critical traffic can stay at the front of the queue when capacity runs short.

Next, ask whether application priority ends at the branch or follows the application across the WAN.

The WAN should improve the path applications take

Priority can’t fix a bad route, though. A critical application can have the highest QoS priority and still perform poorly if its traffic runs into latency and packet loss on a long route to the destination. Path quality is the second middle-mile problem, after priority.

Cato sends traffic over the Cato Global Private Backbone, which gives Cato more control over the path between sites, clouds, and applications than a WAN that depends primarily on best-effort public Internet routing. Cato monitors network conditions and can route around degraded links across backbone paths between Cato PoPs. Critical applications can keep performing when a backbone path slows down.

For SaaS and public-cloud applications, Smart Egress adds another routing choice. IT can define application-level policy so selected traffic exits from a Cato PoP close to the application instance serving the organization. The traffic stays on the backbone for more of the trip, so employees can see faster response times from those applications.

Then ask whether the WAN can improve the route to the application, or whether the middle mile stays largely outside its control.

A refresh should reduce day-two operations work

Much of the work in an SD-WAN lifecycle happens after deployment.

New branches, policy changes, software updates, troubleshooting, and changing bandwidth requirements all create ongoing work. If that work still happens box by box and site by site, a refresh may replace the hardware without changing the operating model.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT manages routing and application policy centrally through the Cato Management Application, while Cato Sockets support zero-touch deployment at new locations.

Because the WAN runs as a cloud service, IT can spend less time on the patch and replacement cycles that appliance-based designs require.

Finally, ask how much day-two work each option still leaves with your team.

Measure the refresh by what improves after deployment

Newer edge infrastructure is the minimum an SD-WAN refresh should deliver.

Performance and operations are only part of the refresh decision. You also need to decide whether the WAN should secure remote users and cloud access, or leave that job to a separate security stack.

The right choice gives IT a WAN that keeps improving long after the new edge goes in.

Title: Protecting operational technology and edge devices
Context: Insecure connectivity in OT and edge devices is known to be targeted by malicious actors to cause disruption and harm to critical services
Full Text:
This alert is relevant to Australian businesses and organisations that operate operational technology including refrigeration and cooling technology. The alert is intended for technical audiences and those responsible for operational technology in their organisation.

Background

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) is aware of cyber security incidents affecting commercial refrigeration systems overseas.

While ASD's ACSC has not seen active targeting in Australia, businesses and organisations should remain vigilant. ASD's ACSC strongly recommends that any Australian organisations and businesses that operate internet-connected operational technology (OT), including commercial refrigeration systems, assess their exposure to cyber security risks and follow ASD’s ACSC existing guidance on operational technology environments and securing edge devices.

Insecure connectivity in OT and edge devices is known to be targeted by malicious actors to cause disruption and harm to critical services. ASD’s ACSC guidance helps businesses to make decisions when designing, putting in place, and managing secure OT environments and edge devices.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises Australian organisations to take the following steps:

Ensure that OT environments and interfaces, and edge devices, are not directly exposed to the internet (particularly for older devices and systems, and those with remote access).

Identify and patch any vulnerabilities promptly.

Apply strong authentication, access controls, and network segmentation.

Monitor systems for unusual automated activity and review security logs regularly.

Businesses should review and act on ASD’s ACSC existing guidance on operational technology environments, including guidance on securing edge devices and secure connectivity principles for operational technology.

Where to get help

Organisations that identify suspicious activity, attempted exploitation, or vulnerabilities affecting their systems, can contact ASD via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371), or at www.cyber.gov.au/submit-a-report

Title: Taking the cloud out of the sky.
Context: First observed in 2022, XWorm gives attackers extensive control over infected Windows systems. Researchers caution that the documents haven’t been independently authenticated, but say they illustrate how effectively attackers can exploit human trust.
Full Text:
French supermarkets lose their cool in a refrigeration cyberattack. Anthropic pulls the plug on AI agents behaving badly. A Canadian ransomware negotiator is arrested in the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. XWorm expands its surveillance capabilities. A Dutch grocery giant suffers a cyberattack. Leaked files reveal Luna Moth’s playbook. Monday business brief. Our guest is Tim Starks from CyberScoop discussing how major rules for federal contractors handling sensitive data are nearing the finish line. Six digits sink Danish security.

Today is Tuesday October 13th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Ukrainian drones strike Russian data centers.

Ukrainian drone strikes have hit three of Russian technology giant Yandex’s six data centers, disrupting digital services across Russia. The attacks began October 7th, targeting facilities in Ryazan, Kaluga, and Vladimir. Two data centers have shut down completely, while a third sustained infrastructure damage.

The outages have affected Yandex Cloud, payment systems, taxi bookings, food deliveries, and numerous third-party services. Yandex says its remaining infrastructure is unstable and cannot provide a timeline for full recovery. The targeted facilities also house powerful supercomputers used for artificial intelligence, although any damage to those systems remains unconfirmed.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, which disrupted internet access for thousands of households in September.

A cyberattack targets supermarket refrigeration systems in France.

A cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigeration systems has disrupted at least 380 stores across France, forcing some retailers to throw away entire inventories of fresh and frozen food.

The attack affected refrigeration management systems manufactured by Danish company Danfoss, including equipment used by the Intermarché, Netto, and Coopérative U chains. Monoprix stores were also affected. Danfoss says the attack primarily affected older systems that no longer receive security updates.

Some supermarkets managed to intervene before food spoiled, while others suffered substantial losses. One retailer estimates that refrigeration failures could cost larger stores more than $200,000. French prosecutors are investigating the attack, including reports of food spoilage and fires. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not identified the attackers. A similar attack targeted commissaries on U.S. military bases in late August.

Anthropic limits internal AI model evaluations on government and other websites.

Anthropic has cut off internet access for its internal AI model evaluations after several agents took unauthorized actions on government and other websites. The incidents included models exploiting server vulnerabilities, bypassing data access restrictions, and circumventing safeguards designed to prevent unwanted activity. In one case, Claude Haiku 4.5 fabricated and submitted a homicide tip to Philadelphia police. Another model exploited a university server to complete a scientific calculation.

Anthropic believes its reinforcement learning process may have encouraged models to find unauthorized workarounds rather than abandon blocked tasks. The company says the incidents caused minimal real-world harm, but notified the White House and moved all internal evaluations offline until stronger safeguards are in place. The decision follows earlier incidents involving malicious package uploads and unauthorized system access.

A Canadian ransomware negotiator has been arrested in connection with the ShinyHunters cyberattack on the FBI.

A prominent Canadian ransomware negotiator has reportedly been arrested in connection with the ShinyHunters cyberattack on the FBI. Reuters identifies the suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a longtime cybersecurity executive known for negotiating with ransomware gangs. FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the breach of FBIjobs.gov, which exposed sensitive information about bureau employees.

Dubrovsky faces federal charges involving conspiracy to commit cyber extortion and interference with commerce through threats. The allegations have not been proven in court. The arrest has surprised Canadian cybersecurity professionals familiar with Dubrovsky’s work.mShinyHunters, a prolific data theft and extortion group, claimed responsibility for the FBI breach last month, describing it as retaliation against the agency.

The FBI says it intends to pursue the group and its associates.

XWorm evolves.

The XWorm remote access trojan is evolving into a more powerful surveillance platform, according to researchers at Netskope. First observed in 2022, XWorm gives attackers extensive control over infected Windows systems. Its developers have expanded its available plugins from 35 to 46, adding capabilities including location tracking, live microphone monitoring, and webcam access.

A particularly concerning addition, called HBrowser, lets attackers remotely control authenticated browser sessions, effectively bypassing multifactor authentication without stealing credentials. Netskope observed more than 1,200 XWorm incidents across 100 organizations during the third quarter.

The malware’s development has accelerated since its builder was cracked and its source code leaked in 2025, making the toolkit more widely accessible. Researchers expect further enhancements and continued use of XWorm by cybercriminals.

A Dutch grocery chain suffers a data breach.

Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize has taken some systems offline following a cyberattack. The company says its stores remain open and customer service is unaffected, although local reports indicate disruptions to deliveries and online orders in Belgium and the Netherlands. There are reports that U.S. operations may also be affected.

It’s unclear whether the incident is connected to recent cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Ahold Delhaize previously suffered a ransomware attack in 2024 that compromised personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people.

Leaked documents expose Luna Moth.

Leaked internal documents have exposed what appears to be a surprisingly organized operation behind the Luna Moth cyber extortion group, also known as Silent Ransom Group. According to Check Point researchers, the group operates much like a business, with specialized roles, detailed scripts, and carefully coordinated social engineering attacks.

Operators impersonate IT support personnel, persuading employees to install remote access software. While one attacker keeps the victim engaged on the phone, another quietly takes control of the computer. The two coordinate through a messaging service. The leaked instructions even include techniques for overcoming suspicious or reluctant victims.

Researchers caution that the documents haven’t been independently authenticated, but say they illustrate how effectively attackers can exploit human trust. Their advice: verify unexpected IT requests independently and restrict unauthorized remote access tools.

Monday business brief.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with five companies announcing new financing rounds. California-based Armadin leads the pack, raising $255.5 million to expand its agentic security platform. Amsterdam’s Hadrian secured $40 million for its AI-powered offensive security technology, while privacy-focused networking startup doxx.net raised $38 million.

Italian compliance automation provider Complaion collected $15.1 million, and Luxembourg-based risk intelligence company Osavul raised $9.5 million. On the mergers and acquisitions front, Quantum eMotion agreed to acquire Canadian cybersecurity firm Plurilock. Germany’s Sequrio acquired three domestic security service providers, while South Africa’s Risk X Group purchased Wolfpack Information Risk.

Swiss certification company SGS acquired Nashville-based Prescient Security. And Dynatrace completed its acquisition of AI evaluation platform Arize, aiming to combine AI testing capabilities with its existing observability tools. The activity reflects continued investor interest in AI security, compliance automation, and cybersecurity services.

Six digits sink Danish security.

Denmark is investigating a massive breach of its national population register, and the alleged point of entry is a password that practically qualifies as an invitation. According to Danish media, an attacker accessed the system through an IT company’s account protected by the password “123456.” At least three accounts reportedly shared that password, including an administrator account. The attacker allegedly conducted 14 million automated searches over ten days, accessing information belonging to 8.8 million people.

The intrusion went undetected until a government employee noticed an unusually large bill for database activity. The company, Pays ApS, has confirmed its access was exploited but hasn’t addressed the password allegations. The person claiming responsibility says they don’t intend to sell or leak the data. Apparently, the password wasn’t the only thing missing a few safeguards.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.

Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.

To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.

In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.

What we enabled

GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:

Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.

Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.

We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.

Secret scanning blocks a commit with push protection after the model detects a secret on line 5 of the file.

Why secrets are hard to detect

Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.

Likely real credential

Likely harmless lookalike

A password assigned beside a production database URL

The same password-shaped value in a test fixture

A connection string in deployment configuration

A localhost connection string in a setup guide

A high-entropy value bound to an API credential

A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash

These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.

That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:

Candidate generation: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.

Context-aware classification: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.

Impact:

11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.

86% faster post-push secret detection execution time.

More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.

How our pipeline works

As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.

HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS

Broad first, careful second

STEP 1

Scan

Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces.

STEP 2

Generate candidates

Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.

STEP 3

Classify

Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.

STEP 4

Alert or suppress

High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.

The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

The classifier model makes a best effort to distinguish “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real

Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.

ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.

We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.

That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.

How we trained

The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:

Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.

High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.

Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.

Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.

Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.

Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.

We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.

The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.

The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.

We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment.

Offline evaluation: On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved 13% higher precision and 19% higher recall than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic.

Online evaluation: We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%. We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average.

Take this with you

The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.

For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.

Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.

We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.

This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:

Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.

Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.

Title: Defenders Reluctant to Deploy Agentic AI as a Cybersecurity Tool
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Companies have invested more resources than ever into agentic AI as a cyber defense tool amid growing AI-enabled cyber threats to enterprise networks from. However, the majority of cybersecurity teams remain reluctant to deploy the technology due to concerns over their effectiveness.

Published on October 13, The Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 from Flashpoint suggested that despite the ongoing discussion surrounding the potential cyber risks around offensive agentic AI, just a quarter (25%) of cybersecurity teams are actively using agentic AI tools as part of their active cyber defense strategy.

While three quarters of security teams have yet to fully investigate the potential deployment of AI tools into their security operations, 20% of those surveyed said that they are running a closed pilot scheme, and a further 35% said they are examining the potential of adoption within the next 12 to 24 months. The remaining 20% of respondents said they have no plans to test out agentic AI as part of their cyber defense as things stand.

Of those who are using or are piloting AI agents, tasks these tools are involved in include information retrieval and alert prioritization, as well as more active tasks such as blocking IP addresses, updating blacklists and monitoring suspicious traffic.

Some organizations have also used AI to help with more advanced activity, including taking automated action that can directly affect security operations. However, many remain wary of providing an AI agent with this amount of decision-making authority.

When AI Agents Are ‘Confidently Wrong’

Some cybersecurity professionals expressed concerns about agents making wrong decisions.

“An agent that’s confidently wrong is worse than one that’s slow,” said one respondent.

Other hurdles to deployment of AI agents in cyber defense include concerns about data leakage, auditability, regulatory requirements and cost, as well as the level of control agents should have over security workflows.

While many organizations are toying with the investment in and deployment of agentic AI as a cyber defense tool, many are still reluctant to go all in until they have done more research into whether AI agents can be trusted with tasks.

“The opportunity for agentic AI on the defensive side is significant, and our research shows security leaders are ready to invest. But they aren't swayed by the hype,” said Josh Lefkowitz, founder and CEO of Flashpoint.

“They're holding agentic AI to a high bar, and they want to know where it improves their work, whether they can trust the output, and where human judgment must remain part of the process."

While cybersecurity teams are still testing the waters with agentic AI, the report also suggests that boards and executive funding providers appear keen on the adoption of the technology, with over half expecting a significant budget increase to aid with the investigation of agentic AI for cyber defense.

More than a third (35%) said that over the next 12 months, they expect their budget to rise by over 10%, while a further 15% suggested they expect to see an increase of up to 10%. Zero respondents said they believed their cybersecurity budget is set to decrease.

Title: Why AI Red Teaming Belongs at the Core of Your AI Security Program
Context: Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage
Full Text:
Enterprises are putting AI applications and agents to work on sensitive data and business workflows, while attackers look for new ways to manipulate the models and exploit the tools connected to them. Security leaders need to know whether those systems will hold up against a real attack, and AI red teaming gives them that answer by testing AI the way an attacker would.

What AI red teaming is

AI red teaming is the process of proactively testing models, agents, applications, and other AI systems to find the weaknesses an attacker could exploit. It simulates techniques such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, and model manipulation to see how a system responds under pressure.

Because AI systems and the attacks against them change all the time, red teaming works best as a continuous loop: test real-world behavior, find what fails, use that evidence to strengthen the protections that guard AI in production, and test again.

Why AI systems need continuous testing

Attack methods keep evolving. Threat actors constantly develop new ways to manipulate models and abuse connected tools and APIs. Because these techniques evolve as fast as AI itself, a system that passed last quarter’s tests may not hold up against this month’s attacks. Security teams need to test continuously for new attack techniques, not just the ones they already know.

Model choices change the risk profile. As token costs shape decisions, teams may switch models to lower-costs, or alternatively, switch to more capable, or different models to better fit their AI application. Each switch can change how a system responds to attacks and which safeguards it needs.

What red teaming achieves

Done well, AI red teaming delivers two outcomes: reduced business risk and proof that your AI controls work.

Red teaming shows which weaknesses matter

Red teaming exposes weaknesses before attackers find them and shows which of those weaknesses matter most.

Not every unexpected model response is a real risk, and testing for weaknesses no attacker could realistically exploit wastes effort. Good red teaming focuses on the attack paths that matter for your applications and data and ranks findings by realistic impact, so teams can choose models and design guardrails that align with real risk.

Red teaming produces the evidence compliance teams need

Governance, risk, and compliance teams increasingly need evidence that safeguards withstand realistic attacks, that AI systems don’t expose sensitive or regulated information, and that each application aligns with internal policy.

Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage. To counter them, Gartner recommends testing AI applications early and using the results to improve runtime controls.

Frameworks including the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, MITRE ATLAS, and the EU AI Act also call for adversarial testing and ongoing evaluation. Red teaming produces the record these frameworks expect: what was tested, what failed, how risks were prioritized, and how the organization responded.

Red teaming shows where your AI can be exploited

Treating red teaming as a prelaunch checkbox leaves a gap between what was tested and what runs in production, because models and connected tools keep changing after launch.

A mature AI security program should include three layers of defense: discovery, posture control, and runtime guardrails. Discovery answers “What AI do we have?” Red teaming sits within posture control and answers the next question: “Where can it be exploited?”

Those results help teams choose models that fit their risk profile and design guardrails around proven attack paths instead of generic assumptions.

What to look for in AI red teaming

A strong AI red teaming approach should include:

Continuous, proactive testing that keeps pace as models and attack techniques change or new models are adopted.

Actionable risk visibility that prioritizes tests by exploitability and impact, so teams focus on the risks that matter when choosing models and designing guardrails.

Audit-ready reporting that maps results to the risk and compliance frameworks governance teams already use.

Integrated remediation that connects findings to the policies and protections that address them, without stitching together disconnected tools.

Research quality matters too. Generic prompt libraries catch generic problems, while testing built on new attack research catches the techniques advanced attackers use.

Cato connects red teaming to runtime protection

At Cato, we believe red teaming delivers the most value when it combines deep attack research with the platform that protects AI in production. That research comes from Cato AI Labs, the team behind EchoLeak, the first reported zero-click AI vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot, and CurXecute, a remote code execution flaw in the Cursor IDE. The team turns discoveries like these into realistic attack scenarios and adds new techniques as threats evolve, so testing reflects how attackers actually operate.

Cato AI Red Teaming puts that research to work. It continuously tests AI models with context-aware adversarial scenarios, prioritizes findings by realistic risk, maps them to leading frameworks, and turns them into policy and model recommendations inside the same AI Security solution that protects AI interactions at runtime.

With testing and protection on one platform, security teams can find AI risk and close the gaps before attackers exploit them.

Title: ClickFix to BEC in 24 Hours: Tragic Quadrant | Huntress
Context: Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems
Full Text:
Most cyber threats start out small and unassuming before they turn into the OH $#!T moments that put your whole business at risk. They can creep up fast during a normal day with a website you trust and a habit you don't question. You ask your favorite AI platform for help, follow "fix it" instructions when it hits a snag, and get back to work without thinking twice.

Nothing feels risky on the surface. But underneath, the "normal" AI search result you clicked and the "fix it" instructions you followed just helped an attacker gain access to your Microsoft 365 account. While you move on to the next task in your day, they walk straight into your inbox without a password or MFA prompt, looking just like you. They read through your messages and create hidden inbox rules that hide their tracks. That stealthy intrusion is mailbox manipulation, and in this case, it can escalate into full-blown business email compromise (BEC) within hours.

Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems. Chained together, they give an attacker everything they need to set up an OH $#!T moment that no one sees coming until it's too late.

Meet Doris and her ClickFix problem

Principal Product Researcher Truman Kain shows what this looks like in practice and how easily it blends into a normal workflow.

Meet Doris Stewart, a fictional finance employee at a company called Speedway Laundry, owned by Speedway Industries. Doris wants help responding to an email, so she goes to Google and searches for ChatGPT. She clicks what appears to be a normal sponsored result and, unknowingly, lands on a custom attacker-built GPT. But there are no obvious tells that this custom GPT is malicious. And Doris trusts ChatGPT, which is what the attacker was banking on.

Here's where things start to get sketchy. The custom GPT tells her there's a service issue and sends her to a fake verification page. Doris is prompted to press Command+Space, paste a command into Terminal, and press Enter. She doesn't recognize that this is a ClickFix scam, and by following those steps, the attacker has tricked her into compromising her own machine.

Now, the attacker runs a script to retrieve cookies and spots Doris' Microsoft session cookie, the one that keeps her logged in to Outlook without entering a password or MFA code each time she needs access. By dropping that cookie into a fresh browser using a free extension and refreshing the page, the attacker is now sitting in Doris' inbox with full control. There was no password and no MFA prompt to get past. The session was already authenticated, so the stolen cookie did the work.

This is where the attacker turns access into cash. In Doris' inbox, the attacker finds an invoice awaiting approval, creates an inbox rule named ".." so it gets easily overlooked, and sets it to archive any message containing the invoice number. Then the attacker replies to Treasury as Doris, asking them to send the payment to a new routing number, deletes the sent message to hide the evidence, and empties the trash. Doris never sees any of it, and the whole thing unfolds in about 24 hours.

This attack didn't require lots of time, money, or technical know-how. But it worked fast, and Doris will be left cleaning up a financial mess that she didn't even know existed.

How Doris could have avoided trouble

The good news is that knowing where to break links in the attack chain can stop a bigger business disruption from happening. In this case, on the endpoint side, the initial access shows up as a Mac shell running curl output with the attacker's IP address Base64-encoded inside it, the exact command Doris walked through pasting into Terminal a few minutes earlier. That pattern is worth flagging as suspicious on endpoints until proven otherwise.

On the identity side, the tells are just as suspicious. Two browsers are active in one session; there are two different operating systems tied to the same login; traffic is routed through a VPN with no business reason to be there; and that sketchy, almost invisible inbox rule ("..").

This isn't new tradecraft, but it's effective and convenient for attackers to slip in unnoticed without dropping noisy tooling that'll get flagged by managed security tools.

Getting ahead of OH $#!T moments with the Tragic Quadrant

The Huntress Tragic Quadrant plots threats on two axes, including the ones in this exact attack chain. The x-axis (prevalence) shows how often we see them in the environments we monitor, and the y-axis, or as we all call it, "pucker factor" (which, if you've ever been on the receiving end of these attacks, makes perfect sense), shows how much damage they cause when they land. That view helps you tackle the riskiest gaps first, so you don't end up in an OH $#!T moment like Doris.

On the lower quadrants, you see tactics like AI platform abuse and ClickFix that aren't usually catastrophic on their own, even if we see them often in our telemetry. The real risk happens when attackers chain them together, and the arrows move up and to the right into the OH $#!T quadrant, where a hidden inbox rule can turn into much bigger problems like BEC or ransomware.

When you know which corner a tactic falls into, it gets easier to see which threats deserve your focus right now and how to spot them in your environment.
